12.4 HTTP Headers — The Ones You See Every Day

Headers are key-value pairs that carry metadata. They control caching, authentication, content negotiation, security policies, and more.

📤
Request Headers

Host: Which website (required for virtual hosting). User-Agent: What client is making the request. Accept: What formats the client can handle. Authorization: Bearer tokens, Basic auth. Cookie: Session data. Content-Type: Format of the request body.

📥
Response Headers

Content-Type: JSON, HTML, image/png, etc. Content-Length: Body size in bytes. Set-Cookie: Create/update session cookie. Cache-Control: How long to cache (max-age, no-cache). Location: Where to redirect (301/302).

🛡️
Security Headers

Strict-Transport-Security (HSTS): Always use HTTPS. X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff (prevent MIME sniffing). X-Frame-Options: Prevent clickjacking. Content-Security-Policy (CSP): Limit which resources can load.

🌍
CORS Headers

Access-Control-Allow-Origin: Which domains can call this API. Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET, POST, PUT, DELETE. Access-Control-Allow-Headers: Which custom headers are allowed. ⚠️ CORS is enforced by BROWSERS, not servers. curl bypasses it.

12.5 HTTP/1.1 — The Workhorse (Keep-Alive, Pipelining, HOL Blocking)

HTTP/1.1 has been the dominant web protocol for 25+ years. Its key innovation: Connection: keep-alive — reuse TCP connections for multiple requests instead of opening a new connection for every image, CSS, and JS file. Browsers typically open 6 parallel connections per origin to work around head-of-line blocking.

HTTP/1.1 — 6 Parallel TCP Connections Per Origin
  BROWSER                              SERVER (jobpost.anihpj.com)
  ┌──────┐   TCP Conn 1: GET /index.html ────────▶  ┌──────┐
  │      │   TCP Conn 2: GET /style.css  ────────▶  │      │
  │      │   TCP Conn 3: GET /app.js     ────────▶  │nginx │
  │      │   TCP Conn 4: GET /logo.png   ────────▶  │      │
  │      │   TCP Conn 5: GET /font.woff2 ────────▶  │      │
  │      │   TCP Conn 6: POST /api/data  ────────▶  │      │
  └──────┘                                          └──────┘

  HEAD-OF-LINE BLOCKING: If GET /style.css is slow,
  ALL responses on TCP Conn 2 are delayed.
  Other connections are unaffected — hence 6 connections.
💡 Chunked Transfer Encoding — Sending Data Without Knowing the Size

Normally, HTTP responses include a Content-Length header — the server must know the total size BEFORE sending the first byte. But what about streaming? Live video, real-time events, large file generation — the server doesn't know the final size. Chunked transfer encoding solves this: the server sends data in self-describing chunks. Each chunk starts with its size in hex, then the data, then CRLF. The last chunk has size 0, signaling "done." Example: 7\r\nHello, \r\n6\r\nWorld!\r\n0\r\n\r\n. The client reassembles the chunks into the full response. This is invisible to the application — gunicorn/nginx handle chunking automatically. Key use: Streaming APIs, Server-Sent Events, large file downloads where compression is applied on-the-fly.

12.6 HTTP/2 — Binary Framing & Multiplexing (Deep Dive)

HTTP/2 (standardized 2015, based on Google's SPDY) replaced HTTP/1.1's text-based protocol with a binary framing layer. The key breakthrough: multiplexing — multiple concurrent streams over ONE TCP connection, eliminating the 6-connection limit.

HTTP/2 Multiplexing — How Streams Share a Connection
                     SINGLE TCP CONNECTION
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ STREAM 1: GET /index.html  [HEADERS] [DATA]                  │
  │ STREAM 3: GET /style.css   [HEADERS]        [DATA]           │
  │ STREAM 5: GET /app.js      [HEADERS]              [DATA]     │
  │ STREAM 7: POST /api/login  [HEADERS] [DATA]                  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  All streams multiplexed over ONE TCP connection — no 6-conn limit!
  Frame order: H1 H3 D1 H5 H7 D5 D3 D7 (interleaved!)

  ⚠️ HTTP/2 STILL has TCP HOL blocking:
  If ONE TCP packet is lost, ALL streams stall until retransmission.
💡 Server Push — The Browser Doesn't Have to Ask

HTTP/2 Server Push lets the server proactively send resources the client will need. Example: client requests index.html → server pushes style.css and app.js before the browser parses the HTML and discovers it needs them. This saves one round trip. Stream prioritization: Clients can assign priority (1-256) and dependencies to streams — "load the hero image first, then the footer." ⚠️ Server Push is being removed from Chrome (2022+) because it was often wasted (pushing resources the browser already had cached). The successor: 103 Early Hints.

12.7 HTTP/3 — QUIC & the Future (Deep Dive)

HTTP/3 fixes HTTP/2's remaining weakness: TCP head-of-line blocking. It runs over QUIC (UDP-based transport), where each stream is independent — losing a packet on one stream doesn't affect others.

FeatureHTTP/1.1HTTP/2HTTP/3anihpj use
TransportTCP (6 conns)TCP (1 conn)QUIC (UDP)K8s Ingress
Multiplex6 conn limitStreams (1 TCP)Streams (1 QUIC)TLS+HTTP/2 default
HOL BlockPer-connectionPer-TCP-connPer-stream (none!)
HandshakeTCP+TLS (2-3RTT)TCP+TLS (1.5RTT)QUIC (0-1RTT)
Header CompressNoneHPACKQPACKReduces bandwidth

12.8 curl — The Engineer's HTTP Swiss Army Knife

# Basic: GET request
curl http://jobpost.anihpj.com/api/jobs/

# Verbose: see every header and TLS detail
curl -v https://jobpost.anihpj.com/api/jobs/

# HTTP method override
curl -X POST -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"title":"DevOps Engineer","location":"Remote"}' \
  https://jobpost.anihpj.com/api/jobs/

# Authentication
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $(cat token.txt)" https://api.anihpj.com/

# Follow redirects
curl -L https://anihpj.com   # Follows 301/302

# Timing breakdown (DNS, TCP, TLS, TTFB, Total)
curl -w "@timing.txt" -o /dev/null -s https://jobpost.anihpj.com

# HTTP/2 and HTTP/3
curl --http2 -v https://jobpost.anihpj.com
curl --http3 -v https://jobpost.anihpj.com   # If compiled with QUIC support

# Send cookies
curl -b "sessionid=abc123" https://jobpost.anihpj.com/

# Download with resume support
curl -C - -O https://example.com/large-file.tar.gz

📝 Chapter 12 — Networking Practice Questions

Answer

HTTP/1.1: text-based, 6 connections guous — binary frames have explicit stream IDs, making interleaving safe and parseable.

Explanation

HTTP/2 frames have a 9-byte header: Length (24-bit), Type (8-bit), Flags (8-bit), Stream ID (31-bit). This allows the receiver to demultiplex frames to the correct stream regardless of arrival order. Text-based HTTP/1.1 can't do this because you can't tell which request a line belongs to.

# HTTP: GET/POST /path HTTP/1.1 + Host/Authorization headers -> 200 OK + JSON body
# curl -sv https://HOST/api/endpoint | jq .
Q2
What is HTTP head-of-line (HOL) blocking? How does HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, and HTTP/3 each address it?
Show Answer
Answer

HTTP/1.1: HOL blocking per connection — solved by opening 6 parallel connections. HTTP/2: SOLVES HTTP-level HOL blocking via stream multiplexing, but still has TCP-level HOL blocking (one lost TCP packet blocks all streams). HTTP/3: SOLVES TCP HOL blocking by using QUIC (UDP) — each stream is independent, lost packets only affect their own stream.

# HTTP: REQUEST=GET/POST /path HTTP/1.1\nHost+Auth headers\nRESPONSE=200 OK + JSON/HTML
# curl -sv https://HOST/api -H "Authorization: Bearer TOKEN" | jq .
# Status: 2xx=OK, 3xx=redirect, 4xx=client err, 5xx=server err
Explanation

HOL blocking is a fundamental consequence of ordering guarantees. TCP guarantees in-order delivery, so if packet #3 of a TCP stream is lost, packets #4-10 wait. HTTP/3's QUIC intentionally sacrifices TCP's ordering guarantee for independence between streams.

Q3
What do HTTP status codes 301, 302, 401, 403, 500, 50
# HTTP: GET/POST /path HTTP/1.1 + Host/Authorization headers -> 200 OK + JSON body
# curl -sv https://HOST/api/endpoint | jq .
2, 503, and 504 mean?
Show Answer
Answer

301: Permanent redirect (update your bookmarks). 302: Temporary redirect. 401: Unauthorized — you need to authenticate. 403: Forbidden — you're authenticated but don't have permission. 500: Internal server error — app crashed or bug. 502: Bad gateway — proxy/load balancer got invalid response from backend. 503: Service unavailable — server overloaded or down for maintenance. 504: Gateway timeout — backend didn't respond in time.

# HTTP: REQUEST=GET/POST /path HTTP/1.1\nHost+Auth headers\nRESPONSE=200 OK + JSON/HTML
# curl -sv https://HOST/api -H "Authorization: Bearer TOKEN" | jq .
# Status: 2xx=OK, 3xx=redirect, 4xx=client err, 5xx=server err
Explanation

502 vs 504: 502 means the backend responded with garbage (malformed HTTP, connection reset). 504 means the backend didn't respond at all within the configured timeout. In Kubernetes, an Ingress controller returns 502 if the Service has no healthy endpoints, and 503 if explicitly configured for maintenance mode.

Q4
Explain CORS. Why does a browser block a cross-origin request, but curl succeeds?
Show Answer
Answer

CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is a browser-enforced security policy. When JavaScript on site-a.com tries to fetch api.site-b.com, the browser first sends a preflight OPTIONS request asking "does site-b allow requests from site-a?" If the response lacks the right Access-Control-Allow-Origin header, the browser BLOCKS the actual request. curl doesn't enforce CORS — it sends the request directly. This is why CORS errors happen in browsers but not in curl/Postman.

# SOCKET STATS: ss -tlnp(TCP listening), ss -ulnp(UDP listening), ss -tpn(connections)
# ss -s(summary); lsof -i :PORT; /proc/net/tcp
Explanation

CORS protects users, not servers. Without CORS, malicious-site.com could use your browser's cookies to make authenticated requests to bank.com. The browser enforces CORS to prevent this. Server-to-server calls don't have cookies/credentials for other sites, so CORS isn't needed there.

Q5
What is the Host header and why was it the most important addition in HTTP/1.1?
Show Answer
Answer

The Host header tells the server WHICH website the client wants, enabling virtual hosting — multiple websites on a single IP:port. Before HTTP/1.1, each website needed its own IP address. With the Host header, one nginx server at 10.0.1.5:443 can serve jobpost.anihpj.com, admin.anihpj.com, and api.anihpj.com — the server uses Host to route to the right backend.

# HTTP: GET/POST /path HTTP/1.1 + Host/Authorization headers -> 200 OK + JSON body
# curl -sv https://HOST/api/endpoint | jq .
Explanation

TLS added complexity: the server needs to know which certificate to present BEFORE it sees the Host header (which is inside the encrypted HTTP). SNI (Server Name Indication) solves this by including the hostname in the TLS ClientHello — the server selects the right certificate, decrypts, then reads the Host header from HTTP.

Q6
How does HTTP/3 (QUIC) handle connection migration? Why can't TCP do this?
Show Answer
Answer

QUIC connections are identified by a Connection ID (not the 4-tuple). When a user switches from Wi-Fi (IP 10.0.1.5) to cellular (IP 172.20.3.8), the 4-tuple changes but the Connection ID stays the same — the connection survives. TCP connections are identified by the 4-tuple (src_ip, src_port, dst_ip, dst_port) — any change breaks the connection. This is why your video call or download doesn't drop when you leave WiFi range with HTTP/3.

# HTTP: GET/POST /path HTTP/1.1 + Host/Authorization headers -> 200 OK + JSON body
# curl -sv https://HOST/api/endpoint | jq .
Explanation

Connection migration is built into QUIC at the transport layer. The client sends a PATH_CHALLENGE frame from the new IP, the server responds with PATH_RESPONSE, and the connection migrates without any re-handshake. This is impossible in TCP because the 4-tuple IS the connection identity.

Q7
What does curl -v show? Decode the output including the TLS handshake indicators.
Show Answer
Answer

curl -v shows: (1) TLS handshake: > GET /api/jobs/ HTTP/1.1 (lines with >). (3) Response: < HTTP/1.1 200 OK (lines with <). Also shows: DNS resolution time, TCP connect, SSL handshake progress, certificate chain details.

Explanation

The > prefix means data SENT by curl. The < prefix means data RECEIVED. * means curl metadata (TLS, connection info). This is the fastest way to debug HTTP issues — one command shows DNS, TCP, TLS, and HTTP in sequence.

How does HTTP/2 he

Chapter 14: Advanced HTTP — Load Balancing, Proxies & CDNs

In production, your application isn't served directly to the internet. It sits behind a chain of infrastructure: reverse proxies (nginx, Envoy), load balancers (AWS ALB/NLB, HAProxy), and CDNs (Cloudflare, CloudFront). This chapter covers how these pieces work together to deliver your application at scale.

🟡 Intermediate⏱️ ~1.5 hours🏗️ Architecture

14.1 Reverse Proxies — The Front Door to Your Application

A reverse proxy sits in front of your application servers and handles incoming client requests. Unlike a forward proxy (which sits between clients and the internet — like a corporate proxy), a reverse proxy sits between the internet and your servers. It provides: TLS termination, request routing (path-based: /api/ → backend-a, /admin/ → backend-b), caching, rate limiting, compression, and request buffering (protects slow backends from fast clients).

anihpj Architecture — Request Flow Through nginx Reverse Proxy
  INTERNET
     │
     ▼
  ┌─────────────────────┐
  │  nginx (reverse proxy)│  TLS termination, routing, caching, rate limiting
  │  :443 (HTTPS)       │
  └──┬──────────┬───────┘
     │          │
     ▼          ▼
  /api/*     /admin/*
     │          │
     ▼          ▼
  gunicorn   gunicorn
  :8000      :8001
     │          │
     ▼          ▼
  Django     Django
  (jobpost)  (admin)

14.2 Load Balancing — Spreading the Load

Load balancers distribute traffic across multiple backend servers for scalability and high availability.

💡 Common LB Algorithms

Round Robin: Each backend in turn. Least Connections: Backend with fewest active connections. IP Hash: Hash of client IP → always same backend (session stickiness without cookies). Weighted: Backends with higher weight get more traffic (useful when backends have different capacities). ⚠️ Sticky sessions break when the backend pod restarts (new IP!). Use Redis for session storage instead.

⚠️ Active vs Passive Health Checks — How the LB Knows a Backend Is Dead

Active health checks: The LB periodically sends a request to each backend's health endpoint (e.g., GET /health every 5s). 200 OK = healthy. 3 consecutive failures = mark unhealthy → stop sending traffic. Used by: AWS ALB, nginx (health_check directive), HAProxy. Passive health checks: The LB observes actual traffic — if a backend returns 5xx errors or times out on real requests, it's marked unhealthy. No extra probe traffic. Used by: Envoy (outlier detection), AWS NLB, nginx (passive). Best practice: Use BOTH — active checks catch dead backends quickly, passive checks catch degraded backends. In K8s: readinessProbe = active check for Services. livenessProbe = active check for pod restarts. Always implement a /health endpoint that checks real dependencies (DB, cache) — not just "the process is alive."

14.3 VIPs (Virtual IPs) & High Availability Load Balancing

A VIP (Virtual IP) is an IP address that floats between multiple servers. Only one server (the master) holds the VIP at a time. If the master fails, a backup takes over the VIP — clients see no interruption. This is implemented via VRRP (Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol), with keepalived being the most common Linux implementation.

VRRP — How a Virtual IP Floats Between Nodes
  NORMAL OPERATION:                      FAILOVER:
  ┌──────────────┐                       ┌──────────────┐
  │ Node 1 (MASTER)│                      │ Node 1 (DEAD) │
  │  10.0.1.10    │                       │  ╳ offline   │
  │  VIP: 10.0.1.100│                     └──────────────┘
  └──────┬───────┘                              │
         │ VRRP advertisements                  │ No ads received
         │ (multicast every 1s)                  │ for 3+ seconds
         ▼                                       ▼
  ┌──────────────┐                       ┌──────────────┐
  │ Node 2 (BACKUP)│                      │ Node 2 (NEW MASTER)│
  │  10.0.1.11    │                       │  10.0.1.11    │
  └──────────────┘                       │  VIP: 10.0.1.100│
                                          └──────────────┘
                                          1. Assigns VIP to interface
                                          2. Sends GRATUITOUS ARP:
                                          "10.0.1.100 is at MY MAC now!"
                                          3. Switches update MAC tables
                                          4. Traffic flows to Node 2
                                          5. Failover: 1-3 seconds

  # Gratuitous ARP = unsolicited ARP reply that updates everyone's ARP cache
  # Without it, switches would keep sending traffic to the dead node's MAC
# keepalived configuration example (/etc/keepalived/keepalived.conf):
vrrp_instance VI_1 {
    state MASTER           # MASTER or BACKUP
    interface eth0
    virtual_router_id 51   # Must match on all nodes sharing this VIP
    priority 100           # Higher = preferred master
    virtual_ipaddress {
        10.0.1.100/24      # The floating VIP
    }
    track_script {          # Health check: is the service actually working?
        chk_nginx           # If this script fails → demote to BACKUP
    }
}

# In Kubernetes (on-prem):
# kube-vip provides VIPs for the kube-apiserver (HA control plane)
# MetalLB provides VIPs for LoadBalancer-type Services
# Both use ARP/VRRP to float IPs between nodes

14.4 DSR — Direct Server Return (Advanced LB Pattern)

DSR (Direct Server Return) is a high-performance load balancing pattern where the load balancer only handles INBOUND traffic. The backend server sends responses DIRECTLY to the client, bypassing the LB. This is critical for high-throughput scenarios (video streaming, CDN origins) where response traffic is much larger than request traffic.

DSR vs Normal Load Balancing — Traffic Flow Comparison
  NORMAL LB (both directions through LB):
  ┌────────┐  1. Request  ┌──────┐  2. Forward  ┌─────────┐
  │ CLIENT │─────────────▶│  LB  │─────────────▶│ BACKEND │
  │        │◀─────────────│      │◀─────────────│         │
  └────────┘  4. Response └──────┘  3. Response └─────────┘
  LB handles 100% of request AND response traffic → bottleneck at scale

  DSR (response bypasses LB):
  ┌────────┐  1. Request  ┌──────┐  2. Forward  ┌─────────┐
  │ CLIENT │─────────────▶│  LB  │─────────────▶│ BACKEND │
  │        │◀─────────────│      │              │  (VIP on │
  │        │  3. Response └──────┘              │  loopback)│
  └────────┘  (DIRECT from backend)            └─────────┘
  LB handles ~5% of traffic (requests only). Response = 95% → direct.

  HOW DSR WORKS (L2 DSR):
  1. Client sends packet: Src=ClientIP, Dst=VIP, MAC=LB's MAC
  2. LB rewrites dst MAC to Backend's MAC (IP stays the same!)
  3. Backend has VIP on loopback (lo:0) → accepts packet addressed to VIP
  4. Bsame L2 network as LB (MAC rewrite only)
  ✓ 
# LB/REVERSE PROXY: nginx proxy_pass http://backend:8000; health checks GET /healthz
# Algorithms: round-robin, least-conn, ip-hash, weighted
Backend must have VIP on loopback: ip addr add 10.0.1.100/32 dev lo
  ✓ Backend must NOT respond to ARP for VIP: arp_ignore=1, arp_announce=2

A CDN (Content Delivery Network) is a globally distributed network of caching servers that serve content from the location closest to the user. Instead of every user hitting your origin server in us-east-1, users in Tokyo get content from a Tokyo edge node. CDNs cache static assets (

What's the difference between a forward proxy and a reverse proxy? Give examples of each.
Show Answer
Answer
Forward Proxy: Sits between clients and the internet. Clients configure it explicitly. Used for: corporate web filtering, anonymous browsing, caching. Example: Squid, corporate HTTP proxy. Reverse Proxy: Sits between the internet and backend servers. Clients are unaware of it. Used for: TLS termination, load balancing, caching, security. Example: nginx, Envoy, AWS ALB.

alf of CLIENTS; reverse proxy acts on behalf of SERVERS. Forward proxy: many clients → one proxy → many servers. Reverse proxy: many clients → one proxy → many backend servers. The proxy is a bottleneck/concentration point in both cases.
Q2
What is the difference between Layer 4 and Layer 7 load balancing? When would you use each?
Show Answer
Answer

L4 (TCP): Routes based on IP:Port (5-tuple). Can't inspect HTTP. Higher throughput, lower latency. Use for: non-HTTP protocols (MySQL, Redis, gRPC without TLS termination), simple TCPe>curl localhost:8000/health) to determine if the service is actually working — not just if th"eq-question">What does a CDN do? How does it reduce latency and protect against DDoS?

Show Answer
Answer

A CDN caches content at edge locations worldwide. Latency reduction: Users in Tokyo fetch from Tokyo edge (5ms) instead of us-east-1 origin (150ms). Edge nodes cache static assets (images, CSS, JS) and even API responses. DDoS protection: CDNs have massive distributed capacity (terabits/second). Attack traffic is absorbed and scrubbed at the edge — your origin server never sees it. CDNs also provide WAF (Web Application Firewall), bot detection, and rate limiting at the edge.

Explanation

For anihpj: Cloudflare caches /static/* and /media/* at 300+ edge locations globally. Dynamic API calls (/api/jobs/) pass through to the origin. Cache-Control headers control behavior: public, max-age=31536000, immutable for od restart changes its IP, breaking IP-based stickiness. Cookie-based stickiness survives pod restarts (the cookie still routes to the Service, which load-balances to any pod). But if you need the SAME pod (e.g., WebSocket connection), use consistent hashing or a headless Service with StatefulSet.

Q7
What headers does a reverse proxy typically add to requests? Why does the backend need them?
Show Answer
Answer

X-Forwarded-For: The original client IP (proxies append, comma-separated). Without it, the backend sees the proxy's IP. X-Forwarded-Proto: The original protocol (http/https). The backend needs this to know if the client used HTTPS — critical for redirects and security checks. X-Real-IP: The original client IP (single value, nginx-specific). X-Forwarded-Host: The original Host header. These are essential for logging, rate limiting, geo-IP, and generating correct absolute URLs in responses.

Explanation

In Django: configure SECURE_PROXY_SSL_HEADER = ('HTTP_X_FORWARDED_PROTO', 'https') and add your proxy's IP to ALLOWED_HOSTS. Otherwise, request.is_secure() returns False and redirect URLs use http:// instead of https://.

Q8
How does an L7 load balancer perform health checks? What happens when a backend fails?
Show Answer
Answer

The LB periodically sends HTTP requests to a health check endpoint (e.g., GET /health every 5 seconds). If the backend responds with 200 OK, it's healthy. If it fails N consecutive checks (typically 2-3), the LB marks it unhealthy and stops sending traffic to it. Active connections to the failed backend get RST (reset). Passive health checking: The LB observes actual traffic failures (5xx errors, connection timeouts) and ejects the backend without explicit health checks.

Explanation

In Kubernetes: the readinessProbe is the health check for Services. If readinessProbe fails, the pod is removed from Endpoints → no traffic. The livenessProbe restarts the pod if it's stuck. Always implement a /health endpoint that checks actual dependencies (database, cache) — not just "the process is alive."

Q9
What is the difference between an ALB (Application Load Balancer) and an NLB (Network Load Balancer) in AWS?
Show Answer
Answer

ALB (L7): Routes HTTP/HTTPS based on URL path, host headers, query params. Terminates TLS. Integrates with AWS WAF and Cognito. Slower (adds latency) but feature-rich. NLB (L4): Routes TCP/UDP/TLS based on IP:Port. Can preserve source IP. Does NOT terminate TLS (passthrough) unless you configure TLS listener. Higher throughput (millions of RPS), lower latency. Use NLB for: non-HTTP workloads, extreme performance, static IP requirements.

Explanation

Common pattern: NLB → ALB (NLB handles the internet-facing IP, ALB does HTTP routing). NLB provides a static IP (important for IP allowlisting), ALB does the HTTP-level work. In Kubernetes: AWS Load Balancer Controller can create either based on Service/Ingress annotations.

Q10
How does the nginx Ingress Controller route traffic in Kubernetes? Walk through from external request to pod.
Show Answer
Answer

(1) External request hits the cloud LB (ALB/NLB) → forwards to nginx Ingress Controller pods (NodePort or LoadBalancer Service). (2) nginx reads the Ingress resource rules: Host header + path → which backend Service. (3) nginx resolves the Service name to ClusterIP via DNS. (4) nginx sends the HTTP request to the Service ClusterIP:port. (5) kube-proxy (iptables) DNATs the ClusterIP to a random healthy pod IP. (6) The pod (gunicorn) receives the HTTP request on port 8000. Note: nginx does NOT use kube-proxy if configured with endpoint discovery — it watches Endpoints and sends directly to pod IPs (bypassing Service proxy).

Explanation

The Ingress Controller is just an nginx pod with a Go controller that watches the K8s API for Ingress resources and rewrites nginx.conf. Each Ingress resource becomes a server block (Host) with location blocks (paths). Changes are applied via nginx reload (or dynamically via Lua/OpenResty to avoid reloads).

🐳 Part 5: Container Networking — Docker Under the HoodCh 15-17

Chapter 15: Docker Networking Fundamentals

Docker networking is how containers communicate — with each other, with the host, and with the outside world. Under the hood, Docker uses Linux kernel features like network namespaces (isolation), veth pairs (virtual cables), and bridges (virtual switches) to create container networks. Understanding these primitives is essential for debugging container connectivity and designing secure, performant container architectures.

🟡 Intermediate⏱️ ~2 hours🐳 Docker🔧 Practical

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ How Docker uses Linux network namespaces, veth pairs, and bridges to create isolated networks
  • ✅ Every Docker network driver — bridge, host, none, overlay, macvlan, ipvlan — and when to use each
  • ✅ What happens when you run docker run -p 8000:8000 — NAT, iptables, and port mapping deep dive
  • ✅ Docker's built-in DNS — how containers find each other by name

15.1 How Docker Creates Isolated Networks

Docker gives every container its own network namespace (netns) — a private copy of the network stack: interfaces, routing tables, iptables rules, and sockets. Containers in different netns can't see each other's interfaces. Docker connects containers using veth (virtual Ethernet) pairs — a tunnel with two ends: one end goes into the container (as eth0), the other stays on the host (as vethXXXXX). All container veth ends plug into a virtual switch — the docker0 bridge.

Docker Default Bridge Network — Under the Hood
                          HOST (Linux)
  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    iptables (NAT rules)                        │
  │  -A POSTROUTING -s 172.17.0.0/16 ! -o docker0 -j MASQUERADE   │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐
  │Container │    │Container │    │Container │
  │  anihpj  │    │ postgres │    │  redis   │
  │172.17.0.2│    │172.17.0.3│    │172.17.0.4│
  │ eth0     │    │ eth0     │    │ eth0     │
  └────┬─────┘    └────┬─────┘    └────┬─────┘
       │veth           │veth            │veth
       │pair           │pair            │pair
  ┌────┴─────┐    ┌────┴─────┐    ┌────┴─────┐
  │ vethXXX  │    │ vethYYY  │    │ vethZZZ  │
  └────┬─────┘    └────┬─────┘    └────┬─────┘
       └───────────────┼───────────────┘
                       │
              ┌────────┴────────┐
              │   docker0 bridge │ ← 172.17.0.1 (host's view)
              └────────┬─
# DOCKER NET: bridge(default,docker0 172.17.0.0/16), host(shares NS), none
# docker network ls; docker run --network=host IMAGE
───────┘
                       │
              ┌────────┴────────┐
              │   eth0 (host)   │ ← Real NIC → Internet
              └─────────────────┘
💡 Network Namespace (netns) — The Secret Sauce

A network namespace is Linux's way of giving a process its own isolated network stack. Think of it as a separate "mini-Linux" with its own interfaces, routes, and firewall rules. Docker creates a netns for each container, then moves the container's veth end into it. The container sees eth0 and thinks it's a real NIC — it has no idea it's sharing a physical NIC with other containers. Check: lsns -t net lists all network namespaces. ip netns manages them. Docker hides netns from ip netns by default — use nsenter or docker exec to enter a container's namespace.

# Kernel-level netns exploration:
# Docker doesn't register netns in /var/run/netns, so ip netns shows nothing.
# But you CAN find them via /proc:

# 1. Find a container's PID
docker inspect -f '{{.State.Pid}}' web    # → 12345

# 2. Enter its network namespace
sudo nsenter -t 12345 -n ip addr         # See interfaces from INSIDE the container
sudo nsenter -t 12345 -n ip route        # See routing table
sudo nsenter -t 12345 -n ss -tlnp        # See listening sockets

# 3. The netns is at /proc/<pid>/ns/net
ls -la /proc/12345/ns/net                # → net:[4026532...] (unique netns ID)

# 4. All containers on the same Docker network share the SAME veth host ends
#    plugged into the same bridge. This is why they can ping each other.
ip link show type veth                    # See all veth interfaces on the host
bridge fdb show dev docker0              # See MAC addresses on the bridge

15.2 Docker Network Drivers — The Complete Guide

Docker supports multiple network drivers — each with different trade-offs for isolation, performance, and multi-host support.

# DOCKER NET: bridge(default,docker0 172.17.0.0/16), host(shares NS), none
# docker network ls; docker run --network=host IMAGE
DriverIsolationPerformanceMulti-HostBest For
bridgeMediumGood❌Dev, single-host apps
hostNoneBest❌High-perf, monitoring agents
noneMaximumN/A❌Batch jobs, build agents
overlayMediumGood*✅Docker Swarm (legacy)
macvlanHighBest❌Legacy apps needing own MAC on LAN
ipvlanHighBest❌When macvlan MAC limits hit

bridge —
# IPTABLES: PREROUTING(DNAT)->FORWARD(filter)->POSTROUTING(SNAT)
# INPUT->local->OUTPUT; iptables -L -nv --line-numbers
Default Driver

The default. All containers on the same bridge network can communicate by IP. DNS-based name resolution works between containers. NAT (MASQUERADE) allows outbound internet access. docker network create my-net creates a custom bridge with automatic DNS — always prefer custom bridges over the default bridge for production.

host — No Isolation

The container shares the host's network stack directly — no separate netns. The container sees the host's interfaces, uses the host's IP, and binds to host ports directly. Advantage: zero NAT overhead, max network performance. Disadvantage: port conflicts — two containers can't both bind to port 8000. Use for: performance-critical services (load balancers, proxies), network monitoring tools that need host-level visibility.

# DOCKER NET: bridge(docker0 172.17.0.0/16, veth pairs), host(shares host NS), none
# Overlay(VXLAN for Swarm); docker network ls; docker run --network=host IMG

none — No Networking

The container has a network namespace but only the loopback interface (lo). No external connectivity. Use for: security-sensitive workloads that need zero network access, offline batch processing, build containers that only need local filesystem.

overlay — Multi-Host

Connects containers across multiple Docker hosts (Swarm mode). Uses VXLAN encapsulation to tunnel L2 traffic over L3 networks. Here's how VXLAN works at the packet level: (1) Container A on Host 1 sends a packet to Container B on Host 2 (same overlay subnet, e.g., 10.0.1.5 → 10.0.1.9). (2) Host 1's kernel determines the destination is on Host 2 (via the overlay's routing table). (3) The original Ethernet fr

docker network ls

# 2. Inspect the default bridge — see all containers on it
docker network inspect bridge

# 3. Compare network modes
docker run --rm -it --network bridge alpine ip addr   # Has eth0 + Docker IP
docker run --rm -it --network host alpine ip addr      # Sees HOST's interfaces!
docker run --rm -it --network none alpine ip addr      # Only loopback (lo)

# 4. Create a custom network
docker network create --driver bridge anihpj-net

# 5. Connect containers
docker run -d --name db --network anihpj-net postgres:16
docker run -d --name web --network anihpj-net -p 8000:8000 anihpj
docker exec web ping db         # Test DNS resolution
docker exec web nc -zv db 5432  # Test port connectivity

# 6. Connect a RUNNING container to an additional network
docker network create secondary
docker network connect secondary web   # web now has eth0 + eth1!
docker exec web ip addr                # See both interfaces
docker exec web ping db                # Still works via original network
docker network disconnect secondary web

# 7. Check iptables rules Docker created
sudo iptables -t nat -L -n | grep 8000
sudo iptables -t nat -L DOCKER -n

    Q1
    How does Docker isolate container networks? Explain network namespaces and veth pairs.
    Show Answer
    Answer

    Docker uses veth pairs — a virtual cable with two ends: one end goes into the container's netns (as eth0), the other stays on the host. All host-side veth ends plug into the docker0 bridge (a virtual switch) for L2 connectivity.

    Explanation

    This is the same technology Kubernetes uses. The pause container in each pod creates the netns, and the CNI plugin moves veth ends into it. Understanding Docker networking directly tra NS), none # docker network ls; docker run --network=host IMAGE"exam-question-item">Q2

    What's the difference between the default bridge (trong> No DNS resolution between containers (must use --link or IPs). Containers can only communicate by IP. Custom bridge: Automatic DNS resolution — container names resolve to IPs via Docker's embedded DNS at 127.0.0.11. Container isolation can be controlled. Always use custom bridges for multi-container applications. docker network create my-net creates a custom bridge network.

    Explanation

    This is a common gotcha: containers on the default bridge CAN ping each other by IP, but DNS doesn't work. On a custom bridge, both IP and DNS work. Docker Compose automatically creates a custom bridge network.

    Q3
    What happens at the iptables level when you run docker run -p 8000:8000?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    Docker creates a DNAT rule: traffic to host:8000 → container_IP:8000. This is in the DOCKER chain of the nat table. For outbound, Docker creates a MASQUERADE rule: traffic from container subnet (172.17.0.0/16) → SNAT to host IP (so the internet can reply). Check: iptables -t nat -L DOCKER -n shows DNAT rules. iptables -t nat -L POSTROUTING -n shows MASQUERADE.

    Explanation

    Without -p, the container is only reachable from other containers on the same network. The EXPOSE instruction in the Dockerfile does NOT publish the port — it's purely documentation. The actual port publishing happens via iptables rules created by dockerd when you use -p.

    # DOCKER NET: bridge(default,docker0 172.17.0.0/16), host(shares NS), none
# docker network ls; docker run --network=host IMAGE
    Q4
    When would you use --network host? What are the trade-offs?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    Use --network host when: (1) You need maximum network performance (zero NAT overhead). (2) The container needs access to the host's real network interfaces. (3) You're running a network monitoring tool. Trade-offs: No network isolation — the container sees all host interfaces. Port conflicts — only one container on the host can bind to port 8000. Less secure — the container shares the host's network namespace.

    Explanation

    host networking is how kube-proxy and many CNI daemonsets run in Kubernetes — they need host-level network access to configure iptables, routes, and interfaces. Sometimes performance requirements outweigh isolation concerns.

    Q5
    How does Docker's embedded DNS work? What's the difference between Docker DNS and Kubernetes CoreDNS?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    Docker's embedded DNS server runs at 127.0.0.11 inside each container (on custom networks). It resolves container names to their IPs. /etc/resolv.conf in the container points to 127.0.0.11. Docker DNS vs CoreDNS: Docker DNS is per-host, simple name→IP mapping for containers on the same network. CoreDNS is cluster-wide, watches the Kubernetes API for Services/Pods, supports plugins (cache, forward, rewrite, prometheus), and provides the cluster domain (svc.cluster.local). Docker DNS is simpler; CoreDNS is far more powerful and extensible.

    Explanation

    In Docker Compose, service names automatically become DNS hostnames. This is why docker-compose.yml doesn't need explicit DNS configuration — the embedded DNS server hanIMAGE

    Q9
    Your container can't reach the internet. pi rule is missing or broken. Docker creates a SNAT rule that translates container IPs (172.17.0.x) to the host IP for outbound traffic. If this rule is missing (iptables was flushed, firewalld/ufw interfered, or Docker daemon restarted incorrectly), containers can route internally but can't reach outside. Fix: sudo systemctl restart docker (rebuilds iptables rules). Or check: iptables -t nat -L POSTROp_forward should be 1).

    Explanation

    Docker relies heavily on iptables. Never run iptables -F (flush all rules) on a Docker host — it will break all container networking. If you need to manage iptables manually, use custom chains and be careful not to touch Docker's chains (DOCKER, DOCKER-USER).

    How would you connect a running container to a second Docker network? Why would you do this?

    docker network connect anihpj-net <container>

# Verify: docker exec <container> ip addr

    Why: (1) Multi-tier architecture — web container needs to talk to both a frontend network (nginx) and a backend network (database). (2) Gradual migration — connect container to new network while still serving on old one. (3) API gateway pattern — a proxy container connected to multiple isolated service networks. Disconnect: docker network disconnect anihpj-net <container>.

    Chapter 16: Docker Compose Networking

    Docker Compose automates multi-container application networking. With one YAML file, you define services, networks, and volumes — Compose creates everything and wires them together. DNS just works: every service name becomes a hostname that resolves to the container's IP.

    🟡 Intermediate⏱️ ~1 hour🐳 Compose

    16.1 How Docker Compose Creates Networks

    When you run docker-compose up, Compose: (1) Creates a default bridge network named <project>_default (e.g., anihpj_default). (2) Creates containers and attaches them to this network. (3) Sets up DNS — each service name becomes a hostname resolvable by all containers on that network. (4) If you define custom networks in the compose file, Compose creates those instead.

    Show Answer
    Answer

    Compose automatically: (1) Creates a custom bridge network per project. (2) Attaches all services to it. (3) Enables DNS resolution — service names become hostnames. With plain Docker, you must manually: docker network create, docker run --network for each container, and remember IPs (or use --link). Compose eliminates all this manual wiring.

    Explanation

    Compose uses the project name (directory name or -p flag) to namespace networks: anihpj_default, anihpj_frontend, anihpj_backend. This prevents network name conflicts between different projects on the same host.

    Q2
    In the anihpj compose file, why are there two networks (frontend and backend)?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    Plain depends_on: Only controls STARTUP ORDER — Compose starts db before web, but web may start before db is actually ready to accept connections. condition: service_healthy: Compose waits until the dependency's HEALTHCHECK passes before starvice.

    Explanation

    In production (Docker Swarm), depends_on is IGNORED — services may start on different nodes. Use application-level retry logic (connection pooling with retries, exponential backoff) instead of relying on startup order.

    Q4
    What are network aliases in Docker Compose? Give a practical use case.
    Show Answer
    Answer

    Network aliases give a service additional DNS names on a specific network. Use case: Migration — you rename "old-db" to "postgres" but want existing apps that hardcode "old-db" to keep working: networks: backend: { aliases: [postgres, old-db] }. Other use: read replicas — "postgres-write" and "postgres-read" pointing to different services. Syntax: Under networks: <name>: { aliases: [...] }.

    Explanation

    Aliases are per-network. A service can have different aliases on different networks. This is useful for multi-tenant setups where different networon">How does Docker Compose DNS resolve service names? Walk through a ping db from the web container.

    Show Answer
    Answer

    (1) web container's /etc/resolv.conf points to 127.0.0.11 (Docker's embedded DNS). (2) ping db triggers a DNS query to 127.0.0.11:53. (3) Docker DNS checks: is "db" a service name on any network this container is connected to? Yes — "db" is on the backend network (which web is also on). (4) Docker DNS returns the db container's IP on the backend network. (5) web sends ICMP to that IP — reaches db.

    Explanation

    Docker DNS is scope-aware — it only resolves services on networks the querying container is connected to. If web isn't on the network db is on, the resolution fails. This provides automatic network isolation.

    Q6
    You run docker-compose up but web can't connect to db. db is running. What are three things to check?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    (1) Networks: Are web and db on the same network? Check docker-compose.yml — db might only be on "backend" but web is only on "frontend." (2) DNS name match: Does the web container reference the correct service name? DATABASE_URL=postgres://...@db:5432/... — "db" must match the service name in compose. (3) Timing: Is web starting before db is ready? Use depends_on: { condition: service_healthy } or add retry logic in the app. Test: docker-compose exec web nc -zv db 5432.

    Q7
    What's the difference between a Docker Compose network and a Kubernetes Service?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    Compose network: L2/L3 network connecting containers on the same host. DNS resolves names to container IPs directly. Service discovery is implicit — service name

    # DOCKER NET: bridge(default,docker0 172.17.0.0/16), host(shares NS), none
# docker network ls; docker run --network=host IMAGE
    = hostname. Kubernetes Service: A virtual IP (ClusterIP) that load-balances across multiple pods. DNS resolves to the Service IP, not individual pod IPs. Provides load balancing, session affinity, and health checking. Compose networks are simpler (single-host, direct IP) while K8s Services are designed for distributed systems (multi-node, load-balanced, self-healing).

    Explanation

    Compose is designed for development and single-host deployments. For production at scale, the Service abstraction (with kube-proxy or eBPF load balancing) is essential — pods come and go, but the Service IP and DNS name remain stable.

    Q10
    How would you design a Docker Compose network topology for a microservices app with 5 services (web, api, auth, db, cache)?
    Show Answer
    Answer
    networks:
  public:     # nginx ↔ web (internet-facing)
  api:        # web ↔ api ↔ auth (internal APIs)
  data:       # api ↔ db, api ↔ cache (data layer isolation)

# web:    [public, api]     — serves frontend, calls internal APIs
# api:    [api, data]       — business logic, accesses db/cache
# auth:   [api]             — authentication only, no data access
# db:     [data]            — database, isolated from everything
# cache:  [data]            — cache, same isolation as db

    Principle: Least privilege. Each service connects only to networks it absolutely needs. db and cache are on the data network only — even if the auth service is compromised, the attacker can't reach the database directly. This is Defense in Depth applied to networking.

    Explanation

    This maps directly to Kubernetes NetworkPolicies. Design your Docker networks the same way you'd design K8s network policies — the principles are identical. Compose networks are a great way to prototype and test network segmentation before deploying to K8s.

      # DOCKER NET: bridge(docker0 172.17.0.0/16, veth pairs), host(shares host NS), none # Overlay(VXLAN for Swarm); docker network ls; docker run --network=host IMG============================================== FROM python:3.12-slim AS builder RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \ build-essential libpq-dev && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* WORKDIR /app COPY requirements.txt . # Copy requirements FIRST (cached layer!) RUN pip install --user --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt # ============================================================ # STAGE 2: RUNTIME — Minimal image, only what's needed # ============================================================ FROM python:3.12-slim AS runtime RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \ libpq-dev curl && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* # Create non-root user (security: never run as root in production!) RUN groupadd -r anihpj && useradd -r -g anihpj -d /app anihpj WORKDIR /app # Copy Python packages from builder stage (not the build tools!) COPY --from=builder /root/.local /usr/local # Copy application code COPY . . # Collect static files RUN python manage.py collectstatic --noinput # Switch to non-root user USER anihpj # EXPOSE is documentation only — doesn't publish the port! EXPOSE 8000 # H/ || exit 1 # CMD with exec form (JSON arraynefits

      The builder stage installs compilers (gcc, build-essential) to compile Python packages, but the runtime image doesn't include these — saving hundreds of MB. The final image contains only: Python runtime, compiled dependencies, and your code. This is the #1 technique for keeping Docker images small and secure.

      ⚠️ Exec Form vs Shell Form — Why It Matters for Container Lifecycle

      Exec form: CMD ["gunicorn", "-b", "0.0.0.0:8000", "myapiner — not from the Docker bridge, not from port mapping, not from other containers. Always use python manage.py runserver 0.0.0.0:8000 for containerized Django dev. This is the #1 Docker networking mistake for Django developers.

      🔐
      Use Non-Root User + Drop Capabilities

      Never run containers as root in production. If an attacker compromises a root container, they have root on the host (uny keep what's needed). Root in a container ≠ root on the host — user namespaces map container root to a non-root user on the host. Enable: userns-remap in Docker daemon config. In Kubernetes: securityContext: { runAsNonRoot: true, capabilities: { drop: [ALL] }, readOnlyRootFilesystem: true }. The principle: least privilege at every layer.

    📝 Chapter 17 — Networking Practice Questions

    Q1
    What is a multi-stage Docker build? How does it benefit the anihpj Dockerfile?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    A multi-stage build uses multiple FROM statements in one Dockerfile. Builder stage: Install compilers (gcc) and build dependencies, compile Python packages. Runtime stage: Start fresh from a slim base image, COPY only the compiled artifacts from the builder. Benefits: (1) Smaller image (no compilers, headers, or build tools). (2) Smaller attack surface (fewer binaries for an attacker to exploit). (3) Faster pulls and deploys. The final anihpj image is ~200MB with multi-stage vs ~800MB without.

    Explanation

    The key pattern: COPY requirements.txt FIRST (before code). Docker caches layers — if requirements.txt hasn't changed, the pip install layer is reused. This makes rebuilds after code changes nearly instant (seconds vs minutes).

    Q2
    Why should Django apps bind to 0.0.0.0 in containers, not 127.0.0.1? Explain with packet flow.
    Show Answer
    Answer

    127.0.0.1 is the loopback interface — only accessible FROM INSIDE the container. When Docker port-maps or routes traffic to the container, it arrives on the eth0 interface (from the veth pair). A process listening on 127.0.0.1:8000 never sees that traffic — it's on the wrong interface. 0.0.0.0 means "listen on ALL interfaces" — loopback, eth0, everything. Traffic from the Docker bridge, other containers, and port mapping all reach the process. gunicorn: --bind 0.0.0.0:8000. Django runserver: 0.0.0.0:8000.

    Explanation

    This is the #1 Docker networking gotcha for beginners. The container has its own network stack — 127.0.0.1 means the container's loopback, not the host's. Docker's port mapping DNATs traffic to the contaq-number">Q3

    What's the difference between CMD exec form and shell form? Why does it matter for networking?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    Networking impact: Shell form causes connection resets on shutdown; exec form allows graceful connection draining.

    Explanation

    In Kubernetes, this matters even more. Pod termination sends SIGTERM → wait gracePeriodSeconds → SIGKILL. With exec form, gunicorn can drain connections during the grace period. With shell form, the grace period is wasted because the signal never reaches gunicorn.

    Q4
    What does HEALTHCHECK do in a Dockerfile? How does Kubernetes use it?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    Docker HEALTHCHECK: Runs a command inside the container periodically. If it returns 0, the container is "healthy." If it fails N times (retries), the container is "unhealthy." Docker shows status in docker ps. Kubernetes: Uses livenessProbe and readinessProbe (separate concepts) — HEALTHCHECK is NOT used by default in K8s. However, if no probes are defined, some K8s setups may use the Docker HEALTHCHECK as a fallback. Best practice: define explicit Kubernetes probes in your pod spec, don't rely on DocessProbe (stop sending traffic if not ready), startupProbe (give slow-starting apps time). Docker HEALTHCHECK is simpler but K8s probes are the production standard.

    Q5
    What files should be in .dockerignore for a Django project? Why does it matter for networking security?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    Must exclude: .env (contains SECRET_KEY, DB_PASSWORD — secrets in images are a MAJOR security risk), db.sqlite3 (local dev database — shouldn't be in the image), __pycache__/, *.pyc (compiled Python, not needed), .git/ (repository history, can contain secrets), env/, venv/ (virtual environments), media/, staticfiles/ (generated at build/runtime). Networking security: If .env leaks into the image and the image is pushed to a registry, anyone with access to that registry can extract your database credentials, API keys, and secret key — they can connect to your production database directly.

    Why use a non-root user in a container? What networking capabilities>

    Root in a container can: (1) Bind to ports < 1024 (well-known ports like 80, 443). (2) Modify iptables rules (change routing, block/allowing traffic). (3) Change network interface configuration. (4) Open raw sockets (craft arbitrary packets). (5) Access /proc/net/* without restrictions. Why non-root: If an attacker compromises a root container, they can escape the container more easily, modify host networking, and pivot to other containers. A non-root user limits the attack surface. Bind to port 80 as non-root: Use setcap 'cap_net_bind_service=+ep' or use a higher port (8000, 8080) with a reverse proxy handling port 80/443.

    Explanation

    In Kubernetes, you can enforce non-root with securityContext: { runAsNonRoot: true }. Combined with readOnlyRootFilesystem: true and allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, you get a hardened container that's much harder to exploit.

    Q7
    How does layer caching in Dockerfiles work? How should you order COPY commands for optimal networktruction as a layer. If a layer's inputs haven't changed, the cached layer is reused. Optimal ordering for fast rebuilds: (1) COPY requirements.txt (changes rarely → cached). (2) RUN pip install (cached unless requirements change). (3) COPY . (chan. Bad ordering: COPY . first → RUN pip install → code changeild after changing one line of Django code should take seconds, not minutes. The networking dependency (COPY . being last) means your app's network configuration files are always fresh while dependencies are cached.

    Show Answer
    Answer

    (1) Compose creates two networks: anihpj_frontend and

    Explanation

    The network boundary between frontend and backend is the web container. It's the only service with interfaces on both networks. This creates a natural security boundary — even if nginx is compromised, the attacker has no direct network path to the database.

    . Why? How do you fix it?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    Most likely: Docker is using a cached layer from a previous build where the code was in a different state. The cache is invalidated if any file in the build context has changed — but Docker dohpj . (force full rebuild). Or add ARG CACHEBUST=unknown before COPY and build with --build-arg CACHEBUST=$(date +%s) to force cache invalidation at that point.

    Also check: (1) Is your code mounted as a volume? ddiv class="eq-question">How would you deploy the anihpj Dockerfile to Kubernetes? What networking changes are needed from Docker Compose?

  namespace: anihpj

    ☸️ Part 6: Kubernetes Networking — The Full StackCh 18-23

    Chapter 18: The Kubernetes Networking Model

    Kubernetes networking is fundamentally different from Docker networking. While Docker focuses on single-host container connectivity, Kubernetes requires a flat, NAT-less network where every pod can communicate with every other pod across all nodes without Network Address Translation. This is achieved through the CNI (Container Network Interface) — a pluggable system that lets you choose how pod networking works.

    🔴 Advanced⏱️ ~2.5 hours☸️ Kubernetes🎯 Critical

    🎯 What You'll Learn

    • ✅ The 4 fundamental K8s networking requirements — and why they exist
    • ✅ CNI — how the plugin system works, from kubelet to pod network
    • ✅ Deep comparison of CNI plugins: Calico, Cilium, Flannel, Weave
    • ✅ Overlay vs underlay networking — VXLAN encapsulation deep dive

    18.1 The 4 Fundamental Networking Requirements

    Kubernetes mandates four networking rules that every CNI plugin must satisfy:

    1️⃣
    Pods Can Communicate Across Nodes Without NAT

    Pod A on Node 1 (10.244.1.5) can reach Pod B on Node 2 (10.244.2.8) directly — no NAT, no port mapping. The source IP the destination sees is the pod's real IP. This is the hardest requirement and what CNI plugins solve.

    2️⃣
    Node Agents Can Communicate With All Pods

    kubelet, kube-proxy, and daemonsets on a node can reach all pods on that node directly. This enables health checks (kubelet → pod), log collection, and monitoring without NAT.

    3️⃣
    Pods See Their Own IP as Others See It

    A pod sees its own IP (e.g., 10.244.1.5) as its source address. Other pods see the same IP. No NAT within the cluster — IP transparency for logging, tracing, and network policies.

    4️⃣
    Host-Network Pods Communicate Without NAT

    Pods using hostNetwork: true can communicate with all other pods on all nodes without NAT. These pods use the node's IP but can still reach the pod network.

    💡 Why a Flat, NAT-Less Network? — The Design Philosophy

    Kubernetes chose a flat network model for a fundamental reason: IP identity = pod identity. In traditional networks, NAT hides real IPs — making logging, tracing, and security policies nearly impossible. In Kubernetes, every pod has a unique, routable IP that IS its identity. NetworkPolicies work because pod IPs are stable within the pod's lifetime. Service meshes work because the real source IP is visible. This was a deliberate choice: complexity at the infrastructure layer (CNI) in exchange for simplicity at the application layer (apps just use IPs). The alternative — NAT'd container networks like Docker's default bridge — works for single-host but collapses at cluster scale because IPs are no longer unique or routable across nodes.

    💡 Why These 4 Rules Exist — The Design Philosophy Behind Flat Networking

    These rules weren't chosen arbitrarily. Rule 1 (no NAT between pods): If pods were NAT'd, every pod would see traffic from the node's IP — making it impossible to distinguish which pod sent a request. NetworkPolicies would be useless because every request would appear to come fr

    • CNI: ADD/DEL/CHECK/VERSION operations; config in /etc/cni/net.d/
    • veth pairs: one end in pod NS, other attached to cni0 bridge on node
    • IP-per-pod model: every pod gets a unique, routable IP

    • Container port conflicts within a pod (shared NS means shared ports!)

    om the node. Service meshes would break because mTLS identity is tied to pod IP. Distributed tracing would show all spans originating from node IPs. Rule 2 (node agents can reach pods): The kubelet must be able to call each pod's health check endpoint directly — without this, liveness/readiness probes fail. kube-proxy must reach pod IPs to populate Endpoints. Log collectors must reach pod filesystems. Rule 3 (pods see their real IP): If a pod saw a different source IP than what other pods see, applications would log incorrect IPs, rate limiters would target wrong clients, and any IP-based authentication would break. Rule 4 (host-network pods can reach pod network): Host-network pods (kube-proxy, CNI agents, monitoring daemonsets) need to reach the pod network to do their jobs. Without this, the entire cluster control plane couldn't function.

    18.2 CNI — The Plugin That Makes It Work

    CNI (Container Network Interface) is a specification, not a product. It defines how the container runtime (containerd/CRI-O) calls a plugin to set up networking for a pod. The flow: kubelet → CRI → CNI binary → IPAM → configure pod netns.

    Kubernetes CNI Execution Flow — From Pod Creation to Network Ready
      1. kubelet receives PodSpec (from API server)
  2. kubelet calls CRI (Container Runtime Interface): "create pod"
  3. CRI (containerd) creates pod sandbox (pause container + netns)
  4. CRI calls CNI plugin with CNI_ARGS (pod name, namespace,
     container ID, network namespace path)
  5. CNI plugin:
     a. Calls IPAM plugin → get IP for this pod (e.g., 10.244.1.5)
     b. Creates veth pair: one end in pod netns, one on host
     c. Assigns IP to pod's eth0 (inside pod netns)
     d. Adds routes (default via bridge/host)
     e. Adds iptables rules (network policy, masquerade)
  6. CNI plugin reports result (IP, routes, DNS) back to CRI
  7. CRI returns success → kubelet updates pod status → Pod Running
    CNI PluginEncapsulationNetworkPolicyEncryptioneBPFBest For
    CalicoBGP/IPIP/VXLAN✅WireGuard✅Production K8s with NetworkPolicy
    CiliumVXLAN/Geneve✅WireGuard/IPSec✅eBPF-native, Hubble observability
    FlannelVXLAN/HostGW❌❌❌Simple, minimal setup
    AWS VPC CNINative (ENI IPs)❌*❌❌EKS — pod IPs from VPC subnet

    Calico (eBPF + BGP)

    Calico is the most popular CNI for production Kubernetes. It supports multiple dataplanes depending on your network environment.

    Calico — Three Dataplane Modes
      BGP MODE (underlay — fastest):
  ┌──────────┐  BGP: "I can reach 10.244.1.0/24"  ┌──────────┐
  │ Node 1   │◀══════════════════════════════════▶│ Node 2   │
  │10.244.1.x│  Pod IPs routable on physical net   │10.244.2.x│
  └──────────┘  No encapsulation! Zero overhead.    └──────────┘
  Requires BGP on routers/switches (or Calico Route Reflectors).

  IPIP/VXLAN MODE (overlay — cloud-friendly):
  ┌──────────┐  IPIP: pod packet inside IP packet  ┌──────────┐
  │ Node 1   │═════════════════════════════════════│ Node 2   │
  │10.244.1.x│  or VXLAN: pod packet inside UDP    │10.244.2.x│
  └──────────┘  Works on ANY network (no BGP req)  └──────────┘

  eBPF MODE (kernel-native):
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Pod A ──▶ eBPF map lookup ──▶ Pod B                    │
  │  No iptables. No kube-proxy. Direct kernel routing.     │
  │  WireGuard encryption at kernel level.                  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    Cilium (eBPF-Native)

    Cilium uses eBPF to program the Linux kernel directly — no iptables, no proxies per service.

    Cilium — eBPF Data Path & Hubble Observability
      CILIUM eBPF DATA PATH (kernel-level, no iptables):
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ POD A (10.244.1.5)          POD B (10.244.2.8)            │
  │  │                           ▲                            │
  │  │ packet sent               │ packet received            │
  │  ▼                           │                            │
  │ ┌──────────────────────┐     │                            │
  │ │ eBPF Program (TC hook)│─────┼── Direct kernel routing   │
  │ │ • Service lookup      │     │  No iptables chain walk   │
  │ │ • NetworkPolicy check │     │  Per-endpoint LB          │
  │ │ • Encapsulation       │     │                            │
  │ │ • Encryption (WG)     │     │                            │
  │ └──────────────────────┘     │                            │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  HUBBLE OBSERVABILITY (built-in, zero-config):
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  ┌─────────┐   ┌─────────┐   ┌─────────┐                  │
  │  │ jobpost │──▶│postgres │──▶│  redis  │                  │
  │  │ 45ms    │   │ 30ms    │   │  2ms    │                  │
  │  └─────────┘   └─────────┘   └─────────┘                  │
  │  Service map + latency + packet drops + HTTP status       │
  │  L7 POLICIES: allow GET /api/*, deny DELETE /admin/*       │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    Flannel (VXLAN — Simplest Option)

    Flannel is the simplest CNI — designed to "just work" with minimal configuration.

    Flannel VXLAN — Node Subnet Allocation
      FLANNEL OVERLAY NETWORK (10.244.0.0/16):

  ┌─────────────────────────┐    ┌─────────────────────────┐
  │ NODE 1 (192.168.1.10)   │    │ NODE 2 (192.168.1.11)   │
  │ Pod CIDR: 10.244.1.0/24 │    │ Pod CIDR: 10.244.2.0/24 │
  │                         │    │                         │
  │ Pod A: 10.244.1.2       │    │ Pod C: 10.244.2.2       │
  │ Pod B: 10.244.1.3       │    │ Pod D: 10.244.2.3       │
  │ ... up to 254 pods      │    │ ... up to 254 pods      │
  │                         │    │                         │
  │ flannel.1 (VXLAN dev)   │    │ flannel.1 (VXLAN dev)   │
  └───────────┬─────────────┘    └───────────┬─────────────┘
              │                               │
              └──── VXLAN tunnel ─────────────┘
                   (UDP port 8472)

  SIMPLE: One DaemonSet, one ConfigMap, pods get IPs.
  LIMITS: No NetworkPolicy, no encryption, no eBPF.
  UPGRADE PATH: Keep Flannel for networking + add Calico for policy.

    Weave Net

    Weave creates a full mesh overlay — every node connects directly to every other node via UDP tunnels.

    Weave Net — Full Mesh Overlay with Fast Datapath
      WEAVE FULL MESH (every node ↔ every node):

       ┌──────────┐
       │  Node 1  │
       │10.32.0.x │
       └────┬─┬───┘
            │ │
     ┌──────┘ └──────┐
     ▼               ▼
  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐
  │  Node 2  │◀─│  Node 3  │  All nodes peer directly!
  │10.44.0.x │  │10.48.0.x │  No central switch/bridge.
  └──────────┘  └──────────┘

  WEAVE ROUTER (on each node):
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ • Discovers peers via multicast/broadcast  │
  │ • Establishes UDP tunnels to all peers     │
  │ • Encrypts with NaCl (fast, secure)        │
  │ • Fast datapath: bypasses Linux bridge     │
  │   (kernel module for wire-speed)           │
  │ • NetworkPolicy via ODP (Open vSwitch)     │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  POD CIDR: 10.32.0.0/12 (default, configurable)
  Smaller community than Calico/Cilium but battle-tested.
    💡 CNI IPAM — How Pods Get Their IPs

    IPAM (IP Address Management) is the CNI sub-plugin that allocates IPs. host-local: Each node gets a /24 subnet, pods get sequential IPs (Flannel default). calico-ipam: IP pools with block affinity — each node gets a /26 block (62 pod IPs), allocation is persisted. AWS VPC IPAM: Pods get actual VPC IPs from ENI secondary addresses — no overlay needed. ⚠️ IP exhaustion: Pod stays "ContainerCreating" with "failed to allocate IP." AWS t3.medium = 2 ENIs × 3 IPs = 4 pod IPs (after subtracting 2 primary). Use larger instances or switch CNI for more pods per node.

    ⚠️ NetworkPolicy — Kubernetes Firewall Fundamentals

    A NetworkPolicy is an L3/L4 firewall for pods — think "security group per pod." Pods are selected by labels; traffic is controlled by ingress/egress rules specifying: from/to pods (podSelector), namespaces (namespaceSelector), or IP blocks (ipBlock). ⚠️ CRITICAL: If NO NetworkPolicy selects a pod, ALL traffic is allowed (default-allow). Once ANY policy selects a pod, it becomes default-DENY — only traffic explicitly allowed by policies is permitted. ⚠️ NetworkPolicies are namespace-scoped. A policy in namespace "anihpj" only affects pods there. ⚠️ The CNI MUST support NetworkPolicy: Calico ✅, Cilium ✅, Flannel ❌ (add Calico for policy), AWS VPC CNI ❌.

    18.3 Overlay vs Underlay — How Pod Networks Actually Work

    Overlay: Pod traffic is encapsulated inside another packet (VXLAN, Geneve). The original pod packet becomes payload inside a UDP packet sent between nodes. Underlay: Pod IPs are routable on the physical network — no encapsulation. BGP or static routes tell the physical network how to reach pod subnets.

    VXLAN Encapsulation — What Actually Hits the Wire
      OUTER ETHERNET │ OUTER IP │ UDP  │ VXLAN │ INNER ETHERNET + IP + TCP + HTTP
  (node MACs)    │(node to  │(4789)│(VNI)  │ (original pod packet)
                 │  node)   │      │       │
  ───────────────┼──────────┼──────┼───────┼────────────────────────────────
  14 bytes       │ 20 bytes │8 bytes│8 bytes│ original pod packet (up to 1450)

  TOTAL OVERHEAD = 14 + 20 + 8 + 8 = 50 bytes
  Max pod MTU on 1500 MTU link = 1500 - 50 = 1450 bytes

  ⚠️ If firewall blocks UDP port 4789 between nodes → cross-node pod traffic breaks SILENTLY!

    18.4 [LAB 🛠️] CNI Exploration & Troubleshooting Lab

    # === PHASE 1: Identify your CNI ===
kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep -E 'calico|cilium|flannel|weave'
kubectl get nodes -o wide                       # PodCIDR per node
kubectl describe pod <cni-pod> -n kube-system    # CNI pod details

# === PHASE 2: Inspect CNI configuration (on a node) ===
ls /etc/cni/net.d/                               # CNI config files (.conf/.conflist)
cat /etc/cni/net.d/*.conf                        # Read the config
ls /opt/cni/bin/                                 # CNI plugin binaries
# Each binary = one CNI command (ADD/DEL/CHECK)

# === PHASE 3: Troubleshooting — pod stuck in ContainerCreating ===
kubectl describe pod <stuck-pod>                 # Events show CNI errors
kubectl logs -n kube-system <cni-pod> --tail=50  # CNI pod logs
# Common errors in logs:
# "failed to allocate IP" → IP pool exhausted (node CIDR full)
# "failed to find plugin" → /opt/cni/bin/ missing binary
# "timeout" → CNI socket unreachable

# === PHASE 4: Check CNI health ===
kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=calico-node
kubectl exec -n kube-system <cni-pod> -- <health-check-cmd>
# Calico: calicoctl node status
# Cilium: cilium status; cilium connectivity test

    📝 Chapter 18 — Networking Practice Questions

    Q1
    What are the 4 fundamental Kubernetes networking requirements?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    (1) Pods can communicate with all other pods on all nodes without NAT. (2) Node agents (kubelet) can communicate with all pods on that node. (3) Pods see their own IP as the IP others see them as. (4) Host-network pods can communicate with all pods without NAT. These requirements create a flat, NAT-less network where every pod has a unique, routable IP.

    Q2
    What is CNI? Walk through the CNI execution flow when a pod is created.
    Show Answer
    Answer

    CNI is a specification defining how container runtimes call plugins to configure pod networking. Flow: kubelet → CRI → CNI binary (with pod name, namespace, netns path) → IPAM (allocates IP) → creates veth pair → assigns IP to eth0 → adds routes → adds iptables rules → reports result back. The CNI config file at /etc/cni/net.d/*.conf specifies which plugin and configuration to use.

    Q3
    Compare Calico and Cilium as CNI plugins. When would you choose one over the other?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    Calico: Mature, BGP-native, simpler architecture, excellent NetworkPolicy, WireGuard encryption. Best for: teams that want battle-tested stability, BGP networking, or simpler operations. Cilium: eBPF-native, Hubble observability, L7 network policies (HTTP/Kafka/gRPC), Cluster Mesh. Best for: teams that want cutting-edge performance, deep observability, or application-layer security policies. Both support eBPF kube-proxy replacement.

    Q4
    What is the difference between overlay and underlay networking in Kubernetes?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    Overlay: Pod packets are encapsulated (VXLAN/Geneve) inside UDP packets between nodes. 50-byte overhead. Works on any network — the physical network only sees node-to-node UDP. Underlay: Pod IPs are routable on the physical network — BGP or static routes tell routers how to reach pod subnets. No encapsulation overhead. Faster but requires network configuration (BGP on switches or cloud route tables). Calico BGP mode is the most common underlay approach.

    Q5
    What happens if UDP port 4789 is blocked between K8s nodes running Flannel VXLAN?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    Cross-node pod-to-pod communication breaks SILENTLY. Pods on the same node can still communicate (local bridge). Pods on different nodes see timeouts. There's no error message — packets are simply dropped by the firewall. Debug: tcpdump -i eth0 'udp port 4789' on both nodes — you'll see packets sent but not received. Fix: Open UDP 4789 in firewall/Security Group between all K8s nodes. VXLAN must be allowed for overlay networking to function.

    Q6
    Why does Flannel not support NetworkPolicy? How can you add policy support?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    Flannel focuses solely on pod networking (IP assignment + cross-node routing). It doesn't implement any network policy engine. Fix: Install Calico for policy only — this is a common pattern: Flannel for networking + Calico for NetworkPolicy. Calico's Felix agent enforces policies via iptables while Flannel handles IP allocation and routing. Alterna
