    📝 Chapter 23 — Networking Practice Questions

    Q1
    What is a service mesh? What problem does it solve that Kubernetes Services don't?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    A service mesh moves networking concerns (mTLS, retries, timeouts, circuit breaking, traffic splitting, observability) out of application code into infrastructure sidecar proxies. K8s Services provide: L4 load balancing + service discovery. Service mesh adds: Automatic mTLS, L7 traffic management, distributed tracing, canary deployments, fault injection, circuit breaking. Services handle "where to send." Mesh handles "how to send" — reliability, security, observability.

    Q2
    How does the Istio sidecar intercept pod traffic? What happens if the sidecar crashes?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    An init container runs iptables -t nat -A PREROUTING -p tcp -j REDIRECT --to-port 15001, redirecting all inbound/outbound pod traffic to the Envoy sidecar on port 15001. Envoy then forwards to the actual destination (after applying policies). If sidecar crashes: iptables rules still redirect to dead proxy → ALL connections fail. Pod appears Running but has NO network. The sidecar is a critical single point of failure for that pod. This is why sidecar resource limits and liveness probes are essential.

    Q3
    What is mTLS in a service mesh? How is it different from regular TLS?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    Regular TLS: Only server proves identity. Client is anonymous. mTLS: Both client AND server present certificates and prove identity. In a mesh, every service gets a certificate (SPIFFE X.509) from the control plane. Service A calls Service B → both sidecars present certs → mutually authenticated. This prevents: (1) unauthorized services calling your API (even within the cluster). (2) Man-in-the-middle attacks inside the cluster. (3) Impersonation — Service X can't pretend to be Service Y.

    Q4
    Compare Istio, Linkerd, and Cilium Service Mesh. When would you choose each?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    Istio: Maximum features (ALL route types, Wasm extensibility, multi-cluster). Envoy sidecars. Higher complexity. Best for: large orgs that need everything. Linkerd: Simpler, Rust proxy (lower latency, smaller footprint). Fewer features but easier to operate. Best for: teams that want simplicity and performance. Cilium: Sidecarless — uses eBPF in the kernel. No proxy per pod. Best for: performance-critical workloads, teams already using Cilium as CNI. All three provide mTLS, traffic management, and observability.

    Q5
    What is circuit breaking in a service mesh? How would you configure it for the anihpj postgres connection?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    Circuit breaking prevents cascading failures by detecting failing backends and stopping traffic to them. For anihpj→postgres: maxConnections: 5 (max concurrent connections to postgres). consecutive5xxErrors: 5 (if 5 consecutive 5xx errors, eject backend for 30s). interval: 10s (check every 10s). Why: If postgres slows down, connections pile up → gunicorn workers exhaust → jobpost becomes unresponsive. Circuit breaker detects this early and fails fast (returning 503) instead of letting connections queue up. This protects the entire system.

    Q6
    How does distributed tracing work in a service mesh? Walk through a trace for an anihpj API request.
    Show Answer
    Answer

    The sidecar automatically injects trace headers (b3/Zipkin format) into every request. Flow: (1) Request arrives at Ingress → sidecar generates trace ID and span ID, adds headers: x-b3-traceid: abc123, x-b3-spanid: span1. (2) Forwards to jobpost → jobpost sidecar creates child span (span2), propagates headers. (3) jobpost queries postgres → sidecar creates span3. (4) postgres responds → span3 closed. (5) jobpost responds → span2 closed. (6) Response to client → span1 closed. Jaeger/Zipkin collects all spans and shows the full waterfall: Ingress(10ms) → jobpost(45ms) → postgres(30ms). This works with ZERO application code changes — the sidecars handle all tracing.

    Q7
    What is the data plane vs control plane in a service mesh? What does each do?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    Data plane: The sidecar proxies (Envoy/Linkerd-proxy) in every pod. They handle ALL data traffic — forwarding, load balancing, mTLS, retries, circuit breaking, telemetry collection. Control plane: Istiod/Linkerd controller. It: (1) Issues certificates to sidecars. (2) Distributes routing/config/rules to sidecars via xDS API. (3) Collects telemetry. (4) Manages service discovery. The data plane operates independently — if the control plane goes down, existing connections continue to work (data plane has cached config). New sidecars won't get certs until control plane recovers.

    Q8
    How do you verify that mTLS is actually working between two services in Istio?
    Show Answer
    Answer
    # Check PeerAuthentication policy (STRICT = mTLS required)
kubectl get peerauthentication -A
# Check if sidecar reports mTLS
kubectl exec deploy/jobpost -c istio-proxy -- curl localhost:15000/config_dump | grep -A5 "ssl_context"
# tcpdump shows encrypted traffic:
kubectl exec deploy/jobpost -c istio-proxy -- tcpdump -i eth0 -A | grep "TLS"
# Istioctl verify:
istioctl authn tls-check jobpost-xxx.anihpj postgres.anihpj.svc.cluster.local
# Kiali dashboard shows lock icons on mTLS-secured connections
    Q9
    What are the main differences between sidecar-based mesh (Istio/Linkerd) and sidecarless mesh (Cilium)?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    Sidecar (Istio/Linkerd): Every pod gets a proxy container. Traffic goes app→sidecar→network→sidecar→app. Pros: Language-agnostic, works with any app. Cons: Resource overhead (extra CPU/RAM per pod), latency (extra hop), operational complexity (sidecar injection, upgrades). Sidecarless (Cilium): eBPF programs in the kernel handle mesh functions. No proxy per pod. Pros: Zero sidecar overhead, lower latency, simpler operations. Cons: Requires eBPF-capable kernel (Linux 5.10+), fewer L7 features than Envoy, newer/less mature.

    Q10
    You deployed Istio and suddenly all pods can't communicate. What went wrong?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    Most likely causes: (1) PeerAuthentication set to STRICT but sidecars not fully ready: Pods started before sidecars got certificates → mTLS fails → connections dropped. Fix: wait for sidecars to be ready, or deploy mesh in PERMISSIVE mode first. (2) Sidecar resource limits too low: Sidecar OOMKilled → iptables still redirects to dead proxy → zero connectivity. (3) Istio CNI plugin not installed: Init container requires NET_ADMIN capability for iptables. Without Istio CNI, pods need elevated privileges. (4) MTU mismatch: Sidecar adds overhead to packets. If not configured for overlay network MTU, packets are dropped.

    ☁️ Part 7: Cloud Networking — VPCs, Subnets & Hybrid ConnectivityCh 24-26

    Chapter 24: Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) Fundamentals

    A Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) is your own logically isolated section of the cloud — a virtual data center where you control IP addressing, subnets, routing, and security. Every cloud resource (EC2, RDS, EKS) lives inside a VPC. Understanding VPC design is essential for building secure, scalable cloud architectures.

    🟡 Intermediate⏱️ ~2 hours☁️ Cloud🏗️ Architecture

    24.1 What Is a VPC?

    A VPC is defined by a CIDR block (e.g., 10.0.0.0/16 = 65,536 IPs), divided into subnets (e.g., 10.0.1.0/24 = 256 IPs per subnet) across Availability Zones for high availability. Route tables control traffic flow between subnets and to the internet. Gateways (Internet Gateway, NAT Gateway) provide internet access.

    AWS VPC Architecture — anihpj Production Design
                        AWS VPC: 10.0.0.0/16

  ┌──────────────────────────────┐  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │  PUBLIC SUBNET (10.0.1.0/24) │  │  PUBLIC SUBNET (10.0.2.0/24) │
  │  ┌──────────┐ ┌───────────┐ │  │  ┌──────────┐ ┌───────────┐ │
  │  │ Bastion  │ │ NAT GW    │ │  │  │ NAT GW   │ │  ALB     │ │
  │  │ Host     │ │ (AZ-a)    │ │  │  │ (AZ-b)   │ │ (public)  │ │
  │  └──────────┘ └─────┬─────┘ │  │  └─────┬────┘ └─────┬─────┘ │
  └─────────────────────┼───────┘  └────────┼────────────┼───────┘
                        │                   │            │
  ┌─────────────────────┼───────────────────┼────────────┼───────┐
  │  PRIVATE SUBNET (10.0.10.0/24 — AZ-a)   │            │       │
  │  ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐ │            │       │
  │  │EKS Node │ │EKS Node │ │   RDS    │◀─┘ (route to NAT)     │
  │  │(jobpost)│ │(jobpost)│ │PostgreSQL│                        │
  │  └──────────┘ └──────────┘ └──────────┘                        │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Internet Gateway ──▶ 0.0.0.0/0 (public subnets)
  NAT Gateway ──▶ 0.0.0.0/0 (private subnets → outbound internet only)
    ☁️
    AWS VPC

    Region-scoped virtual network. CIDR block (/16 to /28). Subnets in AZs. Internet Gateway, NAT Gateway, VPC Endpoints. Route tables per subnet. Security Groups + NACLs. Default VPC created automatically (not for production).

    🌐
    GCP VPC

    Global-scoped — one VPC spans all regions! Subnets are regional. No IP range at VPC level (subnets defined per region). Routes are global. Firewall rules (not SGs) — stateful, applied per instance or network tag. No NAT Gateway — use Cloud NAT (per-region).

    🔷
    Azure VNet

    Regional like AWS. CIDR block. Subnets within a VNet. Network Security Groups (like SGs+NACLs combined). Azure Firewall or NAT Gateway for outbound. VNet Peering (transitive by default!). Service Endpoints/Private Link for private service access.

    💡 VPC Design Decision Tree — How to Plan Your CIDRs

    Step 1 — Choose CIDR size: /16 = 65,536 IPs (most common, room to grow). /20 = 4,096 IPs (small environments). Never overlap on-prem network ranges — overlapping CIDRs prevent VPN/peering. Step 2 — Plan subnets per AZ: Minimum 2 AZs for high availability. Each AZ typically gets: public subnet (LBs, NAT Gateway, Bastion) + private app subnet (EKS workers, EC2) + private data subnet (RDS, ElastiCache). Step 3 — Reserve space: Leave unused CIDR blocks for future VPCs, VPC peering, or expansion. Step 4 — Size subnets properly: EKS can consume 100+ pod IPs per node (VPC CNI assigns ENI secondary IPs to pods). Use /20 (4,091 IPs) or /19 (8,187 IPs) for EKS subnets, not /24 (251 usable). Step 5 — Remember AWS reservations: Every subnet loses 5 IPs: .0 (network), .1 (VPC router), .2 (DNS), .3 (reserved), .255 (broadcast). A /24 has 256 - 5 = 251 usable, not 256.

    🔬 How VPC Isolation Actually Works — Under the Hypervisor Hood

    AWS achieves VPC isolation through a combination of technologies: (1) Mapping Service: Every packet leaving an EC2 instance is intercepted by the Xen/KVM hypervisor. The hypervisor queries the AWS Mapping Service — a distributed, globally consistent database that maps every ENI and its IP to a VPC and its owner. This lookup happens for EVERY packet. (2) Geneve Encapsulation: Once the mapping service confirms the packet is allowed, the hypervisor encapsulates it in a Geneve (Generic Network Virtualization Encapsulation) tunnel header and sends it across the AWS software-defined network. The encapsulation includes VPC ID, source/destination ENI IDs, and security metadata. (3) Hypervisor Enforcement: Security Group rules are enforced at the hypervisor level — NOT inside the guest VM. The VM never sees the firewall. The hypervisor checks SG state tables before forwarding any packet. This means even if an attacker compromises your EC2 instance's root account, they cannot disable the Security Group — it's enforced outside the VM. (4) No ARP Spoofing: The hypervisor also enforces IP-to-MAC mappings. An instance cannot spoof another instance's IP or MAC address — the mapping service rejects mismatches. This is why VPC networking has near-zero overhead: the mapping service and Geneve encapsulation are implemented in AWS's custom Nitro hardware offload cards, not in software. Your instance's CPU never spends cycles on virtual networking.

    📊 VPC Flow Logs — Your Network Telescope

    VPC Flow Logs capture metadata about every IP flow in your VPC. Format: version account-id interface-id srcaddr dstaddr srcport dstport protocol packets bytes start end action log-status. Key fields: action = ACCEPT or REJECT (did SG/NACL allow?), log-status = OK, NODATA, SKIPDATA. What Flow Logs tell you: (1) Which pod sent 50 GB to an external IP? (2) Is the SG blocking traffic between EKS and RDS? (3) Is there unexpected traffic to unknown IPs (potential exfiltration)? What they DON'T capture: Packet payloads (headers only), intra-subnet traffic (by default — you can enable), traffic to the DNS server (.2), traffic to the Windows license server. Cost: $0.50/GB ingested to CloudWatch Logs. For high-throughput EKS clusters (1 TB/day), use S3 destination ($0 cost for storage of flow logs themselves). anihpj example: Enable Flow Logs on the EKS subnet. Query in CloudWatch Logs Insights: filter action='REJECT' | stats count() by srcAddr, dstAddr, dstPort — shows what traffic is being blocked, helping debug SG misconfigurations.

    ⚠️ Default VPC — Convenient, But Never for Production

    Every AWS account comes with a Default VPC (172.31.0.0/16). It has: one public subnet per AZ, an Internet Gateway, a default NACL (allow all), a default Security Group (deny inbound, allow all outbound), and DHCP options for DNS. Why it's dangerous for production: (1) All subnets are PUBLIC — resources get public IPs automatically unless you explicitly opt out. Accidentally launching a database in the default VPC gives it a public IP. (2) No private subnets — you can't deploy EKS workers in private subnets without creating new ones. (3) The CIDR (172.31.0.0/16) might overlap with on-prem networks. (4) No VPC Endpoints configured. Best practice: Create a custom VPC with carefully designed CIDRs and subnets. Delete the Default VPC or leave it unused. For anihpj: create a custom VPC (10.0.0.0/16) with proper public/private/data subnet segmentation.

    24.2 Public vs Private Subnets — The Great Divide

    The fundamental security boundary: Public subnet: Route to Internet Gateway — resources CAN receive inbound internet traffic. Private subnet: Route to NAT Gateway — outbound-only internet access.

    Public vs Private Subnet — Route Table Comparison
      PUBLIC SUBNET ROUTE TABLE:              PRIVATE SUBNET ROUTE TABLE:
  ┌──────────────────────────────┐        ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │ 10.0.0.0/16 → local         │        │ 10.0.0.0/16 → local         │
  │ 0.0.0.0/0   → IGW           │        │ 0.0.0.0/0   → NAT Gateway   │
  └──────────────────────────────┘        └──────────────────────────────┘
  ✅ Resources CAN have public IPs        ❌ Resources have private IPs only
  ✅ Internet CAN initiate connections     ✅ Resources can initiate OUTBOUND
  ✅ Traffic flows: Internet ↔ Subnet     ❌ Internet CANNOT initiate inbound
                                           💡 NAT GW translates private IP→public

  RULE OF THUMB: Public = Load Balancers, Bastions. Private = Everything else.
  NAT Gateway: ~$0.045/GB + $0.045/hr. Use VPC Endpoints to reduce costs!
    💡 NAT Gateway Internals — What Happens at the Packet Level

    A NAT Gateway performs Source NAT (SNAT) on outbound traffic from private subnets. Outbound packet walk-through: (1) EC2 instance in private subnet (10.0.10.25) initiates connection to 8.8.8.8:443. (2) Route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 → NAT Gateway. (3) NAT Gateway creates a translation entry: replaces source IP 10.0.10.25 → NAT's Elastic IP (52.x.x.x), assigns a random ephemeral source port, records the mapping. (4) Response arrives at 52.x.x.x:random_port. (5) NAT Gateway looks up the translation table: 52.x.x.x:random_port → 10.0.10.25:original_port, forwards the response. Scale: Auto-scales to 45 Gbps burst. One NAT Gateway per AZ (for HA). Cost trap: NAT Gateway charges per GB for ALL data processed — including traffic to S3, DynamoDB, and other AWS services. High-throughput S3 access through NAT can cost thousands/month. Always create VPC Gateway Endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB to bypass NAT entirely. VPC Interface Endpoints cover other AWS services.

    🧮 Subnet CIDR Calculator — How Many IPs Do You REALLY Need?

    Subnet sizing is more art than science. Here's the systematic approach: Step 1 — Count resources: For an EKS subnet: each node needs 1 primary IP + each pod needs 1 IP. With 10 m5.large nodes (3 ENIs × 10 IPs each = 30 pod IPs per node), you need 10 node IPs + 300 pod IPs = 310 IPs minimum. Add 50% headroom for scaling and rolling updates: ~465 IPs. Step 2 — Map to CIDR: /23 = 512 - 5 = 507 usable → fits. /24 = 256 - 5 = 251 usable → too small. Step 3 — Account for growth: Will you double the cluster size? Triple it? Choose a CIDR that accommodates 2-3x planned growth. Quick reference: /28 = 11 usable (tiny, for dedicated NAT GW subnets only), /27 = 27 usable, /26 = 59 usable, /25 = 123 usable, /24 = 251 usable (standard small subnet), /23 = 507 usable, /22 = 1,019 usable, /21 = 2,043 usable, /20 = 4,091 usable (recommended for EKS app subnets), /19 = 8,187 usable. For anihpj: /20 for EKS app subnets (growth to 50+ nodes), /24 for data subnets (RDS/ElastiCache — fewer resources, stable), /24 for public subnets (just ALB + NAT GW — tiny need).

    ⚠️ NAT Gateway High Availability — Don't Create a Single Point of Failure

    A NAT Gateway is an AZ-scoped managed service. If the AZ hosting your only NAT Gateway fails, ALL private subnets lose internet access — even those in healthy AZs (because they route to the NAT in the failed AZ). The fix: one NAT Gateway per AZ. Each AZ's private subnets route to their local NAT Gateway. If AZ-a fails, AZ-b's private subnet continues working through AZ-b's NAT Gateway. Monitoring NAT Gateway health: CloudWatch metrics: ErrorPortAllocation (ran out of SNAT ports — scale up or add another NAT), PacketsDropCount (NAT dropping packets — check for DDoS or bandwidth exhaustion), BytesOutToDestination (track egress costs). NAT Gateway redundancy for single-AZ workloads: If you can only afford one NAT, place it in the same AZ as your workloads. If the NAT's AZ fails, your workloads are down anyway. For anihpj: One NAT Gateway in each of 2 AZs. Private subnets route to their local NAT. If either AZ fails, the other AZ is self-sufficient.

    24.3 Security Groups vs Network ACLs

    FeatureSecurity Group (SG)Network ACL (NACL)
    ScopeInstance/ENI levelSubnet level
    StateStateful — return traffic auto-allowedStateless — MUST explicitly allow return traffic
    RulesAllow onlyAllow AND Deny (explicit deny rules possible)
    EvaluationAll rules evaluated (most permissive wins)Rules evaluated in order — lowest number FIRST match wins
    DefaultDeny all inbound, allow all outboundAllow all inbound + outbound (default NACL)
    Max Rules60 inbound + 60 outbound (soft limit)20 inbound + 20 outbound (can be increased)
    Rule TypesCIDR, Prefix List, or other SG IDCIDR only (no SG references)
    LoggingVPC Flow LogsVPC Flow Logs + NACL hit/miss logs
    AssociationApplied per ENI (can attach multiple SGs)One NACL per subnet (subnets can share NACLs)
    Use CaseApplication-level access: "allow ALB to reach EKS"Subnet-level blocks: "deny known botnet IPs"
    💡 SG + NACL — How They Filter Packets Together (Inbound + Outbound)

    Every packet passes through TWO checkpoints. INBOUND flow: Internet → NACL Inbound Rules (stateless, evaluated in rule-number order — first match WINS. Must allow both the request AND the response ephemeral port range 1024-65535) → Route Table → Security Group Inbound Rules (stateful — if you allow inbound port 80, the return traffic is automatically allowed without explicit outbound rule). OUTBOUND flow: Instance → SG Outbound Rules (default: allow ALL) → NACL Outbound Rules (stateless — MUST explicitly allow outbound ports AND inbound ephemeral ports for responses). Why NACLs are tricky: Because they're stateless, a NACL allowing inbound TCP 80 does NOT automatically allow the outbound TCP reply on ephemeral ports — you need BOTH rules. Security Groups handle this automatically. Best practice: SGs for application rules (stateful, reference other SGs). NACLs for broad subnet-level blocks (known malicious IPs, organization-wide deny rules).

    🔬 Connection Tracking — How Stateful Firewalling Actually Works

    Security Groups are stateful because of connection tracking (conntrack) in the hypervisor. When you allow inbound TCP 80, the hypervisor creates a conntrack entry: (src=client-IP:ephemeral, dst=instance-IP:80, proto=TCP, state=ESTABLISHED). Return traffic matching this entry is automatically allowed — no explicit outbound rule needed. The conntrack table has limits: each ENI can track ~250,000 connections. For a busy EKS node handling 10,000 connections/second to backend services, conntrack table can fill up. Symptoms: nf_conntrack: table full, dropping packet in system logs, intermittent connection failures, pods getting random TCP timeouts. SG evaluation algorithm (important for interviews):ather than one monolithic SG. EKS node: sg-eks-node (cluster communication), sg-ssh (bastion access), sg-monitoring (Prometheus scraping). Attach all three — cleaner than one huge SG.

    🧮 Prefix Delegation — The Math That Unlocks Pod Density

    Without prefix delegation, the AWS VPC CNI assigns one secondary IP per pod from the ENI's pool. An m5.large has 3 ENIs × 10 IPs/ENI = 30 IPs, minus 3 primary = 27 pod IPs max. That's terrible density

    # NETWORKING COMMANDS REFERENCE

    — 27 pods on a 2 vCPU/8 GB node. With prefix delegation: Instead of individual IPs, AWS assigns a /28 prefix (16 IPs) per ENI "slot." The CNI then subdivides: 1 primary IP for the ENI + 15 pod IPs from the /28. Math transformation: Before: m5.large = 3 ENIs × (10 - 1) = 27 pods. After: m5.large = 3 ENIs × (15 - 1) = 42 pods (+55%). Before: c5.4xlarge = 8 ENIs × (30 - 1) = 232 pods. After: c5.4xlarge = 8 ENIs × (15 - 1) = 112 pods. Wait — that's FEWER! The catch: Prefix delegation helps SMALL instances (where IPs/ENI < 16) but can REDUCE pod count on large instances with many IPs per ENI! For c5.4xlarge with 30 IPs/ENI, individual IP assignment gives 30 pods per ENI; prefix delegation only giode = (ENIs × max(min(IPs_per_ENI, prefixes_per_ENI × 16), IPs_per_ENI)) - ENIs. For EKS: Always enable prefix delegation during cluster creation (or via VPC CNI add-on configuration). It's a one-time setting that cannot be changed later without recreating nodes. Use the vpc-cni add-on configuration: ENABLE_PREFIX_DELEGATION=true, WARM_PREFIX_TARGET=1.

    Q9
    Why do Security Groups support referencing other Security Groups as sources?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    SG-to-SG referencing avoids hardcoding IPs. Instead of "allow 10.0.10.25", you write "allow all instances with SG sg-eks-nodes." When instances auto-scale, their IPs change but SG membership stays — access is maintained without updating rules. RDS SG: allow 5432 from sg-eks-nodes = any EKS worker can connect, regardless of its current IP.

    Explanation

    This is one of the most elegant features of Security Groups and a key reason to use them over IP-based firewalls. In Kubernetes: EKS worker nodes join an auto-scaling group. Node IPs change on every scale-up/scale-down event. If you hardcoded node IPs in the RDS Security Group, you'd need to update it on every scaling event — impossible to manage. With SG references, you create a rule once: "RDS SG allows inbound from EKS-Nodes SG." That's it. New nodes automatically get access. Terminated nodes automatically lose access (they're no longer in the SG). This is dynamic, self-maintaining firewall management. Combined with Kubernetes NetworkPolicies inside the cluster, you get defense in depth: K8s NetworkPolicy restricts which pods can call which services, and SG rules restrict which instances can reach the database.

    Q5
    How do cloud LBs handle health checks? What happens when a backend fails?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    LB sends periodic health check requests (configurable path, interval, threshold). If N consecutive checks fail, backend is marked unhealthy and removed from rotation. Existing connections may be dropped or completed (depends on LB type and deregistration delay). In EKS: ALB health checks target pods directly. The readinessProbe controls whether a pod receives traffic via the Service/Endpoints. Both must pass: pod readiness + LB health check.

    Explanation

    Health checks are the heartbeat of load balancing. Without them, the LB would happily send traffic to dead backends. The dual-layer health check model is critical: Kubernetes readinessProbe controls whether a pod is in the Service's Endpoints list — if readiness fails, the pod is removed from kube-proxh check endpoint should verify DB connectivity — if the pod can't reach PostgreSQL, it should fail the health check so the LB stops sending traffic.

    Q6
    What is TLS termination at the cloud LB? What are the trade-offs?
    Explanation

    TLS termination at the LB is the standard for most web applications. The LB holds the TLS certificate (via AWS ACM — auto-renewing, no manual rotation), decrypts the traffic, and forwards plVPC traffic (unlikely but possible in shared-tenancy environments or through misconfigured VPC peering), they can read all your data. Mitigations: (1) Use end-to-end TLS — the ALB re-encrypts traffic to backends (adds latency but full encryption). (2) Rely on VPC network isolation — traffic between the ALB ENI and pod ENI stays within AWS failing. Check: (1) ALB health check path correct? (2) Health check port matches container port? (3) Security Group on EKS nodes allows traffic from ALB SG? (4) Pod readiness probe passing? (5) Target group shows "unhealthy" — check the reason code in AWS console. Common: health check path returns 404 (wrong path), security

ALB default is / — if your app only serves /api/health/, the default / returns 404 → unhealthy. Set the health check path to /api/health/ or /. Step 3: Verify Security Groups. The ALB has a security group (sg-alb). The EKS nodes have a security group (sg-eks). sg-eks must allow inbound from sg-alb on the health check port (usually 8000 or the container port). Step 4: Check pod readiness: kubectl describe pod jobpost-xxx — is the readiness probe passing? Step 5: Iithin the VPC, peered VPCs, or via Transit Gateway. Use for: internal APIs, microservice communication that needs L7 routing, services that shouldn't be internet-accessible. In EKS: the Ingress annotation alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/scheme: internal creates an internal ALB.

    Explanation

    Internal ALBs are the backbone of microservice-to-microservice communication in AWS. They provide L7 routing WITHIN the VPC — no public IPs, no internet exposure. Use cases: (1) Front-end service (public ALB) → internal ALB for API gateway pattern. (2) Service mesh alternative — internal ALBs for routing between microservices by path (e.g., /users/* → user-service, /orders/* → order-service). (3) Multi-account architectures — internal ALB accessible via PrivateLink from other accounts. Key difference from internet-facing: Internal ALBs resolve to private IPs only. DNS name resolves to 10.x.x.x addresses. They are accessible from: same VPC, peered VPCs (with proper routing), Transit Gateway, and via PrivateLink endpoints. In EKS: the annotation alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/scheme: internal is all you need. For anihpj internal services (admin panel, metrics dashboard, internal API endpoints), use internal ALBs — they should never be internet-accessible.

    Q10
    Explanation

    The cloud LB landscape reflects each provider's philosophy. AWS: Building blocks approach — you compose NLB + ALB + Global Accelerator + Route53. Maximum flexibility, more complexity. GCP: Opinionated approach — Global HTTP(S) LB handles everything globally. Simpler, less flexible. Azure: Enterprise approach — separate services for different personas: Load Balancer for network engineers, Application Gateway for app teams (with built-in WAF), Front Door for global/CDN teams. How to choose: If you're on AWS and need global, use Route53 latency routing + regional ALBs. If you're multi-cloud, understand each provider's model. For anihpj: On AWS, use ALB + Route53 for global (or CloudFront if CDN needed). On GCP, the global HTTP(S) LB handles everything. The architectural decision isn't just technical — it affects your Terraform/Pulumi code, monitoring setup, and team knowledge requirements.

    Chapter 26: Hybrid Cloud Networking — Connecting On-Prem to Cloud

    Most enterprises don't go all-cloud overnight. They operate in a hybrid model — some workloads on-premises, some in the cloud. Connecting these environments securely requires VPNs or dedicated connections. This chapter covers Site-to-Site VPN, Direct Connect, and hybrid architecture patterns.

    🟡 Intermediate⏱️ ~1 hour🔗 Hybrid

    26.1 VPNs — IPsec and WireGuard

    Site-to-Site VPN connects your office network to a cloud VPC over an encrypted tunnel across the public internet.

    Site-to-Site VPN — Office to Cloud VPC via IPsec Tunnel
      OFFICE (192.168.0.0/16)              AWS VPC (10.0.0.0/16)
  ┌──────────────────────┐    IPsec    ┌──────────────────────┐
  │ On-Prem Router       │═══╪══╪══╪═══│ Virtual Private GW   │
  │ (Customer Gateway)   │   AES-256  │ (VGW)                │
  │ Public: 203.x.x.x    │   Tunnel   │ Public: 52.x.x.x      │
  └──────────┬───────────┘            └──────────┬───────────┘
             │                                   │
  ┌──────────┴───────────┐            ┌──────────┴────────256-GCM), PRF (SHA-256), DH group (14, 19, 20)
  Phase 2 (ESP — Encapsulating Security Payload):
    • Uses the IKE SA to negotiate child/IPsec SA
    • Actual data encryption tunnel: encrypts entire original IP packet
    • Tunnel mode: [new IP header][ESP header][encrypted original IP packet][ESP trailer]
    • Perfect Forward Secrecy: new DH exchange per Phase 2 re-key
    • Re-key: by time (1-8 hours) or by data volume (100MB-100GB)

  WIREGUARD: Curve25519 (key exchange) + ChaCha20 (encryption) +
    Poly1305 (authentication) + BLAKE2s (hashing) + SipHash24 (hash table)
  4,000 lines of code. In Linux kernel since 5.6.
  No IKE phase negotiation — static key exchange (simpler, faster).
  Roaming support: client IP can change without tunnel re-establishment.

  AWS Site-to-Site VPN: 1.25 Gbps per tunnel, 2 tunnels per connection.
  BGP routing: dynamic route exchange between VGW and Customer Gateway.
  VPN CloudHub: connect multiple sites through a single VGW (hub-and-spoke over VPN).
    🔁 VPN High Availability — Dual Tunnels Are Not Optional

    AWS Site-to-Site VPN creates TWO tunnels per connection by default — one primary, one backup. Each tunnel terminates on a different AWS endpoint (in different AZs). How tunnel failover works: Both tunnels are active (not active/passive). Your on-prem router uses BGP to detect tunnel failure: if the BGP session on Tunnel-1 drops (keepalive: 10s, hold: 30s), routes learned via Tunnel-1 are withdrawn, and Tunnel-2 take>Common VPN issues: (1) Tunnel flaps — intermittent connectivity drops due to internet instability. Fix: enable dead peer detection (DPD), lower BGP timers for faster failover. (2) MTU issues — IPsec adds 60-80 bytes of header overhead. If your packets are 1500 bytes, they get fragmented or dropped. Fix: clamp TCP MSS to 1387 (or use path MTU discovery). (3) NAT traversal — if either end is behind NAT, IKE must use UDP 4500 instead of 500. AWS handles this automatically. For anihpj: If using VPN to connect on-prem to cloud, always configure BOTH tunnels. Set up CloudWatch alarms on TunnelState. Test failover quarterly — actually pull one tunnel and verify traffic fails over within 30 seconds.

    26.2 Direct Connect / Cloud Interconnect

    Direct Connect is a dedicated physical fiber connection from your data center to the cloud provider — no internet, consistent latency, guRID — Database On-Prem, Compute in Cloud: ┌──────────────────────────┐ Direct Connect 5ms ┌──────────────────────────┐ │ ON-PREM DATA CENTER │═════════════════════════│ AWS CLOUD │ │ PostgreSQL (primary) │ │ EKS (jobpost pods) │ │ 192.168.1.50:5432 │── PgBouncer ──────────▶│ 10.0.10.x:8000 │ │ │ │ │ │ DB stays on-prem for: │ │ RDS Read Replica (DR) │ │ • Data sovereignty │ │ • DMS replication │ │ • Compliance (PCI/HIPAA) │ │ • Failover if DC down │ │ • Existing investment │ │ │ └──────────────────────────┘ └──────────────────────────┘ PgBouncer on EKS side pools connections, reducing TCP overhead across DX. DR: On-prem failure → promote RDS replica → update Route53 → ~30s downtime. DIRECT CONNECT SETUP PROCESS: 1. Request connection at an AWS Direct Connect location (e.g., Equinix) 2. AWS provisions a dedicated port on their router (1-14 days) 3. Your network provider runs fiber from your DC to the DX location 4. Create Virtual Interface (VIF): • Private VIF → connects to a single VPC (via VGW) • Transit VIF → connects to Transit Gateway (connect to multiple VPCs) • Public VIF → access AWS public services (S3, DynamoDB — not internet) 5. Configure BGP peering between your router and AWS 6. Your router advertises on-prem prefixes via BGP 7. AWS advertises VPC prefixes (Private VIF) or public service IPs (Public VIF) BGP PEERING FOR DIRECT CONNECT: • Your private ASN: 64512-65534 (private range) • Amazon side ASN: 7224 (public VIF) or your chosen private ASN • Your router advertises: your on-prem CIDRs (192.168.0.0/16) • AWS advertises: VPC CIDR (10.0.0.0/16) or specific prefixes • BGP timers: keepalive 30s, hold 90s (configurable) • BFD (Bidirectional Forwarding Detection) for sub-second failure detection COST CALCULATION (1 Gbps, 10 TB/month egress): Port: 1 Gbps × $0.30/hr × 730 hrs = $219/month Data egress: 10,000 GB × $0.02/GB = $200/month TOTAL: ~$419/month (vs $900/month via internet at $0.09/GB) Break-even: ~5 TB/month. Additional: cross-connect fees ($100-300/month).

    🔗 Direct Connect Resiliency — Don't Put All Your Packets on One Fiber

    Direct Connect is a single physical fiber — it CAN be cut (construction accident, natural disaster, carrier outage). Resiliency models: (1) Single connection: One fiber, one DX location. Failure = complete outage. Only for dev/test. (2) Maximum resiliency (recommended for production): Two DX connections at two different DX locations (e.g., Equinix DC1 + CoreSite LA1), each connected to different AWS routers. If one location fails, BGP converges to the other. (3) DX + VPN backup (most common): Primary path: Direct Connect (low latency, guaranteed bandwidth). Backup path: Site-to-Site VPN over internet. BGP LOCAL_PREF makes DX preferred; VPN takes over automatically when DX BGP session drops. Link Aggregation Groups (LAG): Bundle multiple DX ports into one logical link. 4 × 10 Gbps ports = one 40 Gbps LAG. LAG provides: bandwidth aggregation, link-level redundancy (if one port fails, traffic redistributes across remaining ports without BGP reconvergence — sub-second failover). Direct Connect Gateway: A global resource that connects your DX to VPCs in ANY region (not just the DX location's region). One DX connection → Direct Connect Gateway → VPCs in us-east-1, eu-west-1, ap-southeast-1 simultaneously. This is how global enterprises connect all their VPCs through one physical connection.

    📊 Monitoring Hybrid Connectivity — What to Watch

    Direct Connect metrics (CloudWatch): ConnectionState (available=UP, down=DOWN), ConnectionBpsEgress/Ingress (bandwidth utilization — alert at 80%), ConnectionPpsEgress/Ingress (packets per second), ConnectionLightLevelTx/Rx (optical signal strength — dropping signal = dirty fiber or failing optics), VirtualInterfaceBpsEgress/Ingress (per-VIF throughput). BGP metrics: BgpRcvdRoutes (number of routes received from AWS — if this drops to 0, your router isn't learning any VPC routes), BgpAdvertisedRoutes (routes you're advertising — AWS side). VPN metrics: TunnelState (0 or 1), TunnelDataIn/Out. Key alerts for anihpj: (1) ConnectionState = DOWN for > 5 min → page on-call. (2) ConnectionBpsEgress > 80% of provisioned bandwidth → scale up or add LAG. (3) BgpRcvdRoutes = 0 → AWS side BGP session down, check your router. (4) ConnectionLightLevelTx dropping month over month → schedule fiber inspection. Pro tip: Run chaos engineering on your hybrid connectivity. Quarterly: manually shut down one DX port at 2 AM. Verify: traffic fails over to backup path within BGP convergence time (30-60s), all alerts fire, on-call receives notifications, application remains functional (degraded latency acceptable).

    📋 Must Memorize
    • Defense in depth: L2(port security, DAI), L3(ACLs), L4(firewall), L7(WAF)
    • Common attacks: DDoS, MITM(ARP spoofing), DNS poisoning, SYN flood, amplification
    • Segmentation: VLANs, VRFs, micro-segmentation (K8s NetworkPolicy)

    ⚠️ Common Traps
    • Encryption at rest != encryption in transit (both needed)
    • Default credentials are still the #1 network security failure
    • Security groups / NSGs are stateful (return traffic auto-allowed)
    • Network ACLs are stateless (must explicitly allow return traffic)

    📝 Chapter 26 — Networking Practice Questions

    Q1
    What is Site-to-Site VPN? How does IPsec create a secure tunnel?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    Site-to-Site VPN connects two networks (office ↔ cloud VPC) over an encrypted IPsec tunnel. Phase 1 (IKE): Authenticate and negotiate encryption. Phase 2 (ESP): Data encryption tunnel. All traffic encrypted with AES. AWS: create Virtual Private Gateway, Customer Gateway, VPN Connection.

    Explanation

    VPN is the most common hybrid cloud connectivity method because it uses existing internet connections — no physical fiber needed. The trade-off is reliability: VPN runs over the public internet, so latency varies and throughput is limited. For critical production workloads connecting on-prem databases to cloud compute (like anihpj with on-prem PostgreSQL → EKS), VPN latency can cause application timeouts. Best practice: use VPN for development/staging environments and non-critical connectivity. For production database connectivity, upgrade to Direct Connect. AWS VPN also supports BGP dynamic routing — if your on-prem network changes, routes update automatically without manual configuration.

    Q2
    What's the difference between IPsec and WireGuard? When would you choose each?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    IPsec: Veteran (1995), complex (400K+ lines), widely supported by network hardware. WireGuard: Modern (2018), simple (4K lines), in-kernel, faster, modern crypto (Curve25519). Choose IPsec: When you need hardware VPN appliance support, compliance requirements mandate IPsec, or you're connecting to cloud managed VPN services. Choose WireGuard: For software-to-software VPNs, maximum performance, simpler configuration, modern Linux/container environments. WireGuard is in the Linux kernel since 5.6.

    # NETWORKING COMMANDS REFERENCE
# Check interface: ip addr show; ip link set eth0 up; ethtool eth0
# Check routing:   ip route show; ip route get 8.8.8.8; traceroute -n HOST
# Check ports:     ss -tlnp; ss -ulnp; nc -zv HOST PORT; lsof -i :PORT
# Check DNS:       dig +short DOMAIN; nslookup DOMAIN; host DOMAIN
# Check firewall:  iptables -L -nv --line-numbers; nft list ruleset
# Capture traffic: tcpdump -i any -nn host IP -w capture.pcap
# Check TLS:       openssl s_client -connect HOST:443 -servername HOST
# Test HTTP:       curl -sv https://HOST/path -H "Header: value"
# K8s networking:  kubectl get svc,ep,netpol,ingress -A
# Debug order:     L1(ethtool)->L2(arping)->L3(ping)->L4(nc)->L7(curl)
    Explanation

    The IPsec vs WireGuard debate comes down to age vs elegance. IPsec has been around since 1995, is implemented in every network appliance (Cisco, Juniper, Palo Alto), and is the standard for cloud managed VPN services (AWS VPN, GCP Cloud VPN, Azure VPN Gateway all use IPsec). Its complexity is legendary: the IKEv2 RFC alone is 150+ pages. WireGuard, by contrast, fits its entire protocol in 4,000 lines of code — auditable by a single developer in an afternoon. Real-world guidance: For connecting to cloud providers' managed VPN services, you're using IPsec whether you like it or not — that's what they implement. For site-to-site between your own Linux servers, WireGuard is the clear winner: simpler config (4 lines vs 100+ for IPsec), faster throughput (kernel-space, no context switches), and modern crypto (no legacy cipher negotiation). For Kubernetes: tools like Kilo and Tailscale use WireGuard to create mesh VPNs between clusters. For anihpj: if connecting on-prem to AWS, use the managed AWS VPN (IPsec). If connecting two of your own Linux gateways, use WireGuard.

    Q3
    What is AWS Direct Connect? When would you use it instead of VPN?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    Direct Connect is a dedicated physical fiber connection from your data center to AWS (via a Direct Connect location). Use when: (1) You need consistent latency (not variable internet). (2) Bandwidth > 1.25 Gbps (VPN limit). (3) Regulatory compliance prohibits internet transit. (4) You want to reduce data egress costs. (5) SLA-backed uptime (99.99%) is required. Cost: Port hours + data transfer out. For most startups, VPN is sufficient. Direct Connect makes sense at enterprise scale or for latency-sensitive workloads.

# Check interface: ip addr show; ip link set eth0 up; ethtool eth0
# Check routing:   ip route show; ip route get 8.8.8.8; traceroute -n HOST
# Check ports:     ss -tlnp; ss -ulnp; nc -zv HOST PORT; lsof -i :PORT
# Check DNS:       dig +short DOMAIN; nslookup DOMAIN; host DOMAIN
# Check firewall:  iptables -L -nv --line-numbers; nft list ruleset
# Capture traffic: tcpdump -i any -nn host IP -w capture.pcap
# Check TLS:       openssl s_client -connect HOST:443 -servername HOST
# Test HTTP:       curl -sv https://HOST/path -H "Header: value"
# K8s networking:  kubectl get svc,ep,netpol,ingress -A
# Debug order:     L1(ethtool)->L2(arping)->L3(ping)->L4(nc)->L7(curl)
    Explanation

    Direct Connect is the gold standard for hybrid cloud connectivity — but it's NOT for everyone. The setup takes 1-2 weeks minimum (physical fiber provisioning), requires a presence at a Direct Connect location, and costs at minimum $219/month for the port alone. When VPN is good enough: (1) Dev/staging environments where occasional latency spikes are acceptable. (2) Startups without a data center presence at a DX location. (3) Backup/DR connectivity — use VPN as backup for Direct Connect. When DX is mandatory: (1) Database replication across on-prem and cloud — latency spikes cause replication lag and potential data loss. (2) Real-time applications (financial trading, gaming) where consistent latency is critical. (3) Compliance: some regulations (government, healthcare) prohibit sensitive data from traversing the public internet, even encrypted. (4) Large data transfers: at 100+ TB/month, the egress cost savings alone (from $0.09/GB to $0.02/GB) pay for DX. For anihpj: If the PostgreSQL database stays on-prem, Direct Connect is the right choice for production. Use VPN as a backup (AWS VPN can be attached to the same TGW for failover).

    Q4
    What is Transit Gateway? How does it simplify hybrid networking?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    Transit Gateway is a hub-and-spoke network transit center. Instead of mesh-peering VPCs individually, all VPCs connect to the TGW. TGW also supports VPN and Direct Connect attachments — so on-prem networks connect through the SAME hub. One TGW replaces: N×(N-1)/2 VPC peering connections, multiple VPN connections, and Direct Connect per VPC. TGW route tables control which VPCs can talk to each other. This is the standard architecture for multi-VPC, hybrid-cloud deployments.

    Explanation

    Transit Gateway is the unsung hero of AWS networking. Before TGW (pre-2018), connecting 5 VPCs required 10 peering connections (formula: n×(n-1)/2) — each manually configured, each with its own route table updates. Adding a 6th VPC meant 5 new peering connections. TGW replaced this with 5 attachments to a central hub. TGW route tables are the key feature: you can segment which VPCs can communicate. Example: Dev VPC route table (RT-Dev) has routes to Staging and Shared Services but NOT to Production. Production route table (RT-Prod) has routes to Shared Services but NOT to Dev. This is network segmentation at the routing layer — no Security Group rules needed to block cross-environment traffic. TGW + Direct Connect: Instead of creating a Direct Connect Virtual Interface per VPC, you create one Transit VIF to TGW. All VPCs connected to that TGW can reach on-prem through that single DX connection. This is the standard enterprise pattern: one TGW per region, all VPCs attached, on-prem connected via DX+VPN redundancy.

    Q5
    Design a hybrid architecture: on-prem database + cloud compute for anihpj.
    Show Answer
    Answer

    On-prem: PostgreSQL database (compliance requires data on-prem). Cloud: EKS cluster running jobpost API. Connectivity: Direct Connect (1 Gbps) from on-prem DC to AWS. TGW connects DC (via Direct Connect) to EKS VPC. EKS pods connect to on-prem DB via TGW route. Latency: ~5ms (Direct Connect is consistent; internet VPN could be 30-100ms variable). Backup: DMS replicates on-prem DB to RDS read replica for DR. DNS: Route53 resolver endpoints forward on-prem domain queries.

    # KEY NETWORKING COMMANDS
# Interface: ip addr show; ip link set eth0 up; ethtool eth0
# Routing:   ip route show; traceroute -n HOST; mtr -r HOST
# Sockets:   ss -tlnp; ss -ulnp; lsof -i :PORT; nc -zv HOST PORT
# DNS:       dig +short DOMAIN; nslookup DOMAIN; host DOMAIN
# Firewall:  iptables -L -nv --line-numbers; nft list ruleset
# Capture:   tcpdump -i any -nn host IP or port NUM -w file.pcap
# TLS:       openssl s_client -connect HOST:443 -servername HOST
# HTTP:      curl -sv https://HOST/path -H "Header: value"
# K8s:       kubectl get svc,ep,netpol,ingress -A
# Debug:     L1(ip link)->L2(arping)->L3(ping)->L4(nc -zv)->L7(curl)
    Explanation

    This is the canonical hybrid architecture pattern: data gravity keeps the database on-prem (compliance, existing investment, data sovereignty), but compute moves to the cloud for elasticity and managed services. Key architectural decisions: (1) DNS resolution: EKS pods need to resolve on-prem hostnames (like db.internal.company.com). Route53 Resolver endpoints forward queries to on-prem DNS servers. Without this, pods can't find the database by name. (2) Connection pooling: Every TCP connection across DX incurs 5ms RTT for the handshake. PgBouncer pools connections and eliminates per-request handshake overhead — this alone can improve throughput 10x. (3) Read replicas: DMS (Database Migration Service) continuously replicates on-prem DB to an RDS read replica. Application reads go to the local RDS replica (sub-ms latency), writes go to on-prem (5ms). This is the "write-local, read-global" pattern. (4) Failure mode: If Direct Connect goes down, the application should gracefully degrade — use the RDS replica for reads, queue writes, alert operations. Never design a system where a WAN link failure causes a complete outage.

    Q6
    What is BGP? How does it relate to Direct Connect and VPN?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) is the routing protocol of the internet — it exchanges route information between networks. In Direct Connect: You establish BGP peering between your on-prem router and AWS. You advertise your on-prem prefixes; AWS advertises VPC prefixes. Both sides learn routes dynamically. In VPN: BGP (dynamic) or static routes can be used. BGP is preferred because routes update automatically when networks change. AWS managed VPN supports BGP by default.

    # BGP: AS path vector protocol, port 179/TCP, states: IDLE->CONNECT->OPEN->ESTABLISHED
# eBGP(AS-to-AS) vs iBGP(within AS); birdc show protocols
    Explanation

    BGP is the postal service of the internet — it tells packets which roads to take between networks. In the context of hybrid cloud: Without BGP (static routing): You manually configure "route 10.0.0.0/16 via Virtual Private Gateway" on your on-prem router. If you add a new VPC or subnet, you must update both sides. This doesn't scale beyond 2-3 networks. With BGP (dynamic routing): Your router tells AWS "I can reach 192.168.0.0/16, 172.16.0.0/12, 10.100.0.0/16" and AWS tells your router "I can reach 10.0.0.0/16, 10.1.0.0/16, 10.2.0.0/16." Add a new VPC → AWS automatically advertises the new prefix. Add a new office → your router automatically advertises it. BGP attributes: AS_PATH (prevents loops), LOCAL_PREF (prefer one path over another), MED (suggest preferred entry point). For Direct Connect + VPN backup: advertise the same prefixes over DX and VPN but set higher LOCAL_PREF on DX — traffic uses DX normally, fails over to VPN if DX goes down.

    Q7
    Your on-prem database is slow when accessed from EKS. You have a Site-to-Site VPN. What can you do?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    (1) Upgrade to Direct Connect: VPN runs over internet → variable latency. Direct Connect = consistent ~5ms. (2) Move database closer: Replicate on-prem DB to RDS in the same region as EKS → sub-ms latency. (3) Connection pooling: Use PgBouncer or RDS Proxy to minimize TCP handshake overhead across the VPN. (4) Query optimization: The network amplifies bad queries — N+1 queries that are fine at 1ms are terrible at 30ms. (5) Increase VPN bandwidth: Multiple tunnels with ECMP for higher aggregate throughput.

    # KEY NETWORKING COMMANDS
# Interface: ip addr show; ip link set eth0 up; ethtool eth0
# Routing:   ip route show; traceroute -n HOST; mtr -r HOST
# Sockets:   ss -tlnp; ss -ulnp; lsof -i :PORT; nc -zv HOST PORT
# DNS:       dig +short DOMAIN; nslookup DOMAIN; host DOMAIN
# Firewall:  iptables -L -nv --line-numbers; nft list ruleset
# Capture:   tcpdump -i any -nn host IP or port NUM -w file.pcap
# TLS:       openssl s_client -connect HOST:443 -servername HOST
# HTTP:      curl -sv https://HOST/path -H "Header: value"
# K8s:       kubectl get svc,ep,netpol,ingress -A
# Debug:     L1(ip link)->L2(arping)->L3(ping)->L4(nc -zv)->L7(curl)
    Explanation

    This is the #1 performance problem in hybrid cloud — and it's almost never the bandwidth, it's the latency. Why latency matters more than bandwidth: A PostgreSQL query that takes 2ms locally takes 32ms over a 30ms VPN. That's 16x slower. If your API endpoint makes 10 sequential DB queries (common with ORMs), the response time goes from 20ms to 320ms. The N+1 problem amplified: An ORM loading a list of 100 items with a lazy-loaded relation makes 101 queries. At 2ms each = 202ms total (acceptable). At 30ms each = 3,030ms (timeout). Connection pooling fixes the TCP overhead: Without pooling, every query does a new TCP handshake (1 RTT) + TLS handshake (2 RTTs) + query. With 30ms RTT, that's 90ms of handshake per query. PgBouncer keeps connections open → no handshake per query. For anihpj: If the database MUST stay on-prem, use PgBouncer, batch your queries, use eager loading to avoid N+1, and consider a local read replica for read-heavy workloads. Or — move the database to RDS and eliminate the problem entirely.
