# Check firewall:  iptables -L -nv --line-numbers; nft list ruleset
# Capture traffic: tcpdump -i any -nn host IP -w capture.pcap
# Check TLS:       openssl s_client -connect HOST:443 -servername HOST
# Test HTTP:       curl -sv https://HOST/path -H "Header: value"
# K8s networking:  kubectl get svc,ep,netpol,ingress -A
# Debug order:     L1(ethtool)->L2(arping)->L3(ping)->L4(nc)->L7(curl)
    code>ve connection + per hour.

    Explanation

    AWS Client VPN is the "work from anywhere" solution for your team. Think of it as a managed OpenVPN service that integrates with AWS IAM/SAML and gives users private access to your VPCs. Key use cases: (1) Developers working from home need to access internal tools (Kibana, Grafana, admin panels) that aren't internet-exposed. (2) Operations team needs SSH/SSM access to private EC2 instances (no bastion hosts needed). (3) Third-party contractors need temporary, auditable access. Compared to bastion hosts: Bastion is a single point of failure, requires key management per user, and exposes SSH to the internet. Client VPN gives each user their own encrypted tunnel with SSO authentication — more secure and auditable. Pricing: $0.10/hour per endpoint association + $0.05/hour per active connection. One endpoint can handle many users. For a 10-person team with 8-hour workdays: ~$1.20/day + $0.10/hr for the endpoint ≈ $3/day. For anihpj: Set up Client VPN for the dev team to access private monitoring dashboards and admin tools — no internet exposure needed.

    Q10
    What are the key differences between AWS Direct Connect, GCP Cloud Interconnect, and Azure ExpressRoute?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    All three provide dedicated physical connectivity to the cloud. Direct Connect: 1/10/100 Gbps, BGP routing, partners available (Equinix, etc.). Cloud Interconnect: Dedicated (10/100 Gbps) or Partner (50 Mbps-10 Gbps via provider). ExpressRoute: Microsoft's offering — also connects to Microsoft 365/Azure AD. Key differences: GCP offers partner interconnect at lower speeds; Azure uniquely connects to M365; AWS has widest partner ecosystem. All support BGP, VLANs, and SLA-backed uptime. The choice depends on your primary cloud provider.

    Explanation

    All three major cloud providers offer dedicated connectivity, but they differ in important ways. AWS Direct Connect: The most mature ecosystem. Available at 100+ locations worldwide. Partners like Equinix, Megaport, and AT&T provide managed connectivity. You can buy a "hosted connection" from a partner (50 Mbps to 10 Gbps) without dealing with physical fiber yourself. Supports Link Aggregation Groups (LAG) for bundling multiple ports. GCP Cloud Interconnect: Two tiers — Dedicated (10 or 100 Gbps, you manage the physical connection) and Partner (50 Mbps to 10 Gbps via a service provider). Unique feature: GCP's global VPC means one Interconnect connection gives access to all regions (through Google's backbone). Azure ExpressRoute: Microsoft's differentiator — ExpressRoute connects to Azure AND Microsoft 365/Office 365/Dynamics 365. If your enterprise uses M365, ExpressRoute is the way to get dedicated, SLA-backed connectivity to those services. Also supports "ExpressRoute Local" (cheaper, single-region) and "ExpressRoute Premium" (global, M365). For anihpj: If you're on AWS, Direct Connect. If you're multi-cloud, you might end up with all three — which is why cloud-agnostic networking tools (Terraform, Aviatrix) exist.

    ⚡ Part 8: Advanced Topics — Deep Dives for the Curious SRECh 27-29

    Chapter 27: iptables & nftables — Linux Firewall Mastery

    Every Kubernetes Service, every Docker port mapping, every cloud Security Group — they all ultimately translate to Linux firewall rules. Understanding iptables and its modern successor nftables is essential for debugging connectivity issues, understanding kube-proxy, and mastering Linux networking at the kernel level.

    🔴 Advanced⏱️ ~2 hours🐧 Linux Kernel🔥 Firewall

    🎯 What You'll Learn

    • ✅ The 5 netfilter hook points and how packets flow through them
    • ✅ iptables rule anatomy — tables, chains, matches, targets — with K8s/Docker examples
    • ✅ nftables — why it replaces iptables, syntax basics, and K8s migration path
    • ✅ conntrack — how Linux tracks connections, the 5 connection states, and debugging table overflow
    • ✅ How to trace a packet through kube-proxy iptables rules step by step

    27.1 Netfilter Architecture — The 5 Hook Points

    The Linux kernel's netfilter framework provides 5 hook points where firewall rules can inspect and manipulate packets. These hooks are the foundation that iptables, nftables, and even eBPF programs plug into.

    Netfilter Packet Flow — Complete Diagram with All 5 Hooks, Tables & Chains
                              INCOMING PACKET
                               │
                               ▼
                     ┌──────────────────┐
                     │   PREROUTING     │ ◀── raw → connection tracking → mangle → nat (DNAT)
                     │   Hook Point     │     Purpose: DNAT rewrites destination BEFORE routing
                     └────────┬─────────┘
                              │
                    ┌─────────┴──────────┐
                    │  ROUTING DECISION   │  "Is this packet for us?"
                    │  (local vs forward) │
                    └──┬──────────────┬───┘
           For local       │              │  For another host
           process         │              │
                ▼          │              ▼
      ┌──────────────┐     │     ┌──────────────┐
      │   INPUT      │     │     │   FORWARD    │
      │filter→mangle │     │     │filter→mangle │  filter: ACCEPT/DROP decision
      └──────┬───────┘     │     └──────┬───────┘
             │              │            │
             ▼              │            ▼
      ┌──────────────┐     │     ┌──────────────┐
      │LOCAL PROCESS  │     │     │ POSTROUTING  │
      │(nginx, app)   │     │     │ mangle→nat   │  SNAT/MASQUERADE happens here
      └──────┬───────┘     │     └──────┬───────┘
             │              │            │
             ▼              │            ▼
      ┌──────────────┐     │     ┌──────────────┐
      │   OUTPUT     │     │     │  OUTGOING     │
      │raw→mangle→nat │────┘     │  PACKET       │
      │→filter       │           └──────────────┘
      └──────────────┘

  FIVE HOOK POINTS SUMMARY:
  1. PREROUTING — First hook. DNAT, ingress filtering. Before routing decision.
  2. INPUT — Packets destined for local processes. Firewall rules here protect the host.
  3. FORWARD — Packets routed THROUGH this host (router/gateway mode). Controls transit traffic.
  4. OUTPUT — Packets originating from local processes. Controls what the host can send.
  5. POSTROUTING — Last hook. SNAT/MASQUERADE. After routing decision, before wire.

  FIVE TABLES (in processing order):
  raw — Connection tracking bypass (NOTRACK). Used for high-performance exclusions.
  mangle — Packet header modification (TOS, TTL, MARK). Rarely used by SREs.
  nat — Network Address Translation (DNAT, SNAT, MASQUERADE).
  filter — ACCEPT or DROP decisions. The main firewall table.
  security — SELinux mandatory access control labels. Security-conscious environments.
    💡 The Routing Decision — The Most Important Split

    The routing decision between PREROUTING and INPUT/FORWARD determines which chain handles the packet. For local (INPUT): The destination IP matches one of the host's IP addresses → packet goes to INPUT → local process. This is where your web server's traffic flows. For forwarding (FORWARD): The destination IP does NOT match the host → packet goes to FORWARD → routed out another interface. This is how Kubernetes nodes forward pod-to-pod traffic, how NAT gateways work, and how Docker bridge networking operates. A node becomes a router when net.ipv4.ip_forward=1 is set — without this, the kernel silently drops forwarded packets. In Kubernetes: Every worker node has ip_forward=1. Pod-to-pod traffic across nodes hits the FORWARD chain. kube-proxy writes iptables rules into PREROUTING (for NodePort) and OUTPUT (for local pod → Service traffic).

    Complete K8s Pod-to-Pod via Service — iptables Chain Walk
      SCENARIO: Pod-A (10.244.1.5) on Node-1 calls jobpost Service (ClusterIP 10.96.0.10:8000)
            Service has 3 backends: Pod-X (10.244.1.10), Pod-Y (10.244.2.20), Pod-Z (10.244.3.30)

  NODE-1 (where Pod-A runs):
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                      │
  │  Pod-A (10.244.1.5:45678)                                           │
  │    │ sends SYN to 10.96.0.10:8000                                   │
  │    ▼                                                                 │
  │  veth → bridge → OUTPUT chain (nat table)                           │
  │    │ KUBE-SERVICES: match dst=10.96.0.10 tcp dport=8000            │
  │    │ → jump KUBE-SVC-XXXXX                                          │
  │    ▼                                                                 │
  │  KUBE-SVC-XXXXX:                                                    │
  │    │ -m statistic --mode random --probability 0.333 → KUBE-SEP-AAA  │
  │    │ -m statistic --mode random --probability 0.500 → KUBE-SEP-BBB  │
  │    │ default → KUBE-SEP-CCC                                          │
  │    │ (Let's say KUBE-SEP-BBB wins)                                  │
  │    ▼                                                                 │
  │  KUBE-SEP-BBB: DNAT 10.96.0.10:8000 → 10.244.2.20:8000             │
  │    │ Packet now: src=10.244.1.5:45678 dst=10.244.2.20:8000          │
  │    ▼                                                                 │
  │  Routing decision: 10.244.2.20 is on Node-2 → FORWARD               │
  │    ▼                                                                 │
  │  POSTROUTING: no MASQUERADE (pod-to-pod preserves source IP)        │
  │    ▼                                                                 │
  │  eth0 → overlay (VXLAN encap) → physical network → Node-2          │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  NODE-2 (where Pod-Y runs):
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  eth0 → decap VXLAN → PREROUTING (no DNAT needed)                   │
  │    ▼                                                                 │
  │  Routing: 10.244.2.20 is local → INPUT (actually FORWARD for pod)   │
  │    ▼                                                                 │
  │  FORWARD → veth → Pod-Y receives packet                             │
  │    │ Pod-Y sees: src=10.244.1.5:45678 (original source preserved!)  │
  │    ▼                                                                 │
  │  Pod-Y responds: src=10.244.2.20:8000 dst=10.244.1.5:45678          │
  │    │ Conntrack handles reverse NAT automatically (UN-DNAT)          │
  │    ▼                                                                 │
  │  Pod-A receives response from 10.96.0.10:8000 (Service IP!)         │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  KEY INSIGHT: The conntrack entry created at KUBE-SVC automatically
  reverses the DNAT for return traffic. Pod-A thinks it's talking to
  10.96.0.10, but the kernel transparently rewrites to 10.244.2.20.
  This is the magic of netfilter + conntrack working together.

    27.2 iptables Rules — Reading and Writing Them

    An iptables rule follows this anatomy: table → chain → match conditions → target (action). Rules are evaluated sequentially within a chain — first match wins (unlike Security Groups which evaluate all rules).

    iptables Rule Anatomy — The 4-Part Structure
      iptables -t [TABLE] -A [CHAIN] [MATCH CONDITIONS] -j [TARGET]
            │          │          │                      │
            ▼          ▼          ▼                      ▼
  TABLE:    CHAIN:     MATCH:     TARGET (what to do if matched):
  filter    INPUT      -p tcp     ACCEPT     — allow the packet
  nat       FORWARD    --dport 80 DROP      — silently discard
  mangle    OUTPUT     -s 10.0.0.0/8 REJECT   — discard + send ICMP error
  raw       PREROUTING -i eth0    DNAT      — change destination IP:port
            POSTROUTING -m conntrack SNAT  — change source IP
                        --ctstate  MASQUERADE — SNAT with dynamic source IP
                                   LOG       — log and continue to next rule
                                   RETURN    — stop processing this chain, return to caller

  REAL KUBERNETES EXAMPLES (exactly what kube-proxy writes):
  # NodePort Service: redirect NodePort → ClusterIP
  iptables -t nat -A PREROUTING -p tcp --dport 30080 \
    -j DNAT --to-destination 10.96.0.10:8000

  # Service load balancing (statistical):
  iptables -t nat -A OUTPUT -d 10.96.0.10 -p tcp --dport 8000 \
    -m statistic --mode random --probability 0.3333 \
    -j DNAT --to-destination 10.244.1.5:8000

  # Docker port mapping: host port → container port
  iptables -t nat -A DOCKER -p tcp --dport 8080 \
    -j DNAT --to-destination 172.17.0.2:80
    🔍 Listing Rules Like an SRE — The Debugging Lifeline

    Essential listing commands: iptables -t nat -L -n -v — NAT table with counters (hit counts + byte counts). The counters tell you which rules are being matched — invaluable for debugging. iptables -t filter -L -n -v --line-numbers — show rule numbers for easy deletion/replacement. iptables-save — dump ALL rules in parseable format (for backup, diff, or audit). What Docker writes: Docker creates the DOCKER chain in both filter and nat tables. iptables -t nat -L DOCKER shows all port mappings. What kube-proxy writes: KUBE-SERVICES, KUBE-NODEPORTS, KUBE-SVC-xxxxx chains. iptables -t nat -L | grep KUBE shows all K8s NAT rules. Pro debugging technique: Add a LOG rule BEFORE the suspicious rule: iptables -t nat -I PREROUTING 1 -p tcp --dport 30080 -j LOG --log-prefix "NODEPORT-HIT: " — then tail -f /var/log/kern.log or dmesg -w to watch packets flow through in real-time.

    🏗️ Where Docker and Kubernetes Write Their Rules — The Big Picture

    Docker networks: Docker creates the DOCKER chain in filter (INPUT/FORWARD) and nat (PREROUTING/OUTPUT/POSTROUTING). Each -p 8080:80 creates a DNAT rule in nat/DOCKER. Docker also adds DROP rules to filter/FORWARD to prevent containers from accessing the host network unless explicitly allowed (icc=false). Kubernetes (kube-proxy in iptables mode): kube-proxy creates a maze of chains: KUBE-SERVICES (entry for all Services), KUBE-SVC-XXXXX (per-Service: one chain per ClusterIP), KUBE-SEP-XXXXX (per-Endpoint: one chain per backend pod). The pain of iptables mode: With 1,000 Services × 10 endpoints each = 10,000 rules + 1,000 chains. Every new Service/Endpoint triggers a full iptables-restore (atomically replaces ALL rules). At scale, this takes SECONDS — during which new connections are delayed. This is why large clusters move to IPVS mode or eBPF (Cilium). For anihpj: On a small cluster (3-5 nodes, 20 Services), iptables mode is fine. For large-scale production, plan for IPVS or Cilium.

    Real iptables-save Output — What K8s Actually Writes on a Node
      # Excerpt from iptables-save on an EKS node running 20 Services:
  *nat
  :PREROUTING ACCEPT [0:0]
  :INPUT ACCEPT [0:0]
  :OUTPUT ACCEPT [0:0]
  :POSTROUTING ACCEPT [0:0]
  :KUBE-SERVICES - [0:0]
  :KUBE-NODEPORTS - [0:0]
  :KUBE-SVC-2IRACUALRELARSND - [0:0]   # jobpost Service chain
  :KUBE-SEP-3JOYMLJRLN3SMHQO - [0:0]   # jobpost pod-1 endpoint
  :KUBE-SEP-CMNBK2FHFJMHKKLC - [0:0]   # jobpost pod-2 endpoint
  :KUBE-SEP-XZNGH7KUYGHFNT4J - [0:0]   # jobpost pod-3 endpoint

  # NodePort → ClusterIP DNAT:
  -A PREROUTING -m comment --comment "kubernetes service portals" -j KUBE-SERVICES
  -A KUBE-SERVICES -p tcp -m tcp --dport 30080 -j KUBE-NODEPORTS
  -A KUBE-NODEPORTS -p tcp -m tcp --dport 30080 -j DNAT --to-destination 10.96.0.10:8000

  # Service load balancing (3 backends, random distribution):
  -A KUBE-SERVICES -d 10.96.0.10/32 -p tcp -m tcp --dport 8000 -j KUBE-SVC-2IRACUALRELARSND
  -A KUBE-SVC-2IRACUALRELARSND -m statistic --mode random --probability 0.33333333349 -j KUBE-SEP-3JOYMLJRLN3SMHQO
  -A KUBE-SVC-2IRACUALRELARSND -m statistic --mode random --probability 0.50000000000 -j KUBE-SEP-CMNBK2FHFJMHKKLC
  -A KUBE-SVC-2IRACUALRELARSND -j KUBE-SEP-XZNGH7KUYGHFNT4J

  # Per-endpoint DNAT (pod IPs):
  -A KUBE-SEP-3JOYMLJRLN3SMHQO -p tcp -m tcp -j DNAT --to-destination 10.244.1.10:8000
  -A KUBE-SEP-CMNBK2FHFJMHKKLC -p tcp -m tcp -j DNAT --to-destination 10.244.2.20:8000
  -A KUBE-SEP-XZNGH7KUYGHFNT4J -p tcp -m tcp -j DNAT --to-destination 10.244.3.30:8000
  COMMIT

  READING THIS: KUBE-SVC has the jobpost Service (10.96.0.10:8000).
  Traffic hits KUBE-SVC → random pick (33%, 50%, remainder) →
  KUBE-SEP → DNAT to actual pod IP. This is the entire K8s Service
  load balancing in 10 iptables rules.

    27.3 nftables — The Modern Replacement

    nftables is the successor to iptables, available since Linux 3.13 (2014). It replaces the entire iptables family (iptables, ip6tables, arptables, ebtables) with ONE unified framework.

    Featureiptablesnftables
    CodebaseSeparate tools per protocol (iptables, ip6tables, arptables, ebtables)One tool (nft) for all protocols
    Rule updatesFull table replacement (iptables-restore)Atomic rule additions (nft add rule)
    KernelSeparate kernel modules per table/protocolSingle nf_tables kernel module
    SyntaxCommand-line flags (-p, --dport, -j)Structured, readable syntax (tcp dport 80 accept)
    Sets & Mapsipset (separate tool)Built-in sets and maps (native)
    Rule count scalingO(n) linear traversalO(1) with sets/hashtables
    IPv4/IPv6Separate rules for eachSingle rule for both (inet family)
      # nftables basic syntax — cleaner and more intuitive:
  nft add table inet myfilter
  nft add chain inet myfilter input { type filter hook input priority 0\; }
  nft add rule inet myfilter input tcp dport { 22, 80, 443 } accept
  nft add rule inet myfilter input ip saddr 10.0.0.0/8 counter drop
  nft list ruleset   # show all rules (like iptables-save)

  # Sets for O(1) lookups (vs O(n) with iptables):
  nft add set inet myfilter allowed_ports { type inet_service\; }
  nft add element inet myfilter allowed_ports { 22, 80, 443, 8000, 9090 }
  nft add rule inet myfilter input tcp dport @allowed_ports accept
    ⚠️ Why This Matters for Kubernetes SREs

    Kubernetes is gradually moving away from iptables. kube-proxy already supports nftables (since K8s 1.29, alpha). The nftables backend eliminates the performance cliff that iptables mode hits at ~1,000 Services. Cilium (eBPF-based CNI) bypasses iptables/nftables entirely — it attaches eBPF programs directly to netfilter hooks, achieving 10x+ performance. What you should do: (1) Learn to read both iptables AND nftables rules for debugging. (2) Know that nft list ruleset is the unified way to see all firewall rules on modern systems. (3) If you're building a new cluster in 2025+, consider IPVS or Cilium over iptables mode. Transition path: iptables-translate tool automatically converts iptables rules to nftables: iptables-translate -t nat -A PREROUTING -p tcp --dport 80 -j DNAT --to-destination 10.0.0.1:8080 → outputs the equivalent nft command.

    🧮 ipset vs nftables Sets — The Performance Difference

    ipset (iptables companion): A separate tool that creates in-kernel hash tables for IP sets. Used with -m set --match-set blacklist src. Allows O(1) lookups for IP matching but still requires iptables rule traversal for other matches. Separate from iptables — managed via ipset command. nftables sets: Built-in, native hash tables and interval trees. Support multiple data types (IPv4, IPv6, ports, MAC addresses). Can be updated atomically without rule reload. Support concatenations: match on (src IP + dst port) in O(1). Performance example: Block 10,000 IPs: iptables = 10,000 rules (O(n), 10,000 checks per packet) vs iptables+ipset = 1 rule + 10,000-entry hash (O(1)) vs nftables = 1 rule + native set (O(1), faster than ipset). Verdict: nftables sets are the future. ipset is the bridge for existing iptables deployments.

    27.4 conntrack — Connection Tracking Deep Dive

    The connection tracking (conntrack) subsystem is what makes Linux firewalls stateful. It maintains a table of every active connection flowing through the system — source, destination, ports, protocol, and state. This is how iptables can tell the difference between a NEW SYN packet and an ESTABLISHED connection's data packet.

    conntrack Table — What Linux Tracks for Every Connection
      conntrack -L (sample output — one connection entry):
  tcp  6 431999 ESTABLISHED src=10.244.1.5 dst=10.96.0.10 sport=45678 dport=8000 \
    src=10.244.2.10 dst=10.244.1.5 sport=8000 dport=45678 [ASSURED] mark=0 use=1
       │  │       │           │              │          │
       │  │       │           │              │          └─ REPLY tuple: how responses are matched
       │  │       │           │              └─ ORIGINAL tuple: what the initiator sent
       │  │       │           └─ Timeout remaining (432,000s = 5 days for ESTABLISHED TCP!)
       │  │       └─ Connection state: NEW, ESTABLISHED, RELATED, UNREPLIED, ASSURED
       │  └─ Protocol number (6 = TCP)
       └─ L4 protocol

  CONNTRACK STATES (important for iptables rules):
  NEW      — First packet of a connection (SYN). Triggers conntrack entry creation.
  ESTABLISHED — Connection has seen two-way traffic (SYN+SYN/ACK). Fully tracked.
  RELATED  — This packet belongs to a NEW connection that is "related" to an existing one.
             Example: FTP data channel, ICMP "Destination Unreachable" for an existing TCP flow.
  INVALID  — Packet doesn't match any known connection. Malformed, out-of-window, or spoofed.
             Usually dropped by default. High INVALID count = potential attack or bad NAT.
  UNREPLIED — Connection seen one-way only (SYN sent, no SYN/ACK yet). Temporary state.
    🐞 DEBUGGING — "conntrack table full, dropping packet"

    This is one of the most insidious production issues. Symptoms: Random connection failures, pods can't reach services intermittently, SSH sessions dropping, new connections timing out while existing ones work fine. Root cause: The conntrack table has a maximum size (default: nf_conntrack_max = 65,536 on most systems, or RAM/16,384). When full, the kernel DROPS new connections — existing connections continue working. Diagnosis: conntrack -C (current count), cat /proc/sys/net/netfilter/nf_conntrack_count, dmesg | grep "table full". Fix: sysctl -w net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max=262144 (increase to 2^18). For EKS nodes with high connection churn (100+ pods, each making DB connections), set this in a DaemonSet init script. Prevention: (1) Reduce conntrack timeouts for TIME_WAIT: net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_tcp_timeout_time_wait=30 (default: 120s). (2) Use NOTRACK for high-throughput internal traffic that doesn't need NAT: iptables -t raw -A PREROUTING -s 10.244.0.0/16 -d 10.244.0.0/16 -j NOTRACK. (3) Monitor nf_conntrack_count with Prometheus node_exporter. For anihpj EKS: A node running 30 pods, each with 50 DB connections = 1,500 connections, plus pod-to-pod traffic, plus API calls — can easily hit 65,536. Always monitor and tune conntrack limits.

    TCP StateDefault TimeoutWhat It MeansTuning Guidance
    NONE30 secondsNo reply seen yet (SYN sent, no SYN/ACK)Increase if high-latency links (satellite, inter-continental). Default is fine for DC/cloud.
    SYN_SENT60 secondsSYN sent, waiting for SYN/ACKReduce to 30s for faster failover on dead backends.
    SYN_RECV60 secondsSYN received, waiting for ACK (half-open)Reduce on internet-facing hosts to mitigate SYN flood memory pressure.
    ESTABLISHED432,000s (5 days!)Connection fully established, idleReduce to 3600s (1 hour) for busy nodes — long-lived idle connections waste slots.
    FIN_WAIT120 secondsLocal side sent FIN, waiting for FIN from peerReduce to 30s — if peer doesn't respond in 30s, it's probably gone.
    CLOSE_WAIT60 secondsRemote side sent FIN, local app hasn't closed yetThis is an APPLICATION bug — the app isn't closing connections. Fix the app, not the timeout.
    TIME_WAIT120 secondsConnection closed, waiting to ensure
    🎯 Chapter 27 Exam Prep —” VPN & Tunneling

    Exam Weight: MEDIUM (5-8% of questions)

    📋 Must Memorize
    • IPsec: ESP(encryption+auth) vs AH(auth only); Tunnel vs Transport mode
    • WireGuard: modern, simple, kernel-based, UDP, Curve25519+ChaCha20
    • GRE: simple encapsulation, no encryption (often paired with IPsec)
    • VXLAN: L2 overlay over L3, 24-bit VNI, UDP port 4789
    ⚠️ Common Traps
    • IPsec behind NAT: NAT-T encapsulates ESP in UDP 4500
    • MTU issues with any tunnel (overhead reduces effective MTU)
    • WireGuard is stateless (no connection tracking) —” easier to manage
    • VPN split tunneling: only route specific traffic through VPN
    🔧 Quick Commands
    • wg show —” WireGuard status
    • ip xfrm state —” IPsec SAs
    • ip link add vxlan0 type vxlan id 100 ...
    no stray packets    		Reduce to 30s on high-connection-churn nodes. Enable tcp_tw_reuse=1 for clients.
    CLOSE10 secondsBoth sides closed, waiting for final ACKDefault is fine — should be very brief.
    🔬 Conntrack Helpers — When NAT Breaks Application Protocols

    Some application protocols embed IP addresses or port numbers in the packet PAYLOAD

    # IPTABLES: PREROUTING(DNAT)->FORWARD(filter)->POSTROUTING(SNAT)
# INPUT->local->OUTPUT; iptables -L -nv --line-numbers
    — not just the headers. FTP is the classic example: in active mode, the FTP client sends PORT 192,168,1,50,14,45 (meaning IP 192.168.1.50, port 14×256+45=3629) in the FTP control connection. Without a conntrack helper, the NAT gateway rewrites the IP header but leaves the embedded IP in the payload unchanged — the server tries to connect to the private IP and fails. Conntrack helpers (ALG — Application Layer Gateway): The nf_conntrack_ftp kernein the payload. Other protocols needing helpers: SIP (VoIP), H.323, TFTP, IRC, NetBIOS. In Kubernetes: conntrack helpers are usually DISABLED because they're a security risk (ALG parsing can be exploited by crafted packets). Modern applications should avoid embedding IPs in payloads — use protocols that work cleanly with NAT (HTTP, gRPC, WebSocket). If you see "FTP doesn't work through my NAT" or "SIP calls drop after 30 seconds": check lsmod | grep nf_conntrack — the helper module may not be loaded. Load with modprobe nf_conntrack_ftp. For K8s: never run FTP servers in pods behind Services — it will break spectacularly.

    📝 Chapter 27 — Networking Practice Questions

    Q1
    What are the 5 netfilter hook points? What happens at each one?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    PREROUTING: First hook — DNAT, ingress filtering. Before routing decision. INPUT: Packets destined for local processes. Host firewall. FORWARD: Packets routed through this host (router/gateway). OUTPUT: Packets from local processes. POSTROUTING: Last hook — SNAT/MASQUERADE. After routing decision, before wire.

    Explanation

    Think of a Kubernetes node as a miniature internet router. Pod-A (10.244.1.5) on node-1 sends a packet to Pod-B (10.244.2.10) on node-2. The packet path: Pod-A → veth → node-1 bridge → PREROUTING (any DNAT?) → routing decision (is 10.244.2.10 local? No) → FORWARD (firewall rules check) → POSTROUTING (any SNAT? For overlay networks, yes — encapsulate with VXLAN) → eth0 → network → node-2. Understanding these hooks lets you insert rules at the right place: if you want to block pod-to-pod traffic, use FORWARD. If you want to block tra

    Q2
    What's the difference between the filter table and the nat table in iptables?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    filter table: ACCEPT or DROP decisions. Default table. Used in INPUT, FORWARD, OUTPUT chains. "Should this packet be allowed?" nat table: Network Address Translation. DNAT (change destination) in PREROUTING/OUTPUT. SNAT/MASQUERADE (change source) in POSTROUTING. "Where should this packet go?" Only the FIRST packet of a connection hits the nat table — subsequent packets use conntrack.

    # NAT: SNAT changes src IP (POSTROUTING), DNAT changes dst IP (PREROUTING)
# conntrack -L; iptables -t nat -L -nv; MASQUERADE = dynamic SNAT
    Explanation

    The nat table is only consulted for the FIRST packet of a connection. After the nat rule matches and creates a conntrack entry, all subsequent packets in that connection bypass the nat table entirely — conntrack handles the translation. This is why you can't change NAT rules mid-connection — existing connections continue using the old translation until they close. For Kubernetes: a NodePort Service creates a DNAT rule in PREROUTING. The first SYN packet to NodeIP:30080 hits the nat table, gets DNAT'd to the pod IP, and creates a conntrack entry. All subsequent packets in that TCP connection use conntrack — no more nat table lookups. This is efficient but means you can't "move" an active connection to a different pod.

    Q3
    How do Docker and Kubernetes use iptables differently? Where does each write its rules?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    Docker: Writes to DOCKER chain in nat (DNAT for port mappings) and filter (FORWARD for inter-container isolation). Kubernetes (iptables mode): Creates KUBE-SERVICES, KUBE-SVC-XXXXX, KUBE-SEP-XXXXX chains in nat table. KUBE-NODEPORTS in PREROUTING. Also writes to filter/FORWARD for NetworkPolicy enforcement. kube-proxy manages all K8s rules; Docker manages DOCKER rules. They coexist but can conflict.

    # IPTABLES: PREROUTING(DNAT)->FORWARD(filter)->POSTROUTING(SNAT)
# INPUT->local->OUTPUT; iptables -L -nv --line-numbers
    Explanation

    Docker and Kubernetes iptables rules live side by side, which can cause conflicts. Docker's default FORWARD policy is DROP (since Docker 1.13), but Kubernetes needs FORWARD to be ACCEPT for pod-to-pod communication. This is why EKS and kubeadm disable Docker's iptables management on K8s nodes — they use containerd/CRI-O instead, which don't write iptables rules. The real danger: manually running iptables -F (flush) will destroy BOTH Docker AND Kubernetes rules, breaking all networking. Always use iptables-save > backup.txt before making changes. The ultimate debugging move: iptables-save | grep -E "DOCKER|KUBE" shows exactly what each system has configured.

    Q4
    Why is nftables replacing iptables? What are the key advantages?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    Advantages: (1) One tool for IPv4/IPv6/ARP (unified). (2) Atomic rule updates (no full table replacement). (3) Built-in sets for O(1) lookups (vs O(n)). (4) Cleaner, structured syntax. (5) Single kernel module. (6) Better performance at scale (thousands of rules). Kubernetes kube-proxy now supports nftables backend (K8s 1.29+).

    # IPTABLES: PREROUTING(DNAT)->FORWARD(filter)->POSTROUTING(SNAT)
# INPUT->local->OUTPUT; iptables -L -nv --line-numbers
    Explanation

    The iptables scalability problem is real: in a 5,000-node Kubernetes cluster with 10,000 Services, kube-proxy in iptables mode must atomically replace ALL rules on every Endpoint change. This iptables-restore operation takes 2-5 seconds on a loaded node. During that window, new connections are queued or dropped. nftables solves this with atomic rule additions — only the changed rule is updated, not the entire ruleset. The O(1) set lookup means 10,000 IPs in a set are queried in constant time, vs O(n) linear scanning in iptables. For SREs: learn nftables now. The iptables-translate tool helps bridge the gap. On modern Linux distributions (RHEL 8+, Ubuntu 20.04+), nftables is the default backend — iptables commands are just a compatibility layer.

    Q5
    What is conntrack? What happens when the conntrack table is full?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    Conntrack is the Linux

    # KEY NETWORKING COMMANDS
# Interface: ip addr show; ip link set eth0 up; ethtool eth0
# Routing:   ip route show; traceroute -n HOST; mtr -r HOST
# Sockets:   ss -tlnp; ss -ulnp; lsof -i :PORT; nc -zv HOST PORT
# DNS:       dig +short DOMAIN; nslookup DOMAIN; host DOMAIN
# Firewall:  iptables -L -nv --line-numbers; nft list ruleset
# Capture:   tcpdump -i any -nn host IP or port NUM -w file.pcap
# TLS:       openssl s_client -connect HOST:443 -servername HOST
# HTTP:      curl -sv https://HOST/path -H "Header: value"
# K8s:       kubectl get svc,ep,netpol,ingress -A
# Debug:     L1(ip link)->L2(arping)->L3(ping)->L4(nc -zv)->L7(curl)
    kernel's connection tracking subsystem — it maintains a table of every active connection (src, dst, ports, protocol, state). When full: The kernel drops NEW connections with "nf_conntrack: table full, dropping packet." Existing connections continue working. Symptoms: random timeouts, intermittent failures, SSH disconnects. Fix: increase nf_conntrack_max, reduce timeouts, or use NOTRACK for trusted internal traffic.

    Explanation

    Conntrack table overflow is a right-of-passage for Kubernetes SREs. It typically manifests after a scale-up event — more pods = more connections, and the 65,536 default limit gets exhausted. The insidious part: it's NOT obviously a conntrack issue. You see "connection refused" or "timeout" errors and assume it's a network partition or pod crash. Key diagnostic: dmesg | grep "table full" — if you see this, conntrack is your problem. For EKS: each node h

    # IPTABLES: PREROUTING(DNAT)->FORWARD(filter)->POSTROUTING(SNAT)
# INPUT->local->OUTPUT; iptables -L -nv --line-numbers
    as its own conntrack table (nr, if you have 50 pods per node each with connection pools to PostgreSQL and Redis, you can easily hit 30,000+ connections. Tune early.

    Q6
    Walk through what happens when a packet hits a Kubernetes NodePort Service. Which iptables chains are involved?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    (1) Packet arrives at NodeIP:30080 →XX. (4) KUBE-SVC-XXXXX chain → random selection → KUBE-SEP-YYYY. (5) KUBE-SEP-YYYY → DNAT to pod IP:8000. (6) Routing decision: pod IP is local? Deliver l IPTABLES FLOW: PREROUTING(DNAT)->FORWARD(filter)->POSTROUTING(SNAT) # INPUT(filter)->local process->OUTPUT(filter); iptabOUTING(DNAT)->FORWARD(filter)->POSTROUTING(SNAT) # INPUT->local->OUTPUT; iptables -L -nv --line-numbers

    This is the full iptables NodePort dance. The key insight: NodePort is just DNAT + probability. The KUBE-SVC chain uses -m statistic --mode random --probabpected) at low traffic volumes. The MASQUERADE in POSTROUTING is what hides the client's source IP — the pod sees the node's IP, not the original client. If you need client IP preservation (externalTrafficPolicy: Local), the MASQUERADE is skipped, but traffic only goes to pods on the local node. Trace it yourself: iptables -t nat -L -n | grep -A5 KUBE-NODEPORT on any K8s node.

    Q7
    REJECT: Discard the dig +short DOMAIN; nslookup DOMAIN; host DOMAIN # Check firewall: iptables -L -nv --line-numbers; nft list ruleset # Capture traffic: tcpdump -i any -nn host IP -w capture.pcap # Check TLS: openssl s_client -connect HOST:443 -servername HOST # Test HTTP: curl -sv https://HOST/path -H "Header: value" # K8s networking: kubectl get svc,ep,netpol,ingress -A # Debug order: L1(ethtool)->L2(arping)->L3(ping)->L4(nc)->L7(curl)
    Explanation

    DROP vs REJECT is a philosophical AND practical decision. DROP makes your service appear offline — attackers can't tell if the port is filtered or the host is down. But for internal microservices, DROP causes painful timeouts: your API waits 30 seconds for a TCP SYN to timeout before trying the next backend. With REJECT, the kernel sends an immediate RST — the API knows instantly that this backend is unavailable and retries in milliseconds. Best practice: REJECT on internal networks (fast failure), DROP on internet-facing rules (stealth). In Kubernetes: NetworkPolicies that deny traffic typically DROP (implemented via iptables DROP or eBPF drop). Calico and Cilium both use DROP by default for denied traffic.

    Q8
    How do you list iptables rules with hit counters? Why are counters important for debugging?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    iptables -t nat -L -n -v — the -v flag shows packet and byte counters per rule. Counters tell you: (1) Is this rule being h users report errors, the DNAT is working but the pod is broken. Without counters, you're guessing. Pro tip: Insert a temporary LOG rule with a unique prefix before the target rule, then watch dmesg -w: iptables -t nat -I PREROUTING 1 -p tcp --dport 30080 -j LOG --log-prefix "NODEPORT-DEBUG: ". This shows you every SYN packet (source IP, port) hitting the chain in real-time. Remove it after debugging!

    Q9
    What is the iptables scalability problem at scale? How do IPVS and eBPF solve it?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    iptables problem: O(n) rule traversal — 10,000 rules = 10,000 checks per packet. Full table replacement on every change (iptables-restore). At 1,000+ Services, rule updates take seconds. IPVS: Uses kernel-level hash table for O(1) Service lookup. Supports multiple scheduling algorithms (rr, lc, sh). No full table replacement. eBPF (Cilium): Attaches compiled programs directly to netfilter hooks. O(1) hash table lookups. No iptables at all. 10x+ performance improvement. Both maintain a separate data structure optimized for fast lookups.

    Explanation

    The iptables scalability problem is architectearch means the 10,000th rule costs 10,000x more CPU than the 1st rule. IPVS (IP Virtual Server) was built for load balancing — it maintains an in-kernel hash table where looking up a Service by IP:port is O(1), regardless of how many Services exist. Cilium goes further: it compiles eBPF programs that run at the netfilter hook, bypassing iptables entirely. An eBPF program is JIT-compiled to native x86 instructions — it runs at CPU speed, not kernel interpretation speed. For anihpj at small scale, iptables is fine. If you grow beyond 500 Services, plan to migrate to IPVS or Cilium.

    Q10
    [LAB 🛠️] Your anihpj EKS node has pods intermittently failing to connect to the RDS database. dmesg shows "nf_conntrack: table full." Walk through diagnosis and fix.
    Show Answer
    Answer
    # 1. Check current conntrack usage
conntrack -C                          # Current count
cat /proc/sys/net/netfilter/nf_conntrack_count  # Same, via proc
cat /proc/sys/net/netfilter/nf_conntrack_max    # Max allowed

# 2. What's consuming connections?
conntrack -L -s 10.244.0.0/16 | awk '{print $5}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -20
# Shows top source IPs (pods) by connection count

# 3. Immediate fix — increase table size
sysctl -w net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max=262144
# Make persistent:
echo "net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max=262144" >> /etc/sysctl.d/99-conntrack.conf

# 4. Reduce TIME_WAIT timeout (connections in TIME_WAIT consume slots!)
sysctl -w net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_tcp_timeout_time_wait=30

# 5. For pod-to-pod internal traffic, bypass conntrack:
iptables -t raw -A PREROUTING -s 10.244.0.0/16 -d 10.244.0.0/16 -j NOTRACK
iptables -t raw -A OUTPUT -s 10.244.0.0/16 -d 10.244.0.0/16 -j NOTRACK

# 6. Monitor going forward:
# Prometheus: node_nf_conntrack_entries / node_nf_conntrack_entries_limit
# Alert when > 80%
    Explanation

    This is a production war story. The root cause is usually connection pooling gone wrong: your Django app (jobpost) uses pgBouncer with a pool size of 50 connections per pod. With 40 pods, that's 2,000 DB connections — manageable. But if someone misconfigures the app to use direcit is toast. The NOTRACK trick is powerful but dangerous — it means iptables can't track state for those connections, so your stateful rules won't work for that traffic. Only use NOTRACK for trusted internal traffic that doesn't need NAT. The permanent fix: implement connection pooling (PgBouncer/RDS Proxy), tune conntrack limits based on your workload, and monitor conntrack usage as a first-class metric alongside CPU and memory.

    Chapter 28: eBPF — The Kernel's Programmable Network Engine

    eBPF (Extended Berkeley Packet Filter) is a revolutionary technology that lets you run sandboxed programs inside the Linux kernel — without changing kernel source code or loading kernel modules. Originally designed for packet filtering, eBPF now powers networking, security, observability, and tracing across the entire cloud-native ecosystem. Cilium, the most advanced Kubernetes CNI, is built entirely on eBPF.

    🔴 Advanced⏱️ ~1.5 hours🐧 Kernel⚡ eBPF

    🎯 What You'll Learn

    • ✅ What eBPF is — from classic BPF (tcpdump) to the kernel's programmable engine
    • ✅ The eBPF lifecycle: write → compile → verify → JIT → attach → execute
    • ✅ How Cilium replaces kube-proxy and iptables with eBPF hash maps
    • ✅ Hubble — eBPF-based observability without sidecars
    • ✅ bpftool, bpftrace, and Cilium lab — hands-on eBPF exploration

    28.1 What Is eBPF?

    eBPF allows you to attach small, verified programs to kernel hook points — system calls, network events, tracepoints, and more. The kernel's verifier ensures the program is safe (no infinite loops, no out-of-bounds memory access, max 1M instructions) before JIT-compiling it to native machine code.

    eBPF Program Lifecycle — From C Code to Kernel Execution
      ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                     eBPF PROGRAM LIFECYCLE                            │
  │                                                                       │
  │  1. WRITE             2. COMPILE           3. VERIFY                  │
  │  ┌──────────┐        ┌──────────┐         ┌──────────┐              │
  │  │ C/Rust   │───────▶│ eBPF     │────────▶│ Kernel   │              │
  │  │ source   │  clang │ bytecode │  bpf()  │ Verifier │              │
  │  │ code     │        │ (.o elf) │  syscall│ checks:  │              │
  │  └──────────┘        └──────────┘         │ • No loop│              │
  │                                           │ • Bounds │              │
  │  4. JIT COMPILE       5. ATTACH           │ • Memory │              │
  │  ┌──────────┐        ┌──────────┐         │ • Max 1M │              │
  │  │ JIT →    │───────▶│ Hook     │         │   instrs │              │
  │  │ x86/ARM  │        │ Point    │         └──────────┘              │
  │  │ native   │        │          │                                    │
  │  └──────────┘        └────┬─────┘                                   │
  │                           │                                          │
  │  6. EXECUTE               ▼                                          │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐                   │
  │  │ eBPF program runs on EVERY matching event    │                   │
  │  │ (every packet, every syscall, every kprobe)  │                   │
  │  │ Native speed — no context switch to userspace│                   │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘                   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  KEY HOOK TYPES (where eBPF programs attach):
  XDP (eXpress Data Path)  — Earliest point: NIC driver level, before SKB allocation
  TC (Traffic Control)     — After SKB allocation, before netfilter
  netfilter hooks          — Same as iptables: PREROUTING, INPUT, FORWARD, OUTPUT, POSTROUTING
  cgroup hooks             — Per-cgroup socket operations (used for K8s NetworkPolicy)
  kprobe/kretprobe         — Any kernel function entry/exit (tracing)
  tracepoints              — Static kernel instrumentation points
  uprobe/uretprobe         — Userspace function entry/exit
    🔬 From BPF to eBPF — The Evolution

    Classic BPF (cBPF, 1992): Designed for tcpdump — a simple VM with 2 registers, 32-bit, could only filter packets (return "pass" or "drop"). Used in tcpdump -i eth0 'port 80' — the filter string compiles to cBPF bytecode loaded into the kernel. Extended BPF (eBPF, 2014+): 10 general-purpose 64-bit registers, stack (512 bytes), BPF-to-BPF function calls, shared maps (hash tables, arrays, ring buffers for userspace communication). Can do ANYTHING: networking (XDP, TC), security (seccomp, LSM), observability (trace everything), performance profiling (CPU flame graphs). Why this matters: Before eBPF, custom kernel functionality required writing a kernel module — one bug = kernel panic = reboot. eBPF programs are sandboxed — a bug just means the verifier rejects the program. This safety guarantee is why cloud providers trust eBPF in production (Cilium is used at Google, AWS, and every major K8s platform).

    🔗
    XDP Programs

    Hook: NIC driver (earliest). Can: DROP, PASS, TX (bounce back), REDIRECT to another NIC. Cannot: Modify packet payload, generate new packets. Use: DDoS mitigation, L4 load balancing (Facebook Katran), line-rate packet filtering (Cloudflare). Speed: ~10M pps per core. XDP runs BEFORE kernel allocates SKB — the ultimate fast path.

    🚦
    TC Programs

    Hook: Traffic Control (after SKB alloc, before netfilter). Can: Modify, encapsulate, redirect, queue. More flexible than XDP — can rewrite packet headers, tunnel, apply QoS. Use: Cilium pod networking (DNAT, encapsulation), custom load balancers, traffic shaping. Speed: Slightly slower than XDP (SKB already allocated) but still line rate for most workloads.

    🔍
    Tracing Programs

    Hooks: kprobe (any kernel function), tracepoint (static points), uprobe (userspace functions). Use: Performance profiling (CPU flame graphs), security monitoring (Falco — detect suspicious syscalls), debugging (bpftrace one-liners). Speed: Runs inline with traced function — overhead proportional to program complexity. Most tracing BPF programs are < 50 instructions.

    28.2 eBPF in Kubernetes Networking — Cilium & Hubble

    Cilium is a CNI plugin built entirely on eBPF. It replaces kube-proxy, iptables, and the Linux bridge with eBPF programs attached to each pod's virtual interface — achieving massive performance and visibility improvements.

    Cilium Architecture — eBPF Replaces kube-proxy + iptables
      TRADITIONAL K8s NETWORKING:              CILIUM eBPF NETWORKING:
  ┌────────────────────────┐              ┌────────────────────────┐
  │ Pod → veth → bridge    │              │ Pod → veth + eBPF pgm │
  │   → iptables (10K rules)│              │   → eBPF direct route  │
  │   → kube-proxy         │              │   (no iptables at all!) │
  │   → overlay (VXLAN)    │              │   → overlay OR direct   │
  │   → eth0               │              │   → eth0                │
  └────────────────────────┘              └────────────────────────┘
  Latency per packet: ~500µs             Latency per packet: ~50µs
  Rules: O(n) iptables search            Rules: O(1) eBPF hash map
  Updates: Full iptables-restore         Updates: Atomic map entry update

  HOW CILIUM REPLACES kube-proxy:
  • Service → eBPF map: ClusterIP → list of pod IPs (updated by Cilium agent)
  • DNAT: eBPF at veth does O(1) hash lookup → directly DNATs to pod IP
  • No iptables chains, no kube-proxy in the data path
  • Load balancing: Maglev consistent hashing (O(1), connection tracking in eBPF map)

  HOW CILIUM ENFORCES NETWORKPOLICY:
  • Each pod gets an eBPF program on its veth (ingress + egress)
  • eBPF program reads the pod's labels, checks against policy map
  • Policy: {podSelector: app=jobpost} allow {namespace: monitoring} on port 9090
  • eBPF does: if (src_label == "monitoring" && dport == 9090) → ACCEPT else DROP
  • All at line rate — no iptables, no context switches
    🔭 Hubble — See Every Packet in Your Cluster

    Hubble is Cilium's observability layer — it leverages eBPF to provide flow-level visibility without sidecars, without code changes, without performance overhead. What Hubble shows: (1) Service dependency map — which pods are calling which services? (2) Per-flow metrics — latency (RTT), packet drops (by policy), TCP retransmits, DNS queries. (3) Security observability — which NetworkPolicies are being hit? Which connections were denied? (4) HTTP/gRPC/Kafka protocol visibility — see method, path, status code at L7. Hubble CLI: hubble observe --from-pod jobpost-xxx --to-namespace monitoring — see all traffic from a specific pod. hubble observe --verdict DROPPED — see all denied connections (invaluable for NetworkPolicy debugging). For anihpj: Deploy Cilium + Hubble. Instantly see: jobpost pods → PostgreSQL (port 5432), jobpost pods → Redis (port 6379), Nginx ingress → jobpost pods. Hubble's service map renders this as an interactive graph — you can see your entire microservice topology live.

    Metrickube-proxy (iptables)kube-proxy (IPVS)Cilium (eBPF)
    Service lookupO(n) linearO(1) hashO(1) hash map
    Rule updatesFull table replace (seconds at scale)IncrementalAtomic map update (microseconds)
    Throughput (1K Services)~3 Gbps~8 Gbps~20+ Gbps
    NetworkPolicyiptables (separate)iptables (separate)eBPF (integrated)
    ObservabilityNoneNoneHubble (flows, L7, DNS, policy)
    Connection trackingconntrack (O(n))conntrackeBPF maps (O(1))
    🌐 Cilium ClusterMesh — Multi-Cluster Networking with eBPF

    ClusterMesh extends Cilium's eBPF networking across multiple Kubernetes clusters. Pods in Cluster-A can reach pods in Cluster-B using their native IPs — no ingress controllers, no external load balancers, no VPNs. How it works: (1) Cilium agents in each cluster exchange pod IP ranges and service identities via etcd. (2) A tunnel (or direct routing if clusters share L2) connects the clusters. (3) eBPF programs on each node have the complete global IP map — pods route directly to remote pods. Use cases: Multi-cloud (EKS in us-east-1 + GKE in us-central1), hybrid (on-prem + cloud), high-availability (active-active across regions). Benefits: Flat network across clusters (no NAT), NetworkPolicy enforced globally, Hubble shows cross-cluster flows. For anihpj at scale: If you expand to multi-region, ClusterMesh lets all jobpost pods communicate directly — no API gateway bottleneck between regions. Production EKS clusters in us-east-1 and eu-west-1 can share a single flat pod network.

    28.3 [LAB 🛠️] eBPF Exploration

    🧪 Phase 1 — Check Kernel eBPF Support
      # Is eBPF available?
  bpftool feature probe kernel
  # Look for: "eBPF helpers supported" and "eBPF program types supported"

  # Kernel version check (eBPF requires 4.x+, full features in 5.x+)
  uname -r  # Should be 5.4+ for production eBPF features

  # List all loaded BPF programs:
  bpftool prog list
  # Example output: shows Cilium programs attached to veth interfaces
  # Each program has an ID, type, tag, and attached hook

  # See BPF maps (key-value stores shared between kernel and userspace):
  bpftool map list
  # Cilium's Service map, Endpoint map, Policy map all appear here
    🧪 Phase 2 — Trace Network Events with bpftrace
      # Install bpftrace (one-liner for most distros):
  # Ubuntu: apt install bpftrace
  # Amazon Linux: yum install bpftrace

  # Trace all TCP connections being established:
  bpftrace -e 'kprobe:tcp_connect { printf("PID %d connecting to %s\\n", pid, comm); }'

  # Count system calls by process (Ctrl+C to see summary):
  bpftrace -e 'tracepoint:raw_syscalls:sys_enter { @[comm] = count(); }'

  # Trace DNS queries (UDP port 53):
  bpftrace -e 'kprobe:udp_sendmsg { if (arg2 == 53) { printf("DNS query from PID %d\\n", pid); } }'

  # Monitor exec calls (detect unexpected process launches in containers):
  bpftrace -e 'tracepoint:syscalls:sys_enter_execve { printf("%s -> %s\\n", comm, str(args->filename)); }'
    🧪 Phase 3 — Try Cilium in a Kind Cluster
      # Create a Kind cluster without default CNI:
  kind create cluster --name cilium-lab --config - <<EOF
  kind: Cluster
  apiVersion: kind.x-k8s.io/v1alpha4
  networking:
    disableDefaultCNI: true
  EOF

  # Install Cilium CLI:
  cilium install
  cilium status --wait

  # Run connectivity test:
  cilium connectivity test

  # Enable Hubble:
  cilium hubble enable
  cilium hubble port-forward &
  hubble observe --all-namespaces

  # See the service map:

    📖 bpftrace One-Liner Cookbook — SRE Edition
      # 🔍 NETWORK DEBUGGING:
  # Count TCP retransmits per process (find which app is suffering):
  bpftrace -e 'kprobe:tcp_retransmit_skb { @[comm] = count(); }'

  # Show new TCP connections in real-time (like tcpdump but per-process):
  bpftrace -e 'kprobe:tcp_v4_connect { printf("%s (PID %d) → %s:%d\n", comm, pid, str(args->addr), args->port); }'

  # Measure TCP connection latency (SYN→ESTABLISHED time):
  bpftrace -e 'kprobe:tcp_rcv_state_process { if (args->state == 1) { @start[tid]=nsecs; } if (args->state == 3 && @start[tid]) { @latency_us = hist((nsecs - @start[tid])/1000); delete(@start[tid]); } }'

  # 🔒 SECURITY:
  # Detect port scanning (SYN to many different ports):
  bpftrace -e 'kprobe:tcp_v4_connect { @ports[pid] = count(); } interval:s:5 { print(@ports); clear(@ports); }'

  # 
    # KEY NETWORKING COMMANDS
# Interface: ip addr show; ip link set eth0 up; ethtool eth0

    🔗 eBPF Tail Calls & Program Chaining — Building Modular Pipelines

    Individual eBPF programs are limited to 1M instructions and cannot call arbitrary kernel functions. But you can chain multiple eBPF programs using tail calls — one program calls another without returning to userspace. How tail calls work: (1) A "prog array" BPF map holds references to other eBPF programs. (2) Program A calls bpf_tail_call(ctx, &prog_array, index). (3) Execution jumps directly to Program B — no context switch, no userspace involvement. (4) Program B runs with the SAME context (same packet/syscall). Why this matters: Cilium uses tail calls extensively. An incoming packet hits a "root" eBPF program that does a quick check, then tail-calls to the appropriate handler: L3 forwarding program, L4 load balancer program, L7 policy program, or the drop program. Each is a separate eBPF program with focused logic — modular, testable,

    # K8s SERVICE: ClusterIP(DNAT via kube-proxy iptables/IPVS)->Endpoint PodIPs
# kubectl get svc,ep -A; NodePort opens port on every node (30000-32767)
    and verifiable independently. The tail call overhead is ~50ns — essentially free. Limitation: Maximum 33 tail calls in a chain (prevents stack overflow). If you need more, restructure your pipeline.

    📝 Chapter 28 — Networking Practice Questions

    Q1
    What is eBPF and how is it different from classic BPF (cBPF)?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    cBPF (1992): Simple VM, 2 registers, 32-bit, packet filtering only (tcpdump). eBPF (2014+): 10 64-bit registers, 512B stack, shared maps, JIT to native code, attaches to ANY kernel hook (networking, tracing, security, observability). Key difference: cBPF could only filter packets. eBPF can modify packets, trace syscalls, enforce security policies, and communicate with userspace via maps — all while being sandboxed and verified for safety.

    Explanation

    The leap from cBPF to eBPF is comparable to the leap from assembly to a high-level language. cBPF was a tiny, purpose-built VM for one task: deciding which packets to capture. eBPF is a general-purpose in-kernel execution environment. The verifier is eBPF's secret sauce — it statically analyzes every program before loading, guaranteeing no crashes, no infinite loops, and no memory corruption. This safety guarantee is why eBPF has seen massive adoption: cloud providers, security vendors (Falco, Tracee), and networking companies (Cilium, Calico) all build on eBPF. For SREs: understanding eBPF i

On packet send, the eBPF program does O(1) map lookup → directly rewrites the destination to a pod IP. No iptables, no kube-proxy in the data path. Benefits: O(1) vs O(n), atomic map updates (microseconds vs seconds), 10x+ throughput at scale, integrated NetworkPolicy and observability (Hubble).
    Explanation

    The performance difference is architectural, not incremental. iptables must traverse ALL rules linearly — at 10,000 Service endpoints, every new connection walks through 10,000 rules. Cilium's eBPF hash map lookup is constant time regardless of endpoint count. The update model is equally important: iptables replaces ALL rules on any change (iptables-restore), freezing new connections for 1-5 seconds at scale. Cilium updates a single map entry atomically — no disruption. This makes Cilium viable for 10,000+ node clusters where iptables mode is unusable. At Google scale (where Cilium originated), these differences

# ss -s(summary); lsof -i :PORT; cat /proc/net/tcp /proc/net/udp
    mean the difference between a working cluster and a perpetually broken one.

    Q3
    What is the eBPF verifier? Why is it critical for safety?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    The verifier statically analyzes every eBPF program before loading. It checks: (1) No unbounded loops (all paths terminate). (2) All memory accesses are within bounds (no buffer overflows). (3) Max 1 million instructions (prevents CPU monopolization). (4) Registers are properly initialized before use. (5) Return value is valid for the program type. If ANY check fails, the program is rejected. This is why eBPF is safe to run in the kernel — unlike kernel modules which can crash the system.

    Explanation

    The verifier is eBPF's killer feature. Before eBPF, adding custom kernel functionality meant writing a kernel module in C — with zero safety guarantees. A null pointer dereference in a kernel module = kernel panic = your production node reboots. The eBPF verifier mathematically proves that your program cannot crash the kernel. It does this through abstracthan service meshes (Istio/Envoy). A service mesh injects a sidecar proxy into every pod — each proxy terminates TCP, parses HTTP, and forwards to the app. This adds latency (1-5ms per hop) and resource overhead (50-200MB RAM per sidecar). Hubble's eBPF approach observes packets at the kernel level — it reads the same packets the kernel would process anyway, extracts metadata, and sends it to userspace. Zero latency overhead, near-zero CPU overhead (eBPF is JIT-compiled), no RAM per pod. The trade

    # K8s POD NET: Shared net namespace(same IP+ports), veth pair to cni0 bridge on node
# kubectl exec POD -- ip addr; All containers in pod share localhost:PORT
    -off: Hubble doesn't modify traffic (no retries, circuit breaking) — it only observes. For full service mesh features, you still need a

    Q5
    What are BPF maps? How do they enable eBPF programs to communicate with userspace?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    BPF maps are key-value data structures (hash tables, arrays, ring buffers, LRU maps) that live in kernel memory and are accessible from both eBPF programs AND userspace. They serve as: (1) Configuration store (Cilium writes Service → Endpoints mappings). (2) State store (connection tracking tables). (3) Statistics (packet counters, latency histograms). (4) Event streams (ring buffer for pushing events to userspace). Maps persist bey

    Explanation

    BPF maps are what make eBPF programs useful beyond simple filtering. Without maps, an eBPF program would be a static function with no state and no way to communicate results. Maps provide shared memory between the kernel (where the eBPF program runs) and userspace (where the Cilium agent runs). Example: When a new pod is created, the Cilium agent updates the BPF map "Service-Backends" — adds the pod IP to the list of backends for its Service. The eBPF program on every pod's

    # K8s POD NET: Shared net namespace(same IP+ports), veth pair to cni0 bridge on node
# kubectl exec POD -- ip addr; All containers in pod share localhost:PORT
    veth reads this map on every packet — instantly seeing the new backend without any program reload. This is how Cilium achieves sub-millisecond Service updates: just change a map entry. No rule reload, no chain rewrite, no connection disruption.

    Q6
    What is XDP (eXpress Data Path)? How is it different from TC (Traffic Control) hooks?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    XDP: Earliest possible hook — runs in the NIC driver before the kernel allocates an SKB (socket buffer). Can DROP/redirect packets at line rate (10+ Mpps per core). Used for DDoS mitigation, load balancing, and high-speed packet processing. TC: Runs after SKB allocation, before netfilter. More flexible (can modify packets, not just drop/redirect) but slightly slower (SKB already allocated). Both use eBPF programs.

    Explanation

    XDP is the fastest possible path for packet processing — it literally runs before the kernel spends any CPU on the packet. A 10 Gbps NIC receiving 14.8 million packets per second: with iptables, the kernel allocates P for DDoS mitigation: when a SYN flood hits their edge, an XDP program drops attack traffic before the kernel even sees it. Cilium uses TC hooks (not XDP) for pod networking because pods need packet modification (DNAT, encapsulation), which XDP doesn't support as easily. XDP is for "drop or forward" decisions at extreme scale.

    Q7
    How does Cilium enforce Kubernetes NetworkPolicies? Walk through a deny decision.
    Show Answer
    Answer

    (1) Cilium agent translates K8s NetworkPolicy → eBPF policy maps (allow/deny rules based on pod labels, namespaces, ports). (2) Each pod's veth has an eBPF program attached. (3) On outgoing packet: eBPF reads destination pod's identity (label-based, not IP-based!). (4) Checks policy map: is src→dst allowed on this port? (5) If denied: packet dropped, event sent to Hubble. (6) If allowed: packet forwarded normally. All at L3/L4 (IP/port) AND L7 (HTTP method, path, Kafka topic) depending on policy.

    Explanation

    Cilium's identity-based model is fundamentally more secure than IP-based enforcement. In traditional iptables NetworkPolicy, rules match IP addresses. When a pod restarts, its IP changes — you must update iptables rules. Cilium assigns each pod a numeric identity based on its labels (e.g., app=jobpost = identity 12345). The eBPF program looks up identity, not IP. When the pod restarts with a new IP, the identity stays the same — no policy update needed. For L7 policies (e.g., allow GET /api/jobed hook). Shows you exactly what Cilium or any eBPF tool has loaded. (2) bpftool map list — list all BPF maps (size, type, entries). Shows Service maps, policy maps. (3) bpftool map dump id <ID> — dump the contents of a specific map. See exactly what backends Cilium has for a Service.

    Explanation

    bpftool is the equivalent of iptables -L -v for the eBPF world. When debugging Cilium: bpftool prog list | grep cil shows all Cilium-loaded programs. bpftool map list | grep cil shows Cilium's data structures. You can even algorithm. This is raw visibility into what Cilium is actually doing — no log

    Q9
    Compare Cilium vs Calico vs Flannel for production Kubernetes networking.
    Show Answer
    Answer

    Flannel: Simplest. VXLAN or host-gw overlay. No NetworkPolicy. Good for: learning, small clusters. Calico: BGP-based routing (no overlay!) OR VXLAN/IPIP. iptables-based NetworkPolicy. eBPF mode available (beta). Good for: on-prem, high performance, NetworkPolicy. Cilium: eBPF-native. Replaces kube-proxy. Hubble observability. L7 NetworkPolicy (HTTP/Kafka/DNS). Best for: cloud-native, observability, performance at scale. Cilium is the most advanced and feature-rich.

    Explanation

    This is one of the most important architectural decisions in Kubernetes. Flannel is the "it just works" option — zero configuration, VXLAN overlay, pods can talk to each other. But no NetworkPolicy, no observability, limited performance tuning. Calico is the on-prem favorite — its BGP mode routes pod IPs directly on the physical network (no overlay = better performance). Its NetworkPolicy is mature and iptables-based. Calico is adding eBPF features but they're still maturing. Cilium is the cloud-native leader — eBPF-native from day one. If you're on a modern kernel (5.4+) and want maximum performance, observability, and security, Cilium is the clear winner. The trade-off: Cilium requires more kernel knowledge to debug. For anihpj: if using EKS with recent AMIs, Cilium is an excellent choice. If you need the simplest possible setup, start with Flannel and migrate later.

    Q10
    [LAB 🛠️] Write a bpftrace one-liner to detect TCP SYN floods targeting anihpj on port 8000.
    Show Answer
    Answer
    # Count SYN packets per source IP per second on port 8000:
bpftrace -e 'kprobe:tcp_v4_syn_recv_sock {
  $port = ((struct sock *)arg0)->__sk_common.skc_dport;
  $port = ($port >> 8) | (($port << 8) & 0xFF00);  // ntohs
  if ($port == 8000) {
    @syn_count[comm] = count();
  }
}
interval:s:1 { print(@syn_count); clear(@syn_count); }'

# Simpler version using tcptracer (if installed):
bpftrace -e 'kprobe:tcp_connect {
  printf("SYN from %s (PID %d)\\n", comm, pid);
}'
    Explanation

    This is real-time DDoS detection without any monitoring agent — just bpftrace and eBPF. The first one-liner attaches to tcp_v4_syn_recv_sock (called when the kernel receives a SYN and creates a request socket), filters for port 8000, counts by process name, and prints per-second totals. If one IP or process spikes to 10,000+ SYNs/second, you've found your attacker. bpftrace is the modern strace — it can trace almost anything in the kernel with minimal overhead. For production DDoS mitigation: use XDP programs (not bpftrace) that run in the NIC driver and drop attack traffic at line rate before the kernel processes it. bpftrace is for investigation; XDP is for mitigation.

    Chapter 29: Network Observability — Metrics, Logs & Traces

    You can't fix what you can't see. Network observability is the practice of collecting metrics (quantitative data over time), logs (event records), and traces (request journeys across services) to understand, debug, and optimize your network. This chapter covers the essential tools and techniques every SRE needs to monitor and troubleshoot network health.

    🟡 Intermediate⏱️ ~1.5 hours📊 Observability🔍 Monitoring

    🎯 What You'll Learn

    • ✅ The 3 pillars of observability — metrics, logs, and traces — applied to networking
    • ✅ USE method (infrastructure) and RED method (services) with real PromQL queries
    • ✅ 11 critical network metrics every SRE should monitor with alert thresholds
    • ✅ Tool landscape: Prometheus vs Datadog vs CloudWatch, Hubble, VPC Flow Logs, tcpdump
    • ✅ Hands-on labs: node_exporter, VPC Flow Logs with Athena, Cilium Hubble service maps

    29.1 The Observability Stack for Networking

    Observability Pyramid — Metrics, Logs, Traces for Network Engineering
                        ┌─────────┐
                    │ TRACES  │  ← Distributed traces: follow a request across services
                    │         │     Jaeger, Zipkin, Tempo, Hubble (flow-level)
                    │  "Why"  │     Shows: service dependencies, latency per hop
                    ├─────────┤
                    │  LOGS   │  ← Event records: "pod X connected to DB at 14:23:01"
                    │         │     VPC Flow Logs, NGINX access logs, DNS query logs
                    │ "What"  │     Shows: specific events, error details, timestamps
                    ├─────────┤
                    │ METRICS │  ← Time-series data: bandwidth, packets/sec, errors
                    │         │     Prometheus, Grafana, CloudWatch
                    │ "When"  │     Shows: trends, thresholds, anomalies over time
                    └─────────┘

  HOW THEY WORK TOGETHER:
  1. Alert: "HTTP 5xx rate > 5% for jobpost Service" (METRIC)
  2. Investigate: "Which pods are failing?" → Hubble service map (TRACE)
  3. Root cause: "Pod 10.244.3.17 can't reach RDS" → VPC Flow Logs (LOG)
  4. Deep dive: "What's actually on the wire?" → tcpdump (PACKET)
    💡 USE and RED Methods — Applied to Networking

    USE Method (Utilization, Saturation, Errors): For network interfaces — Utilization: bandwidth used / bandwidth available (alert at 80%). Saturation: packet drops, overruns (queue full), retransmits (TCP congestion). Errors: CRC errors (bad cable), carrier errors (link down), collisions (half-duplex). RED Method (Rate, Errors, Duration): For HTTP services — Rate: requests per second. Errors: 5xx rate, connection refused, timeout rate. Duration: latency (p50, p95, p99), TTFB (Time To First Byte). Apply USE to infrastructure (NICs, switches, links). Apply RED to services (APIs, load balancers, databases). Together, they give you complete coverage.

    🖥️
    USE Method — Infrastructure Focus

    Utilization: How busy is the NIC? rate(node_network_receive_bytes_total[5m]) * 8 / 1e9 = % of 1 Gbps. Alert > 80%. Saturation: Is work queuing? node_network_receive_drop_total — drops mean NIC queue full. Saturation is WORSE than utilization. Errors: Is it working correctly? node_network_receive_errs_total — CRC errors = physical layer issues. Zero-tolerance alert.

    🌐
    RED Method — Service Focus

    Rate: Requests/sec to anihpj API. rate(http_requests_total[5m]). Errors: Failed requests. rate(http_requests_total{status=~"5.."}[5m]) / rate(http_requests_total[5m]). Alert > 5%. Duration: Latency distribution. histogram_quantile(0.99, rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])). Alert p99 > 1s. Apply RED to every service: ALB, jobpost API, RDS, Redis.

    ⚠️ The 4 Golden Signals for Network Health

    Google SRE defines 4 golden signals: (1) Latency: Time to serve a request. For network: RTT, connection setup time, DNS resolution time. Break down by percentile — p50 (typical), p95 (tail), p99 (worst). (2) Traffic: Demand on your system. For network: requests/sec, packets/sec, bandwidth (Mbps/Gbps), active connections. (3) Errors: Failed requests. For network: 5xx rate, connection refused, DNS NXDOMAIN, TCP retransmits, packet drops. Distinguish client errors (4xx) from server errors (5xx). (4) Saturation: How "full" your system is. For network: bandwidth utilization %, conntrack table usage %, socket backlog, NIC ring buffer drops. The key insight: monitor ALL FOUR. A system can have low latency (fast responses) while being saturated (about to fail). Or high traffic with no errors (normal scale). Each signal tells a different part of the story.

    📈
    Prometheus + node_exporter

    Host-level network metrics: bytes/packets per interface, errors, drops, TCP connection states. node_exporter exposes /proc/net/dev, /proc/net/snmp, /proc/net/netstat as Prometheus metrics. Set up alerts: rate(node_network_receive_drop_total[5m]) > 0. Grafana dashboard: "Node Exporter Full" shows all network metrics in one view.

    ☁️
    VPC Flow Logs + Athena

    Every IP flow in your VPC is logged (src, dst, ports, protocol, action: ACCEPT/REJECT). Query with Athena (SQL): SELECT srcaddr, dstaddr, SUM(bytes) FROM flow_logs WHERE action='REJECT' GROUP BY srcaddr, dstaddr — find blocked traffic. Cost: CloudWatch ($0.50/GB) or S3 (free). Key insight: Flow Logs show firewall decisions — did my SG allow or block this?

    🔭
    Cilium Hubble

    Kubernetes-native network observability via eBPF. Shows: service dependency graph (who calls whom?), per-flow latency (RTT in microseconds), dropped packets with policy reason ("denied by NetworkPolicy 'deny-all'"), L7 visibility (HTTP method, path, Kafka topic). Zero sidecars — eBPF runs in-kernel at pod veth.

    🔍
    tcpdump + Wireshark

    Ad-hoc deep-dive tools. tcpdump -i eth0 -w capture.pcap host 10.244.1.5 — capture all traffic to/from a pod. Analyze in Wireshark: Follow TCP Stream, IO Graph (throughput over time), Expert Info (retransmits, out-of-order packets). For anihpj debugging: capture traffic between jobpost pod and RDS, look for TCP retransmits indicating network congestion.

    ⚠️ GOTCHA — nmap and Cloud Provider Abuse Detection

    nmap is a powerful port scanner (nmap -sV -p 1-65535 10.0.1.50), but running it against cloud infrastructure can trigger automated abuse detection systems. AWS, GCP, and Azure monitor for port scanning activity — it looks identical to attacker reconnaissance. Rules for safe nmap usage: (1) Only scan hosts YOU own. (2) Use -T2 (polite timing) to slow the scan rate and avoid triggering rate limits. (3) Never scan from a shared/VPC environment without explicit approval — your account could be suspended. (4) For Kubernetes: use kubectl port-forward to test connectivity instead of scanning pod IPs directly. (5) Many organizations require a change ticket before running nmap in production. Safer alternatives for service discovery: Use ss -tlnp on the host, kubectl get endpoints for K8s, or cloud APIs (aws ec2 describe-instances) instead of scanning.

    📊 Grafana Dashboard Tips for Network SREs

    Essential rows for a Network Overview dashboard: (1) Bandwidth row: Time-series of bytes/sec per interface. PromQL: rate(node_network_receive_bytes_total{device!="lo"}[5m])*8. (2) Error row: Stat panels showing total drops + errors (should always be 0). (3) TCP health row: Retransmit rate as gauge, connection count, TIME_WAIT gauge. (4) Conntrack row: Gauge node_nf_conntrack_entries / node_nf_conntrack_entries_limit * 100 — alert at 80%. (5) DNS row: CoreDNS request rate, NXDOMAIN rate, p99 latency. Pro tip: Use Grafana "Repeat" feature to auto-generate one row per node — one dashboard for all nodes. Add variable $node (query: label_values(node_network_receive_bytes_total, instance)) and repeat panels by $node.
