    📐 SLIs, SLOs, and SLAs — The Reliability Stack for Networking

    SLI (Service Level Indicator): A measured metric. Example: "99.5% of HTTP requests to jobpost API complete successfully within 500ms over the last 30 days." Measured by Prometheus: sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{le="0.5"}[30d])) / sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_count[30d])). SLO (Service Level Objective): The target you commit to. Example: "99.9% of requests complete within 500ms." This is a promise to your users. Your error budget = 100% - SLO = 0.1% allowed failures. SLA (Service Level Agreement): The contract with penalties. Example: "If we fail to meet 99.5% for 2 consecutive months, customers get 25% credit." SLAs have financial consequences — set them looser than SLOs. Network-specific SLIs: (1) Availability: % of successful TCP connections to the API endpoint. (2) Latency: p95/p99 of TCP connect time + TLS handshake + HTTP response. (3) Throughput: requests per second sustained. (4) Packet loss: % of TCP segments retransmitted. (5) DNS: % of successful DNS resolutions. For anihpj: Internal SLO: 99.9% availability, p99 < 500ms. SLA to customers: 99.5% availability, p99 < 2s. The gap between SLO and SLA is your safety buffer. Never set SLO = SLA — you'll violate the SLA every time you miss the SLO.

    📈 Network Capacity Planning — Pr
    # KEY NETWORKING COMMANDS
# Interface: ip addr show; ip link set eth0 up; ethtool eth0
# Routing:   ip route show; traceroute -n HOST; mtr -r HOST
# Sockets:   ss -t per AZ (Mbps), peak connections per node, peak packets per second, peak DNS queries per second. Collect 90 days of data. Step 2 — Model growth: If traffic grows 15% month-over-month, in 6 months you'll need current × 1.15^6 = current × 2.31 — more than double. Step 3 — Identify bottlenecks: Which resource hits its limit first? For EKS: usually pod IP exhaustion (VPC CNI ENI led peak. If peak is 7 Gbps, you need 10 Gbps capacity. If conntrack peaks at 50,000, you need 65,536 × 1.3 = 85,197 — increase to 131,072. Step 5 — Test: Run load tests at 2× current peak to find the REAL bottleneck — theory meets reality. For anihpj: Track: (a) pod count growth → ENI IP consumption, (b) request rate growth → bandwidth + conntrack, (c) new microservices → Service count → iptables rule count. Plot trend lines. Alert when any resource projects to exceed 70% within 90 days. Capacity planning is proactive SRE — you fix the problem before users notice.

    📝 Chapter 29 — Networking Practice Questions

    Q1
    What is the difference between metrics, logs, and traces? How do they complement each other for network debugging?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    Metrics: Time-series data (bandwidth, packets/sec). Answers "WHEN did the problem start?" Logs: Event records ("connection refused at 14:23:01"). Answers "WHAT happened?" Traces: Request journey across services. Answers "WHY is it slow?" Together: Alert from metric → investigate with trace → root cause from log → deep dive with packor all four and you'll catch problems before (saturation), during (latency, errors), and after (traffic patterns). The key insight: NO single signal is sufficient. A service can have perfect latency and zero errors while being 99% saturated and about to fail.

    Q3
    What are VPC Flow Logs? What do they capture and what do they NOT capture?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    VPC Flow Logs capture metadata about every IP flow: src/dst IP, ports, protocol, packets, bytes, start/end time, and ACTION (ACCEPT/REJECT by SG/NACL). They do NOT capture: Packet payloads (headers only), intra-subnet traffic by default, traffic to DNS (.2), traffic to Windows KMS, DHCP traffic, traffic to the VPC router (.1). Stored in CloudWatch Logs or S3. Query with CloudWatch Insights or Athena.

    # NETWORKING COMMANDS REFERENCE
# Check interface: ip addr show; ip link set eth0 up; ethtool eth0
# Check routing:   ip route show; ip route get 8.8.8.8; traceroute -n HOST
# Check ports:     ss -tlnp; ss -ulnp; nc -zv HOST PORT; lsof -i :PORT
# Check DNS:       dig +short DOMAIN; nslookup DOMAIN; host DOMAIN
# Check firewall:  iptables -L -nv --line-numbers; nft list ruleset
# Capture traffic: tcpdump -i any -nn host IP -w capture.pcap
# Check TLS:       openssl s_client -connect HOST:443 -servername HOST
# Test HTTP:       curl -sv https://HOST/path -H "Header: value"
# K8s networking:  kubectl get svc,ep,netpol,ingress -A
# Debug order:     L1(ethtool)->L2(arping)->L3(ping)->L4(nc)->L7(curl)
    Explanation

    VPC Flow Logs are like NetFlow/sFlow for the cloud — they answer "who talked to whom?" at the network layer. The ACTION field is the most valuable for debugging: ACCEPT means SG+NACL allowed the traffic; REJECT means one of them blocked it. This instantly tells you if a connection failure is a firewall issue or an application issue. The limitation: Flow Logs are sampled at the hypervisor level — very short-lived flows (single SYN) might be missed. They're also eventually consistent — logs appear 5-10 minutes after the flow ends. For real-time debugging, use tcpdump or Hubble. For auditing, compliance, and pattern analysis, Flow Logs are essential.

    Q4
    How do you monitor TCP retransmissions? What do high retransmissions indicate?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    Monitor: node_netstat_Tcp_RetransSegs (total segments retransmitted). Calculate retrans rate: rate(node_netstat_Tcp_RetransSegs[5m]) / rate(node_netstat_Tcp_OutSegs[5m]). Alert when > 1%. High retransmits indicate: (1) Network congestion (packets dropped at switch/router). (2) Bad NIC/cable (CRC errors causing drops). (3) MTU mismatch (packets too large, fragmented/dropped). (4) Overloaded server (TCP buffer full, drops packets). (5) Firewall silently dropping packets (no RST, just timeout).

    # NETWORKING COMMANDS REFERENCE
# Check interface: ip addr show; ip link set eth0 up; ethtool eth0
# Check routing:   ip route show; ip route get 8.8.8.8; traceroute -n HOST
# Check ports:     ss -tlnp; ss -ulnp; nc -zv HOST PORT; lsof -i :PORT
# Check DNS:       dig +short DOMAIN; nslookup DOMAIN; host DOMAIN
# Check firewall:  iptables -L -nv --line-numbers; nft list ruleset
# Capture traffic: tcpdump -i any -nn host IP -w capture.pcap
# Check TLS:       openssl s_client -connect HOST:443 -servername HOST
# Test HTTP:       curl -sv https://HOST/path -H "Header: value"
# K8s networking:  kubectl get svc,ep,netpol,ingress -A
# Debug order:     L1(ethtool)->L2(arping)->L3(ping)->L4(nc)->L7(curl)
    Explanation

    TCP retransmission is the canary in the network coal mine. Normal retrans rate is < 0.1% — anything above 1% is a problem. How TCP retransmission works: The sender starts a timer after sending a segment. If no ACK arrives within RTO (Retransmission Timeout, typically 200ms-1s), the segment is retransmitted. Each retransmission doubles the RTO (exponential backoff). After net.ipv4.tcp_retries2 (default 15) retransmissions, the connection is aborted. For anihpj: If jobpost pods show 5% retrans rate to RDS, the database connection pool is experiencing packet loss — queries will be slow, timeouts will occur. Check: (1) ethtool -S eth0 | grep drop on the node. (2) VPC Flow Logs for REJECT between EKS and RDS subnets. (3) CloudWatch metrics for NetworkIn/Out on the RDS instance for bandwidth saturation.

    Q5
    What is the USE method? Apply it to a network interface.
    Show Answer
    Answer

    USE = Utilization, Saturation, Errors. For a NIC: Utilization: rate(node_network_receive_bytes_total[5m]) * 8 / 1e9 = % of 1 Gbps used. Saturation: node_network_receive_drop_total (packets dropped because queue full), node_network_transmit_carrier_total (carrier sense errors). Errors: node_network_receive_errs_total (CRC errors, frame errors). Alert: Util > 80%, Saturation > 0/sec sustained, Errors > 0.

    # KEY NETWORKING COMMANDS
# Interface: ip addr show; ip link set eth0 up; ethtool eth0
# Routing:   ip route show; traceroute -n HOST; mtr -r HOST
# Sockets:   ss -tlnp; ss -ulnp; lsof -i :PORT; nc -zv HOST PORT
# DNS:       dig +short DOMAIN; nslookup DOMAIN; host DOMAIN
# Firewall:  iptables -L -nv --line-numbers; nft list ruleset
# Capture:   tcpdump -i any -nn host IP or port NUM -w file.pcap
# TLS:       openssl s_client -connect HOST:443 -servername HOST
# HTTP:      curl -sv https://HOST/path -H "Header: value"
# K8s:       kubectl get svc,ep,netpol,ingress -A
# Debug:     L1(ip link)->L2(arping)->L3(ping)->L4(nc -zv)->L7(curl)
    Explanation

    The USE method is brilliantly simple — for EVERY resource, check utilization, saturation, and errors. Utilization answers "how busy is it?" — at 80% utilization, you have headroom but should plan. Saturation answers "is work queuing?" — drops mean the NIC queue is full, packets are being thrown away BEFORE processing. Saturation is worse than utilization. Errors answers "is it working correctly?" — CRC errors mean bits are being corrupted on the wire. For network interfaces: saturation = drops (rx_missed_errors, rx_fifo_errors). If drops are increasing but utilization is only 50%, the problem might be CPU interrupts or NIC driver — not bandwidth. The USE method forces you to look at all three dimensions, not just "is the link up?"

    Q6
    What metrics would you monitor for DNS health in a Kubernetes cluster?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    CoreDNS exposes Prometheus metrics on :9153. Key metrics: coredns_dns_requests_total (query rate by type: A, AAAA, SRV), coredns_dns_responses_total{rcode="NXDOMAIN"} (failed lookups), coredns_dns_request_duration_seconds (latency percentiles), coredns_panics_total (CoreDNS crashes). Alert: NXDOMAIN rate > 5%, p99 latency > 100ms, panic count > 0. Also monitor CoreDNS pod restarts and node-level DNS from kubelet (kubelet_runtime_operations_duration_seconds).

    # DNS RESOLUTION: Browser cache -> OS hosts -> resolver -> root->TLD->authoritative NS
# dig +trace DOMAIN; nslookup DOMAIN; /etc/resolv.conf nameserver
    Explanation

    DNS is the silent killer of Kubernetes — when CoreDNS is slow or failing, pods can't resolve Service names, and EVERYTHING breaks. The symptoms are confusing: "connection refused," "timeout," "no route to host" — all because the DNS lookup never returned. CoreDNS cache is critical: enable the cache plugin with a 30s TTL. A cache hit takes microseconds; a cache miss requires an upstream query (potentially 50ms+). Monitor cache hit rate: coredns_cache_hits_total / (coredns_cache_hits_total + coredns_cache_misses_total). For anihpj: If jobpost pods suddenly can't connect to PostgreSQL, check CoreDNS first: kubectl logs -n kube-system deployment/coredns. The #1 cause of "mysterious" pod connectivity issues is DNS failure. Always monitor DNS as a first-class service.

    Q7
    How does Hubble differ from traditional monitoring tools? What unique visibility does it provide?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    Hubble is eBPF-based, so it provides kernel-level visibility without sidecars or application instrumentation. Unique capabilities: (1) Service dependency map (auto-generated in real-time). (2) Policy verdict (DROPPED + reason: "denied by NetworkPolicy X"). (3) L7 protocol parsing (HTTP method/path/status, Kafka topic, DNS query name). (4) Per-flow RTT latency at microsecond precision. (5) Zero overhead — eBPF runs in-kernel alongside the packet path. Traditional tools require sidecars (Istio/Envoy) or application-level agents (Datadog APM).

    # KEY NETWORKING COMMANDS
# Interface: ip addr show; ip link set eth0 up; ethtool eth0
# Routing:   ip route show; traceroute -n HOST; mtr -r HOST
# Sockets:   ss -tlnp; ss -ulnp; lsof -i :PORT; nc -zv HOST PORT
# DNS:       dig +short DOMAIN; nslookup DOMAIN; host DOMAIN
# Firewall:  iptables -L -nv --line-numbers; nft list ruleset
# Capture:   tcpdump -i any -nn host IP or port NUM -w file.pcap
# TLS:       openssl s_client -connect HOST:443 -servername HOST
# HTTP:      curl -sv https://HOST/path -H "Header: value"
# K8s:       kubectl get svc,ep,netpol,ingress -A
# Debug:     L1(ip link)->L2(arping)->L3(ping)->L4(nc -zv)->L7(curl)
    Explanation

    Hubble represents a paradigm shift: observability WITHOUT agents. Traditional APM tools (Datadog, New Relic, Dynatrace) require you to install an agent in every pod or language library in every application. A service mesh like Istio injects Envoy sidecars into every pod — adding latency and RAM to every request. Hubble's eBPF approach observes the same packets the kernel processes, extracts metadata, and reports it — with zero added latency and near-zero CPU. The trade-off: Hubble doesn't provide application-level context (user IDs, business transactions) — it's network-level observability. For full APM, you still need application instrumentation. For network observability, Hubble is the most efficient approach available.

    Both are essential and complementary. Blackbox monitoring catches problems your internal metrics might miss: an AWS outage that makes your ALB unreachable even though pods are healthy.     never run nmap against pod IPs — use kubectl port-forward to test connectivity.

    Q10
    [LAB 🛠️] An alert fires: "anihpj API p99 latency > 2s." Walk through systematic diagnosis using observability tools.
    Show Answer
    Answer
    # 1. CHECK METRICS — Isolate the problem dimension:
# Grafana: is it all endpoints or one pod?
kubectl top pods -n anihpj  # CPU/Memory spike?

# 2. CHECK TRACES — Where is time being spent?
# Jaeger: filter by service=jobpost, operation=/api/jobs/
# Is time spent in: app code? DB query? External API call? DNS?

# 3. CHECK LOGS — Look for errors at the time:
kubectl logs -n anihpj deployment/jobpost --since=5m | grep -i error

# 4. CHECK NETWORK — Packet loss? Retransmits?
# On the node:
ss -ti | grep retrans  # TCP retransmit counts
ethtool -S eth0 | grep drop  # NIC drops

# 5. CHECK DEPENDENCIES — Is PostgreSQL slow?
# VPC Flow Logs: any REJECT between EKS and RDS?
# RDS CloudWatch: DatabaseConnections, ReadLatency, WriteLatency

# 6. CHECK DNS:
kubectl logs -n kube-system deployment/coredns | tail -20
    Explanation

    This walkthrough demonstrates the systematic debugging methodology using the observability pyramid: Metrics → Traces → Logs → Packet. Start broad (metrics tell you WHEN and WHERE). Narrow with traces (WHICH service is slow). Pinpoint with logs (WHAT error occurred). Confirm with packet capture (WHY at the protocol level). The most common causes of high p99 latency in order: (1) DB query running slow (missing index, lock contention) — Jaeger will show the DB span taking 1.8s of the 2s. (2) External API timeout — Jaeger will show the HTTP client span timing out after 5s. (3) DNS resolution slow — CoreDNS logs show NXDOMAIN or upstream timeout. (4) Network congestion — TCP retransmits in ss -ti. (5) Garbage collection pause — application logs show GC events. Each cause has a distinct signature in different observability tools. Learning to navigate between them quickly is the hallmark of an expert SRE.

    🟡 Intermediate⏱️ ~1.5 hours🐞 Debugging🔍 Methodology

    🎯 What You'll Learn

    • ✅ The layered debugging approach — always start at the bottom and work up
    • ✅ Connection Refused vs Connection Timeout vs No Route to Host — the 3 error signatures
    • ✅ The First 5 Minutes checklist — 10 commands every SRE should run immediately
    • ✅ How to separate "network problem" from "application problem" definitively
    • ✅ A debugging decision tree that works for EVERY incident

    30.1 The Layered Approach — Always Start at the Bottom

    The OSI model isn't just theory — it's your debugging compass. Start at Layer 1 and verify each layer before moving up. Jumping straight to L7 ("the app is broken!") wastes time when the problem is often at L1-L4.

    Network Debugging Decision Tree — Start Here for Every Incident
      🚨 INCIDENT: "Users can't reach the jobpost app"

  Q1: Is the link up? (L1 — Physical)
  ├── ip link show eth0 → state UP?
  │   └── NO → Check cable, switch port, NIC driver (dmesg | grep eth0)
  │
  Q2: Is ARP resolving? (L2 — Data Link)
  ├── ip neigh show → gateway MAC present? REACHABLE or STALE?
  │   └── NO → L2 issue: VLAN, switch config, duplicate IP, cable problem
  │
  Q3: Is routing OK? (L3 — Network)
  ├── ping 8.8.8.8 → replies?
  │   └── NO → ip route get 8.8.8.8 → check default route exists
  │       └── No default route? → ip route add default via 10.0.1.1
  │   └── YES (ping works) → L3 is fine, move to L4
  │
  Q4: Is the port open? (L4 — Transport)
  ├── nc -zv 10.0.10.50 8000 → Connection refused OR timeout?
  │   └── REFUSED → service not running on that port (app problem!)
  │   └── TIMEOUT → firewall blocking (SG/NACL/iptables/NetworkPolicy)
  │   └── SUCCESS → L4 is fine, move to L7
  │
  Q5: Is DNS resolving? (Application dependency)
  ├── dig api.anihpj.com → returns correct IP?
  │   └── NO → Check CoreDNS pods, /etc/resolv.conf, upstream DNS
  │
  Q6: Is the app healthy? (L7 — Application)
  ├── curl -v http://10.0.10.50:8000/api/health/ → 200 OK?
  │   └── NO → Check pod logs, readiness probe, DB connection, app config
  │   └── YES → Issue is upstream (LB, ingress, DNS, client-side)

  GOLDEN RULE: Never skip a layer. L3 working doesn't mean L2 is fine.
  A flapping link can pass ping 99% of the time and drop 1% of packets —
  your app sees random timeouts that make no sense until you check ethtool -S.
    💡 The Layer-by-Layer Tool Cheatsheet

    L1 (Physical): ip link show (UP/DOWN), ethtool eth0 (speed, duplex, link detected), ethtool -S eth0 (NIC statistics: drops, errors, CRC), dmesg | grep -i "link\|eth0\|network" (driver messages). L2 (Data Link): ip neigh show (ARP table), arping -I eth0 10.0.1.1 (send ARP request manually), bridge fdb show (MAC forwarding table on bridges). L3 (Network): ip route show (routing table), ip route get 8.8.8.8 (which route would be used?), traceroute -n 8.8.8.8 (path discovery). L4 (Transport): ss -tlnp (listening TCP sockets), nc -zv HOST PORT (port connectivity test), ss -ti (TCP info: RTT, retransmits, CWND). L7 (Application): curl -v http://HOST/health (HTTP response), openssl s_client -connect HOST:443 (TLS debugging).

    30.2 The First 5 Minutes — 10 Commands for ANY Network Issue

    When you're paged, run these commands in order. They cover 80% of network incidents in 5 minutes. Don't think — just run them and review the output.

      # ═══ THE SRE FIRST 5-MINUTE NETWORK CHECKLIST ═══

  # 1. Are all interfaces UP?
  ip link show | grep -E "state (UP|DOWN)"

  # 2. Do we have the right IP addresses?
  ip -br addr show

  # 3. Is there a default route?
  ip route show default

  # 4. Can we reach the gateway? (ARP working?)
  ip neigh show

  # 5. Is DNS working?
  dig +short kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local

  # 6. What's listening on this machine?
  ss -tlnp

  # 7. Any firewall rules blocking?
  iptables -L -n -v | head -20   # Check hit counters!

  # 8. Are pods communicating?
  kubectl get pods -o wide        # All Running? Any restarts?

  # 9. What do the logs say?
  dmesg -T | tail -30             # Kernel messages (conntrack, OOM, NIC errors)

  #10. Can we reach the service locally?
  curl -v --connect-timeout 5 http://localhost:8000/api/health/
    ⚠️ The Most Common First-Minute Mistake

    New SREs often jump straight to kubectl describe pod or application logs — skipping L1-L4 entirely. They spend 15 minutes debugging the app only to discover the NIC was down because someone unplugged a cable, or the route table was modified by a Terraform apply, or conntrack was full. Train your muscle memory: ip link → ip route → ss -tlnp → THEN check the app. The first 3 comman

    🎯 Chapter 30 Exam Prep —” IPv6 Essentials

    Exam Weight: MEDIUM (8-10% of questions)

    📋 Must Memorize
    • 128-bit address (8 groups of 4 hex digits); compression: omit leading zeros, :: for zeros
    • Types: ::1/128(loopback), fe80::/10(link-local), fc00::/7(ULA), 2000::/3(global unicast)
    • No broadcast! Uses multicast (ff02::1=all nodes, ff02::2=all routers)
    • SLAAC: router sends prefix, host generates IID; DHCPv6 for stateful addressing
    ⚠️ Common Traps
    • IPv6 is enabled by default on most OS —” security implications!
    • Dual-stack: run IPv4 AND IPv6 simultaneously (not migration, coexistence)
    • NAT not needed in IPv6 (address abundance) —” firewall still needed!
    • /64 is the standard subnet size (not /24 like IPv4)
    🔧 Quick Commands
    • ip -6 addr show —” IPv6 addresses
    • ping6 fe80::1%eth0 —” Link-local ping
    • traceroute6 HOST —” IPv6 traceroute
    ds take 10 seconds and eliminate the most common causes. If you're debugging with a colleague and they say "the app is broken," ask: "Did you check ip link? Did you check the route? Did you check the port?" Until those three are verified, don't look at application code.

    30.3 Connection Refused vs Connection Timeout — The Crucial Difference

    These three error messages look similar but mean completely different things. Learning to read them instantly saves hours of debugging in the wrong direction.

    Three Scenarios — Same curl Command, Three Different Failures
      SCENARIO A: curl -v http://10.0.10.50:8000
  * connect to 10.0.10.50 port 8000 failed: Connection refused
  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  WHAT HAPPENED: Client sent SYN → 10.0.10.50 received it → kernel
  checked: is anything listening on port 8000? → NO → kernel sent RST
  MEANING: The host IS reachable. The network WORKS. The service is
  not running (or listening on a different port).
  FIX: Check `ss -tlnp | grep 8000` on the target. Start the service.

  SCENARIO B: curl -v --connect-timeout 5 http://10.0.99.50:8000
  * connect to 10.0.99.50 port 8000 failed: Connection timed out
  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  WHAT HAPPENED: Client sent SYN → no response → retransmitted SYN
  → still no response → timeout after --connect-timeout seconds
  MEANING: The destination is UNREACHABLE. Packets are being silently
  dropped somewhere (firewall, routing black hole, host down, wrong IP).
  FIX: Check firewall rules (SG, NACL, iptables), routing (ip route get),
  and host status. Use traceroute to find where packets stop.

  SCENARIO C: curl -v http://10.0.99.50:8000
  * connect to 10.0.99.50 port 8000 failed: No route to host
  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  WHAT HAPPENED: The kernel couldn't find a route to 10.0.99.50.
  It didn't even send a SYN — the error comes from the local kernel.
  MEANING: Local routing table has no entry matching the destination.
  FIX: `ip route get 10.0.99.50` shows "unreachable". Add a route
  or check why the subnet isn't in the routing table.

  ⚡ QUICK REFERENCE:
  Connection Refused = RST received → SERVICE PROBLEM, not network!
  Connection Timed Out = SYN dropped → NETWORK/FIREWALL PROBLEM
  No Route to Host    = Local routing failure → ip route missing
    🐞 The RST vs Drop Mindset Shift

    Connection Refused (RST): This is the BEST error to get during debugging. It means the network path is complete — packets are flowing end-to-end. The target host received your SYN, processed it, and actively decided to reject it. The problem is local to the target: wrong port, service not started, or process crashed. Connection Timeout (silent drop): This is the WORST error. It could be: a firewall dropping your packets, a routing loop, a host that's completely down (no RST response), a black-hole route, or packets being dropped at the NIC level. Silent drops give you zero feedback — you have to traceroute or check every hop. Pro tip: If you get "Connection refused" from a pod that should be running, DON'T check the network — check kubectl logs and kubectl describe pod. The network is fine. The app is broken.

    30.4 Separating "Network Problem" from "Application Problem"

    The most expensive debugging mistake: spending hours diagnosing the network when the application is broken, or vice versa. Use these definitive tests to isolate the layer.

    ✅
    Test 1: Curl from the SAME machine

    curl localhost:8000/api/health/ — if this works, the app is running correctly and listening. The problem is definitely NETWORK (someone else can't reach it) or DNS (wrong address). If this FAILS: the application is not running or not listening — an app problem, not network.

    ✅
    Test 2: Curl from another pod (same namespace)

    kubectl exec -it debug-pod -- curl http://jobpost-service:8000/api/health/ — if this works from another pod, the K8s Service and pod are fine. The problem is external to the cluster (ingress, LB, DNS). If this FAILS from another pod but works locally: NetworkPolicy or CNI issue.

    ✅
    Test 3: Ping works but curl doesn't

    Ping (ICMP) working means L3 routing is correct and the host is up. If ping works but curl doesn't, the problem is at L4+: port blocked (iptables/SG/NetworkPolicy), service not listening on that port, or application-level issue (TLS, HTTP config). Check ss -tlnp on the target.

    ✅
    Test 4: TCP handshake succeeds but no HTTP response

    nc -zv host 8000 succeeds (TCP connected) but curl hangs. This means the TCP stack is working, the port is open, but the APPLICATION is not responding. Check: app hung (CPU 100%?), stuck on DB query, thread pool exhausted, or application firewall (mod_security).

    🎯 The Definitive Isolation Test

    Can you reproduce the problem with nc or curl from the same machine? YES → app or local config problem (not network). NO (works locally but not remotely) → network path problem. Then test from another machine in the same subnet: YES it works → problem is routing/firewall between subnets. NO it fails → problem is within the target machine (iptables, SG on ENI, host-level firewall). This three-step isolation (local → same-subnet → cross-subnet) pinpoints the exact hop where the failure occurs.

    🔧 netcat (nc) — The SRE's Swiss Army Knife for Connectivity

    netcat is the most versatile network debugging tool — it can be a client, server, port scanner, or proxy. Essential patterns: (1) Port check: nc -zv host 8000 — just test TCP handshake (no data). -z = zero I/O mode (don't send data), -v = verbose. (2) Banner grab: echo "" | nc host 22 — see SSH version banner. echo -e "GET / HTTP/1.0\r\n\r\n" | nc host 80 — raw HTTP request. (3) Listen mode: nc -l 9999 — start a simple TCP server on port 9999. Connect from another machine to test end-to-end connectivity without deploying a real service. (4) File transfer: Receiver: nc -l 9999 > file.txt, Sender: nc host 9999 < file.txt — quick file transfer without scp. (5) Port range scan: nc -zv host 8000-9000 2>&1 | grep succeeded — find which ports are open. (6) UDP test: nc -zuv host 53 — test UDP connectivity (DNS). Pro tip: nc -w 3 sets a 3-second timeout — always use a timeout to avoid hanging forever on unresponsive hosts. For K8s debugging: kubectl run nc-test --rm -it --image=busybox -- nc -zv service-name 8000 — instant connectivity test from a throwaway pod.

    📦 tcpdump Crash Course — The SRE's Packet-Level Microscope

    tcpdump captures packets at the network interface level — it shows you EXACTLY what's on the wire. Essential filters (always use them — unfiltered tcpdump on a busy interface will flood your terminal): (1) Host filter: tcpdump -i eth0 host 10.244.1.5 — all traffic to/from that IP. (2) Port filter: tcpdump -i eth0 port 8000 — only port 8000. (3) Protocol filter: tcpdump -i eth0 tcp, tcpdump -i eth0 icmp, tcpdump -i eth0 arp. (4) TCP flags: tcpdump -i eth0 'tcp[tcpflags] & (tcp-syn|tcp-fin) != 0' — only SYN or FIN packets (connection start/end). tcpdump -i eth0 'tcp[tcpflags] & tcp-rst != 0' — only RST packets (connection refused!). (5) Combined: tcpdump -i eth0 host 10.244.1.5 and port 5432 and tcp. Output control: -n (no DNS resolution — faster, doesn't generate extra traffic), -nn (no port name resolution), -v/-vv/-vvv (increasing verbosity), -c 100 (stop after 100 packets), -w capture.pcap (write to file for Wireshark analysis), -r capture.pcap (read from file). Real SRE pattern: tcpdump -i any -nn -c 200 -w /tmp/debug.pcap host 10.96.0.10 — capture 200 packets to/from a K8s Service IP, save to file, analyze offline in Wireshark. This is how you prove whether traffic is reaching the pod or being dropped by iptables.

    🔬 strace — When You Need to See What the Application Is Actually Doing

    Sometimes the network is fine but the application is making bad decisions. strace shows every system call an application makes — including socket(), connect(), sendto(), recvfrom(). Network-specific strace: strace -e trace=network -p <PID> — show only network syscalls. strace -e trace=connect,sendto,recvfrom -p <PID> — show connection attempts and data transfers. What strace reveals: (1) Which IP/port is the app ACTUALLY connecting to? (Maybe DNS resolved wrong, or config has wrong value). (2) Is connect() returning -1 ECONNREFUSED or -1 ETIMEDOUT? (Tells you the exact error the app is seeing). (3) Is the app trying IPv6 first and falling back to IPv4? (Happy Eyeballs adds 300ms delay). (4) What socket options is the app setting? (SO_REUSEADDR, TCP_NODELAY?). Essential flags: -f (follow child processes/threads), -tt (microsecond timestamps), -o /tmp/strace.log (output to file). For K8s: kubectl exec -it pod -- strace -e trace=network -p 1 (PID 1 in the container). strace has overhead — don't run it in production for long periods. Use it for 30-second diagnostic captures.

    📝 Chapter 30 — Networking Practice Questions

    Q1
    What is the layered debugging approach? Why should you always start at Layer 1?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    Start at the physical layer (L1) and verify each layer before moving up: L1 (link up?), L2 (ARP?), L3 (routing/ping?), L4 (port open?), L7 (app responding?). Starting at L1 prevents wasting time debugging higher layers when the problem is fundamental — a disconnected cable, a missing route, or a down interface. Jumping to L7 first means you might debug application code for 30 minutes before realizing the NIC is down.

    Explanation

    The OSI model is the most practical debugging tool in networking. Every SRE has a war story of debugging an application for hours only to find the cable was unplugged. The layered approach is fail-safe: you verify the foundation before building on it. L1 is binary — link is UP or DOWN, no ambiguity. L2 is local — ARP works or it doesn't. L3 is reachable — ping works or it doesn't. By the time you reach L7, you have 100% confidence that L1-L4 are working, so any remaining problem IS the application. This eliminates the "is it the network or the app?" debate entirely.

    Q2
    What's the difference between "Connection Refused" and "Connection Timed Out"? Why does it matter?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    Connection Refused (ECONNREFUSED): SYN reached the host, kernel sent RST because nothing is listening on that port. Network WORKS — app problem. Connection Timed Out (ETIMEDOUT): SYN was sent but never received a response (RST or SYN/ACK). Packets are being silently dropped somewhere — network/firewall problem. The distinction is critical: "Refused" means debug the service; "Timed Out" means debug the network path.

    Explanation

    This distinction is the #1 time-saver in network debugging. I've watched engineers spend 2 hours checking firewalls, routing tables, and VPC configurations when the error was "Connection refused." They were debugging the network when the network was perfectly fine — the service just wasn't running. Conversely, "Connection timed out" on a service you KNOW is running means your packets are hitting a firewall or routing black hole. The RST packet in "Connection refused" is a gift — it tells you the destination is alive and reachable. Treasure it.

    Q3
    You run "No route to host." What does this mean? How do you fix it?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    "No route to host" (EHOSTUNREACH) means the LOCAL kernel couldn't find a routing table entry for the destination IP. No SYN was ever sent. Fix: ip route get <dest-ip> to see which route would be used. Add a route: ip route add <dest-subnet> via <gateway>. In K8s: check if the pod network CIDR has routes on the node. In cloud: check VPC route tables — the destination subnet may not have a route.

    # ROUTING: Longest prefix match; ip route show; traceroute -n HOST
# Default route: 0.0.0.0/0 via GW; Static routes for specific subnets
    Explanation

    EHOSTUNREACH is unique because it comes from YOUR kernel, not from the remote host. Your machine looked at its routing table, couldn't find any entry matching the destination, and immediately returned the error — zero packets were sent. This is fundamentally different from "Connection timed out" where packets ARE sent but never acknowledged. Common causes in K8s: (1) The pod network CIDR isn't in the node's routing table (CNI not configured correctly). (2) The node's default route was deleted. (3) You're trying to reach an IP in a subnet that doesn't exist in your VPC. Fix is always local: add the missing ro">What are the 10 commands in the "First 5 Minutes" network checklist?

    Show Answer
    Answer

    (1) ip link show — interfaces UP? (2) ip -br addr show — correct IPs? (3) ip route show default — default route? (4) ip neigh show — ARP working? (5) dig +short kubernetes.default — DNS working? (6) ss -tlnp — what's listening? (7) iptables -L -n -v — firewall counters? (8) kubectl get pods -o wide — pods running? (9) dmesg -T | tail -30 — kernel errors? (10) curl localhost:8000/health — app responding?

    # KEY NETWORKING COMMANDS
# Interface: ip addr show; ip link set eth0 up; ethtool eth0
# Routing:   ip route show; traceroute -n HOST; mtr -r HOST
# Sockets:   ss -tlnp; ss -ulnp; lsof -i :PORT; nc -zv HOST PORT
# DNS:       dig +short DOMAIN; nslookup DOMAIN; host DOMAIN
# Firewall:  iptables -L -nv --line-numbers; nft list ruleset
# Capture:   tcpdump -i any -nn host IP or port NUM -w file.pcap
# TLS:       openssl s_client -connect HOST:443 -servername HOST
# HTTP:      curl -sv https://HOST/path -H "Header: value"
# K8s:       kubectl get svc,ep,netpol,ingress -A
# Debug:     L1(ip link)->L2(arping)->L3(ping)->L4(nc -zv)->L7(curl)
    Explanation

    This checklist covers 80% of network incidents. The order matters: you verify connectivity BEFORE checking the application. Running dmesg at step 9 catches the silent killers: conntrack table full, OOM killer terminating pods, NIC driver errors, and filesystem errors. The iptables -L -n -v at step 7 is crucial — the -v flag shows rule hit counters. If the rule blocking your traffic shows 0 hits, traffic isn't reaching that chain (wrong port/protocol). If it shows millions of hits, it's actively blocking traffic. Without counters, you can't distinguish "rule exists but not matching" from "rule actively blocking."

    Q5
    How do you definitively determine if a problem is "network" or "application"?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    Run the 3-step isolation test: (1) Local: curl localhost:PORT. Works = app is fine, problem is external. Fails = app problem. (2) Same-subnet: curl from another machine in the same subnet. Works = subnet-local networking is fine, problem is cross-subnet routing/firewall. Fails = host-level firewall or app config (listening on 127.0.0.1 only?). (3) Cross-subnet: curl from a different subnet. Works = full path OK. Fails = routing/firewall between subnets. This 3-step test definitively isolates the layer of failure.

    # KEY NETWORKING COMMANDS
# Interface: ip addr show; ip link set eth0 up; ethtool eth0
# Routing:   ip route show; traceroute -n HOST; mtr -r HOST
# Sockets:   ss -tlnp; ss -ulnp; lsof -i :PORT; nc -zv HOST PORT
# DNS:       dig +short DOMAIN; nslookup DOMAIN; host DOMAIN
# Firewall:  iptables -L -nv --line-numbers; nft list ruleset
# Capture:   tcpdump -i any -nn host IP or port NUM -w file.pcap
# TLS:       openssl s_client -connect HOST:443 -servername HOST
# HTTP:      curl -sv https://HOST/path -H "Header: value"
# K8s:       kubectl get svc,ep,netpol,ingress -A
# Debug:     L1(ip link)->L2(arping)->L3(ping)->L4(nc -zv)->L7(curl)
    Explanation

    This isolation test is the most powerful debugging technique that almost nobody uses systematically. Most engineers try random things — "let me check the SG, let me restart the pod, let me check the logs." The 3-step test gives you a definitive answer in 30 seconds. The critical insight is step 1: if curl localhost:8000 works, STOP looking at the application. The app is running, listening, and responding correctly. Every failure from another machine is a NETWORK problem — the app is innocent. At anihpj, if you can curl the health endpoint from within the pod but the ALB shows 503, the problem is between the ALB and the pod — check Security Groups, target group registration, and pod readiness.

    Q6
    How do you debug a scenario where ping works but HTTP/curl doesn't?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    Ping (ICMP) working means L3 is fine. The problem is at L4+. Debug: (1) nc -zv HOST PORT — does TCP connect? (2) ss -tlnp on target — is anything listening on that port? (3) Check firewall rules: iptables (filter table, not nat!), Security Groups, NetworkPolicy. (4) Check if the service is listening on 0.0.0.0 vs 127.0.0.1 (only local). (5) curl -v — does TCP handshake complete but HTTP hangs? → application stuck. ICMP is often allowed when TCP is blocked — never assume ping=everything works.

    <
    # TROUBLESHOOTING: L1(ip link, ethtool)->L2(arping, ip neigh)->L3(ping, traceroute)
# ->L4(ss, nc -zv)->L7(curl, dig, openssl); tcpdump -i any -nn host IP
    div class="eq-explanation">
    Explanation

    "Ping works but the app doesn't" is the classic L3-vs-L4 debugging scenario. ICMP (ping) and TCP use different protocols (IP protocol 1 vs 6). Firewalls often allow ICMP (for network diagnostics) while blocking TCP ports. Security Groups have separate rules for ICMP and TCP — an SG allowing ICMP from 0.0.0.0/0 does NOT allow TCP 8000. In K8s: NetworkPolicies that allow all ingress may still block specific ports. In cloud: NACLs are stateless — allowing outbound ICMP doesn't automatically allow inbound ICMP replies. At anihpj: if ping from the ALB to the EKS node works but health checks fail on port 8000, the issue is the EKS node SG doesn't allow TCP 8000 from the ALB SG. The fix: add the inbound TCP rule for port 8000.

    Q7
    What does `ss -ti` show? How do you use it for debugging?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    ss -ti shows TCP socket info: state (ESTAB, LISTEN, TIME_WAIT), RTT (round-trip time in ms), retransmits count, cwnd (congestion window), bytes_acked, and more. Debugging: High retransmits = packet loss (network congestion or bad hardware). High RTT = latency problem (far endpoint or network saturation). Tiny cwnd = TCP thinks the network is congested. TIME_WAIT buildup = app creating/destroying connections too fast. Use ss -ti state time-wait | wc -l to count TIME_WAIT sockets.

    # TROUBLESHOOTING: L1(ip link, ethtool)->L2(arping, ip neigh)->L3(ping, traceroute)
# ->L4(ss, nc -zv)->L7(curl, dig, openssl); tcpdump -i any -nn host IP
    Explanation

    ss -ti is the Swiss Army knife for transport-layer debugging. It shows TCP's internal state — information that TCP itself uses to make decisions but rarely exposes. The RTT field is gold: if ss -ti shows RTT=50ms for a connection to a service in the same VPC (should be < 1ms), your traffic is taking a strange path (maybe going through NAT Gateway and back?). The retransmits counter increments on every TCP retransmission — 0 is normal, 1-5 is concerning, 50+ on a single connection means severe packet loss. For anihpj: ss -ti | grep -A2 postgres shows the health of every DB connection — critical for diagnosing "the database is slow" complaints.

    Q8
    Users report "the website is down." Walk through your systematic debugging approach.
    Show Answer
    Answer

    (1) Verify scope: is it everyone or just one user/region? (2) DNS: dig api.anihpj.com — correct IP? (3) LB health: check ALB target group — healthy hosts? (4) K8s Service: kubectl get endpoints jobpost-service — any endpoints? (5) Pods: kubectl get pods — all running? (6) App: kubectl exec -it pod -- curl localhost:8000/health — responds? (7) Network: SG rules, route tables, NACLs allowing traffic? (8) Recent changes: kubectl get events --sort-by='.lastTimestamp' — any recent failures?

    # TROUBLESHOOT: L1(ethtool,ip link)->L2(arping,ip neigh)->L3(ping,traceroute)
# ->L4(ss,nc -zv)->L7(curl,dig,openssl); TCPdump: tcpdump -i any -nn host IP
    Explanation

    This is the systematic "outside-in" approach. Start from the user's perspective (DNS) and trace the request path inward. At each hop, you verify that hop is working before moving to the next. The ALB target group health is often the smoking gun: if all targets are unhealthy, the problem is at the pod level (app crashed, wrong port, readiness probe failing). If targets are healthy but users still can't connect, the problem is upstream (DNS pointing to wrong ALB, ALB security group blocking, or route53 misconfiguration). The kubectl get events at step 8 is crucial — K8s records important events (pod evictions, health check failures, resource pressure) that tell you WHAT happened before you even look at logs.

    Q9
    What is the difference between `ping`, `traceroute`, and `mtr`? When do you use each?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    ping: Tests L3 reachability. Measures RTT and packet loss. "Can I reach this host?" traceroute: Shows the path (each router hop) to the destination. "Which path do my packets take? Where do they stop?" mtr: Combines ping + traceroute continuously. Shows per-hop latency and packet loss over time. "Is this intermittent? Which hop is losing packets?" Use ping for quick reachability checks. Use traceroute when ping fails — find WHERE it fails. Use mtr for intermittent problems — continuous monitoring reveals the flapping hop.

    # ICMP: Type8=EchoReq, 0=EchoReply, 3=DestUnreach, 11=TTLexceeded
# ping tests L1-L3 only (does NOT test TCP ports!); mtr combines ping+traceroute
# traceroute: sends packets with TTL=1,2,3... reads ICMP Time Exceeded replies
    Explanation

    mtr is the most underrated network diagnostic tool. traceroute shows a single snapshot — if the problem is intermittent, you might get a clean trace while the issue is happening. mtr runs continuously, updating per-hop statistics every second. After 60 seconds of mtr, you see: hop 5 has 2% packet loss → that's your problem hop. Reading mtr output: Loss at a middle hop that DOESN'T propagate to later hops is normal (routers deprioritize ICMP replies). Loss that STARTS at hop N and continues through ALL subsequent hops = the problem is at hop N or between N-1 and N. For cloud debugging: traceroute across the internet is unreliable (ISPs filter ICMP). Use traceroute -T -p 443 (TCP SYN to port 443) instead — TCP packets are less likely to be filtered than ICMP.

    Q10
    [LAB 🛠️] A pod can't reach an external API at api.github.com. Walk through diagnosis using the layered approach.
    Show Answer
    Answer
    # L1: Is the pod's interface up?
kubectl exec -it jobpost-xxx -- ip link show eth0
# Look for: state UP

# L2: ARP working? (less relevant for external — gateway handles ARP)
kubectl exec -it jobpost-xxx -- ip neigh show

# L3: Can we reach the internet?
kubectl exec -it jobpost-xxx -- ping -c 3 8.8.8.8
# Fails → routing or NAT issue. Check:
kubectl exec -it jobpost-xxx -- ip route show
# Should have default route via node or CNI gateway

# L3b: DNS resolution?
kubectl exec -it jobpost-xxx -- nslookup api.github.com
# Fails → CoreDNS issue. Check CoreDNS pods and /etc/resolv.conf

# L4: Can we connect to port 443?
kubectl exec -it jobpost-xxx -- nc -zv api.github.com 443
# Timeout → firewall blocking outbound 443. Check:
# - NAT Gateway (private subnet needs NAT for internet)
# - Security Group outbound rules
# - NetworkPolicy egress rules

# L7: HTTPS working?
kubectl exec -it jobpost-xxx -- curl -v https://api.github.com
# Shows exactly where the failure occurs
    Explanation

    This is the real-world layered debugging applied to Kubernetes. The most common cause at L3: the pod is in a private subnet with no NAT Gateway route. The ping 8.8.8.8 test is definitive — if ICMP to a public IP fails, you have no internet route. The second most common cause at L3b: CoreDNS is down or misconfigured. Test with nslookup — if it hangs, CoreDNS is unreachable (check kube-dns service and CoreDNS pod status). If nslookup returns NXDOMAIN, DNS is working but the domain doesn't exist (or CoreDNS upstream is wrong). The third most common at L4: NetworkPolicy blocking egress. By default, K8s allows all egress — if someone added a deny-all egress NetworkPolicy, pods lose internet access. Check kubectl get networkpolicies -A.

    Chapter 31: Common Network Failure Scenarios — Full Walk-Throughs

    Theory is important, but real debugging happens when something is broken right now. This chapter walks through 5 of the most common network failure scenarios in production — each with the exact commands, expected output, diagnostic reasoning, and the final fix. These are based on real incidents every SRE encounters.

    🟡 Intermediate⏱️ ~2 hours🐞 Debugging🔥 Real Incidents

    🎯 What You'll Learn

    • ✅ Scenario 1: Pod can't reach the database — K8s Service + NetworkPolicy debugging
    • ✅ Scenario 2: External users can't reach the app — DNS → LB → K8s path tracing
    • ✅ Scenario 3: Intermittent timeouts — conntrack, MTU, TCP retransmit analysis
    • ✅ Scenario 4: DNS failures inside K8s — CoreDNS debugging and config validation
    • ✅ Scenario 5: TLS certificate errors — openssl chain validation and common pitfalls

    31.1 Scenario 1: "The Pod Can't Reach the Database"

    🐞 Incident: Django app returns "could not connect to server: Connection refused"
      SYMPTOMS:
  • jobpost pods restarting with "OperationalError: could not connect to server"
  • kubectl logs jobpost-xxx shows: "Is the server running on host
    postgres-service.anihpj.svc.cluster.local and accepting TCP/IP
    connections on port 5432?"

  DEBUG WALK-THROUGH:

  STEP 1 — Test connectivity from the pod:
  kubectl exec -it jobpost-xxx -- nc -zv postgres-service 5432
  # OUTPUT: nc: connect to postgres-service port 5432 (tcp) failed: Connection refused
  # ANALYSIS: Connection REFUSED → RST received → the host is reachable but
  # nothing is listening on port 5432, OR the service name resolves to wrong IP

  STEP 2 — Verify DNS resolution:
  kubectl exec -it jobpost-xxx -- nslookup postgres-service
  # OUTPUT: Name: postgres-service.anihpj.svc.cluster.local
  #         Address: 10.96.50.100
  # ANALYSIS: DNS resolves correctly. Check if this ClusterIP has endpoints.

  STEP 3 — Check K8s Service endpoints:
  kubectl get endpoints postgres-service
  # OUTPUT: NAME               ENDPOINTS     AGE
  #         postgres-service           5d
  # ANALYSIS: NO ENDPOINTS! The Service selector doesn't match any pods.

  STEP 4 — Check the Service selector vs pod labels:
  kubectl get svc postgres-service -o jsonpath='{.spec.selector}'
  # OUTPUT: {"app":"postgres","tier":"database"}
  kubectl get pods -l app=postgres,tier=database
  # OUTPUT: No resources found.
  # ANALYSIS: The pod labels don't match. Check actual pod labels.

  STEP 5 — Check actual pod labels:
  kubectl get pods -l app=postgres --show-labels
  # OUTPUT: postgres-xxx   app=postgres,tier=db  (NOT "database"!)
  # ROOT CAUSE: Service selector says tier=database but pod label says tier=db.
  # FIX: Update Service selector to tier=db, OR pod label to tier=database.

  kubectl patch svc postgres-service --type=json -p \
    '[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/selector/tier","value":"db"}]'
  kubectl get endpoints postgres-service
  # OUTPUT: NAME               ENDPOINTS           AGE
  #         postgres-service   10.244.2.15:5432    5d
  # ✅ FIXED: Service now has endpoints!
    ⚠️ Alternative Root Causes for "Pod Can't Reach Database"

    Cause 2 — NetworkPolicy blocking: kubectl get networkpolicies -A — if a deny-all or restrictive egress policy exists, pods can't reach the DB. Test: kubectl exec -it jobpost-xxx -- nc -zv 10.244.2.15 5432 (use pod IP directly, bypassing Service). If direct IP works but Service doesn't → Service issue. If neither works → NetworkPolicy or firewall. Cause 3 — PostgreSQL not listening on all interfaces: PostgreSQL's listen_addresses might be set to localhost instead of *. Check: kubectl exec -it postgres-xxx -- psql -c "SHOW listen_addresses;". Cause 4 — Wrong namespace: The Service name postgres-service without namespace suffix resolves within the same namespace. If the DB is in namespace data and the app is in anihpj, you need postgres-service.data.svc.cluster.local. Cause 5 — PostgreSQL connection limit: kubectl exec -it postgres-xxx -- psql -c "SELECT count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity;" — if count = max_connections (default 100), new connections are rejected.

    31.2 Scenario 2: "External Users Can't Reach the App"

    🐞 Incident: "https://api.anihpj.com is down" — users seeing 503 or timeout
      DEBUG WALK-THROUGH (Outside-In):

  STEP 1 — DNS check:
  dig api.anihpj.com +short
  # OUTPUT: 34.120.45.67
  # Quick check: is this the ALB IP? If it changed recently, DNS cache
  # might be stale (TTL too high). If NO answer → DNS record deleted!

  STEP 2 — LB health check (AWS ALB):
  aws elbv2 describe-target-health --target-group-arn arn:aws:elasticloadbalancing:...
  # OUTPUT: "TargetHealth": {"State": "unhealthy", "Reason": "Health checks failed"}
  # ANALYSIS: All targets unhealthy. LB has no backends to send traffic to.

  STEP 3 — Check K8s Service:
  kubectl get svc jobpost-service
  # OUTPUT: TYPE=ClusterIP, CLUSTER-IP=10.96.0.10, PORT=8000
  kubectl get endpoints jobpost-service
  # OUTPUT: 10.244.1.5:8000,10.244.2.8:8000,10.244.3.12:8000
  # ANALYSIS: Service has endpoints. Pods exist. Why are they unhealthy?

  STEP 4 — Check pod health:
  kubectl get pods -l app=jobpost
  # OUTPUT: All Running, but READY shows 0/1 for 2 of 3 pods
  kubectl describe pod jobpost-xxx | grep -A10 "Conditions:"
  # OUTPUT: Ready: False. Readiness probe failed: HTTP probe returned 500

  STEP 5 — Check the readiness probe:
  kubectl get pod jobpost-xxx -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[0].readinessProbe}'
  # OUTPUT: {"httpGet":{"path":"/api/health/","port":8000},"periodSeconds":10}
  # The /api/health/ endpoint returns 500 → pod not ready → removed from endpoints

  STEP 6 — Check the health endpoint:
  kubectl exec -it jobpost-xxx -- curl localhost:8000/api/health/
  # OUTPUT: {"status":"unhealthy","database":"disconnected"}
  # ROOT CAUSE: The app can't connect to its database, so health check fails.
  # Follow Scenario 1 to debug database connectivity.
  # FIX: Restore DB connectivity → health check passes → pod becomes Ready →
  # endpoints populated → ALB health check passes → service restored.
    🔗 The Full Request Path — Every Hop That Can Fail

    User → DNS (Route53) → ALB (internet-facing) → Target Group → K8s NodePort/Ingress → Service (ClusterIP) → kube-proxy/iptables → Pod (veth). Each hop is a potential failure point: (1) DNS: wrong record, expired domain, Route53 health check failing. (2) ALB: security group blocking, TLS cert expired, listener rule misconfigured. (3) Target Group: health checks failing (wrong path, wrong port, timeout), targets deregistered. (4) K8s Service: no endpoints (label mismatch), wrong port, type=ClusterIP not NodePort/LoadBalancer. (5) Pod: readiness probe failing, app crashed, OOMKilled, resource limits. Systematic approach: ALWAYS test each hop independently. curl the pod IP directly (bypasses Service). curl the Service ClusterIP (bypasses LB). curl the ALB DNS (full path). This isolates exactly which hop is broken.

    31.3 Scenario 3: "Intermittent Timeouts Between Services"

    🐞 Incident: 5xx errors appearing randomly, lasting 1-2 minutes, then disappearing
      SYMPTOMS:
  • Grafana shows 5xx spikes every 15-30 minutes
  • "upstream connect error or disconnect/reset before headers"
  • No pod restarts, no OOMKills, CPU/memory normal

  DEBUG WALK-THROUGH:

  STEP 1 — Check TCP retransmits (THE smoking gun for intermittent issues):
  # On the node where the client pod runs:
  ss -ti | grep -B1 retrans
  # OUTPUT: retrans:5/12    ← 5 retransmitted segments out of 12 sent!
  # ANALYSIS: 41% retrans rate — severe packet loss. Normal is <0.1%.

  STEP 2 — Check NIC statistics for drops:
  ethtool -S eth0 | grep -E "drop|err|discard"
  # OUTPUT: rx_dropped: 0  tx_dropped: 0  (NIC level is clean)
  # The drops are happening at a higher layer.

  STEP 3 — Check conntrack table:
  conntrack -C
  # OUTPUT: 65432 (current count)
  cat /proc/sys/net/netfilter/nf_conntrack_max
  # OUTPUT: 65536
  # ANALYSIS: Conntrack table is 99.8% full! Any new connection triggers
  # "nf_conntrack: table full, dropping packet" → random timeouts!

  dmesg -T | grep "table full" | tail -5
  # OUTPUT: [timestamp] nf_conntrack: table full, dropping packet
  # CONFIRMED: Conntrack table overflow is the root cause.

  STEP 4 — Identify what's consuming connections:
  conntrack -L -p tcp | awk

    Exam Weight: MEDIUM (5-8% of questions)
    📋 Must Memorize
    • 3-tier: Access(distribution)→’Aggregation→’Core (traditional DC)
    • Spine-Leaf: every leaf connects to every spine (modern DC, equal-cost paths)
    • Hub-and-Spoke: central hub connects all sites (VPN, transit gateway)
    • Mesh: full(expensive) vs partial(selective peering)
    ⚠️ Common Traps
    • Oversubscription ratio: access-to-aggregation (3:1 to 20:1 typical)
    • East-West traffic dominates in modern DCs (spine-leaf optimized for this)
    • Single points of failure in hub-and-spoke (hub redundancy critical)
    • ECMP: equal-cost multi-path for load distribution across parallel links
    🔧 Quick Commands
