    31.4 Scenario 4: "DNS Resolution Fails Inside Kubernetes"

    🐞 Incident: Pods can't resolve service names — "Name or service not known"
      SYMPTOMS:
  • kubectl exec -it pod -- nslookup kubernetes.default → "server can't find..."
  • Pods can ping IPs but not resolve hostnames
  • New pods affected, old pods still working (DNS cache)

  DEBUG WALK-THROUGH:

  STEP 1 — Test DNS from a debug pod:
  kubectl run -it --rm debug --image=busybox -- nslookup kubernetes.default
  # OUTPUT: ;; connection timed out; no servers could be reached
  # ANALYSIS: DNS server is completely unreachable.

  STEP 2 — Check CoreDNS pods:
  kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns
  # OUTPUT: coredns-xxx 0/1 CrashLoopBackOff
  # ANALYSIS: CoreDNS is down! Check logs.

  kubectl logs -n kube-system coredns-xxx
  # OUTPUT: "plugin/loop: Loop (127.0.0.1:xxxxx → :53) detected for zone '.'
  #          ... CoreDNS detects a forwarding loop and shuts down"
  # ROOT CAUSE: CoreDNS config has a forwarding loop — it forwards to itself!

  STEP 3 — Check CoreDNS ConfigMap:
  kubectl get configmap -n kube-system coredns -o yaml
  # Look for the forward directive:
  # forward . /etc/resolv.conf  ← This forwards to the node's /etc/resolv.conf
  # If the node's resolv.conf points to 127.0.0.1 (which goes back to CoreDNS)
  # → infinite loop → CoreDNS crashes.

  ALTERNATIVE ROOT CAUSES:
  • CoreDNS pods evicted (node resource pressure)
  • kube-dns Service IP changed (check: kubectl get svc -n kube-system kube-dns)
  • NetworkPolicy blocking UDP port 53 to kube-system namespace
  • Node's /etc/resolv.conf has unreachable upstream DNS servers

  FIX: Update CoreDNS ConfigMap to forward to a valid external DNS:
  kubectl edit configmap -n kube-system coredns
  # Change: forward . 8.8.8.8 1.1.1.1  (or your VPC DNS resolver .2)

    31.5 Scenario 5: "TLS Certificate Errors"

    🐞 Incident: curl fails with "SSL certificate problem: unable to get local issuer certificate"
      SYMPTOMS:
  • curl https://api.anihpj.com → certificate error
  • Browser shows "NET::ERR_CERT_AUTHORITY_INVALID"
  • Worked fine yesterday, no config changes

  DEBUG WALK-THROUGH:

  STEP 1 — Inspect the certificate chain:
  openssl s_client -connect api.anihpj.com:443 -showcerts
  # OUTPUT: Shows the server certificate and intermediate certificates.
  # Look for: "verify error:num=21:unable to verify the first certificate"
  # This means the certificate chain is INCOMPLETE — intermediate certs missing.

  STEP 2 — Check certificate details:
  echo | openssl s_client -connect api.anihpj.com:443 2>/dev/null | \
    openssl x509 -noout -dates -subject -issuer
  # OUTPUT:
  # notBefore=Jan 10 00:00:00 2025 GMT
  # notAfter=Apr 10 23:59:59 2026 GMT  ← NOT expired
  # subject=CN=api.anihpj.com  ← Correct hostname
  # issuer=CN=R3,O=Let's Encrypt,C=US  ← Let's Encrypt intermediate

  STEP 3 — Verify the full chain (local file check):
  openssl verify -CAfile /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt cert.pem
  # OUTPUT: cert.pem: CN=api.anihpj.com
  #         error 20 at 0 depth lookup: unable to get local issuer certificate
  # ANALYSIS: The certificate file is missing the intermediate certificate(s).
  # The server only sent the leaf cert + one intermediate, but the root CA
  # is missing from the 
    # K8s POD NETWORKING: Shared net namespace, veth pair to cni0 bridge
# kubectl exec POD -- ip addr; All containers in pod share localhost
    chain OR the intermediate is wrong.

  COMMON ROOT CAUSES:
  • Intermediate certificate NOT included in the server config
    (nginx: ssl_certificate should include full chain, not just leaf)
  • Certificate EXPIRED (check notAfter date — Let's Encrypt = 90 days!)
  • Wrong hostname in certificate (CN or SAN doesn't match the URL)
  • System clock skew (cert appears expired because clock is wrong)
  • Root CA not trusted by client (self-signed or internal CA)
  • ALB/Ingress has old certificate ARN while ACM auto-renewed

  FIX: Ensure the full chain is served:
  # For nginx: cat server.crt intermediate.crt > fullchain.pem
  # For ALB: ACM handles this automatically — check the correct cert ARN
  # For Let's Encrypt: certbot renew --dry-run to test auto-renewal
    🔍 dig Deep Dive — Understanding Every Line of Output

    dig is the definitive DNS diagnostic tool. Understanding its full output is essential for debugging any name resolution issue. Key sections: (1) HEADER: status: NOERROR (success), NXDOMAIN (domain doesn't exist), SERVFAIL (DNS server error). flags: qr aa rd ra — qr=query response, aa=authoritative answer, rd=recursion desired, ra=recursion available. (2) QUESTION SECTION: What you asked for. (3) ANSWER SECTION: The actual records. 300 IN A 10.0.1.50 — 300s TTL, INternet class, A record. (4) AUTHORITY SECTION: Which nameservers are authoritative for this domain. Appears for referrals. (5) ADDITIONAL SECTION: Glue records — IPs of the authoritative nameservers. Essential dig flags: +short (just the answer), +trace (follow dugging pattern: dig +trace api.anihpj.com shows every delegation step — if it stops at a nameserver, that's where the problem is. dig api.anihpj.com @10.0.0.2 tests VPC DNS resolver directly. Compare results from different resolvers to isolate DNS vs. app issues.

    For anUse the status code to jump directly to the right debugging layer.

    ⏱️ curl -w Timing Breakdown — The Network vs App Split in One Command
    200ms, OCSP/CRL issue. TTFB (server):0.250s ← App processing time: 250ms - 12ms = 238ms for app. Total Time: 0.250s ← Total user experience. THE NETWORK-APP SPLIT: Network time = DNS + TCP + TLS = 5 + 12 + 23 = 40ms App time = TTFB - TCP = 250 - 12 = 238ms App is responsible for 85% of latency → debug the application, not the network. If TCP Connect is 2000ms but TTFB is also ~2000ms → network is 99% of latency. If TCP Connect is 5ms but TTFB is 5000ms → app is the problem (DB query, etc).

    📝 Chapter 31 — Networking Practice Questions

    Q1
    Your pod gets "Connection refused" when connecting to postgres-service. K8s endpoints show ``. What's the most likely cause?
    Show Answer
    # K8s POD NET: Shared net namespace(same IP+ports), veth pair to cni0 bridge on node
# kubectl exec POD -- ip addr; All containers in pod share localhost:PORT
    Q2
    Users report 503 errors from the ALB. K8s pods are Running. What's the debug flow?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    (1) Check ALB target group health: aws elbv2 describe-target-health — are targets healthy? (2) Check K8s Service endpoints: kubectl get endpoints — populated? (3) Check pod readiness: kubectl get pods — READY column 1/1? (4) Test locally: kubectl exec -it pod -- curl localhost:8000/health — responds? (5) Check SG: does EKS node SG allow inbound from ALB SG on the target port? Most common: readiness probe failing → pod removed from endpoints → target group unhealthy.

    Explanation

    ALB 503 means the LB has no healthy targets. The chain of responsibility: ALB → Target Group → registered targets → K8s pods. At each hop, health is independently verified. The ALB checks the target group's health check path. The target group registers pod IPs (in IP mode)

    # K8s POD NET: Shared net namespace(same IP+ports), veth pair to cni0 bridge on node
# kubectl exec POD -- ip addr; All containers in pod share localhost:PORT
    . The pod is registered only if its readiness probe passes. So 503 cascade: readiness probe fails → pod removed from Service endpoints →
    # K8s POD NETWORKING: Shared net namespace, veth pair to cni0 bridge
# kubectl exec POD -- ip addr; All containers in pod share localhost
    AWS Load Balancer Controller removes pod IP from target group → target group shows unhealthy → ALB returns 503. Fix the readiness probe and everything recovers automatically. No manual intervention needed at the ALB level.

    Q3
    Your services have intermittent 5xx errors every 15 minutes. Pods are healthy. What's likely happening?
    Show Answer
    # K8s POD NET: Shared net namespace(same IP+ports), veth pair to cni0 bridge on node # kubectl exec POD -- ip addr; All containers in pod share localhost:PORT class="eq-answer-label">Answer

    Intermittent failures with healthy pods point to infrastructure: (1) Conntrack table full — check conntrack -C and dmesg | grep "table full". (2) MTU mismatch — VXLAN/Geneve encapsulation adds 50+ bytes overhead, packets >1500 MTU get fragmented/dropped. (3) Network saturation — check ethtool -S for drops, ss -ti for retransmits. (4) kube-proxy iptables rule sync — at scale, iptables-restore takes seconds, blocking new connections. (5) DNS intermittent failures — CoreDNS pod restarting or upstream timeout.

    Explanation

    Intermittent failures are the hardest to debug because they're gone by the time you investigate. The key is to catch them in the act. For conntrack: the failures happen exactly when the table hits max capacity, then existing connections expire, making room, and everything works again — until it fills up again. The pattern is a sawtooth: 5 minutes of failures, 10 minutes of success, repeat. For MTU issues: large HTTP responses (with big payloads)

    # SOCKET STATS: ss -tlnp(TCP listening), ss -ulnp(UDP listening), ss -tpn(connections)
# ss -s(summary); lsof -i :PORT; /proc/net/tcp
    get fragmented while small requests succeed — users see "sometimes images don't load" or "large file uploads fail." Use ping -M do -s 1472 <target> to test MTU (1472 + 28 ICMP/IP headers = 1500). If it fails, reduce by 50 for VXLAN overhead.

    Q4
    CoreDNS pods are in CrashLoopBackOff. What are the likely causes and fixes?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    (1) Loop detection: CoreDNS detects it's forwarding to itself (node resolv.conf → 127.0.0.1 → CoreDNS → loop). Fix: change ConfigMap forward to external DNS (8.8.8.8, VPC .2). (2) OOMKilled: Too many DNS queries, CoreDNS memory limit too low. Fix: increase memory limit. (3) ConfigMap syntax error: Invalid Corefile syntax. Fix: validate with coredns -dns.port=1053 -conf Corefile. (4) Node pressure: Node has no CPU/memory to schedule CoreDNS pods. Fix: add nodes or reduce other workloads. (5) Broken plugin: Custom plugin causing panic. Check logs.

    Explanation

    The loop detection is the most common CoreDNS failure — and the most confusing because the logs clearly say "loop detected" but engineers don't know what it means. Here's the cycle: pod queries CoreDNS → CoreDNS looks at its Corefile → forward rule says "use /etc/resolv.conf" → node's resolv.conf has nameserver 127.0.0.1 (which IS CoreDNS!) → CoreDNS forwards to itself → detects loop after 10 iterations → shuts down with "Loop detected." The fix is to change the forward destination to an external resolver. For EKS: use the VPC .2 resolver (forward . 10.0.0.2) for internal+external resolution. Add policy: random for cache distribution and health plugin for liveness probe.

    Q5
    curl fails with "SSL certificate problem." The cert isn't expired. What else could be wrong?
    Show Answer
    Answer# HTTP: GET/POST /path HTTP/1.1 + Host/Authorization headers -> 200 OK + JSON body # curl -sv https://HOST/api/endpoint | jq .>

    (1) Missing intermediate cert: Server only sends leaf cert, not full chain. Browser may cache intermediates, curl doesn't. Fix: concatenate leaf + intermediate into fullchain.pem. (2) Wrong hostname: Certificate CN/SAN doesn't match the URL you're curling. Check with openssl s_client -connect 

    # SOCKET STATS: ss -tlnp(TCP listening), -ulnp(UDP listening), -tpn(all connections)
# ss -s(summary); lsof -i :PORT; cat /proc/net/tcp /proc/net/udp
    HOST:443 | openssl x509 -text | grep DNS:. (3) System clock skew: Cert appears expired/not-yet-valid because clock is wrong. Check date. (4) Untrusted CA: Self-signed or internal CA not in trust store. Use curl --cacert ca.pem or add to system trust store.

    Explanation

    TLS errors are almost always one of four things: expired, wrong hostname, missing intermediate, or untrusted CA. The diagnostic tool is openssl s_client -showcerts. Look at the output carefully: if you see "verify error:num=21:unable to verify the first certificate" — that's a missing intermediate. If you see "verify error:num=10:certificate has expired" — check the clock AND the cert dates. Pro tip: run openssl s_client -connect HOST:443 to auto-close the connection (non-interactive). For anihpj: if using ACM on ALB, the cert auto-renews but you must use the SAME cert ARN — ACM creates a new cert ARN on renewal, so your infrastructure must reference the new ARN or use aws acm list-certificates to find the latest.

    Q6
    How do you test if a K8s NetworkPolicy is blocking traffic between two pods?<
    # HTTP: REQUEST=GET/POST /path HTTP/1.1\nHost+Auth headers\nRESPONSE=200 OK + JSON/HTML
# curl -sv https://HOST/api -H "Authorization: Bearer TOKEN" | jq .
# Status: 2xx=OK, 3xx=redirect, 4xx=client err, 5xx=server err
    /div>
    Show Answer
    Answer

    (1) List all NetworkPolicies: kubectl get networkpolicies -A. (2) Test connectivity directly: kubectl exec -it pod-a -- nc -zv <pod-b-ip> <port>. (3) If it fails, temporarily create an allow-all policy to confirm it's a policy issue: kubectl apply -f allow-all.yaml. (4) Describe the suspect policy: kubectl describe networkpolicy <name> — check podSelector, ingress/egress rules, namespaceSelector. (5) Verify pod labels match the policy's podSelector. (6) With Calico/Cilium: use calicoctl get networkpolicy or Hubble to see denied flows.

    Explanation

    NetworkPolicy debugging is label-matching puzzle. A NetworkPolicy with podSelector: {app: jobpost} applies to pods with label app=jobpost. If your pod has app: jobpost-api instead, the policy doesn't apply. The ingress.from.namespaceSelector and ingress.from.podSelector combine with AND logic: BOTH must match. The temporary allow-all test is the quickest way to confirm it's a policy issue — create an allow-all ingress policy, test again, if it works → your original policy is too restrictive. For anihpj: always have a "break-glass" allow-all NetworkPolicy in your toolkit for emergency debugging. Apply it, verify it fixes the issue, then refine the real policy.

    Q7
    What does `
    # MTU: Ethernet=1500, Jumbo=9000, VXLAN overhead=50->inner MTU=1450
# PMTU black hole: ICMP frag-needed blocked->TCP stalls; ping -M do -s 1472 HOST
    ss -ti` show, and how do you interpret retrans:5/12?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    ss -ti shows per-socket TCP information. retrans:5/12 means 5 segments retransmitted out of 12 sent — a 41% retransmission rate. Normal is 0 or < 1%. High retransmits mean: severe packet loss (congestion, bad hardware, MTU mismatch), or the remote endpoint is unreachable and TCP keeps retrying. Other key fields: rtt:2.5/1.2 (current RTT 2.5ms, variance 1.2ms), cwnd:10 (congestion window = 10 segments — TCP is throttled), bytes_acked:1234567 (how much data was acknowledged).

    Explanation

    TCP retransmits at the socket level are the definitive indicator of network packet loss. You can have 0 interface errors and 0 switch port errors but STILL see TCP retransmits — the loss is happening somewhere beyond your visibility (upstream router, internet congestion, remote host dropping packets). ss -ti gives you per-connection granularity: which specific connection is suffering? Filter with grep: ss -ti | grep -B1 "retrans:". If ALL connections to the same destination show high retransmits, the problem is in the path. If only ONE connection shows high retransmits, the problem is that connection's specific traffic pattern or the remote host's handling of that connection.

    Q8
    Walk through debugging "Connection timed out" from a pod to an external API.
    Show Answer
    Answer

    (1) Test with nc -zv api.example.com 443 or direct IP. (2) If direct IP works but hostname fails → DNS issue. (3) If both fail → check routing: ip route get 8.8.8.8 — default route exists? (4) Check NAT: is the pod in a private subnet with a NAT Gateway route? (5) Check egress firewall: SG outbound rules, NACL outbound, NetworkPolicy egress. (6) Check if it's ALL external or just this API: ping 8.8.8.8 — if ICMP works but TCP 443 doesn't → firewall allowing ICMP but not TCP 443. (7) Check if the external API has IP allowlisting — your NAT Gateway IP might not be whitelisted.

    Explanation

    External connectivity debugging adds the NAT layer. Private subnets have no direct internet — traffic must go through a NAT Gateway (AWS) or Cloud NAT (GCP). If the route table for the pod's subnet doesn't have 0.0.0.0/0 → NAT Gateway, the pod has NO internet route. Also check: does the NAT Gateway have an Elastic IP? Is the NAT Gateway in a PUBLIC subnet (must be for internet access)? Many "can't reach external API" issues are actually "NAT Gateway is misconfigured" issues. For anihpj: EKS pods in private subnets → NAT Gateway in public subnet → internet. If the NAT Gateway is in a private subnet, it can't reach the internet either.

    Q9
    What is MTU mismatch? How does it cause intermittent failures, and how do you detect it?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    MTU (Maximum Transmission Unit) mismatch occurs when a packet is larger than a hop's MTU. With DF (Don't Fragment) set, the router drops it and sends ICMP "Fragmentation Needed." If ICMP is blocked (common in cloud), the packet is silently dropped. Why intermittent: Only LARGE packets are dropped — small requests succeed, large responses fail. Detection: ping -M do -s 1472 <target> (increment -s until it fails). VXLAN overhead = 50 bytes, so effective MTU = 1450 instead of 1500. Fix: reduce pod MTU (ip link set eth0 mtu 1450) or enable TCP MSS clamping on the CNI.

    Explanation

    MTU issues are the silent killer of overlay networks. VXLAN adds 50 bytes of header (8 VXLAN + 8 UDP + 20 IP + 14 Ethernet). If your physical network MTU is 1500, packets from the pod (also 1500) become 1550 after encapsulation — too big. The router drops them, but if ICMP "fragmentation needed" messages are filtered (AWS drops ICMP between subnets in some configurations), TCP never learns about the MTU and keeps retransmitting the full-size packet. This is called a "PMTUD black hole" (Path MTU Discovery black hole). Symptoms: SSH works fine (small packets), but curl for large pages hangs or times out. TLS handshake works (small), but large HTTP responses fail. Fix for EKS: the AWS VPC CNI can automatically set pod MTU — enable AWS_VPC_K8S_CNI_EXTERNALSNAT=true and set pod MTU to 9001 (AWS Jumbo Frames supported on VPC).

    Q10
    [LAB 🛠️] Users report "the app is slow." You have 5 minutes to identify if it's a network or application problem. Walk through your approach.
    Show Answer
    Answer
    # MINUTE 1 — Quick network health check:
ip link show | grep DOWN     # Any interfaces down?
ping -c 5 8.8.8.8           # Packet loss?
ss -ti | grep retrans       # TCP retransmits?

# MINUTE 2 — Application-level latency:
curl -w "@curl-format.txt" -o /dev/null -s http://localhost:8000/api/jobs/
# curl-format.txt:
# time_namelookup: %{time_namelookup}\n
# time_connect: %{time_connect}\n
# time_starttransfer: %{time_starttransfer}\n
# time_total: %{time_total}\n
# If time_connect > 100ms → network latency
# If time_starttransfer - time_connect > 1s → app processing time
# If time_total is high but time_connect is low → app problem!

# MINUTE 3 — Check database latency:
kubectl exec -it jobpost-xxx -- time nc -zv postgres-service 5432

# MINUTE 4 — Check resource saturation:
top -bn1 | head -5          # CPU saturation?
free -h                     # Memory pressure?
df -h                       # Disk full?

# MINUTE 5 — Recent changes:
kubectl get events -n anihpj --sort-by='.lastTimestamp' | tail -20
    Explanation

    The curl -w timing breakdown is the single most powerful "network vs app" diagnostic. time_namelookup: DNS resolution time (DNS problem?). time_connect: TCP handshake time (network RTT). time_starttransfer: time to first byte (app processing + network). time_total: total time. If time_connect is 5ms but time_starttransfer is 2000ms, the network is fast (5ms to connect), but the app took 1995ms to start responding — the problem IS the application (slow DB query, thread pool exhaustion, GC pause). If time_connect is 2000ms, the network is slow — check routing, MTU, congestion. This one-liner gives you a definitive split between network time and app time in 2 seconds.

    Chapter 32: Network Performance Analysis & Tuning

    "The network is slow" is the most common — and least useful — complaint. Slow compared to what? This chapter teaches you how to MEASURE network performance objectively, understand what "fast" means at each layer, and tune Linux TCP settings for production workloads. You'll learn to use iperf3, measure bandwidth-delay product, and optimize TCP congestion control.

    🔴 Advanced⏱️ ~1.5 hours📈 Performance⚡ Tuning

    🎯 What You'll Learn

    • ✅ The components of network latency — propagation, serialization, queuing, processing
    • ✅ Bandwidth-Delay Product — why more bandwidth doesn't fix latency problems
    • ✅ iperf3, mtr, httping, qperf — measuring real network performance between hosts
    • ✅ TCP tuning for production — BBR congestion control, buffer sizes, TCP Fast Open
    • ✅ Kernel sysctl parameters that dramatically affect network performance

    32.1 Understanding Network Latency

    Latency is NOT a single number. It's the sum of four independent components. Understanding each one tells you WHERE to optimize — and what you CAN'T optimize.

    The Four Components of Network Latency
      TOTAL LATENCY = Propagation + Serialization + Queuing + Processing

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                       │
  │  PROPAGATION DELAY  (physics — you CAN'T beat the speed of light)    │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ Light in fiber: ~200,000 km/s (2/3 of vacuum speed)             │ │
  │  │ New York → London (5,500 km): ~27ms ONE WAY (55ms RTT minimum)  │ │
  │  │ Same AZ (1 km): ~0.005ms — essentially zero                     │ │
  │  │ Cross-region (US East → US West, 4,500 km): ~22ms one way      │ │
  │  │ RULE: ~1ms RTT per 100 km of fiber distance                     │ │
  │  │ VERDICT: You can't change this. Design around it.               │ │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                       │
  │  SERIALIZATION DELAY  (how fast bits go onto the wire)               │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ 1500-byte packet: 1 Gbps → 12µs | 100 Mbps → 120µs | 10 Mbps → │ │
  │  │ 1.2ms. At 10 Gbps+, serialization is negligible (< 1µs).        │ │
  │  │ VERDICT: Almost never the bottleneck in cloud (1-10 Gbps links).│ │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                       │
  │  QUEUING DELAY  (packets waiting in buffers at routers/switches)     │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ When a link is saturated, packets queue. Queue depth × serial-  │ │
  │  │ ization time = queuing delay. At 90% utilization, queuing delay │ │
  │  │ can be 10x serialization delay. At 99% = 100x.                  │ │
  │  │ VERDICT: The #1 cause of "the network is slow." Fix congestion. │ │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                       │
  │  PROCESSING DELAY  (router/switch CPU time per packet)               │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ Modern routers process packets in ASIC hardware at line rate     │ │
  │  │ (microseconds). Software firewalls (iptables, proxies) add more. │ │
  │  │ VERDICT: Negligible in cloud unless you added software hops.    │ │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    📐 Bandwidth-Delay Product — Why More Bandwidth Doesn't Fix Latency

    The Bandwidth-Delay Product (BDP) is the amount of data "in flight" at any moment: BDP = bandwidth × RTT. For a 1 Gbps link with 50ms RTT: BDP = 1,000,000,000 × 0.05 = 50,000,000 bits = ~6.25 MB. This means 6.25 MB of data is in transit before the sender sees the first ACK. Why this matters: TCP's congestion window (cwnd) limits how much unacknowledged data can be in flight. If cwnd < BDP, the sender is IDLE waiting for ACKs — the link is underutilized. Adding bandwidth makes this WORSE: at 10 Gbps with 50ms RTT, BDP = 62 MB — TCP needs a huge cwnd to fill the pipe. The practical impact: For cross-region database replication (50ms RTT), a single TCP connection can never exceed ~500 Mbps regardless of available bandwidth — unless you tune TCP buffers. Solution: Use multiple parallel connections (iperf3 -P 10), enable BBR congestion control (better at filling high-BDP pipes), or increase TCP buffer sizes (tcp_rmem/tcp_wmem).

    32.2 Measuring Network Performance — Tools & Techniques

    📏
    iperf3 — Bandwidth Testing

    Server: iperf3 -s. Client: iperf3 -c <server-ip> -P 10 -t 30 (10 parallel streams, 30s test). Shows: throughput (Gbps), retransmits, CPU utilization. Single-stream (-P 1) tests TCP window behavior. Multi-stream (-P 10) tests aggregate throughput. In K8s: kubectl run iperf-server --image=networkstatic/iperf3 -- -s then kubectl run -it iperf-client --rm --image=networkstatic/iperf3 -- -c <server-pod-ip>.

    🛤️
    mtr — Continuous Path Monitoring

    mtr -r -c 100 <target> (100 pings per hop, report mode). Shows per-hop loss% and latency. Unlike traceroute's single snapshot, mtr reveals intermittent problems. Reading: loss at hop N that doesn't continue to N+1 → router deprioritizing ICMP (ignore). Loss at hop N that continues through all subsequent hops → real problem at hop N.

    🌐
    httping — HTTP-Level Latency

    httping -c 10 -g http://api.anihpj.com/api/health/. Measures full HTTP transaction time (DNS + TCP + TLS + HTTP). Different from ping (ICMP only) and iperf3 (TCP throughput only). Shows what USERS experience.

    📡
    netperf — TCP/UDP Benchmarking

    netserver on server, netperf -H <server> -t TCP_STREAM on client. Tests: TCP_STREAM (throughput), TCP_RR (request/response latency), UDP_STREAM. More granular control than iperf3 — test specific message sizes, socket buffer sizes, and CPU affinity. netperf -H server -t TCP_RR -- -r 1,1 tests single-byte request/response (peak PPS capability).

    ⚡
    qperf — Zero-Config Bandwidth Test

    qperf server-ip tcp_bw tcp_lat — tests bandwidth AND latency without installing a separate server binary (qperf handles both sides via SSH or a listener). qperf -t 30 server-ip tcp_bw udp_bw tcp_lat runs a 30-second comprehensive test. Great for quick ad-hoc checks: no server setup, just point at the remote host.

    ⚠️ iperf3 Gotchas — Don't Trust Single-Stream Results

    Gotcha 1 — Single-stream TCP bottleneck: iperf3 -c server (default, single stream) is often bottlenecked by TCP window size, not available bandwidth. A 50ms RTT with default 256KB TCP buffer = max ~40 Mbps per stream. Use -P 10 for 10 parallel streams to measure real aggregate throughput. Gotcha 2 — CPU bottleneck: At 25 Gbps+, iperf3 itself becomes CPU-bound. Use -Z (zero-copy mode) or DPDK-based tools for 40 Gbps+ testing. Gotcha 3 — Reverse direction: iperf3 -c server -R tests DOWNLOAD (server → client). Without -R, it tests UPLOAD (client → server).

    32.3 TCP Tuning for Performance

    Linux TCP defaults are conservative — designed for 1990s internet. Modern cloud networks can handle much more aggressive settings. These tunings can 2-10x your throughput on high-latency links.

    ParameterDefaultRecommendedWhat It Does
    net.ipv4.tcp_congestion_controlcubicbbr# HTTP: GET/POST /path HTTP/1.1 + Host/Authorization headers -> 200 OK + JSON body # curl -sv https://HOST/api/endpoint | jq .strong>BBR (Bottleneck Bandwidth and RTT) is Google's congestion control. Models the path instead of reacting to loss. Much better for high-BDP links and bufferbloat. Enable: modprobe tcp_bbr; sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_congestion_control=bbr.
    net.core.rmem_max212992134217728 (128MB)Max receive buffer. For 10 Gbps at 50ms RTT, BDP = 62.5 MB. Buffer must be ≥ BDP. Too small = TCP window limited.
    net.core.wmem_max212992134217728Max send buffer. Same logic as rmem_max.
    net.ipv4.tcp_rmem4096 131072 62914564096 87380 134217728Auto-tuning: min, default, max. Kernel auto-scales within this range.
    net.ipv4.tcp_fastopen13TCP Fast Open: skip 1 RTT on repeat connections. 3 = enable for both client and server. Requires app support (curl --tcp-fastopen).
    net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse01Reuse TIME_WAIT sockets for new connections (client-side only). Safe for cloud environments. Reduces connection exhaustion.
    net.core.somaxconn1284096Max SYN backlog per socket. If your service has connection spikes, increase this. Also set net.ipv4.tcp_max_syn_backlog=4096.
    net.ipv4.tcp_slow_start_after_idle10Disable slow start restart after idle. Keeps cwnd from resetting on idle connections (important for DB connection pools).
    🎯 BBR vs CUBIC — The Congestion Control Revolution

    CUBIC (default since Linux 2.6.19): Loss-based. Increases cwnd ag, Linux 4.9+): Model-based. Continuously estimates the path's bandwidth and RTT. Doesn't rely on packet loss as a signal — maintains high throughput even at 1-5% packet loss where CUBIC collapses. BBR results: 20-100x better on lossy paths, 2-4x better on high-BDP paths. YouTube uses BBR — average throughput increased 4% globally, 14% in developing regions. Enable BBR on all production nodes: echo "net.core.default_qdisc=fq" >> /etc/sysctl.conf && echo "net.ipv4.tcp_congestion_control=bbr" >> /etc/sysctl.conf && sysctl -p. Verify:

    🔧 NIC Ring Buffers & Offloading — Hardware Tuning for Performance

    Modern NICs have hardware features that dramatically affect performance. 

    # PERF: iperf3 -c SERVER(bandwidth), ping -c 100 SERVER(latency/loss), mtr -r SERVER
# TCP retransmits = packet loss signal; ss -tin | grep retrans
    Ring buffers: The NIC stores incoming packets in a circular buffer (ring) in RAM before the kernel processes them. ethtool -g eth0 shows current and max ring sizes. Rx ring full = packet drops at the hardware level — before the kernel even sees them. At 10 Gbps with small packets, the default 256-entry ring can overflow in microseconds. Fix: ethtool -G eth0 rx 4096 tx 4096 (increase to maximum). NIC offloading: The NIC hardware can handle TCP operations that would otherwise use CPU: (1) TSO (TCP Segmentation Offload): NIC splits large TCP segments into MTU-sized packets. Saves CPU but can mask MTU issues. (2) GSO (Generic Segmentation Offload): Software equivalent — kernel does segmentation, NIC gets pre-split packets. (3) GRO (Generic Receive Offload): NIC merges multiple incoming packets into one large segment — reduces kernel interrupt count.
    # PERF: iperf3 -c SERVER(bandwidth), ping -c 100 SERVER(latency/loss), mtr -r SERVER
# TCP retransmits = packet loss signal; ss -tin | grep retrans
    (4) LRO (Large Receive Offload): Hardware GRO — faster but can break packet inspection (tcpdump sees merged packets). Check offloading: ethtool -k eth0 shows all offload features. When to disable: If you're running a firewall/proxy (iptables, nginx) — GRO/LRO can cause issues because the merged packet may not match firewall rules correctly. Disable with: ethtool -K eth0 gro off lro off. For anihpj EKS nodes: increase ring buffers to max via a DaemonSet init script. Leave TSO/GSO on for throughput. Consider disabling LRO if you run NetworkPolicy-heavy workloads.

    🚦 tc (Traffic Control) — Linux QoS, Shaping & Policing

    tc (traffic control) is Linux's Quality of Service framework — it can delay, drop, reorder, or rate-limit packets. Key concepts: (1) qdisc (queuing discipline): The algorithm that decides which packet to send next. Attached to each network interface. (2) Classes: Sub-divisions of a qdisc for different traffic types. (3) Filters: Rules that classify packets into classes. Common qdiscs: pfifo_fast (default — 3-band priority FIFO), fq_codel (Fair Queuing with Controlled Delay — reduces bufferbloat), htb (Hierarchical Token Bucket — bandwidth limits per class), netem (Network

    # PERF: iperf3 -c SERVER(bandwidth), ping -c 100 SERVER(latency/loss), mtr -r SERVER
# TCP retransmits = packet loss signal; ss -tin | grep retrans
    Emulator — add artificial latency/loss for testing!). SRE use cases: (1) Simulate network problems: tc qdisc add dev eth0 root netem delay 50ms loss 1% — adds 50ms latency and 1% packet loss. Test how your app behaves under degraded network! tc qdisc del dev eth0 root — remove simulation. (2) Rate-limit a service: tc qdisc add dev eth0 root htb default 1; tc class add dev eth0 parent 1: classid 1:1 htb rate 100mbit — limit eth0 to 100 Mbps. (3) Check current qdisc: tc qdisc show dev eth0. BBR requires fq qdisc: tc qdisc replace dev eth0 root fq. If you enable BBR without fq, it falls back to less optimal pacing. # HTTP: REQUEST=GET/POST /path HTTP/1.1\nHost+Auth headers\nRESPONSE=200 OK + JSON/HTML # curl -sv https://HOST/api -H "Authorization: Bearer TOKEN" |own interfaces, routes, iptables rules, and sockets. They're what containers use for network isolation, and they're an invaluable debugging tool. Create and use: ip netns add test-ns (create namespace), ip netns exec test-ns ip link show (run command in namespace — sees only loopback initially), ip link add veth0 type veth peer name veth1 (create veth pair), ip link set veth1 netns test-ns (move one end into namespace), ip netns exec test-ns ip addr add 10.0.99.1/24 dev veth1 (assign IP). Debugging use: (1) Start a process in an isolated namespace — test if a problem is network-config-relateping -c 100 SERVER(latency/loss) # ss -tin | grep retrans(retransmits=packet loss); mtr -r SERVER(per-hop stats). (3) Test iptables rules in isolation — add rules to the namespace's stack without affecting host rules. List namespaces: ip netns liste the pod's network config from the node's perspective.

    📝 Chapter 32 — Networking Practice Questions

    Q1
    What are the 4 components of network latency? Which ones can you control?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    Propagation: Speed of light in fiber (~200,000 km/s). NOT controllable — physics. Serialization: Bits onto the wire (~12µs foode># KEY NETWORKING COMMANDS # Interface: ip addr show; ip link set eth0 up; ethtool eth0 # Routing: ip route show; traceroute -n HOST; mtr -r HOST # Sockets: ss -tlnp; ss -ulnp; lsof -i :PORT; nc -zv HOST PORT # DNS: dig +short DOMAIN; nslookup DOMAIN; host DOMAIN # Firewall: iptables -L -nv --line-numbers; nft list ruleader: value" # K8s: kubectl get svc,ep,netpol,ingress -A # Debug: L1(ip link)->L2(arping)->L3(ping)->L4(nc -zv)->L7(curl)on dominates. In the same data center, queuing dominates at high utilization.

    Explanation

    The key insight: for cross-region traffic (50ms RTT), propagation delay IS the latency. You cannot "fix" it with more bandwidth. A 1 Gbps link and a 100 Gbps link both have the same propagation delay. The only way to reduce latency over distance is to MOVE THE DATA CLOSER (CDN edge cache, read replicas, multi-region deployment). For same-AZ traffic (< 1ms), queuing delay is the main source of jittebursts without queuing.

    Q3
    What is BBR congestion control? How is it different from CUBIC, and when should you use it?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    CUBIC: Loss-based. Increases cwnd until packet loss → backs off. Good on clean networks, terrible on lossy links. BBR: Model-based. Continuously estimates bandwidth and RTT. Doesn't use loss as congestion signal. 2-4x better on high-BDP links, 20-100x better on lossy links. When to use: Cross-region traffic, any path with > 0.1% packet loss, bufferbloat-prone links (home internet, WiFi), cloud inter-AZ traffic. BBR is safe for all workloads — Google uses it for ALL YouTube and Google.com traffic. Enable on all nodes.

    Explanation

    BBR represents a fundamental shift in congestion control philosophy. CUBIC and all previous algorithms (Reno, NewReno) assume packet loss = congestion. This was true in the 1990s when routers had tiny 

    # NETWORKING COMMANDS REFERENCE
# Check interface: ip addr show; ip link set eth0 up; ethtool eth0
# Check routing:   ip route show; ip route get 8.8.8.8; traceroute -n HOST
# Check ports:     ss -tlnp; ss -ulnp; nc -zv HOST PORT; lsof -i :PORT
# Check DNS:       dig +short DOMAIN; nslookup DOMAIN; host DOMAIN
# Check firewall:  iptables -L -nv --line-numbers; nft list ruleset
# Capture traffic: tcpdump -i any -nn host IP -w capture.pcap
# Check TLS:       openssl s_client -connect HOST:443 -servername HOST
# Test HTTP:       curl -sv https://HOST/path -H "Header: value"
# K8s networking:  kubectl get svc,ep,netpol,ingress -A
# Debug order:     L1(ethtool)->L2(arping)->L3(ping)->L4(nc)->L7(curl)
    buffers. Today, with bufferbloat (routers have MBs of buffer), packets are lost for many reasons: WiFi interference, bad cables, switch buffer overflow (not congestion), and random bit errors. BBR builds a model of the path — it periodically probes for more bandwidth and measures RTT changes. When RTT starts increasing (buffer filling), BBR backs off BEFORE packet loss occurs. This means BBR maintains high throughput while keeping buffers empty (low latency) — the holy grail of congestion control. For anihpj: enable BBR on all EKS nodes via a DaemonSet init script. The difference for cross-AZ database replication can be dramatic.

    Q4
    You run `iperf3 -c server` and get 40 Mbps. You know the link is 1 Gbps. Why?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    Single-stream TCP is limited by the congestion window, not available bandwidth. At 50ms RTT with default 256KB TCP buffer: max throughput ≈ buffer/RTT = 256KB/0.05s ≈ 40 Mbps. Solutions: (1) iperf3 -c server -P 10 (10 parallel streams = 10× throughput). (2) Increase TCP buffers: iperf3 -c server -w 4M (4MB window ~640 Mbps at 50ms). (3) Run on both directions: -R for download test. (4) Verify NIC speed: ethtool eth0 | grep Speed — is it actually 1 Gbps?

    Explanation

    This is the #1 iperf3 "false negative." Engineers run a single-stream test, see 40 Mbps, and panic: "The network is broken!" But the network is fine — TCP's congestion control is the bottleneck, not the link. Always test with -P 10 to see aggregate throughput. If 10 streams get 900 Mbps, the link is fine — single-stream performance is limited by TCP, not the network. If 10 streams STILL get 40 Mbps, THEN you have a real network problem (bad NIC, switch port negotiated at 100 Mbps, CPU bottleneck, or QoS policy limiting per-IP bandwidth).

    Q5
    What does mtr show that traceroute doesn't? How do you interpret the output?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    mtr combines traceroute + continuous ping — it shows per-hop loss% and latency OVER TIME, not just a single snapshot. Reading: Loss% at hop N that DOESN'T continue to N+1 = router deprioritizing ICMP replies (NORMAL, ignore). Loss% at hop N that CONTINUES through ALL later hops = REAL packet loss at that hop. mtr also shows: best/worst/average latency per hop, standard deviation (jitter), and packet loss over the test duration. Run mtr -r -c 100 target (100 pings, report mode) for a quick check, or mtr target (interactive) for live monitoring.

    Explanation

    mtr is the definitive tool for intermittent network problems. traceroute sends 3 probes per hop, one time — if the problem is intermittent (1% packet loss), you'll probably miss it. mtr sends probes continuously for the duration of the test, accumulating statistics. After 60 seconds, 1% loss becomes visible as 6 dropped packets out of 600. The critical skill is distinguishing "normal" ICMP deprioritization from real loss. Rule: if loss appears at hop 5 (20%) but hop 6 shows 0%, the loss at hop 5 is fake — the router is busy and deprioritized ICMP replies. If loss at hop 5 is 20% AND hop 6+ also show ~20%, the loss is real — packets are being dropped at or before hop 5.

    Q6
    What is TCP Fast Open (TFO)? How many RTTs does it save?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    TCP Fast Open (TFO) allows data to be sent in the SYN packet — saving 1 RTT on REPEAT connections. Normal TCP: SYN → SYN/ACK → ACK → DATA (3 RTTs before first byte). TFO: SYN+DATA → SYN/ACK+DATA → ACK (1 RTT saved). TFO requires: both client and server support it, a TFO cookie from a previous connection (stored client-side), and net.ipv4.tcp_fastopen=3 (enable both client and server). Saves ~50ms on cross-region connections, ~1ms within same AZ. Most impactful for short-lived connections (HTTP requests, DB queries).

    Explanation

    TFO is like having a VIP pass — on your first visit, the server gives you a cookie. On subsequent visits, you show the cookie at the door and skip the line. The TFO cookie is a cryptographic token the server generates and the client caches. On the next connection, the client includes the cookie in the SYN packet along with data. The server verifies the cookie and accepts the data immediately — the application gets the HTTP request BEFORE the 3-way handshake completes. For anihpj: if jobpost pods frequently make short HTTP calls to internal services, enabling TFO can reduce p50 latency by 30-50% on cross-AZ calls. Enable on both the client (curl --tcp-fastopen) and server (nginx: listen 80 fastopen=256).

    Q7
    What kernel parameters should you tune for a high-throughput HTTP server handling 10,000 connections/second?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    (1) net.core.somaxconn=4096 + net.ipv4.tcp_max_syn_backlog=4096 — handle connection spikes without dropping SYNs. (2) net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse=1 — reuse TIME_WAIT sockets for new connections (prevents ephemeral port exhaustion). (3) net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range=1024 65535 — widen ephemeral port range. (4) net.ipv4.tcp_slow_start_after_idle=0 — keep cwnd across idle periods. (5) net.core.netdev_max_backlog=5000 — larger NIC ring buffer for bursty traffic. (6) BBR congestion control.

    Explanation

    At 10,000 connections/second, the default Linux settings become bottlenecks quickly. somaxconn=128 means only 128 pending SYNs can queue — if you get a burst of 200 new connections in 10ms, 72 of them are dropped at the kernel level before your app even sees them. tcp_tw_reuse=1 is critical because each closed connection sits in TIME_WAIT for 60-120 seconds, consuming an ephemeral port. At 10K conns/sec × 60s = 600,000 ports needed — but the default range is 28,000-32,000 (only 28,232 available). Without tcp_tw_reuse, you'll exhaust ephemeral ports and new connections will fail with "Cannot assign requested address." For anihpj at scale: apply these via a DaemonSet that runs sysctl -p /etc/sysctl.d/99-network-tuning.conf on every node.

    Q8
    How do you test network performance between two pods in different availability zones?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    (1) Deploy iperf3 server on a pod in AZ-a: kubectl run iperf-svr --image=networkstatic/iperf3 --overrides='{"spec":{"nodeSelector":{"topology.kubernetes.io/zone":"us-east-1a"}}}' -- -s. (2) Client from AZ-b: kubectl run -it iperf-cli --rm --image=networkstatic/iperf3 --overrides='{"spec":{"nodeSelector":{"topology.kubernetes.io/zone":"us-east-1b"}}}' -- -c <server-pod-ip> -P 10 -t 30. (3) Measure: throughput (Gbps), retransmits. (4) Also test with ping -c 100 <server-pod-ip> for baseline RTT. (5) Test different packet sizes: iperf3 -c <ip> -l 64 (small) vs -l 64K (large) to check MTU issues.

    Explanation

    Cross-AZ performance testing is essential because AZs can be 1-10km apart — close enough for sub-millisecond RTT, far enough for MTU and congestion issues. AWS charges for cross-AZ data transfer ($0.01/GB each way), so understanding your cross-AZ bandwidth usage directly impacts cost. Key metrics: (1) Throughput: should be close to instance network limits (e.g., 5 Gbps for m5.large). (2) Retransmits: should be near 0% — any retransmits on same-region cross-AZ traffic indicate a problem. (3) RTT: typically 0.5-2ms between AZs in the same region. If you see 10ms+ between AZs, your traffic may be routing through an internet gateway or NAT (misconfigured route tables).

    Q9
    What is bufferbloat? How does BBR help, and how do you detect it?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    Bufferbloat is excessive buffering in network equipment (routers, switches). Large buffers cause high throughput BUT also high and variable latency — packets sit in queues for hundreds of milliseconds. Detection: Run a ping while saturating the link: ping target should be 5ms idle. Start iperf3 -c target -t 30 simultaneously — if ping RTT jumps to 500ms, you have bufferbloat. BBR fix: BBR measures RTT continuously and backs off BEFORE buffers fill — maintaining high throughput AND low latency. CUBIC fills buffers until they drop packets (causing both high latency AND packet loss).

    Explanation

    Bufferbloat is why "the internet feels slow" even when bandwidth is high. Your 1 Gbps home connection has 

    # KEY NETWORKING COMMANDS
# Interface: ip addr show; ip link set eth0 up; ethtool eth0
# Routing:   ip route show; traceroute -n HOST; mtr -r HOST
# Sockets:   ss -tlnp; ss -ulnp; lsof -i :PORT; nc -zv HOST PORT
# DNS:       dig +short DOMAIN; nslookup DOMAIN; host DOMAIN
# Firewall:  iptables -L -nv --line-numbers; nft list ruleset
# Capture:   tcpdump -i any -nn host IP or port NUM -w file.pcap
# TLS:       openssl s_client -connect HOST:443 -servername HOST
# HTTP:      curl -sv https://HOST/path -H "Header: value"
# K8s:       kubectl get svc,ep,netpol,ingress -A
# Debug:     L1(ip link)->L2(arping)->L3(ping)->L4(nc -zv)->L7(curl)
    2-3 MB of buffer in the cable modem. When someone uploads a large file (saturating upload), those buffers fill — adding 500ms-2s of latency to every other packet. Your Zoom call freezes, web pages take forever to load, but your speed test shows 900 Mbps. This is bufferbloat: high throughput + terrible latency. BBR addresses this by treating RTT increase (not packet loss) as the congestion signal. It probes for bandwidth, watches RTT rise as buffers fill, and backs off — maintaining most of the throughput while keeping buffers nearly empty. For anihpj: bufferbloat can occur on NAT Gateways and cross-AZ links under load. Monitor: latency during peak traffic. If p99 latency spikes during high throughput periods → bufferbloat. Fix: BBR or traffic shaping.

    Q10
    [LAB 🛠️] Benchmark the network between two EKS pods. Measure throughput, RTT, and packet loss. Write the commands and interpret the output.
    Show Answer
    Answer
    # Server pod:
kubectl run iperf-server --image=networkstatic/iperf3 --restart=Never -- -s
SERVER_IP=$(kubectl get pod iperf-server -o jsonpath='{.status.podIP}')

# Test 1 — Baseline RTT:
kubectl run ping-test --rm -it --image=busybox --restart=Never -- \
  ping -c 100 $SERVER_IP
# EXPECTED: avg RTT < 2ms for same-AZ, < 5ms cross-AZ

# Test 2 — Single-stream TCP throughput:
kubectl run iperf-1 --rm -it --image=networkstatic/iperf3 --restart=Never -- \
  -c $SERVER_IP -t 10
# Check: throughput limited by BDP? If low, TCP window is the bottleneck.

# Test 3 — Multi-stream TCP (aggregate):
kubectl run iperf-10 --rm -it --image=networkstatic/iperf3 --restart=Never -- \
  -c $SERVER_IP -P 10 -t 30
# EXPECTED: aggregate should approach instance network limit

# Test 4 — UDP packet loss:
kubectl run iperf-udp --rm -it --image=networkstatic/iperf3 --restart=Never -- \
  -c $SERVER_IP -u -b 1G -t 10
# Look for: "0% loss" = clean network. Any loss = problem.

# Cleanup:
kubectl delete pod iperf-server
    Explanation

    This lab gives you objective network performance data — no more "the network feels slow." Single-stream TCP tests the BDP limit: if you get 2 Gbps single-stream on a 5 Gbps instance, TCP is the bottleneck, not the network. Multi-stream tests aggregate bandwidth: should approach the instance limit. UDP tests raw packet loss: if UDP shows 0.5% loss but TCP shows full throughput, TCP is successfully hiding the loss (through retransmits) — it's working harder than you think. For anihpj production: run these tests monthly to establish baseline performance. When "the network is slow" tickets come in, re-run the tests and COMPARE to baseline — objective data ends the debate.

    🔑 SPIFFE/SPIRE — Cryptographic Identity for Every Workload

    SPIFFE (Secure Production Identity Framework for Everyone): A standard for workload identity. Every pod gets a SPIFFE ID like spiffe://anihpj.com/ns/production/sa/jobpost — a URI that uniquely identifies the workload. SPIRE (SPIFFE Runtime Environment): The implementation. SPIRE agents run on each node, issue short-lived X.509 certificates to pods, and rotate them automatically. How mTLS works with SPIFFE: Pod-A connects to Pod-B. Both present their SPIFFE certificates. Pod-B checks: "Is spiffe://anihpj.com/ns/production/sa/jobpost allowed to call me?" If the SPIFFE ID is in the allowlist → connection proceeds. If not → rejected. This i INPUT->local->OUTPUT; iptables -L -nv --line-numbers

    33.6 Common Network Attacks and How to Defend

    AttackLayerDetectionMitigation
    SYN FloodL4High SYN rate, many half-open connectionsSYN cookies, rate limiting, cloud scrubbing (AWS Shield)
    DNS AmplificationL7Massive DNS responses to your IPRate-limit DNS, close open resolvers, DNSSEC
    ARP SpoofingL2Duplicate MAC for same IP in ARP tableStatic ARP entries, DHCP snooping, switch port security
    TLS DowngradeL5Weak ciphers in handshakeHarden TLS config, disable TLS 1.0/1.1, enforce strong ciphers
    BGP HijackL3Unexpected AS_PATH changesRPKI, IRR filtering, prefix allowlists
    Credential SniffingL7HTTP (not HTTPS) trafficEnforce TLS everywhere, HSTS, redirect HTTP→HTTPS
    🛡️ DDoS Attack Types — Defense at Every Layer

    Volumetric (L3/L4): Flood the pipe with traffic (e.g., 100 Gbps UDP flood). Defense: cloud scrubbing services (AWS Shield Advanced, Cloudflare Magic Transit), Anycast distribution (spread attack across many points). Protocol (L4): Exhaust server state — SYN flood fills conntrack table. Defense: SYN cookies (cryptographic challenge instead of state), increase conntrack limits, rate limiting per source IP. Application-layer (L7): HTTP floods that look like legitimate requests — hard to distinguis

    # SUBNETTING: /8=255.0.0.0(16M hosts), /16=255.255.0.0(65K), /24=255.255.255.0(256)
# Network=IP&mask; Broadcast=Network|~mask; Hosts=2^(32-prefix)-2
# ipcalnt + WAF at the edge absorbs L3/L4 attacks. ALB + WAF handles L7 attacks. Auto-scaling EKS nodes handle traffic spikes. Never expose your origin servers directly — always put a CDN or DDoS protection service in front.
    📝 WAF Rule Writing — Real Examples for anihpj
      # AWS WAF rules protecting the anihpj API:

  # 1. Rate-based rule: block IPs exceeding 2000 requests per 5 minutes
  aws wafv2 create-rule --name "RateLimit-API" \
    --priority 1 \
    --statement '{"RateBasedStatement":{"Limit":2000,"AggregateKeyType":"IP"}}' \
    --action Block

  # 2. SQL injection protection (AWS Managed Rule):
  # AWSManagedRulesSQLiRuleSet — blocks: ' OR 1=1--, UNION SELECT, etc.

  # 3. Geo-match: allow only US, UK, Nigeria traffic to /api/
  # Block all other countries

  # 4. IP reputation: block known botnets and Tor exit nodes
  # AWSManagedRulesAmazonIpReputationList

  # 5. Size constraint: block requests with body > 8KB (prevent large payload attacks)
  aws wafv2 create-rule --name "BodySize-8KB" \
    --statement '{"SizeConstraintStatement":{"FieldToMatch":{"Body":{}},"ComparisonOperator":"GT","Size":8192}}'

  WAF cost: ~$5/month per Web ACL + $1/rule/month + $0.60/million requests
  For 10M requests/month: ~$25/month — cheap insurance.
    🔐 DNSSEC — Preventing DNS Spoofing and Cache Poisoning

    DNSSEC (DNS Security Extensions) adds cryptographic signatures to DNS records. When you query api.anihpj.com, the DNS resolver can verify that the response was NOT tampered with — it was signed by the legitimate zone owner. How it works: (1) Each DNS zone has a public/private key pair (ZSK — Zone Signing Key). (2) Every DNS record is signee root zone down. DNSSEC prevents: DNS cache poisoning (attacker injects fake records), DNS spoofing (man-in-the-middle DNS), and DNS hijacking. DNSSEC does NOT: Encrypt DNS queries (use DoH/DoT for that), hide which domains you query, or protect against DDoS. For anihpj: Enable DNSSEC on your domain reong>STRIDE is Microsoft's threat modeling framework: Spoofing (pretending to be someone else), Tampering (modifying data), Repudiation (denying actions), Information Disclosure (data leaks), Denial of Service (making unavailable), Elevation of Privilege (gaining higher access). Applied to anihpj: (1) Spoofing: Attacker spoofs jobpost pod IP → mTLS with SPIFFEng> Attacker deletes data and denies it → audit logging (CloudTrail, K8s audit logs) proves actions. (4) Information Disclosure: Attacker reads database → encryption at rest (KMS) + NetworkPolicy limits DB access. (5) Denial of Service: SYN flood, HTTP flood → Shield + WAF + auto-scaling. (6) Elevation of Privilege: Attacker escapes container → pod security context (runAsNonRoot, readOnlyRootFilesystem), seccomp, AppArmor. For every new service: run through STRIDE. Ask "what's the worst that could happen?" Then design controls for each threat. This is proactive security — build defenses before the attack.

    📝 Chapter 33 — Networking Practice Questions

    Q1
    What is defense in depth? Why is it important for network security?
    Show Answer
    Explanation

    The "hard shell, soft center" model (perimeter firewall only) fails catastrophically: once an attacker is inside, nothing stops them. The 2013 Target breach happened because attackers compromised an HVAC vendor, then pivoted from the vendor portal to the payment systems — no internal segmentation. Defense in depth would have limited the HVAC vendor's access to only their portal, preventing the pivot. For anihpj: a defense-in-depth approach means even if a jobpost pod is compromised, the attacker can only reach PostgreSQL (port 5432) and Redis (6379) — they can't reach other namespaces, can't SSH to nodes, and can't exfiltrate data to the internet (egress NetworkPolicy).

    Q2
    What is Zero Trust? How does it differ from traditional perimeter-based security?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    Zero Trust means NO implicit trust based on network location. Every connection must be explicitly authenticated, authorized, and encrypted. Traditional perimeter security trusts everything "inside" the network. Zero Trust assumes the network is already compromised. Key principles: verify explicitly (use all available signals), least privilege access (minimum permissions), assume breach (design for containment). Implementation: SPIFFE/SPIRE for workload identity, mTLS for all connections, NetworkPolicies for micro-segmentation.

    Explanation

    The perimeter model is like a castle wall — once you're inside, you can go anywhere. Zero Trust is like a hotel — you have a key that only opens YOUR room, and the lobby doesn't give you access to the kitchen. In cloud-native environments, the perimeter doesn't really exist — pods come and go, IPs change constantly, and workloads span multiple clusters and clouds. Zero Trust is the only model that works in this environment. Google's BeyondCorp proved this at massive scale: they eliminated their corporate VPN entirely, exposing all internal apps to the public internet behind identity-aware proxies. Every request is authenticated — no VPN means no "inside the network" trust.

    Q3
    What is SPIFFE/SPIRE? How does it enable zero trust in Kubernetes?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    SPIFFE is a standard for workload identity — every pod gets a URI like spiffe://cluster.local/ns/prod/sa/jobpost. SPIRE is the implementation that issues short-lived X.509 certificates to pods. Enables mTLS: Pod-A presents its SPIFFE cert to Pod-B, Pod-B checks "is this SPIFFE ID allowed?" — identity-based access, not IP-based. Certificates auto-rotate (typically 1-hour TTL). Even if an attacker steals an IP address, they can't steal the cryptographic identity.

    Explanation

    Traditional mTLS requires managing certificates manually — generating, distributing, rotating. SPIFFE/SPIRE automates this: (1) SPIRE Agent runs on each K8s node (DaemonSet). (2) When a pod starts, the agent verifies the pod's identity via the K8s API (namespace, service account, labels). (3) The agent issues an X.509 certificate with the pod's SPIFFE ID as the Subject Alternative Name (SAN). (4) The certificate is written to a shared volume mounted in the pod. (5) The application uses this certificate for mTLS. (6) Certificates are short-lived (1 hour default) — compromised certs expire quickly. For anihpj: deploy SPIRE, configure jobpost and postgres pods to use SPIFFE certs, and enforce that only spiffe://.../sa/jobpost can connect to spiffe://.../sa/postgres on port 5432.

    Q4
    What is the difference between East-West and North-South traffic? Why does it matter for security?
    Show Answer
    Explanation

    The East-West security gap is why data breaches are so devastating. Attacker compromises a frontend pod through a vulnerable dependency → pod has unrestricted access to databases, caches, message queues, and internal APIs → attacker exfiltrates data laterally, never touching the perimeter firewall. Traditional security tools (firewalls, IDS) sit at the perimeter and are blind to East-West traffic. Solution: NetworkPolicies (every pod has ingress/egress rules) + mTLS (encrypt pod-to-pod traffic) + Hubble/Cilium (observe East-West flows). For anihpj: a compromised jobpost pod should NOT be able to access monitoring tools, CI/CD systems, or other tenants' databases. NetworkPolicies enforce this isolation.

    Q5
    What is a SYN flood attack? How do SYN cookies defend against it?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    A SYN flood sends massive numbers of SYN packets (without completing the handshake), filling the server's SYN backlog queue. Legitimate clients can't connect — denial of service. SYN cookies: Instead of allocating a connection structure for every SYN, the server encodes connection info into a cryptographic cookie in the SYN/ACK sequence number. Only when the client completes the handshake (ACK) does the server decode the cookie and create the connection. No state stored until 3-way handshake completes — immune to SYN floods. Enable: sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies=1.

    Explanation

    SYN cookies are a brilliant cryptographic solution to a resource exhaustion problem. The key insight: don't allocate memory until the client proves they're real (by completing the handshake). The SYN/ACK sequence number normally just increments — with SYN cookies, it becomes an encoded timestamp + MSS + cryptographic hash of (src IP, dst IP, ports, timestamp, secret). When the ACK arrives, the server verifies the hash — if valid, it knows this was a legitimate handshake and creates the connection. The trade-off: SYN cookies disable TCP options negotiation (window scaling, SACK, etc.) because the cookie takes the space normally used for options. In cloud environments, SYN cookies should ALWAYS be enabled on internet-facing load balancers.

    Q6
    What is ARP spoofing? How do you defend against it?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    ARP spoofing: an attacker sends forged ARP replies claiming their MAC address belongs to the gateway's IP. Victims update their ARP cache → send traffic to the attacker instead of the gateway → attacker can intercept, modify, or drop traffic (Man-in-the-Middle). Defenses: (1) Static ARP entries for critical hosts (but doesn't scale). (2) DHCP snooping + Dynamic ARP Inspection on managed apping service level. Hosts cannot spoof

    # K8s POD NETWORKING: Shared net namespace, veth pair to cni0 bridge
# kubectl exec POD -- ip addr; All containers in pod share localhost
    ARP in a VPC.

    Explanation

    ARP spoofing is a serious threat in physical networks (office LANs, data centers without proper switch security). The reason it works: ARP is a trust-based protocol — any host can claim any IP-to-MAC mapping, and other hosts believe it. There's no authentication in ARP. In cloud environments (AWS VPC, GCP VPC), the hypervisor acts as the ultimate authority — it maintains the true IP-to-MAC mapping in the mapping service, and guest VMs cannot override it. This is one of the security benefits of cloud networking: the virtualization layer eliminates an entire class of L2 attacks. For on-prem Kubernetes: ensure your switches have port security and DAI enabled. For anihpj in AWS: ARP spoofing is not a concern at the VPC level — focus on higher-layer attacks.

    Q7
    How do you defend against DDoS attacks at each layer?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    L3/L4 (Volumetric): Cloud scrubbing (AWS Shield, Cloudflare), Anycast to distribute attack traffic. L4 (Protocol/SYN flood): SYN cookies, rate limiting, connection limits per source IP. L7 (Application/HTTP flood):# K8s POD NETWORKING: Shared net namespace, veth pair to cni0 bridge # kubectl exec POD -- ip addr; All containers in pod share localhoststrong> WAF rate limiting, CAPTCHA, bot detectipre>ching. Defense requires ALL layers: cloud edge absorbs volumetric → WAF filters L7 attacks → your infrastructure only sees legitimate traffic.

    Explanation

    DDoS defense is a layered pipeline: (1) Edge absorption: Cloud providers have massive capacity (AWS Shield can absorb multi-Tbps attacks). Traffic hits their edge first — they scrub volumetric attacks before they reach your VPC. (2) WAF filtering: After volumetric scrubbing, WAF inspects HTTP requests — blocks SQL injection, XSS, rate limits, geo-blocking. (3) Application resilience: Auto-scaling handles legitimate traffic spikes. Rate limiting per user/session prevents abuse. Circuit breakers stop cascading failures. For anihpj: CloudFront + WAF → ALB → EKS. CloudFront absorbs L3/L4, WAF blocks L7 attacks, EKS auto-scales. This pipeline handles both volumetric attacks AND application-level abuse.

    Q8
    What is BGP hijacking? How do RPKI and prefix filtering prevent it?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    BGP hijacking: a rogue Autonomous System (AS) announces IP prefixes that don't belong to it. Other networks accept the false route → traffic destined for the legitimate owner is rerouted to the attacker. Can be accidental (misconfiguration) or malicious. RPKI (Resource Public Key Infrastructure): Cryptographically verifies that an AS is authorized to announce specific prefixes. Routers check RPKI before accepting BGP announcements. Prefix filtering: Your ISP only accepts announcements for prefixes you own (defined in IRR — Internet Routing Registry).

    Explanation

    BGP was designed in 1989 with zero security — any AS can announce any prefix, and the internet will believe it. The most famous BGP hijack: in 2008, Pakistan Telecom accidentally announced YouTube's prefix (208.65.153.0/24) in an attempt to block YouTube in Pakistan. Their upstream provider (PCCW) propagated the route globally → YouTube was inaccessible worldwide for 2 hours. RPKI fixes this by creating a chain of trust: RIRs (ARIN, RIPE) sign ROAs (Route Origin Authorizations) that cryptographically bind prefixes to AS numbers. Routers can validate BGP announcements against the RPKI database. Adoption is growing but not universal — ~40% of routes are RPKI-validated as of 2025. For anihpj: if you own IP space, create ROAs for your prefixes. If you use cloud IPs, the cloud provider handles this.

    Q9
    How does a stateful firewall track connections? What are the security implications?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    A stateful firewall (like AWS Security Groups) maintains a connection tracking table (conntrack). When a SYN packet matches an allow rule, the firewall creates a conntrack entry: (src IP, dst IP, src port, dst port, protocol, state=ESTABLISHED). All subsequent packets matching this entry are auto-allowed — no rule evaluation needed. Security implications: (1) Return traffic is IMPLICITLY allowed — you don't need explicit outbound rules for responses. (2) Conntrack table overflow = denial of service (new connections dropped). (3) Stateful firewalls can be fooled by TCP state manipulation (but modern implementations are robust).

    Explanation

    Stateful firewalls are a double-edged sword. The convenience is massive: you allow inbound TCP 80 and ALL return traffic is automatically allowed — no need for ephemeral port 

    # K8s CNI: Flannel(VXLAN, simple), Calico(BGP, NetPol native), Cilium(eBPF, L7)
# Config: /etc/cni/net.d/*.conf; CNI ops: ADD/DEL/CHECK/VERSION
    rules. But the conntrack table is a limited resource. An attacker can flood a stateful firewall with SYN packets from spoofed IPs → each one creates a conntrack entry → table fills up → legitimate connections are dropped. This is a SYN flood attack exploiting statefulness. Mitigations
    # K8s POD NET: Shared net namespace(same IP+ports), veth pair to cni0 bridge on node
# kubectl exec POD -- ip addr; All containers in pod share localhost:PORT
    : (1) SYN cookies at the firewall level. (2) Aggressive conntrack timeouts for half-open connections. (3) Rate limiting new connections per source IP. For AWS Security Groups: they're implemented at the hypervisor level with massive conntrack capacity — they're resilient but not immune. Always monitor conntrack usage on your instances.

    Q10
    [LAB 🛠️] Design a defense-in-depth security architecture for anihpj on AWS. List every security layer and what it protects against.
    Show Answer# K8s POD NET: Shared net namespace(same IP+ports), veth pair to cni0 bridge on nodANIHPJ DEFENSE-IN-DEPTH ARCHITECTURE: ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ LAYER 1 — Edge DDoS Protection │ │ AWS Shield Standard (free, automatic L3/L4 protection) │ │ Protects: volumetric DDoS, SYN floods, UDP reflection │ ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤ │ LAYER 2 — WAF (Web Application Firewall) │ │ AWS WAF on CloudFront + ALB │ │ Rules: SQL injection, XSS, rate limit (2000 req/5min), │ │ IP reputation, geo-block (non-US/Nigeria) │ │ Protects: L7 attacks, credential stuffing, bots │ ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤ │ LAYER 3 — VPC Security │ │ Public subnet (ALB only) + Private subnets (EKS, RDS) │ │ Security Groups: ALB→EKS:8000, EKS→RDS:5432 │ │ NACLs: broad subnet-level deny rules for known bad IPs │ │ Protects: unauthorized network access, port exposure │ ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤ │ LAYER 4 — TLS Everywhere │ │ ALB: TLS termination (ACM cert, auto-renew) │ │ EKS→RDS: TLS (RDS enforces SSL connections) │ │ EKS→Redis: TLS (ElastiCache encryption in-transit) │ │ Protects: eavesdropping, MITM, data in transit │ ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤ │ LAYER 5 — K8s NetworkPolicy │ │ Default-deny all ingress │ │ Allow: ingress→jobpost:8000, jobpost→postgres:5432 │ │ Allow: jobpost→redis:6379, monitoring→all:9090 │ │ Deny egress from postgres (DB never talks to internet) │ │ Protects: lateral movement, pod compromise │ ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤ │ LAYER 6 — mTLS (SPIFFE/SPIRE) │ │ Every pod gets cryptographic identity 
    # HTTP: GET/POST /path HTTP/1.1 + Host/Authorization headers -> 200 OK + JSON body
# curl -sv https://HOST/api/endpoint | jq .
    │ │ All pod-to-pod traffic encrypted + authenticated │ │ Protects: service impersonation, traffic sniffing │ ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤ │ LAYER 7 — Secrets + Data Encryptiis AUTH token │ │ Protects: data at rest, credential exposure │ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    Explanation

    This 7-layer architecture follows the "assume breach" philosophy. If an attacker bypasses Shield (L1), WAF (L2) still blocks SQL injection. If they get past WAF, SG rules (L3) limit which ports they can reach. If they compromise the ALB, TLS (L4) encrypts traffic so they can't read it. If they compromise a pod, NetworkPolicy (L5) limits which other pods they can reach. If they spoof a pod IP, mTLS (L6) requires a valid SPIFFE certificate. If they somehow access the database, encryption at rest (L7) means the data is unreadable without KMS keys. EacChapter 34: Kubernetes Network Policies — The Pod-Level Firewall

    By default, every pod in Kubernetes can communicate with every other pod — regardless of namespace. This is convenient for development but catastrophic for security. NetworkPolicies give you pod-level firewall rules: exactly which pods can talk to which, on which ports. Combined with defense in depth, they're your primary tool against lateral movement.

The moment you create your FIRST NetworkPolicy that selects a pod, ALL OTHER traffic to that pod is IMPLICITLY DENIED. Only traffic matching your policy's ingress rules is allowed. This means: If you create a policy allowing ingress on port 5432 to postgres pods, suddenly those pods can't receive traffic on ANY other port — including DNS (port 53), health checks, or metrics. Safe approach: Always create a broad "allow necessary infrastructure" policy FIRST (DNS, monitoring, health checks), THEN create restrictive application policies. Test in a dev namespace before applying to production. Use kubectl describe networkpolicy to see which pods are affected.
