    🔍 CiliumNetworkPolicy — L7 Rules Beyond Standard NetworkPolicy

    Standard K8s NetworkPolicies only filter at L3/L4 (IP + port). Cilium extends this with CiliumNetworkPolicy CRDs that filter at L7: HTTP method, path, headers, Kafka topic, DNS query name. Example — allow GET /api/jobs/ but deny POST:

             app: jobpost
    ingress:
    - fromEndpoints:
      - matchLabels:
          app: ingress-nginx
      toPorts:
      - ports:
        - port: "8000"
          protocol: TCP
        rules:
          http:
          - method: GET
            path: "/api/jobs/.*"
          - method: POST
            path: "/api/jobs/"
          # DENIES: DELETE, Cilium can further restrict which HTTP endpoints are accessible. Combined with standard NetworkPolicies, you get: L3/L4 (who can connect) + L7 (what they can do).

    34.2 Writing NetworkPolicies for anihpj

      # ═══ COMPLETE NETWORKPOLICY SET FOR ANIHPJ ═══

  # 1. DEFAULT DENY ALL ingress in the anihpj namespace:
  apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
  kind: NetworkPolicy
  metadata:
    name: deny-all-ingress
    namespace: anihpj
  spec:
    podSelector: {}          # Selects ALL pods in the namespace
    policyTypes:
    - Ingress
    # No ingress rules → denies ALL incoming traffic

  # 2. ALLOW ingress controller → jobpost (port 8000):
  apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
  kind: NetworkPolicy
  metadata:
    name: allow-ingress-to-jobpost
    namespace: anihpj
  spec:
    podSelector:
      matchLabels:
        app: jobpost
    policyTypes:
    - Ingress
    ingress:
    - from:
      - namespaceSelector:
          matchLabels:
            name: ingress-nginx
      ports:
      - ostgres
    namespace: anihpj
  spec:
    podSelector:
      matchLabels:
        app: postgres
    policyTypes:
    - Ingress
    ingrs (port 9090 metrics):
  apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
  kind: NetworkPolicy
  metadata:
    name: allow-monitoring
    namespace: anihpj
  spec:
    podSelector: {}          # All pods
    policyTypes:
    - Ingress
    ingress:
    - from:
      - namespaceSelector:
          matchLabels:
            name: monitoring
      ports:
      - protocol: TCP
        port: 9090

  # 5. ALLOW DNS from all pods (UDP 53 to kube-system):
  apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
  kind: NetworkPolicy
  metadata:
    name: allow-dns
    namespace: anihpj
  spec:
    podSelector: {}
    policyTypes:
    - Egress
    egress:
    - to:
      - namespaceSelector:
          matchLabels:
            kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system
      ports:
      - protocol: UDP
        port: 53
      # Create two test pods in different namespaces:
  kubectl create ns test-a
  kubectl create ns test-b
  kubectl run pod-a --image=nginx -n test-a
  kubectl run pod-b --image=nginx -n test-b

  # BEFORE NetworkPolicy: pod-b can reach pod-a
  kubectl exec -n test-b pod-b -- curl -s --connect-timeout 3 pod-a.test-a:80
  # OUTPUT: <html>...nginx welcome page...</html> ← WORKS (no policies)

  # Apply deny-all to namespace test-a:
  kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
  apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
  kind: NetworkPolicy
  metadata:
    name: deny-all
    namespace: test-a
  spec:
    podSelector: {}
    policyTypes: [Ingress]
  EOF

  # AFTER NetworkPolicy: pod-b CANNOT reach pod-a
  kubectl exec -n test-b pod-b -- curl -s --connect-timeout 3 pod-a.test-a:80
  # OUTPUT: curl: (28) Connection timed out ← BLOCKED!

  # Allow specific pod label:
  kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
  apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
  kind: NetworkPolicy
  metadata:
    name: allow-from-test-b
    namespace: test-a
  spec:
    podSelector: {}
    ingress:
    - from:
      - namespaceSelector:
          matchLabels:
            kubernetes.io/metadata.name: test-b
  EOF

  # With Hubble (if Cilium installed):
  hubble observe --namespace test-a --verdict DROPPED
  # Shows every dropped packet with the reason: "Policy denied"
    🛡️ Kyverno — Enforce NetworkPolicy by Default Across All Namespaces

    You can manually create default-deny policies in every namespace, but that relies on humans remembering. Kyvern class="diagram-box">

      apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
  kind: ClusterPolicy
  metadata:
    name: auto-default-deny
  icy
        name: default-deny
        namespace: "{{request.object.metadata.name}}"
        data:
          spec:
            podSelector: {}
            policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]
  # This creates a deny-all NetworkPolicy in EVERY namespace
  # automatically. Namespaces must then add explicit allow rules.

    Kyverno can also: (1) Require that all pods have a NetworkPolicy selecting them (prevent unmanaged pods). (2) Block pods with hostNetwork: true x. Both implement "policy as code" — infrastructure guardrails that prevent misconfigurations before they reach production.

    🚪 Egress Security — Preventing Data Exfiltration

    Most teams focus on ingress (who can reach my pods?) but neglect egress (where can my pods reach?). A compromised pod can exfiltrate data to an attacker-controlled server if egress is unrestricted. Egress NetworkPolicy best practices: (1) Default-deny egress and explicitly allow only necessary destinations. (2) Allow DNS (UDP 53 to CoreDNS) — pods need this to resolve service names. (3) Allow specific external APIs by CIDR (e.g., api.stripe.com → resolve to IPs, allow those /32 or /24 ranges). (4) BLOCK cloud metadata endpoint (169.254.169.254 on AWS) — prevents IMDSv1 credential theft. Use iptables or NetworkPolicy: ipBlock: {cidr: 169.254.169.254/32} with no corresponding allow rule = blocked. (5) BLOCK internal RFC1918 ranges that pods shouldn't access (other VPCs, on-prem networks). For anihpj: jobpost pods should egress to: DNS (UDP 53), PostgreSQL (TCP 5432 to RDS subnet), Redis (TCP 6379), and specific external APIs (HTTPS 443 to known IPs). Everything else: DENIED. This limits blast radius — even if a pod is compromised, the attacker can't phone home.

    📝 Chapter 34 — Networking Practice Questions

    Q1
    What is the default network policy in Kubernetes? Why is it dangerous?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    With NO NetworkPolicies, ALL traffic between ALL pods in ALL namespaces is allowed. Every pod can reach every other pod on any port. This is dangerous because: (1) A compromised pod can attack any other pod. (2) There's no segmentation between environments (dev/staging/prod if in the same cluster). (3) Sensitive services (databases) accept connections from any pod. First action in any production cluster: apply a default-deny NetworkPolicy to every namespace, then explicitly allow only necessary traffic.

    Explanation

    Kubernetes' "allow all by default" philosophy is the opposite of security best practice. It's a legacy of K8s' origins as a developer-friendly platform where ease of use trumped security. In production, this is unacceptable. A default-deny policy (empty podSelector, no ingress rules) instantly blocks all incoming traffic to pods in that namespace. Then you add allow rules for legitimate traffic. The key insight: NetworkPolicies are namespace-scoped. A default-deny in namespace "anihpj" doesn't affect namespace "monitoring." You must apply policies to every namespace individually. Use tools like Kyverno or OPA Gatekeeper to enforce that every namespace has a default-deny policy.

    Q2
    What happens when you create your FIRST NetworkPolicy that selects a pod?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    The moment a pod is selected by ANY NetworkPolicy, ALL traffic to that pod is IMPLICITLY DENIED — only traffic explicitly allowed by the policy's ingress rules passes. This is the "implicit deny" rule. If your policy only allows port 5432, all other ports (22, 80, 9090, DNS) are blocked — including infrastructure traffic. Always create a broad "allow DNS and monitoring" policy first, then restrictive application policies.

    Explanation

    This is the #1 NetworkPolicy gotcha that causes production outages. Scenario: You create a NetworkPolicy to allow jobpost→postgres on port 5432. Suddenly, Prometheus can't scrape postgres metrics (port 9090 blocked), health checks fail (port 10254 blocked), and DNS stops working for postgres pods (egress to UDP 53 blocked). The fix: always start with infrastructure policies: (1) Allow DNS egress from all pods. (2) Allow monitoring ingress to all pods. (3) Allow ingress controller to all web-facing pods. THEN add restrictive application policies. Remember: NetworkPolicies are additive — you can have multiple policies selecting the same pods, and the UNION of their rules applies.

    Q3
    How do you allow traffic from pods in a specific namespace? From a specific pod label in ANOTHER namespace?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    From a namespace: Use namespaceSelector. From specific pods in another namespace: Use BOTH namespaceSelector AND podSelector in the same from entry — they combine with AND logic. Example: allow from pods with label app: prometheus in namespace with label name: monitoring. From an IP range (outside cluster): Use ipBlock with cidr and optional except.

    Explanation

    The selector logic is: multiple from entries = OR (traffic matching ANY entry is allowed). Multiple selectors within ONE from entry = AND (traffic must match ALL selectors). This is powerful but confusing. Example: from: [{namespaceSelector: {name: monitoring}, podSelector: {app: prometheus}}] means "allow traffic ONLY from pods labeled app=prometheus that are in namespace labeled name=monitoring." Pods labeled app=prometheus in the default namespace are NOT allowed. This AND behavior enables precise cross-namespace access control.

    Q4
    Write a NetworkPolicy that allows jobpost pods to connect to PostgreSQL on port 5432 and denies everything else to PostgreSQL.
    Show Answer
    Answer
    apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: postgres-access
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: postgres
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  ingress:
  - from:
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: jobpost
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 5432
    Explanation

    This policy selects pods with label app: postgres and allows ingress only from pods with label app: jobpost on

    # TLS 1.3: ClientHello->ServerHello{EncExt,Cert,CertVerify,Finished}->ClientFinished
# openssl s_client -connect HOST:443 -showcerts
    TCP port 5432. Because this is the only policy selecting postgres pods, ALL other traffic is implicitly denied. This includes: other pods in the same namespace, pods in other namespaces, monitoring agents (unless they have their own allow policy), and even the kubelet health check. In production, you'd also add policies for: DNS egress from postgres (port 53 UDP), monitoring ingress (port 9090), and potentially backup agent access. The principle: start restrictive, then add exceptions.

    Q5
    What's the difference between ingress and egress NetworkPolicy rules?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    Ingress: Controls traffic COMING INTO pods selected by the policy. "Who can connect TO me?" Egress: Controls traffic LEAVING FROM pods selected by the policy. "Where can I connect TO?" A policy can define both, one, or neither. If policyTypes includes Ingress but has no ingress rules → deny all ingress. Same for Egress. If policyTypes is empty → the policy has no effect (rarely useful).

    Explanation

    Egress rules are often overlooked but are critical for containing compromised pods. If an attacker compromises a jobpost pod, they might try to: (1) Connect to a C2 server on the internet (exfiltrate data). (2) Scan other pods in the cluster. (3) Connect to the cloud metadata endpoint (169.254.169.254) to steal IAM credentials. An egress NetworkPolicy on jobpost pods can restrict outbound traffic to only: DNS (UDP 53), PostgreSQL (TCP 5432), Redis (TCP 6379), and external APIs (TCP 443 to specific IPs). This prevents the attacker from reaching their C2 server or scanning the network. Always pair ingress AND egress policies for defense in depth.

    Q6
    How do NetworkPolicies interact with the CNI? Which CNIs support them?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    NetworkPolicies are enforced by the CNI plugin — NOT by Kubernetes itself. The Kubernetes API just stores the policy objects. The CNI must implement enforcement. CNIs that support NetworkPoling> Flannel (no policy support — use Calico on top), Amazon VPC CNI (requires Calico or Cilium for NetworkPolicy), basic bridge CNI. Check your CNI: kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep -E "calico|cilium|weave|flannel".

    Explanation

    This is a critical architectural dCNI does NOT support NetworkPolicies — you must install Calico or Cilium. AKS (Azure) supports NetworkPolicies with Azure CNI + Calico network policy engine. GKE supports NetworkPolicies natively (they use Calico under the hood). For anihpj on EKS: install Calico for NetworkPolicy support alongside the AWS VPC CNI. Calico handles policy enforcement while VPC CNI handles IP allocation. Verify enforcement: apply a deny-all policy, then test with curl between pods — if it still works, your CNI doesn't support NetworkPolicies.

    Q7
    How do you allow DNS traffic from all pods while denying everything else?
    Show Anname: allow-dns-egress namespace: anihpj spec: podSelector: {} policyTypes: - Egress egress: - to: 
    # TLS 1.3: ClientHello->ServerHello{EncExt,Cert,CertVerify,Finished}->ClientFinished
# openssl s_client -connect HOST:443 -showcerts
    - namespaceSelector: matchLabels: kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system - podSelector: matchLabels: k8s-app: kube-dns ports: - protocol: UDP port: 53
    Explanation

    DNS is the silent dependency that breaks everything when blocked. Pods need DNS to resolve Service names, external APIs, and cloud endpoints. When you create egress policies, always start with DNS allow. The rule above allows UDP 53 to kube-dns pods in kube-system namespace. For CoreDNS, the label is k8s-app: kube-dns. Important: DNS also uses TCP 53 for large responses (>512 bytes) and zone transfers. In practice, UDP 53 covers 99% of DNS traffic. If you see intermittent DNS failures after applying egress policies, add TCP 53 as well. Also: CoreDNS pods may be on different nodes — NetworkPolicy applies regardless of which node the traffic passeer">Q8

    Can NetworkPolicies restrict traffic by HTTP method or path? If not, what can?
    Show AnswerCilium NetworkPolicy# DNS RESOLUTION: Browser cache -> OS hosts -> resolver -> root->TLD->authoritative NS # dig +trace DOMAIN; nslookup DOMAIN; /etc/resolv.conf naNGINX Ingress annotations (only for ingress traffic).     35.3 Mutual TLS (mTLS) — Cryptographic Identity for Every Service

    Mutual TLS (mTLS) is TLS where BOTH sides present certificates. The client verifies the server (standard TLS) AND the server verifies the client (mutual). This gives every connection cryptographic proof of identity — not just encryption.

    Standard TLS vs Mutual TLS (mTLS)
      STANDARD TLS:    1. ClientHello
  2. ← ServerHello + ServerCert         2. ← ServerHello + ServerCert
  3. Client verifies server cert         3. ← CertificateRequest
  4. Key exchange, encrypted channel     4. ClientHello + ClientCert →
                                         5. Server verifies client cert
  Server knows: client IP                6. Key exchange, encrypted channel
  Server does NOT know: WHO the client is
                                         Server knows: SPIFFE ID of client
  ✅ Encryption                          ✅ Encryption + Authentication
  ❌ No client identity                  ✅ Cryptographic client identity

No application code changes needed. Istiod (control plane) distributes certificates. mTLS can be permissive (allow plaintext + TLS) or strict (TLS only). Strict mode = any pod without a sidecar is rejected.

    🦅
    Linkerd — Ultra-Light mTLS

    Linkerd also injects sidecars but is much lighter than Istio (Rust-based proxy, not Envoy). Automatic mTLS with identity based on service account. Linkerd's control plane (identity controller) acts as an internal CA, issuing 24-hour certificates to every proxy. Lower overhead, fewer features — ideal Step by Step

    Phase 1 (Current): TLS on the edge (ALB terminates HTTPS). Pod-to-pod = plain HTTP. NetworkPolicies restrict pod-to-pod traffic by IP/port. Phase 2 (Next): Add mTLS for sensitive services — jobpost→postgres and jobpost→redis connections are TLS-encrypted with client certificates. Phase 3 (Future): Deploy SPIRE for workload identity. Every pod gets a SPIFFE ID. Enforce mTLS mesh-wide — no plaintext traffic anywhere. Phase 4 (Ideal): Full zero trust: SPIFFE identities + NetworkPolicies + mTLS + OPA for authorization. Every connection: authenticated (who are you?), authorized (are you allowed?), encrypted (can anyone listen?).

    📜 Certificate Transparency — Public Audit Logs for TLS Certificates

    Certificate Transparency (CT) is a system that publicly logs ALL TLS certificates issued by participating CAs. Why it exists: In 2011, DigiNotar CA was hacked and issued fraudulent certificateppend-only logs. Domain owners can monitor CT logs for certificates issued for their domains — detecting fraudulent certs in near real-time. How it works: (1) CA submits certificate to CT log. (2) CT log returns an SCT (Signed Certificate Timestamp) — proof the cert was logged. (3) The SCT is embedded in the certificate (or served via OCSP stapling/TLS extension). (4) Browsers require SCTs — certificates without SCTs are rejected (Chrome requires CT since 2015). Monitor your domains: crt.sh/?q=%.anihpj.com — see every certificate ever issued for your domain. Set up alerts via certspotter or Cert Spotter. If you see a certificate you didn't request, your CA or domain might be compromised.

    �rict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains; preload. What happens: (1) Browser visits https://api.anihpj.com → sees HSTS header → remembers for 1 year (max-age). (2) User accidentally types http://api.anihpj.com → browser AUTOMATICALLY rewrites to https:// BEFORE sending any request. (3) If TLS certificate is invalid, browser shows HARD ERROR — user can't bypass (no "proceed anyway" button). includeSubDomains: Applies to ALL subdomains (*.anihpj.com). preload: Submit to Google's HSTS preload list — hardcoded into Chrome/Firefox, so even the FIRST visit is HTTPS. Risks: If you lose TLS capability (cert expired, misconfigured), your site is COMPLETELY inaccessible for max-age duration. Start with short max-age (300 = 5 minutes), test, then increase to 1 year. For anihpj: enable HSTS on your ALB/nginx. Submit to the preload list once stable. Combined with cert-manager auto-renewal, you get permanent HTTPS with zero manual intervention.

    🔧 TLS Cipher Hardening — What to Enable and What to Disable

    Not all TLS is created equal. Older TLS versions and weak ciphers have known vulnerabilities (POODLE, BEAST, CRIME, Heartbleed). Modern TLS configuration (2025 standard): (1) Disable TLS 1.0 and 1.1: Vulnerable to POODLE and BEAST. Minimum TLS 1.2, prefer TLS 1.3. (2) Disable weak ciphers: RC4, 3DES, CBC-mode ciphers. Use only AEAD ciphers (AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305). (3) Enable Perfect Forward Secrecy: ECDHE key exchange (not static RSA). Ensures past sessions can't be decrypted even if the private key is compromised. (4) nginx example: ssl_protocols TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3; ssl_ciphers ECDHE-ECDSA-AES128-GCM-SHA256:ECDHE-RSA-AES128-GCM-SHA256; ssl_prefer_server_ciphers on;. (5) Test your config: sslscan api.anihpj.com or testssl.sh api.anihpj.com — shows all supported protocols and ciphers. (6) SSL Labs rating: aim for A+. For anihpj: ALB with ACM handles TLS negotiation — ACM uses strong defaults. For nginx Ingress: configure the SSL settings above. For internal PostgreSQL: use sslmode=verify-full with strong ciphers.

    📝 Chapter 35 — Networking Practice Questions

    Q1
    What are the 5 stages of the TLS certificate lifecycle?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    (1) Issue: Generate CSR + private key, submit to CA, prove domain ownership. (2) Deploy: Store cert + key as K8s Secret, reference in Ingress or mount in pod. (3) Monitor: Check expiry dates, alert at 30 days remaining. (4) Renew: Get new certificate BEFORE expiry, replace Secret without downtime. (5) Revoke: If key compromised, add cert to CRL or OCSP staple, replace immediately.

    Explanation

    Most certificate

    # TLS 1.3: ClientHello->Serdo stages 1-2 but neglect 3-4. "The certificate expired" is the #1 TLS-related outage — and it's 100% preventable with monitoring and automation. Let's Encrypt issues 90-day certificates specifically to force automation — you can't manually renew every 90 days, you MUST automate. cert-manager handles stages 2-4 automatically: it deploys the cert, monitors expiry, and renews 30 days before. The only manual step is initial setup of the ClusterIssuer. For anihpj: use cert-manager from day one. Set up Prometheus alerts on certmanager_certificate_expiration_timestamp_seconds — alert when fewer than 30 days remain (backup for cert-manager's own renewal).
    Q2
    How does cert-manager auto-renew certificates? What can go wrong?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    cert-manager watches Certificate resources. 30 days before expiry, it initiates renewal: creates a new Order → completes ACME challenge → obtains new cert → updates the referenced Secret. What can go wrong: (1) ACME challenge fails (DNS record not updated, HTTP endpoint unreachable) → renewal fails silently, cert expires. (2) cert-manager pod is down → no renewal. (3) Rate limiting: Let's Encrypt limits 5 duplicate certs per week — if cert-manager retries too aggressively, it gets rate-limited. (4) Secret update fails (RBAC issue) → old cert stays. Monitor: kubectl get certificaterequests -A and kubectl describe certificate for renewal status.

    Explanation

    cert-manager is reliable but not infallible. The most common failure mode is ACME challenge failure. For HTTP-01: the Ingress must be correctly configured to route /.well-known/acme-challenge/ to cert-manager's solver pod. If your Ingress has a catch-all redirect to HTTPS, the HTTP challenge (which requires port 80) gets redirected → challenge fails. For DNS-01: the DNS provider API credentials must be valid and have permission to create TXT records. If someone rotates the API key without updating the Secret, challenges fail. Defense: (1) Set up independent expiry monitoring (don't trust cert-manager alone). (2) Test renewal in staging before production. (3) Keep at least 30 days of buffer — if renewal fails, you have time to fix it.

    Q3
    What is mutual TLS (mTLS)? How is it different from standard TLS?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    Standard TLS: server presents certificate, client verifies server. Client is anonymous. mTLS: BOTH server AND client present certificates. Server verifies client's identity cryptographically. This provides: (1) Authentication — the server knows WHO is connecting (not just IP). (2) Encryption — same as TLS. (3) Authorization — server can allow/deny based on client certificate's identity (SPIFFE ID). mTLS is the foundation of zero trust networking — every connection is authenticated, not just trusted because it's "inside the network."

    Explanation

    Standard TLS answers "can I trust this server?" (prevent MITM). mTLS also answers "should I trust this client?" (prevent unauthorized access). In a microservice architecture, this is transformative: instead of IP-based access control (which breaks when pods restart with new IPs), you use identity-based access control. A PostgreSQL proxy can accept connections only from clients presenting a certificate with SPIFFE ID spiffe://anihpj.com/ns/production/sa/jobpost. Even if an attacker compromises a different pod and gets its IP, they can't connect because they don't have the jobpost SPIFFE certificate. This is defense in depth at the cryptographic level.

    Q4
    What is the difference between HTTP-01 and DNS-01 ACME challenges?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    HTTP-01: CA checks a token at http://domain/.well-known/acme-challenge/<token>. Requires port 80 open. Works only for public-facing domains. DNS-01: CA checks a TXT record at _acme-challenge.domain.com. Requires DNS API access. Works for INTERNAL services and WILDCARD certs (*.anihpj.com). No public port needed. HTTP-01 is simpler; DNS-01 is more flexible and secure (no public exposure needed). Use DNS-01 for production wildcard and internal certificates.

    Explanation

    The choice between HTTP-01 and DNS-01 depends on your infrastructure. HTTP-01 requires that port 80 is publicly accessible and that your Ingress correctly routes the challenge path. This is fine for public APIs but problematic for internal services (databases, message queues) that shouldn't have public endpoints. DNS-01 delegates validation to your DNS provider — the CA never connects to your infrastructure. For anihpj: use HTTP-01 for api.anihpj.com (it's already public). Use DNS-01 for *.internal.anihpj.com (wildcard for internal services — lets you issue one cert for all internal hostnames). The DNS-01 solver in cert-manager supports Route53, Cloudflare, Google Cloud DNS, and 30+ other providers. Configure the solver with your DNS provider's API credentials stored in a K8s Secret.

    Q5
    How do service meshes (Istio, Linkerd) implement mTLS? What's the trade-off?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    Both inject a sidecar proxy into every pod. All pod traffic flows through the sidecar (pod→sidecar→network→sidecar→pod). Sidecars automatically handle mTLS handshake, certificate rotation, and encryption. Trade-offs: (1) Resource overhead: each sidecar uses 50-200MB RAM + CPU for TLS. (2) Latency: 1-5ms added per hop. (3) Complexity: debugging pod-to-pod issues now involves sidecar logs. (4) Benefit: application code doesn't need TLS logic — the mesh handles it transparently. Linkerd is lighter (Rust proxy) but fewer features; Istio is heavier (Envoy) but more capable (L7 routing, circuit breaking).

    Explanation

    Service mesh mTLS is "invisible mTLS" — your application doesn't need to know about certificates, SPIFFE, or TLS libraries. The sidecar transparently upgrades all traffic to mTLS. This is both the biggest benefit and the biggest risk: benefit because you get mTLS everywhere without changing code; risk because you now have a complex distributed system (the mesh) that can fail in subtle ways. For anihpj: start with application-level TLS (Django connects to PostgreSQL with sslmode=require). This gives you encryption without a mesh. Add a service mesh later if you need mesh-wide mTLS, traffic splitting, or advanced observability. Many teams never need a full mesh — application-level TLS + NetworkPolicies covers 90% of security requirements.

    Q6
    L2(arping)->L3(ping)->L4(nc -zv)->L7(curl)summary>
    Answer

    When a certificate expires, clients refuse to connect — browsers show "Your connection is not private," APIs return TLS errors, and inter-service mTLS breaks. This is a HARD outage — no gradual degradation. Prevention: (1) Automate renewal (cert-manager with 30-day buffer). (2) Independent monitoring: check all certs weekly (Prometheus Blackbox Exporter, ssl-cert-check script). (3) Alert at 30 days, page at 14 days. (4) Test renewal process quarterly. (5) Short-lived certs (90 days like Let's Encrypt) force automation — long-lived certs (1 year) rot because nobody remembers to renew. (6) Keep a runbook: "cert expired → run cert-manager renewal OR manually generate + deploy."

    Explanation

    Certificate expiry is the #1 self-inflicted outage. The insidious part: it works perfectly for months, then fails catastrophically at a specific second. Unlike most failures that degrade gradually, certificate expiry is binary. Let's Encrypt's 90-day validity was a deliberate design choice — it forces automation because manual renewal every 90 days is impractical. ACM (AWS Certificate Manager) certificates auto-renew (if DNS-validated) but the renewal creates a NEW cert ARN — your infrastructure must reference the new ARN. This trips up teams that hardcode cert ARNs in Terraform. Best practice: use ACM with DNS validation → cert auto-renews → reference by domain name in ALB listener, not by ARN.

    Q7
    OCSP Stapling: Server periodically fetches OCSP response from CA and "staples" it to the TLS handshake. Client doesn't need to contact CA — faster + more private. All modern servers support OCSP stapling (nginx: ssl_stapling on).

    Explanation

    Revocation is the weak link in TLS security. If your private key is compromised, you MUST revoke the certificate. But how quickly do clients learn about the revocation? CRLs are cached for hours or days — an attacker can use a revoked cert for a long time. OCSP is real-time but has a privacy problem (the CA sees every site you visit) and a performance problem (extra round trip). OCSP stapling solves both: the serveng> enable OCSP stapling on nginx: ssl_stapling on; ssl_stapling_verify on;. cert-manager doesn't handle revocation — if a cert is compromised, you must manually revoke via the CA's

    Q8
    What are the key differences between Let's Encrypt, AWS ACM, and a corporate/internal CA?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    Let's Encrypt: Free, automated, 90-day certs, publicly trusted (all browsers). Requires ACME challenge (domain validation). Best for: public-facing services. AWS ACM: Free, auto-renewing, 13-month certs, publicly trusted. No private key export (must use with AWS services). Best for: AWS-native services (ALB, CloudFront, API Gateway). Corporate/Internal CA: You control everything. Issue certs for internal domains, custom validity periods. NOT publicly trusted (must distribute CA cert to all clients). Best for: internal services, mTLS, service mesh identity.

    Explanation

    The CA choice depends on trust domain. For public APIs (api.anihpj.com): use Let's Encrypt or ACM — they're trusted by all browsers. For internal services (postgres.anihpj.internal): you can use an internal CA because you control all the clients. ACM's limitation is important: you can't export the private key. This means ACM certs only work with integrated AWS services (ALB, CloudFront, API Gateway). You can't use an ACM cert on your own nginx server. For non-AWS services, use Let's Encrypt (via cert-manager) or an internal CA. For anihpj: ACM for the public ALB, cert-manager + Let's Encrypt for nginx Ingress, and a smallstep CA or HashiCorp Vault for internal mTLS certs.

    What is the difference between Active/Passive and Active/Active HA? When would you use each?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    Active/Passive: One path active, one standby. Standby idle until failover. Failover time: 30s-5min (detection + switchover). Cost: 1.5× (idle hardware). Use for: simple apps, databases, legacy systems. Active/Active: All paths carry traffic simultaneously. Failover: instant (traffic already distributed). Cost: 2× (all hardware active). Use for: stateless web services, cloud-native apps, any system that can handle distributed traffic. Active/Active requires careful design for data consistency (conflict resolution).

    Explanation

    The key trade-off is recovery speed vs complexity. Active/Passive is simpler — you just need a heartbeat between the active and passive, and a mechanism to switch. But during failover, the passive takes over with cold caches, no established connections, and potentially stale data. Active/Active eliminates the failover event entirely — both sides are always handling traffic. But you must solve: data synchronization (how do writes in region A appear in region B?), conflict resolution (what if the same record is updated in both regions simultaneously?), and distributed transaction management. For anihpj: stateless jobpost pods → Active/Active across AZs (ALB distributes). Stateful PostgreSQL → Active/Passive within region (RDS Multi-AZ with automatic failover to standby).

    Q2
    What is RTO and RPO? How do they drive network design decisions?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    RTO (Recovery Time Objective): Maximum acceptable downtime. Drives: DNS TTL (lower = faster failover but more queries), automation investment, database failover speed. RPO (Recovery Point Objective): Maximum acceptable data loss. Drives: replication type (sync = 0 loss, async = seconds of loss), backup frequency, WAL archiving. Network design must support both: RTO drives HA architecture (Active/Active vs Active/Passive), RPO drives data replication design (sync vs async, cross-region).

    Explanation

    RTO and RPO are business decisions with technical consequences. If the business says "RTO=5 min, RPO=0," you CANNOT use DNS failover with 300s TTL (RTO would be 5+ minutes just for DNS propagation). You need instant failover (BGP anycast, or Active/Active with health-check-based routing). If RPO=0, you MUST use synchronous replication — which requires low-latency links (same region or metro area). Cross-region sync replication is impractical (50ms+ latency per write). This is why most architectures use: sync within region (RPO=0), async cross-region (RPO=~1s), DNS failover cross-region (RTO=~60s). The network design flows directly from the RTO/RPO requirements.

    Q3
    How does DNS-based failover work? What are its limitations?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    Route53 (or similar) performs health checks on your endpoints. When the primary fails, Route53 stops returning the primary IP and returns the secondary IP. Limitations: (1) TTL-dependent — clients cache the old IP until TTL expires (if TTL=300s, failover takes up to 5 min). (2) Client DNS caching — some clients/browsers ignore TTL and cache longer. (3) Not instantaneous — health check interval (10-30s) + detection threshold + DNS propagation. (4) Connection state lost — existing TCP connections to the failed endpoint are dropped. (5) Sticky sessions broken. Mitigations: low TTL (60s), multiple health checkers, client-side retry logic.

    Explanation

    DNS failover is simple, universal,

    # PERF: iperf3 -c SERVER(bandwidth), ping -c 100 SERVER(latency/loss), mtr -r SERVER
# TCP retransmits = packet loss signal; ss -tin | grep retrans
    and surprisingly effective — but it's NOT instant. The TTL trade-off: low TTL (30s) = faster failover but more DNS queries (higher cost, slightly higher latency for users). High TTL (300s) = fewer queries but slower failover. Many organizations compromise at 60s. The real-world gotcha: some ISPs and corporate DNS resolvers IGNORE low TTLs and cache for their own minimum (often 300s or more). You can't control every resolver between your users and your DNS. For critical applications, combine DNS failover with BGP anycast (instant) or use a global load balancer (Cloudflare, AWS Global Accelerator) that handles failover at the network layer, not DNS.

    Q4
    What is the difference between LACP, ECMP, and BGP for link redundancy?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    LACP (Link Aggregation): Bundles multiple physical links between the SAME two devices into one logical link. L2 only. Both ends must support it. ECMP (Equal-Cost Multi-Path): Multiple equal-cost routes to the same destination. Traffic is distributed across paths (typically by 5-tuple hash). L3. BGP (Border Gateway Protocol): Dynamic routing between different ASes. Can advertise the same prefix via multip

    # KEY NETWORKING COMMANDS
# Interface: ip addr show; ip link set eth0 up; ethtool eth0
# Routing:   ip route show; traceroute -n HOST; mtr -r HOST
# Sockets:   ss -tlnp; ss -ulnp; lsof -i :PORT; nc -zv HOST PORT
# DNS:       dig +short DOMAIN; nslookup DOMAIN; host DOMAIN
# Firewall:  iptables -L  is for two adjacent switches/routers — like bonding 4×25Gbps ports into one 100Gbps logical link between your core switch and top-of-rack switch. ECMP is for routing within a network — if you have two equal-cost paths to destination 10.0.0.0/16, the router hashes flows across both. BGP is for the internet scale — your AS advertises routes to peers, and BGP attributes (AS_PATH, LOCAL_PREF, MED) determine path selection. In AWS: Direct Connect uses BGP for on-prem ↔ AWS routing. ECMP would be used inside your on-prem network if you have multiple equaote DB → redirect traffic. Cost: 10-20% of primary. RTO: 15-60 minutes. Active-Active: Both regions fully scaled, serving traffic. Cost: 2× primary. RTO: instant. Pilot Light is the sweet spot for most organizations — you have the core components running (data replication, minimal compute) but pay a fraction of full Active-Active cost. Use Pilot Light for RTO of 15-60min. Use Active-Active for RTO < 1min.
    Explanation

    Pilot Light is like keeping your car idling instead of driving it around. The engine is running (database replication), but you're not paying for the full experience (compute, bandwidth). When disaster strikes, you "step on the gas" — auto-scale groups expand, RDS replicas are promoted, DNS is updated. The 15-60 minute RTO comes from: (1) Scaling up instances (2-5 min), (2) Promoting DB replica (5-10 min), (3) DNS propagation (1-5 min with low TTL), (4) Warming caches (5-15 min). For anihpj: Pilot Light is ideal. Run a minimal EKS cluster (2 nodes) + RDS read replica in eu-west-1. Replicate data continuously. On US-East failure: scale EU EKS to 6 nodes, promote RDS replica, update Route53. Total RTO: ~15 minutes.

    Q6
    How do you handle database failover in a multi-AZ architecture?
    Show Answer
    L2(arping)->L3(ping)->L4(nc -zv)->L7(curl)-120 seconds: RDS detects failure → promotes standby → updates DNS CNAME → application reconnects. The DNS CNAME (xxx.rds.amazonaws.com) has a 5-second TTL — much faster than typical DNS failover. For anihpj: production uses RDS Multi-AZ within us-east-1 (RPO=0, automatic failover). DR uses cross-region read replica in eu-west-1 (async, RPO=~1s, manual promotion via Lambda automation).

    Q7
    What are the trade-offs between low DNS TTL and high DNS TTL?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    Low TTL (30-60s): ✅ Fast failover (DNS updates propagate quickly). ✅ Quick A/B testute53, slightly higher latency). ❌ If your DNS provider is down, clietice: 60s TTL for critical records, 300s for stable services.

    Explanation

    DNS TTL is a trade-off between agility and stability. For anihpj production: set api.anihpj.com TTL to 60s. This enables fast Route53 failover (~60s instead of 5 min). The cost impact: at 1M queries/day, 60s TTL means clients cache for 60s → ~1M lookups/day. At 300s TTL, clients cache for 300s → ~288K lookups/day. Route53 charges $0.40/million queries — the difference is ~$8/month. That's trivial compared to the cost of 5 extra minutes of downtime. Set your TTL based on your RTO: if RTO=5min, 60s TTL is perfect. If RTO=15min, 300s TTL is fine.

    Scaling Decision Tree — "My App Is Slow Under Load"
      "My app is slow under load" — which scaling to apply?

  Is LATENCY the problem? (each request takes too long)
  ├── YES → Check: DB queries, downstream API calls, CPU bound?
  │         → Fix the bottleneck first. More instances won't help.

  Is THROUGHPUT the problem? (can't handle enough concurrent requests)
  ├── YES → Horizontal scaling: more pods + LB
  │         → Check connection limits: somaxconn, worker_connections

  Is BANDWIDTH the problem? (network interface saturated)
  ├── YES → CDN for static assets, compress responses (gzip/brotli)
  │         → Vertical scaling: upgrade NIC or instance type

  Are connections piling up in TIME_WAIT?
  └── YES → Connection pooling, keep-alive, reduce new connections
    requests served from edge (static assets). Only 5-20% reach origin. CloudFront caches: images, CSS, JS, fonts. Reduces origin bandwidth 5-20×. Also reduces latency (edge is closer to user). Cache-Control headers control what gets cached and for how long.

    🔗
    Connection Pooling

    Reuse TCP connections instead of opening new ones. Reduces handshake overhead 10-100×. PgBouncer for PostgreSQL, Redis connection pooling built-in. ⚠️ Gotcha: Pooling works great until a backend restart breaks ALL pooled connections simultaneously. Always use retry logic with exponential backoff.

    📈 HPA (Horizontal Pod Autoscaler) — Automatic Scaling Based on Real Metrics

    HPA automatically scales pods based on CPU, memory, or custom metrics. Basic HPA: kubectl autoscale deployment jobpost --min=3 --max=30 --cpu-percent=70. When average CPU exceeds 70%, HPA adds pods. When below, it removes them. Advanced — custom metrics: Scale based on requests/second, queue depth, or any Prometheus metric. Requires Prometheus Adapter. Example: scale jobpost when requests/second > 500 per pod. Network-aware scaling: HPA doesn't know about network limits — you can scale to 100 pods and saturate the instance NIC. Combine HPA with Cluster Autoscaler (adds nodes when pods can't schedule). Cool-down periods: --horizontal-pod-autoscaler-downscale-stabilization=5m — wait 5 minutes before scaling down (prevents flapping). For anihpj: CPU-based HPA for jobpost (CPU correlates with request load). Custom metric HPA for worker pods (scale based on queue depth). Always set max replicas to prevent runaway scaling from overwhelming the database or saturating network.

    💰 Network Cost Optimization — Where Your Cloud Bill Goes

    Network costs are the hidden line item that surprises every growing startup. AWS network costs breakdown: (1) NAT Gateway: $0.045/GB processed + $0.045/hour. A single high-traffic app can spend $500+/month on NAT. Fix: VPC Endpoints (S3=free, ECR/DynamoDB=cheaper). (2) Cross-AZ traffic: $0.01/GB each direction. If 50% of your ALB traffic goes cross-AZ, that's half your data at $0.01/GB. Fix: enable cross-zone LB (distributes evenly, same cost) OR deploy pod-affinity to keep traffic in-AZ. (3) Internet egress: $0.09/GB first 10TB, decreasing at higher tiers. 100TB/month = ~$7,000. Fix: CDN (CloudFront = $0.085/GB, cheaper at scale), compress responses (gzip/brotli = 70-90% smaller), VPC Endpoints for AWS services (bypass internet). (4) Direct Connect: $0.30/hr for port + $0.02/GB egress. Break-even vs. internet egress: ~5 TB/month. (5) Inter-region: $0.02/GB. Cross-region RDS replication, multi-region deployments. For anihpj: monthly network cost at 500 RPS (~10TB/month): NAT Gateway=$450 + cross-AZ=$100 + internet egress=$900 = ~$1,450. With optimization (VPC Endpoints + CDN + compression): NAT=$50, cross-AZ=$100, CDN egress=$85 = ~$235. Savings: $1,215/month (84% reduction). Network cost optimization pays for itself immediately.

    📝 Chapter 37 — Networking Practice Questions

    Q1
    How do you estimate the bandwidth needed for a web application?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    Formula: Bandwidth = RPS × Avg Response Size × 8 + overhead. Example: 500 RPS × 20KB response × 8 bits/byte = 80 Mbps. Add 20% for TLS/HTTP headers = 96 Mbps. Plan for peak (3× average) + 30% headroom. Also account for: upload bandwidth (if users upload files), traffic asymmetry, and cross-AZ data transfer (if services span AZs).

    Explanation

    Bandwidth estimation is essential for cloud cost planning — every Mbps costs money. The overhead matters: TLS handshake adds ~5KB per new connection. If you have 500 new connections/second, that's 2.5 MB/s (20 Mbps) just for TLS — nearly as much as the data itself! Use HTTP keep-alive to reuse connections and amortize the TLS overhead. For anihpj at 500 RPS: average bandwidth ~100 Mbps for responses + 20 Mbps for TLS overhead = ~120 Mbps outbound. Add 30% headroom = ~156 Mbps. A single m5.large instance (10 Gbps) provides 6iv class="eq-question">What's the difference between vertical and horizontal scaling? When would you use each?

    Show Answer
    Answer

    Vertical: Bigger/faster hardware (more CPU, RAM, NIC speed). Simple, no code changes, but hits a ceiling. Horizontal: More instances (more pods, more nodes). Scales infinitely, but requires stateless design and load balancing. Use vertical: for databases (hard to distribute), legacy apps, initial scaling. Use horizontal: for stateless web services, API servers, microservices. Cloud-native apps should be designed for horizontal scaling from day one.

    Explanation

    The cloud-native answer is always "horizontal" — but reality is nuanced. PostgreSQL can scale vertically (r5.large → r5.24xlarge = 48× more resources) but horizontal scaling (sharding) is very complex. For jobpost pods: they're stateless — horizontal scaling is trivial. For PostgreSQL: i scaled from 1 to 1000 without any changes.

    Q3
    How does a CDN reduce origin bandwidth? What percentage of traffic can it offload?
    Show Answer
    L2(arping)->L3(ping)->L4(nc -zv)->L7(curl)label">Answer

    A CDN caches static assets (images, CSS, JS, fonts) at edge locations worldwiave 100K page views/day = 200 GB/day of static assets. With a CDN caching for 1 year (max-age=31536000), 99% of these requests are cache hits — only 2 GB/day reaches your origin. The CDN absorbs 198 GB/day — reducing origin bandwidth from 200 GB to 2 GB (99% reduction). At $0.09/GB origin egress, that's $540/month saved. The CDN costs ~$17/month for the same traffic. Net savings: $523/month AND faster page loads for users worldwide.

    Q4
    What is connection pooling? Why does it matter at scale?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    Connection pooling reuses established TCP connections instead of opening new ones for every request. Without pooling: every request = new TCP handshake (1 RTT) + TLS handshake (2 RTTs) + query. With pooling: connection already open → just send query. Reduces latency 3-10× and server overhead 10-100×. Why it matters: At 1000 RPS without pooling, you need 1000 TCP handshakes/second — each creates a conntrack entry. At 1000 RPS with a pool of 50 connections, you reuse those 50 connections. That's 20× fewer conntrack entries and 3 fewer RTTs per query.

    Explanation

    Connection pooling is the difference between a system that handles 100 RPS and one that handles 10,000 RPS on the same hardware. The math: TCP+TLS handshake takes ~3 RTTs. At 1ms RTT, that's 3ms overhead per new connection. At 1000 RPS, that's 3 seconds of CPU time per second just for handshakes — impossible. With pooling, you pay the handshake cost once per connection creation (e.g., 50 connections = 150ms total), then reuse them for hours. For anihpj: configure PgBouncer with a pool of 50 connections per pod. 10 jobpost pods × 50 = 500 total DB connections — easily handled by PostgreSQL. Without pooling, each pod might open 500 connections under load = 5000 total — exceeding PostgreSQL's max_connections (default 100).

    Q5
    Your app is slow under load. Latency per request is fine, but throughput is low. What's likely wrong?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    If latency is fine but throughput is low, the problem is concurrency limits: (1) exhaustion — ip_local_port_range too narrow + TIME_WAIT buildup. Fix: increase all limits (somaxconn=4096, worker_connections=10000, ulimit -n 65536), widen port range, enable tcp_tw_reuse.

    Explanation

    This is the classic "latency vs throughput" diagnostic. Latency = how long ONE request takes (good → server code is fast). Throughput = how many concurrent requests you can handle (bad → you're hitting a connection limit). The most common culprit is somaxconn (default 128). If 200 users connect simultaneously, 72 of them get their SYN dropped at the kernel level — they experience "connection timed out" even though the server is idle. Second culprit: gunicorn with 4 workers can only handle 4 concurrent requests. Others queue

    # SOCKET STATS: ss -tlnp(TCP listening+ 1, or switch to async workers (gevent) for I/O-bound apps like Django. Third culprit: DB connection pool exhausted — all pool connections are in use, new requests wait. Fix: increase pool size or add read replicas.
    ry>
    Answer

    HTTP keep-alive reuses a single TCP connection for multiple HTTP requests/responses — instead of opening a new connection for each resource. Without keep-alive: Each image, CSS file, JS file = new TCP+TLS handshake (3 RTTs). With keep-alive: One handshake, all resources flow over the same connection. Reduces: connection count (fewer conntrack entries), latency (no handshake per resource), CPU (fewer TLS negotiations). Trade-off: Kept-alive connections consume server resources (socket, buffer). Too many idle keep-alive connections = resource waste. Tune keep-alive timeout (nginx: keepalive_timeout 65) and max requests per connection (keepalive_requests 1000).

    Explanation

    HTTP/1.1 defaults to keep-alive, but HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 make it even better — multiplexing multiple requests over a single connection simultaneously. A modern web page loads 50-100 resources. Without keep-alive: 100 TCP handshakes (300 RTTs just for setup). With HTTP/2 multiplexing: 1 connection, all 100 resources streamed concurrently. The performance difference is dramatic — pages load 3-5× fiv>

    Q7
    What happens when connection pooling breaks? How do you handle it?
    Show Answer
    Mitigations: (1) Retry logic with exponential backoff and jitter. (2) Connection health checks before using a pooled connection. (3) Circuit breaker: stop sending to a broken backend for a cooling-off period. (4) Graceful shutdown: backend drains connections before terminating (deregistration delay). (5) Connection pool auto-reconnect: pool detects broken connections and creates new ones.

    User → CloudFront CDN (static cache) → WAF (inspection) → ALB (TLS termination, port 443) → K8s Node via NodePort (30080) → iptables DNAT to ClusterIP (10.96.100.50:8000) → nginx Ingress pod → K8s Service endpoint → jobpost pod (10.244.1.5:8000) → RDS PostgreSQL (TLS-secured, port 5432). Each hop: DNS resolves name, TLS encrypts traffic, iptables/eBPF routes packets, NetworkPolicy authorizes connections, readiness probes verify health.

    Explanation

    This end-to-end journey is the ultimate test of your networking knowledge. At each hop, multiple systems must work: DNS (Route53 resolves api.anihpj.com to ALB IP), TLS (ALB terminates with ACM cert, nginx may re-encrypt), iptables (NodePort DNAT in nat/PREROUTING, Service DNAT in KUBE-SVC chain), CNI (VPC CNI routes pod IPs directly — no overlay), NetworkPolicy (Cilium/Calico enforces which pods can reach PostgreSQL), and application protocols (HTTP 1.1/2 between ALB and pod, PostgreSQL wire protocol between pod and RDS). If ANY hop fails, the request fails. Understanding this full journey is what separates senior SREs from junior ones.

    Show Answer
    Answer

    Multi-stage builds separate build dependencies from runtime. Benefits: (1) Smaller image — build tools (compilers, headers) aren't in the final image. (2) Security — fewer packages = smaller attack surface. (3) Faster pulls — smaller image = faster pod startup. (4) Cleaner — no build artifacts, no secrets in intermediate layers. The production image should contain ONLY the runtime: Python + app + dependencies. No gcc, no git, no dev headers.

    Q3
    What's the difference between a liveness probe and a readiness probe? How do they affect networking?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    Liveness probe: "Is the pod alive?" If it fails, K8s RESTARTS the pod. Readiness probe: "Is the pod ready to serve traffic?" If it fails, K8s REMOVES the pod from Service endpoints. Network impact: Readiness probe failure = pod IP removed from Endpoints → no traffic sent to pod. Liveness probe failure = pod restarted → new pod gets new IP → brief disruption while endpoints update. Readiness probes should check app health (DB connection, cache availability). Liveness probes should be simpler (just check the process is running) — avoid complex checks that could trigger unnecessary restarts.

    Explanation

    Misconfiguring probes is a common cause of cascading failures. If your readiness probe checks database connectivity and the DB is slow (but not down), ALL pods become "not ready" simultaneously → Service has zero endpoints → complete outage. Instead, readiness should check: "can I serve requests?" (process running, dependencies reachable). Liveness should check: "am I deadlocked?" (thread dump, deadlock detection). For anihpj: readiness probe = HTTP GET /api/health/ (checks DB + cache connectivity). Liveness probe = TCP check on port 8000 (is gunicorn still running?). If the DB is slow, readiness fails → pod removed from endpoints — good! Other pods with faster DB connections handle traffic. But liveness should NOT depend on DB — if all pods restart simultaneously because of a slow DB, you get a thundering herd.

    Q4
    Why run containers as non-root? What network security implications does this have?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    Running as non-root limits what a compromised container can do: (1) Can't bind to privileged ports (< 1024). (2) Can't modify system files. (3) Can't install kernel modules. (4) Can't modify network configuration (iptables, routes). Network implications: Binding to ports < 1024 requires root (or CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE). Apps should listen on high ports (e.g., 8000) and use Service/Ingress to map to standard ports (80/443). This adds a layer of security — even if an attacker escapes to the container, they can't easily set up a backdoor on port 22.

    Explanation

    Running as root in containers is dangerous because root in the container CAN be root on the host — unless explicitly blocked by pod security context (runAsNonRoot), seccomp profiles, or AppArmor. The network angle: a root container can modify iptables rules (if NET_ADMIN capability is granted), change routing tables, spoof ARP, and sniff traffic. A non-root container cannot do any of this. For anihpj: the Dockerfile uses USER appuser (UID 1000). The K8s manifest adds securityContext: {runAsNonRoot: true, runAsUser: 1000}. Gunicorn binds to port 8000 (non-privileged). The Service maps :8000 and the Ingress maps :443 → :8000. No root anywhere in the application layer.

    Q5
    How do K8s Ingress annotations affect networking? Give examples from the anihpj manifest.
    Show Answer
    Answer

    Ingress annotations tell the Ingress Controller HOW to configure the underlying load balancer. anihpj examples: (1) alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/scheme: internet-facing → creates a public ALB. (2) alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/target-type: ip → ALB targets pod IPs directly (no NodePort hop). (3) alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/listen-ports: '[{"HTTPS": 443}]' → only HTTPS, no HTTP. (4) alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/healthcheck-path: /api/health/ → ALB uses this path for health checks. Annotations are controller-specific — nginx ingress uses different annotations than ALB ingress.

    Explanation

    Ingress annotations are the bridge between K8s declarative config and cloud-specific implementation. The target-type: ip annotation is particularly important: without it, the ALB sends traffic to NodePort (30000-32767) on the node, which then goes through kube-proxy iptables → pod. This adds a hop and loses source IP. With target-type: ip, the AWS Load Balancer Controller registers pod IPs directly in the target group — traffic goes ALB → pod IP directly. This is faster (fewer hops), preserves client IP, and enables health checks directly against pods. For anihpj on EKS: always use target-type: ip with the AWS VPC CNI (which gives pods VPC-routable IPs).

    Q6
    What is the role of K8s Secrets in the anihpj network architecture?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    K8s Secrets store sensitive configuration: DATABASE_URL, REDIS_URL, API keys, TLS certificates. They're mounted as environment variables or files in pods. Security: Secrets are base64-encoded (not encrypted by default! Enable encryption at rest). Access is controlled via RBAC. Secrets are NOT visible in kubectl describe pod (values are hidden). In the anihpj manifest: DATABASE_URL comes from postgres-secret, avoiding hardcoding credentials in the Deployment YAML. For production: use external secret management (AWS Secrets Manager, Vault) with CSI driver to mount secrets as files — more secure than K8s Secrets.

    Explanation

    K8s Secrets are convenient but have important limitations. By default, they're stored in etcd as base64 (NOT encrypted) — anyone with etcd access can read them. Enable encryption at rest (KMS plugin). Use RBAC to restrict which service accounts can read which secrets (jobpost SA can read postgres-secret, monitoring SA cannot). For anihpj: the application reads DATABASE_URL and REDIS_URL from environment variables injected from Secrets. The connection URLs include credentials — they must never appear in logs, config files, or version control. Use a CSI driver (Secrets Store CSI Driver) to mount secrets from AWS Secrets Manager directly — they never touch K8s Secrets at all, eliminating the etcd exposure risk.

    Q7
    How does the ALB Ingress Controller decide which pods to register as targets?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    The AWS Load Balancer Controller watches K8s Ingress resources. When it sees an Ingress with ingressClassName: alb, it: (1) Creates an ALB (if not exists). (2) Creates a Target Group per backend Service. (3) Watches Endpoints for that Service — each pod IP:port becomes a target. (4) Registers pods whose Readiness Probe passes (K8s removes unready pods from Endpoints → Controller removes them from Target Group). (5) Configures health checks based on annotations. Pod lifecycle: created → readiness passes → added to Endpoints → added to Target Group → receives traffic.

    Explanation

    The ALB Ingress Controller bridges K8s and AWS networking. It translates K8s abstractions (Ingress, Service, Endpoints) into AWS resources (ALB, Target Group, Listener Rules). The flow: (1) Ingress created → Controller creates/modifies ALB. (2) Service with matching backend → Controller creates Target Group. (3) Pod becomes Ready → K8s adds pod IP to Endpoints → Controller adds pod IP to Target Group. (4) Pod becomes NotReady → K8s removes from Endpoints → Controller deregisters from Target Group. (5) ALB health checks run independently — even if a pod is in the Target Group, ALB only sends traffic if health checks pass. This dual health check (K8s readiness + ALB target health) provides defense in depth against routing traffic to broken pods.

    Q8
    What's the purpose of each annotation in the anihpj Ingress manifest?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    (1) scheme: internet-facing → Public ALB with public IPs (vs internal for private VPC access). (2) target-type: ip → Register pod IPs directly (vs instance mode = NodePort). (3) listen-ports: '[{"HTTPS": 443}]' → ALB only listens on HTTPS (no HTTP redirect — add another listener if needed). (4) healthcheck-path: /api/health/ → ALB uses this endpoint for health checks instead of default /. Each annotation corresponds to an AWS ALB configuration setting — the Controller translates them into API calls.

    Explanation

    Understanding each annotation is essential for debugging ALB issues. If users get 503: check healthcheck-path — is the path correct? Does the app return 200? If source IP is lost: you're probably using target-type: instance (default) which goes through NodePort → kube-proxy MASQUERADE. Switch to target-type: ip. If HTTP works but HTTPS doesn't: check listen-ports — maybe only HTTP is configured. If the ALB isn't being created at all: check that ingressClassName: alb is set and the AWS Load Balancer Controller is installed. Run kubectl describe ingress jobpost-ingress to see the status and any error messages from the controller.

    Q9
    How would you scale the anihpj architecture to handle 10× current traffic?
    Show Answer
    Answer

    (1) CDN: Increase cache hit ratio — cache API responses where possible, add edge caching for semi-dynamic content. (2) Horizontal scaling: Increase jobpost replicas (enable HPA: kubectl autoscale deployment jobpost --min=3 --max=30 --cpu-percent=70). (3) Database: Add read replicas for read-heavy workloads. Use connection pooling (PgBouncer). (4) Caching: Redis for query results, session data. (5) EKS nodes: Cluster Autoscaler adds nodes as pod count grows. (6) Network: Verify instance network limits — upgrade instance type if needed (m5.large=10Gbps → m5.4xlarge=25Gbps). (7) Conntrack: Increase limits per node (262K+).

    Explanation

    Scaling 10× requires attacking all layers simultaneously — not just adding pods. The most common bottleneck at 10× is the database: 10× traffic = 10× DB queries. A single RDS instance can't handle it — you need read replicas. Use Django's DATABASE_ROUTERS to route reads to replicas and writes to primary. Second bottleneck: connection limits. 10× pods with direct DB connections = 10× connections in conntrack. Use PgBouncer as a sidecar — each pod has a local PgBouncer that pools connections, reducing DB connections 10-50×. Third bottleneck: network bandwidth. At 10×, your current 1 Gbps might be saturated. Check CloudWatch metrics NetworkOut on EC2 instances. Upgrade to larger instance types with more bandwidth.

    Q10
    [LAB 🛠️] Deploy the complete anihpj stack using the manifests above. Verify every networking layer.
    Show Answer
    Answer
    # 1. Create namespace and apply manifests:
kubectl create ns anihpj
kubectl apply -f jobpost-deployment.yaml
kubectl apply -f jobpost-service.yaml
kubectl apply -f jobpost-ingress.yaml
kubectl apply -f networkpolicy.yaml  # From Ch 34

# 2. Verify pods:
kubectl get pods -n anihpj -o wide
# All Running? READY 1/1?

# 3. Verify Service:
kubectl get svc -n anihpj
kubectl get endpoints -n anihpj
# Endpoints populated?

# 4. Verify Ingress/ALB:
kubectl describe ingress -n anihpj
# Address shows ALB DNS?

# 5. Test end-to-end:
curl -v https://$(kubectl get ingress -n anihpj -o jsonpath='{.status.loadBalancer.ingress[0].hostname}')/api/health/
# Should return 200 OK with {"status":"healthy"}

# 6. Verify NetworkPolicy:
kubectl exec -it some-other-pod -- curl jobpost-service:8000
# Should timeout (blocked by default-deny)
    Explanation

    This lab validates the entire networking stack. Step 5 is the critical end-to-end test — it verifies: DNS (hostname resolves), TLS (SSL handshake succeeds), ALB (routes to targets), K8s Ingress (routes to Service), Service (routes to pod), pod (health endpoint responds), application (database connection works). If any of these fails, you know exactly where to look. Step 6 verifies NetworkPolicy enforcement — cross-pod traffic should be blocked unless explicitly allowed. Run this lab in a staging cluster after every infrastructure change. Automate it: write a shell script or K8s Job that runs these checks and alerts if any fail.
