    🧠 OSI vs TCP/IP — When to Use Which

    TCP/IP (4-layer) is what the Internet actually runs on: Link → Internet → Transport → Application. The OSI model is a teaching & diagnostic framework. When debugging, think in OSI layers to isolate the problem: is it L1 (cable unplugged)? L2 (ARP not resolving)? L3 (route missing)? L4 (port blocked)? L7 (app returning 500)? Golden Rule: Start at the bottom (L1) and work UP. Every SRE should memorize: "Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away" — Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application.

    ip Command — Interface, Address, Route, Neighbor

    🔌 Interface (L1/L2)

    ip link manages the physical/data-link layer — cables, virtual interfaces, bridges, veth pairs, VLAN sub-interfaces. This is where you check if the cable is plugged in and the link is negotiated at the right speed.

    🌐 Address (L3)

    ip addr manages IP addresses assigned to interfaces. One interface can have multiple IPs (useful for BGP anycast or multi-homing). The -br flag gives you quick one-line-per-interface summaries — perfect for scripting.

    🗺️ Route (L3)

    ip route manages the kernel routing table. ip route get DST is the single most useful SRE command — it tells you exactly which interface and next-hop the kernel will use for a given destination without sending any packets.

    📇 Neighbor (L2)

    ip neigh shows the ARP/NDP cache. Stale entries mean the MAC hasn't been refreshed. FAILED entries mean the host is unreachable at L2 — this is often the root cause of "ping fails but IP config looks fine."

      # INTERFACES (L1/L2)
  ip link show                          # List all interfaces + state
  ip link set eth0 up                   # Bring interface UP
  ip -s link show eth0                  # Interface statistics (errors, drops)
  ip -d link show eth0                  # Detailed info (driver, qdisc, bridge)
  ethtool eth0                          # Speed, duplex, link detected
  ethtool -S eth0                       # NIC hardware statistics
  ethtool -i eth0                       # Driver info, firmware version

  # ADDRESSES (L3)
  ip addr show                          # All IPs on all interfaces
  ip -br addr show                      # Brief format (one line per interface)
  ip addr add 10.0.1.50/24 dev eth0     # Add IP address
  ip addr del 10.0.1.50/24 dev eth0     # Remove IP address
  ip addr add 10.0.1.51/24 dev eth0 label eth0:1  # Add secondary IP with label

  # ROUTING (L3)
  ip route show                         # Full routing table
  ip route show default                 # Default route only
  ip route get 8.8.8.8                  # Which route would be used? (MOST USEFUL!)
  ip route add 10.0.0.0/16 via 10.0.1.1 # Add route
  ip route add 10.0.0.0/16 via 10.0.1.1 metric 100  # Add with metric
  ip route del 10.0.0.0/16              # Remove route
  ip route show table all               # ALL routing tables (main, local, custom)

  # POLICY ROUTING (advanced)
  ip rule show                          # Show routing policy rules (RPDB)
  ip rule add from 10.0.1.50 table 100  # Route traffic FROM this IP via table 100
  ip route add default via 10.0.1.254 table 100  # Default route in custom table
  # Use case: dual-homed server — different default routes per source IP

  # NEIGHBORS (L2 — ARP)
  ip neigh show                         # ARP table (IP → MAC)
  ip neigh show nud stale               # Show only stale entries
  ip neigh add 10.0.1.1 lladdr aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff dev eth0  # Static ARP
  ip neigh del 10.0.1.5 dev eth0        # Flush ARP entry (force re-ARP)
  arping -I eth0 10.0.1.1               # Send ARP request manually

  # NETWORK NAMESPACES (critical for container/K8s debugging!)
  ip netns list                         # List all network namespaces
  ip netns add debug-ns                 # Create a new network namespace
  ip netns exec debug-ns ip addr show   # Run command INSIDE namespace
  ip netns exec debug-ns bash           # Open shell inside namespace
  ip link add veth0 type veth peer name veth1  # Create veth pair
  ip link set veth1 netns debug-ns      # Move one end into namespace
  ip netns exec debug-ns ping 8.8.8.8   # Test connectivity from namespace
  # Docker/K8s pods each have their own netns — this is how they're isolated!

    ss — Socket Statistics (Replaces netstat)

    🧠 Why ss > netstat

    ss reads directly from /proc/net/sockstat and the kernel's Netlink socket-diag interface — it's orders of magnitude faster than netstat on machines with thousands of connections. netstat reads /proc/net/tcp and parses text; ss queries the kernel directly via Netlink. On a busy K8s node with 50,000 connections, ss returns in milliseconds while netstat can take seconds. Always use ss.

    🔍 TCP State Mapping

    LISTEN = daemon waiting | ESTAB = active data flow | TIME-WAIT = closed, cleaning up (2MSL) | CLOSE-WAIT = remote closed, local app hasn't called close() — this is a BUG! | SYN-SENT = attempting connection | FIN-WAIT = shutting down. SRE Rule: If you see CLOSE-WAIT accumulating, check your application code — it's leaking file descriptors.

    📊 TCP Info Deep Dive

    ss -ti exposes: rtt (round-trip time in ms), rttvar (RTT variance), cwnd (congestion window in segments), mss (max segment size), retrans (retransmit count — if > 0, investigate!), bytes_acked/bytes_received (data volume), pacing_rate (kernel rate-limiting). This is TCP diagnostic gold.

      # ═══ TCP LISTENING ═══
  ss -tlnp                              # TCP listening sockets (most used!)
  ss -tlnp | grep 8000                  # Is something listening on port 8000?
  ss -tlnp sport = :8000                # Same, using ss filter syntax
  ss -tlnp '( sport = :8000 or sport = :443 )'  # Multiple ports

  # ═══ CONNECTION STATE FILTERS ═══
  ss -t state established               # All established TCP connections
  ss -t state time-wait | wc -l         # Count TIME_WAIT sockets
  ss -t state close-wait | wc -l        # CLOSE_WAIT = application bug!
  ss -t state syn-sent                  # Connections still being established
  ss -t state fin-wait-1                # Active close in progress
  ss -t '( dport = :5432 or sport = :5432 )'  # All connections to/from Postgres

  # ═══ TCP INTERNAL INFO ═══
  ss -ti                                # TCP info: RTT, retransmits, CWND, MSS
  ss -ti | grep -E 'retrans:[1-9]'      # Connections with retransmissions (BAD!)
  ss -ti dst 10.244.1.5                 # TCP info for connections to specific pod
  ss -t -o state established            # Show TCP timers (keepalive, retrans)

  # ═══ PROCESS/AUTH FILTERS ═══
  ss -tlnp '( sport >= :8000 and sport <= :9000 )'  # All listeners in port range
  ss -tnp dst 10.96.0.10                # Connections to K8s ClusterIP
  ss -tnp src 10.244.0.0/16             # Connections FROM pod subnet

  # ═══ SUMMARY ═══
  ss -s                                 # Summary statistics (TCP/UDP counts)
  ss -t -o state established dst 10.0.0.0/8  # Established to private IPs
  ss -4tn                               # IPv4 TCP numeric (no DNS, no ports names)
  ss -6tln                              # IPv6 TCP listeners only

  # ═══ K8s-SPECIFIC PATTERNS ═══
  # Check if kubelet is listening:
  ss -tlnp | grep 10250
  # Check etcd client connections:
  ss -tnp dst :2379
  # Check API server connections:
  ss -tnp dst :6443 | head -20
  # Count total connections on a busy node:
  ss -tan | wc -l

    dig & nslookup — DNS Debugging

    🧠 DNS Response Anatomy

    A dig response has 5 sections: HEADER (flags: qr, aa, tc, rd, ra; status: NOERROR/NXDOMAIN/SERVFAIL), QUESTION (what you asked), ANSWER (the actual records — this is what you want!), AUTHORITY (authoritative nameservers for the domain), ADDITIONAL (glue records — IPs for nameservers). Use +noall +answer to see just the answer. NXDOMAIN = domain doesn't exist. SERVFAIL = DNS server couldn't resolve (timeout, DNSSEC failure, broken delegation).

      # ═══ BASIC QUERIES ═══
  dig api.anihpj.com                    # Full DNS query (A record)
  dig +short api.anihpj.com             # Just the answer IP
  dig api.anihpj.com ANY                # All record types
  dig -x 10.0.1.50                      # Reverse DNS lookup
  dig api.anihpj.com @8.8.8.8           # Query specific DNS server
  dig api.anihpj.com +noall +answer     # Show only answer section
  nslookup api.anihpj.com               # Simple lookup (cross-platform)

  # ═══ RECORD TYPES ═══
  dig api.anihpj.com A                  # IPv4 address
  dig api.anihpj.com AAAA               # IPv6 address
  dig api.anihpj.com MX                 # Mail exchange records
  dig api.anihpj.com TXT                # Text records (SPF, DKIM, verification)
  dig api.anihpj.com CNAME              # Canonical name (alias)
  dig api.anihpj.com NS                 # Nameservers
  dig api.anihpj.com SOA                # Start of Authority (zone metadata)
  dig api.anihpj.com SRV                # Service records (K8s uses these!)
  dig api.anihpj.com PTR                # Pointer record (reverse DNS)

  # ═══ TRACE & DEBUG ═══
  dig +trace api.anihpj.com             # Trace delegation from root (ROOT→TLD→NS→A)
  dig api.anihpj.com +dnssec            # Enable DNSSEC (shows RRSIG records)
  dig api.anihpj.com +tcp               # Force TCP (bypasses UDP truncation)
  dig api.anihpj.com +ttlid             # Show TTL values for each record
  dig api.anihpj.com +stats             # Show query timing breakdown
  dig CHAOS TXT version.bind @8.8.8.8   # Ask DNS server its software version

  # ═══ TTL INTERPRETATION ═══
  # TTL < 60  = dynamic/failover (load balancer DNS, e.g. AWS ELB)
  # TTL 300   = 5 min (typical for services behind CDN)
  # TTL 3600  = 1 hour (standard for stable services)
  # TTL 86400 = 24 hours (static records, email servers)
  # If TTL is 0 → record might rotate every query (DNS-based load balancing)

  # ═══ K8s DNS DEBUGGING ═══
  dig jobpost-service.default.svc.cluster.local  # K8s internal DNS
  dig jobpost-service.default.svc.cluster.local +short  # Just the ClusterIP
  dig -x 10.96.0.10                     # Reverse lookup of ClusterIP
  # CoreDNS config: kubectl get cm coredns -n kube-system -o yaml

    curl — HTTP/HTTPS Debugging

    🧠 curl Timing Template

    Create ~/.curl-format.txt with this content for performance analysis:

         time_namelookup:  %{time_namelookup}\n
      time_connect:  %{time_connect}\n
   time_appconnect:  %{time_appconnect}\n
  time_pretransfer:  %{time_pretransfer}\n
     time_redirect:  %{time_redirect}\n
 time_starttransfer:  %{time_starttransfer}\n
                    ----------\n
         time_total:  %{time_total}\n

    Then: curl -w "@~/.curl-format.txt" -o /dev/null -s https://api.anihpj.com. This breaks down: DNS lookup → TCP connect → TLS handshake → TTFB (time to first byte) → total. If time_appconnect - time_connect > 500ms, TLS negotiation is slow (check cipher suite, OCSP stapling). If time_starttransfer - time_pretransfer > 2s, the backend is slow to respond.

      # ═══ BASIC HTTP ═══
  curl -v http://api.anihpj.com         # Verbose (show headers + handshake)
  curl -I https://api.anihpj.com        # HEAD request (headers only)
  curl -X POST -d '{"key":"val"}' URL   # POST with JSON body
  curl -X PUT -d @file.json URL         # PUT with file as body
  curl -X DELETE URL                    # DELETE request
  curl -L https://bit.ly/xxx            # Follow redirects (max 50 by default)
  curl -L --max-redirs 3 URL            # Follow max 3 redirects

  # ═══ HEADERS & AUTH ═══
  curl -H "Content-Type: application/json" URL  # Set content type
  curl -H "Authorization: Bearer TOKEN" URL      # JWT/OAuth bearer token
  curl -u admin:password URL            # HTTP Basic auth
  curl -b "session=abc123" URL          # Send cookies
  curl -c cookies.txt URL               # Save cookies to file
  curl -b cookies.txt URL               # Use saved cookies

  # ═══ TIMING & PERFORMANCE ═══
  curl -w '@~/.curl-format.txt' -o /dev/null -s URL  # Timing breakdown
  curl --connect-timeout 5 URL           # Timeout after 5s for connection
  curl --max-time 30 URL                # Max total time (connect + transfer)
  curl -w "%{http_code}\n" -o /dev/null -s URL  # Just the HTTP status code
  curl -w "%{remote_ip}:%{remote_port}\n" -o /dev/null -s URL  # Connected IP:port

  # ═══ TLS & PROTOCOLS ═══
  curl -k https://api.anihpj.com        # Ignore TLS errors (testing only!)
  curl --cacert ca.pem URL              # Use custom CA cert
  curl --cert client.pem --key client.key URL  # mTLS client cert
  curl --http2 URL                      # Force HTTP/2
  curl --http3 URL                      # Force HTTP/3 (QUIC) — requires curl 7.88+
  curl -sv URL 2>&1 | grep -E 'ALPN|SSL'  # See TLS version and cipher used

  # ═══ DEBUGGING ═══
  curl -v URL 2>&1 | grep '< HTTP'      # Extract response status line
  curl -D headers.txt URL               # Save response headers to file
  curl -o /dev/null -s -w "%{http_code}" URL  # Just status code (script-friendly)
  curl --resolve api.anihpj.com:443:10.0.1.50 URL  # Override DNS (test specific backend)

    iptables — Quick Reference for SREs

    🧠 iptables Tables & Chains Architecture

    iptables has 5 built-in tables with different purposes: filter (default — INPUT/FORWARD/OUTPUT chains, firewall rules), nat (PREROUTING/INPUT/OUTPUT/POSTROUTING — DNAT, SNAT, MASQUERADE), mangle (all 5 chains — modify packet headers like TOS/TTL/MARK), raw (PREROUTING/OUTPUT — bypass connection tracking with NOTRACK), security (SELinux mandatory access control). Most SRE work is in filter and nat tables. Packet flow: raw.PREROUTING → conntrack → mangle.PREROUTING → nat.PREROUTING (DNAT) → routing decision → filter.FORWARD → mangle.POSTROUTING → nat.POSTROUTING (SNAT/MASQUERADE).

      # ═══ VIEW RULES ═══
  iptables -L -n -v                     # All filter rules with packet/byte counters
  iptables -L -n -v --line-numbers      # With rule numbers (for deletion)
  iptables -t nat -L -n -v              # NAT table rules with counters
  iptables -t mangle -L -n -v           # Mangle table rules
  iptables -S                           # Show rules as iptables commands
  iptables -S INPUT                     # Show INPUT chain only

  # ═══ BACKUP & RESTORE ═══
  iptables-save > rules.txt             # Backup ALL rules (all tables)
  iptables-save -t nat > nat-rules.txt  # Backup only NAT table
  iptables-restore < rules.txt          # Restore from backup (atomic)

  # ═══ ADD/DELETE RULES ═══
  iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 8000 -j ACCEPT  # Append: allow port 8000
  iptables -I INPUT 1 -p tcp --dport 22 -j ACCEPT  # Insert at position 1
  iptables -D INPUT 3                   # Delete rule #3
  iptables -D INPUT -p tcp --dport 8000 -j DROP   # Delete by matching rule
  iptables -R INPUT 2 -p tcp --dport 443 -j ACCEPT  # Replace rule #2

  # ═══ COMMON SRE PATTERNS ═══
  # Block a specific IP range:
  iptables -A INPUT -s 10.0.0.0/8 -j DROP
  # Rate-limit SSH (5 connections per minute):
  iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 22 -m state --state NEW -m recent --set
  iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 22 -m state --state NEW -m recent --rcheck --seconds 60 --hitcount 5 -j DROP
  # Port forwarding (redirect 80→8080):
  iptables -t nat -A PREROUTING -p tcp --dport 80 -j REDIRECT --to-port 8080
  # Log dropped packets (max 5/minute to avoid log flood):
  iptables -A INPUT -j LOG --log-prefix "IPT-DROP: " --log-level 4 -m limit --limit 5/min

  # ═══ DANGER ZONE ═══
  iptables -Z                           # Zero all counters (safe)
  iptables -F                           # FLUSH all rules (DANGER: breaks K8s!)
  iptables -P INPUT ACCEPT              # Set default policy to ACCEPT
  iptables -P INPUT DROP                # Set default policy to DROP (breaks everything if no ACCEPT rules)

    ping, traceroute, mtr — Reachability & Path Diagnostics

    📡 ping

    Tests L3 reachability using ICMP Echo Request/Reply. Measures RTT and packet loss. Gotcha: ping working ≠ TCP working. ICMP is often firewalled separately. MTU test: ping -M do -s 1472 DST — if it fails, path MTU is < 1500. Reduce size until it works to find actual MTU.

    🗺️ traceroute

    Maps the path by sending packets with incrementing TTL. Each router decrements TTL; when TTL=0, router sends ICMP Time Exceeded back. *** = no response (firewall or rate-limiting). Use -T (TCP SYN) to bypass ICMP-only firewalls targeting specific ports.

    📊 mtr (My Traceroute)

    Combines ping + traceroute into continuous path monitoring. Shows per-hop: loss%, sent/received packets, avg/best/worst/StDev RTT. Interpretation: If loss% jumps at hop N and stays high for all subsequent hops → problem is at hop N. If loss% at hop N but hop N+1 is 0% → hop N is just rate-limiting ICMP (false positive).

      # ═══ PING ═══
  ping -c 5 8.8.8.8                    # 5 pings, show RTT + packet loss
  ping -i 0.2 10.0.1.1                  # Fast ping (200ms interval)
  ping -M do -s 1472 10.0.1.1           # Test MTU (1472+28=1500). "Frag needed" = MTU smaller!
  ping -M do -s 8972 10.0.1.1           # Jumbo frame test (9000 MTU)
  ping -W 2 10.0.1.1                    # 2-second timeout per ping
  ping -f 10.0.1.1                      # Flood ping (requires root, stress test)
  ping -a 10.0.1.1                      # Audible ping (beep on each response)

  # ═══ TRACEROUTE ═══
  traceroute -n 8.8.8.8                 # Show path (no DNS, faster)
  traceroute -T -p 443 api.anihpj.com    # TCP SYN trace (bypass ICMP filters — most reliable!)
  traceroute -U -p 53 8.8.8.8           # UDP trace (default, port 33434+)
  traceroute -I 8.8.8.8                 # ICMP trace (often blocked)
  traceroute -m 30 8.8.8.8              # Max 30 hops (default)
  traceroute -q 1 8.8.8.8               # 1 probe per hop (faster, less reliable)

  # ═══ MTR ═══
  mtr -r -c 100 8.8.8.8                 # Report mode, 100 pings per hop
  mtr --tcp -P 443 api.anihpj.com       # MTR with TCP (more reliable than ICMP)
  mtr -n -r -c 50 10.244.1.5            # Trace to specific pod IP
  mtr -o "LRSD NBAW JMXI" 8.8.8.8       # Custom fields in report
  # Key MTR columns: Loss% Snt Last Avg Best Wrst StDev
  # StDev (jitter) > 50ms = unstable link. Loss% > 5% at specific hop = congestion/fault.

  # ═══ PATH MTU DISCOVERY WORKFLOW ═══
  # 1. Start with expected MTU:
  ping -M do -s 1472 -c 3 DEST
  # 2. If "Frag needed" (or DF set and packet too large), reduce:
  ping -M do -s 1400 -c 3 DEST
  # 3. Binary search until you find the max that works
  # 4. Set MTU on interface: ip link set dev eth0 mtu 1450
  # Common issue: VPN/GRE tunnels add overhead → reduce inner MTU

    nc (netcat) — The SRE Swiss Army Knife

    🔌 Port Testing

    nc -zv HOST PORT performs a TCP SYN scan — sends SYN, waits for SYN-ACK, sends RST. "succeeded" = port is open. "Connection refused" = nothing listening. "Connection timed out" = firewall or network issue. Note: -z means zero-I/O mode (don't send data, just check).

    📡 Banner Grabbing

    Many services send a banner on connect: echo | nc HOST 22 shows SSH version, nc HOST 25 for SMTP, nc HOST 80 <<< "HEAD / HTTP/1.1" for HTTP. Banner grabbing is crucial for inventory — knowing exactly what's running on every port.

    📁 File Transfer

    Server: nc -l 9999 > received_file.tar | Client: nc HOST 9999 < file.tar. No encryption — use only on trusted networks. For secure transfer, pipe through: nc -l 9999 | openssl enc -d -aes256 > file.

    🔗 Proxy Testing

    nc -X connect -x proxy:8080 TARGET 443 — test connectivity through an HTTP CONNECT proxy. nc -X 5 -x socks5proxy:1080 TARGET 80 — test through SOCKS5 proxy.

      # ═══ PORT TESTING ═══
  nc -zv host 8000                      # TCP port check (SYN scan)
  nc -zuv host 53                       # UDP port check
  nc -w 3 host 8000                     # Timeout after 3 seconds
  nc -zv host 8000-9000 2>&1 | grep succeeded  # Port range scan
  nc -zv -w 1 host 1-1024 2>&1 | grep -i succeeded  # Well-known port scan

  # ═══ SERVER/LISTENER ═══
  nc -l 9999                            # Start simple TCP server (one connection then exits)
  nc -lk 9999                           # Keep listening after disconnect (-k flag)
  nc -l 9999 > received.txt             # Save incoming data to file
  nc -l -p 9999 -e /bin/bash            # Backdoor shell (DANGER: security risk!)

  # ═══ RAW PROTOCOL TESTING ═══
  echo "GET / HTTP/1.0

" | nc host 80  # Raw HTTP request
  echo "HELO test" | nc host 25         # SMTP EHLO
  echo "stats" | nc localhost 11211     # Memcached stats command
  echo "PING" | nc localhost 6379       # Redis PING
  echo -e "\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00" | nc host 3306  # MySQL handshake probe

  # ═══ CHAT / PIPE TESTING ═══
  # Terminal 1: nc -l 5555
  # Terminal 2: nc localhost 5555
  # (type in either terminal → appears in both — full-duplex pipe!)

  # ═══ TIMING TEST ═══
  time nc -zv host 8000                 # How fast does the handshake complete?
  # Useful for measuring network latency without ping

    openssl s_client — TLS/SSL Debugging

    🧠 When to Use openssl vs curl for TLS debugging

    curl -v shows the TLS handshake at a high level. openssl s_client gives you every certificate in the chain, cipher suite details, server key exchange parameters, and session information. Use openssl when: debugging certificate chain issues, checking cipher suite negotiation, verifying OCSP stapling, testing mTLS, or analyzing any TLS-layer problem.

      # ═══ BASIC TLS CONNECTION ═══
  openssl s_client -connect api.anihpj.com:443  # Full TLS handshake dump
  openssl s_client -connect api.anihpj.com:443 -servername api.anihpj.com  # SNI
  openssl s_client -connect api.anihpj.com:443 -showcerts  # Show all certs in chain
  openssl s_client -connect api.anihpj.com:443 -brief   # Brief output (OpenSSL 1.1.1+)

  # ═══ CERTIFICATE INSPECTION ═══
  echo | openssl s_client -connect api.anihpj.com:443 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -text  # Full cert details
  echo | openssl s_client -connect api.anihpj.com:443 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -dates  # Validity period
  echo | openssl s_client -connect api.anihpj.com:443 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -subject  # Subject DN
  echo | openssl s_client -connect api.anihpj.com:443 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -issuer  # Issuer DN
  echo | openssl s_client -connect api.anihpj.com:443 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -fingerprint -sha256  # Cert fingerprint

  # ═══ CIPHER & PROTOCOL TESTING ═══
  openssl s_client -connect api.anihpj.com:443 -tls1_2  # Force TLS 1.2
  openssl s_client -connect api.anihpj.com:443 -tls1_3  # Force TLS 1.3
  openssl s_client -connect api.anihpj.com:443 -cipher 'ECDHE-RSA-AES256-GCM-SHA384'  # Test specific cipher
  openssl s_client -connect api.anihpj.com:443 -tlsextdebug  # Show TLS extensions

  # ═══ mTLS (MUTUAL TLS) ═══
  openssl s_client -connect api.anihpj.com:443 -cert client.pem -key client.key  # Client certificate
  openssl s_client -connect api.anihpj.com:443 -cert client.pem -key client.key -CAfile ca.pem  # With CA

  # ═══ OCSP STAPLING CHECK ═══
  openssl s_client -connect api.anihpj.com:443 -status  # Check OCSP stapling response

  # ═══ CERTIFICATE DOWNLOAD (for analysis) ═══
  echo | openssl s_client -connect api.anihpj.com:443 2>/dev/null | sed -n '/-----BEGIN/,/-----END/p' > cert.pem
  openssl x509 -in cert.pem -text -noout  # Analyze downloaded cert

    conntrack — Connection Tracking Debugging

    🧠 What is Connection Tracking?

    The Linux kernel's conntrack module maintains a table of all active network connections (TCP, UDP, ICMP, SCTP). Each entry tracks: source/dest IP:port, protocol, state, timeout, and packet/byte counters. This is what enables stateful firewalling (iptables rules with -m state --state ESTABLISHED,RELATED) and NAT (the kernel must remember the original source to "un-NAT" reply packets). Conntrack table full = new connections silently dropped — a classic production outage pattern!

      # ═══ VIEW CONNECTION TRACKING TABLE ═══
  conntrack -L                          # List ALL tracked connections (can be huge!)
  conntrack -L -p tcp                   # TCP connections only
  conntrack -L -s 10.244.1.5            # Connections FROM specific pod IP
  conntrack -L -d 10.96.0.10            # Connections TO specific ClusterIP
  conntrack -L --state ESTABLISHED       # Only established connections
  conntrack -L --state TIME_WAIT         # Only TIME_WAIT connections
  conntrack -C                          # Count total tracked connections (FAST!)

  # ═══ CONNTRACK STATS ═══
  conntrack -S                          # Conntrack subsystem statistics
  cat /proc/sys/net/netfilter/nf_conntrack_count  # Current connection count
  cat /proc/sys/net/netfilter/nf_conntrack_max    # Maximum table size
  # If count ≈ max → TABLE IS FULL → new connections dropped!
  # Fix: sysctl -w net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max=262144

  # ═══ DELETE ENTRIES ═══
  conntrack -D -s 10.244.1.5            # Delete all connections from this IP
  conntrack -D -p tcp --dport 8000       # Delete all connections to port 8000
  conntrack -F                          # FLUSH entire table (DANGER: breaks all connections!)

  # ═══ EVENT MONITORING (real-time) ═══
  conntrack -E                          # Watch all conntrack events in real time
  conntrack -E -e NEW                   # Only NEW connections
  conntrack -E -e DESTROY               # Only destroyed connections (connection ended)
  conntrack -E -s 10.244.0.0/16         # Only for pod subnet

  # ═══ CONNTRACK TIMEOUTS ═══
  sysctl net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_tcp_timeout_established  # Default: 432000 (5 days!)
  sysctl net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_tcp_timeout_time_wait    # Default: 120s
  sysctl net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_tcp_timeout_close_wait   # Default: 60s
  # In high-traffic environments, lower the established timeout to free slots faster

  # ═══ K8s CONNTRACK ISSUES ═══
  # kube-proxy iptables mode creates MANY conntrack entries per Service
  # Common symptom: "Connection refused" on new connections but existing ones work
  # Check: conntrack -C (compare to max)
  # Mitigation: increase nf_conntrack_max, switch to kube-proxy IPVS mode
  # IPVS mode doesn't use conntrack for load balancing — much more scalable!

    📊 Port Range Quick Reference

    Well-known ports (0-1023): Require root/CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE. Assigned by IANA. SSH (22), HTTP (80), HTTPS (443), DNS (53). Registered ports (1024-49151): User applications. PostgreSQL (5432), Redis (6379), K8s API (6443), Prometheus (9090). Dynamic/Ephemeral ports (49152-65535): Temporary client ports. Linux default range: 32768-60999. Widen with: sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range="1024 65535". K8s-specific ranges: NodePort: 30000-32767 (configurable via --service-node-port-range). Container ports: any above 1024 (non-root). Container ports: any above 1024 (non-root). NEVER hardcode ephemeral ports in firewall rules -- they change per connection!

    K8s Port Types - Decoded

    containerPort

    Declared in Pod spec. Informational only -- does NOT open port. App calls bind() inside container. Ex: containerPort: 8000 in jobpost.

    targetPort

    Port on Pod where Service forwards traffic. Where app actually listens. Defaults to port if unset. Ex: gunicorn on targetPort: 8000.

    port (Service)

    Port Service exposes inside cluster. Pods access svc:port. Can differ from targetPort. Ex: Service port: 80 to Pod targetPort: 8000.

    nodePort

    Exposes Service on each Node IP (30000-32767). External: NodeIP:nodePort to Service to Pod. Prefer Ingress/LB for production.

      # K8s Port Flow -- anihpj jobpost Service:
  # External traffic to NodeIP:30001 (nodePort) to ClusterIP:80 (port) to Pod:8000
  apiVersion: v1
  kind: Service
  metadata:
    name: jobpost-service
  spec:
    type: NodePort
    selector:
      app: jobpost
    ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8000
      nodePort: 30001

    Port Checking Commands

      ss -tlnp                              # All TCP listeners with process
  lsof -i :8000                         # Process using port 8000
  fuser 8000/tcp                        # PID using port 8000
  ss -tnp dst :5432                     # Connections TO Postgres
  ss -tnp src :8000                     # Connections FROM gunicorn
  nc -zv localhost 8000-9000 2>&1 | grep succeeded  # Port range scan
  # "Address already in use" error - find culprit:
  ss -tlnp | grep :PORT
  kill -9 $(fuser PORT/tcp 2>/dev/null)

    🔧 Appendix C: tcpdump Filter Cheat SheetREFERENCE

    40+ Essential tcpdump Filters

      # ═══ BASIC FILTERS ═══
  tcpdump -i eth0                       # Capture on eth0 (default: all traffic)
  tcpdump -i any                        # ALL interfaces
  tcpdump -n                            # No DNS resolution (faster, no extra traffic)
  tcpdump -nn                           # No DNS + no port name resolution
  tcpdump -v / -vv / -vvv               # Verbose levels
  tcpdump -c 100                        # Stop after 100 packets
  tcpdump -w capture.pcap               # Write to file (Wireshark-compatible)
  tcpdump -r capture.pcap               # Read from file
  tcpdump -s 0                          # Capture full packet (no truncation)
  tcpdump -tttt                         # Human-readable timestamps

  # ═══ HOST & NETWORK FILTERS ═══
  tcpdump host 10.0.1.50                # Traffic to/from specific host
  tcpdump src 10.0.1.50                 # Traffic FROM specific host
  tcpdump dst 10.0.1.50                 # Traffic TO specific host
  tcpdump net 10.0.1.0/24               # Traffic to/from entire subnet
  tcpdump 'src 10.0.1.0/24 and dst 10.0.2.0/24'  # Cross-subnet

  # ═══ PORT FILTERS ═══
  tcpdump port 8000                     # Traffic on port 8000 (any direction)
  tcpdump src port 8000                 # Traffic FROM port 8000
  tcpdump dst port 443                  # Traffic TO port 443
  tcpdump portrange 8000-9000           # Range of ports

  # ═══ PROTOCOL FILTERS ═══
  tcpdump tcp                           # TCP only
  tcpdump udp                           # UDP only
  tcpdump icmp                          # ICMP only (ping, traceroute)
  tcpdump arp                           # ARP only (L2 address resolution)
  tcpdump ip6                           # IPv6 only

  # ═══ TCP FLAGS (advanced) ═══
  tcpdump 'tcp[tcpflags] & tcp-syn != 0'        # SYN packets (connections starting)
  tcpdump 'tcp[tcpflags] & tcp-rst != 0'        # RST packets (connections refused!)
  tcpdump 'tcp[tcpflags] & tcp-fin != 0'        # FIN packets (connections ending)
  tcpdump 'tcp[tcpflags] & (tcp-syn|tcp-fin) != 0'  # SYN or FIN

  # ═══ COMBINED (REAL SRE PATTERNS) ═══
  tcpdump -i any -nn host 10.244.1.5 and port 5432
  # All traffic to/from a specific pod on PostgreSQL port

  tcpdump -i eth0 -nn -c 100 -w debug.pcap 'tcp[tcpflags] & tcp-rst != 0'
  # Capture 100 RST packets → analyze in Wireshark

  tcpdump -i eth0 -nn 'host 10.96.0.10 and tcp port 8000'
  # Traffic to K8s Service ClusterIP

  tcpdump -i eth0 -nn 'icmp or arp'
  # Only ICMP + ARP (diagnose reachability + L2 issues)

  # ═══ COMMON DEBUGGING WORKFLOWS ═══
  # "Is traffic reaching this pod?"
  tcpdump -i any -nn host 10.244.1.5

  # "Are SYN packets being dropped?"
  tcpdump -i eth0 -nn 'tcp[tcpflags] & tcp-syn != 0' and dst port 8000

  # "Is there a TLS handshake?" (look for ClientHello)
  tcpdump -i eth0 -nn dst port 443 and 'tcp[((tcp[12]>>4)*4)+5]=0x16'

  # "What DNS queries are being made?"
  tcpdump -i eth0 -nn udp port 53

    Wireshark Display Filters — Companion Reference

      # After capturing with tcpdump -w, open in Wireshark and use:
  ip.addr == 10.244.1.5                 # All traffic to/from this IP
  ip.src == 10.0.0.0/16                 # Traffic FROM this subnet
  tcp.port == 8000                      # Traffic on port 8000
  tcp.flags.syn == 1 && tcp.flags.ack == 0  # SYN only (no ACK)
  tcp.flags.reset == 1                  # RST packets (connection refused)
  tcp.analysis.retransmission            # TCP retransmissions
  http.request                           # HTTP requests
  http.response.code >= 500             # HTTP 5xx errors
  dns                                    # All DNS traffic
  tls.handshake.type == 1               # TLS ClientHello (handshake start)
  icmp                                   # All ICMP traffic
  arp                                    # All ARP traffic

  # POWER COMBO: tcpdump capture → Wireshark analysis:
  # 1. tcpdump -i eth0 -w /tmp/capture.pcap host 10.244.1.5
  # 2. scp /tmp/capture.pcap laptop:/tmp/
  # 3. Open in Wireshark → Statistics → IO Graph (throughput)
  #                       → Statistics → TCP Stream Graph → Time-Sequence
  #                       → Analyze → Expert Info (errors, warnings)

    Common K8s Network Errors — Quick Diagnostic Reference

      # "Connection Refused" → service not listening or wrong port
  kubectl exec -it pod -- ss -tlnp | grep PORT
  kubectl exec -it pod -- nc -zv SERVICE PORT

  # "Connection Timed Out" → firewall/NetworkPolicy/SG blocking
  kubectl get networkpolicies -A
  kubectl exec -it pod -- traceroute -n DEST_IP

  # "No Route to Host" → routing table missing route
  kubectl exec -it pod -- ip route show
  kubectl exec -it pod -- ip route get DEST_IP

  # "Name or service not known" → DNS failure
  kubectl logs -n kube-system deployment/coredns
  kubectl exec -it pod -- cat /etc/resolv.conf
  kubectl exec -it pod -- nslookup SERVICE_NAME

  # "Connection reset by peer" → backend crashed mid-connection
  kubectl get pods -o wide  # Check for restarts
  kubectl logs POD_NAME --previous  # Crash logs

  # "Too many open files" → file descriptor limit
  kubectl exec -it pod -- ulimit -n
  kubectl exec -it pod -- cat /proc/sys/fs/file-max

  # "Cannot assign requested address" → ephemeral port exhaustion
  kubectl exec -it pod -- ss -s  # Check TIME_WAIT count

    G.1 Key RFCs Every Network Engineer Should Know

    RFCs (Request for Comments) are the official specifications that define how the Internet works. These are the foundational documents behind every protocol in this guide.

    RFC #TitleWhat It DefinesChapter
    RFC 791Internet Protocol (IPv4)IPv4 header format, addressing, fragmentationCh 5
    RFC 2460IPv6 SpecificationIPv6 header, addressing architectureCh 6
    RFC 793Transmission Control ProtocolTCP header, state machine, flow controlCh 8
    RFC 768User Datagram ProtocolUDP header format (8 bytes)Ch 9
    RFC 792Internet Control Message ProtocolICMP types, codes, echo/ping specCh 7
    RFC 826Address Resolution ProtocolARP packet format, resolution processCh 2
    RFC 1034/1035DNS Concepts & ImplementationDNS hierarchy, record types, resolutionCh 11
    RFC 2616/7230-7235HTTP/1.1HTTP methods, headers, status codesCh 12
    RFC 7540HTTP/2Binary framing, multiplexing, HPACKCh 12
    RFC 9000QUIC (HTTP/3)UDP-based transport, 0-RTT, streamsCh 9
    RFC 8446TLS 1.31-RTT handshake, cipher suitesCh 35
    RFC 1918Private IP Addresses10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16Ch 5
    RFC 2131Dynamic Host Configuration ProtocolDHCP DORA process, optionsCh 14
    RFC 7348VXLANOverlay encapsulation, 24-bit VNICh 18
    RFC 4271BGP-4Path vector routing, AS pathCh 7
    RFC 2328OSPF v2Link-state routing, areas, LSA typesCh 7
    💡 How to Read RFCs

    RFCs use specific keywords defined in RFC 2119: MUST = absolute requirement, MUST NOT = absolute prohibition, SHOULD = recommended but exceptions exist, MAY = optional. When reading RFCs, focus on the abstract, introduction, and packet format sections. The formal grammar (ABNF) sections can be skipped on first read.

    G.2 Linux Kernel Networking Parameters

    These /proc/sys/net/ parameters control the Linux kernel's networking behavior. Understanding them is essential for performance tuning and debugging.

    ParameterDefaultPurposeWhen to Tune
    net.ipv4.tcp_fin_timeout60Seconds in FIN-WAIT-2 before socket diesReduce for high-connection servers (30s)
    net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse0Reuse TIME-WAIT sockets for new connectionsEnable (1) for high-throughput clients
    net.ipv4.tcp_keepalive_time7200Seconds before first keepalive probeLower to 300 for cloud/NAT environments
    net.ipv4.tcp_max_syn_backlog128Max queued SYN requests (SYN_RECV)Increase for high-traffic servers (4096)
    net.core.somaxconn128Max backlog for listen() (ESTABLISHED queue)Increase to 1024 for web servers
    net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range32768 60999Ephemeral port range for outbound connectionsExpand to 1024-65535 for busy clients
    net.ipv4.ip_forward0Enable IP forwarding (router mode)Set to 1 on K8s nodes and routers
    net.ipv4.tcp_congestion_controlcubicTCP congestion algorithmTry BBR for high-BDP networks
    net.core.rmem_max / wmem_max212992Max socket buffer size (bytes)Increase for 10Gbps+ networks (16MB)
    net.ipv4.tcp_rmem / tcp_wmem4096 131072 6291456TCP auto-tuning (min/default/max)Tune max for high-throughput links
    net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max65536Max connection tracking entriesIncrease for NAT gateways (262144+)
    net.ipv4.neigh.default.gc_thresh1128ARP table size thresholdsIncrease for /16 networks (1024+)
    ⚠️ Persistence Note

    These parameters reset on reboot! To make permanent: add to /etc/sysctl.conf or /etc/sysctl.d/99-networking.conf, then run sysctl -p. In Kubernetes: use kubectl edit configmap -n kube-system kube-proxy for conntrack settings, or node tuning via DaemonSet.

    G.4 Kubernetes CNI Specification (v1.0.0)

    The Container Network Interface (CNI) specification defines how container runtimes interact with network plugins. Reference: CNI Spec

      CNI OPERATIONS (Plugin must implement):
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ ADD     (container-id, netns, ifname, config) -> Result  │
  │   Creates interface in container NS, assigns IP, returns │
  │   Result {IPs, routes, DNS}                              │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ DEL     (container-id, netns, ifname, config) -> ()      │
  │   Removes interface, releases IP, cleans up              │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ CHECK   (container-id, netns, ifname, config) -> ()      │
  │   Verifies networking is still correctly configured      │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ VERSION () -> {supported versions}                       │
  │   Reports which CNI spec versions the plugin supports    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  CNI CONFIGURATION (example: /etc/cni/net.d/10-flannel.conflist)
  {
    "cniVersion": "1.0.0",
    "name": "cbr0",                    // Network name
    "plugins": [                         // Plugin chain (can have multiple)
      {
        "type": "flannel",              // Main plugin
        "delegate": {"hairpinMode": true,"isDefaultGateway": true}
      },
      {
        "type": "portmap",              // Port mapping plugin
        "capabilities": {"portMappings": true}
      },
      {
        "type": "bandwidth",            // Bandwidth limiting plugin
        "capabilities": {"bandwidth": true}
      }
    ]
  }
    💡 CNI Plugin Properties
    • Stateless: CNI is stateless — plugins track IP assignments externally (IPAM).
    • Chained: Multiple plugins can be chained (e.g., flannel -> portmap -> bandwidth).
    • Runtime-agnostic: Works with any container runtime (containerd, CRI-O, Docker).
    • IPAM: IP Address Management is a separate concern — host-local, DHCP, or external (Calico IPAM).
